			- PRs ready to be merged EOD.
		</details>

			- <mention-user url="user://2edd872b-594c-8159-a47e-00020c7e3b63"/> to mention SSO support in the new version. 
		</details>

		<summary>**F3 User interface product shop**</summary>

26cc3702-22d5-8016-88aa-d3f676a3262e.title: [Marketing Agencies] Our Partnership Strategy
26cc3702-22d5-8016-88aa-d3f676a3262e.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/26cc370222d5801688aad3f676a3262e as of 2026-04-15T12:57:26.542Z: {"title":"\\[Marketing Agencies\\] Our Partnership Strategy"} ### TL/DR Marketing agencies are reorganizing around AI to move from slow, manual creative work to fast, automated, performance-driven production, supported by internal platforms like Omni, Vermeer, and Song. To serve them, BFL should offer a modular Agency License, API access, dev models, client-hosted rights, and optional reseller terms, anchored in clear licensing and meaningful minimum commits. ## Summary --- 1. Marketing Agencies mainly want AI **to make campaigns faster, cheaper, and more effective;** creating content automatically, updating it in real time, and moving away from slow manual work and hourly fees toward results-driven production. 2. To achieve this, these companies are rapidly re-organizing around by: - Creating **dedicated innovation labs** and **technical teams** that blend creatives, engineers, and data experts. - They are also building **internal AI platforms** that sit across the entire organization, giving thousands of employees access to generative tools inside unified systems (e.g., Omnicom’s “Omni”, Havas’s “Vermeer”, Accenture’s “Song AI”, etc.). - Agencies also aksi **shifting their business models** toward high-velocity, on-brand, AI-assisted production, focusing on workflows like iterative editing, brand-specific generation, and automated content pipelines instead of traditional handcrafted creative. 3. As a result, **Agencies need a flexible AI offering** that allows for API access for thousands of employees, dev models for technical labs to customize and fine-tune, and client-hosted rights for delivery work. Agencies are uniquely positioned to provide brand interpretation and workflow expertise, which would be challenging for BFL to replicate at scale. Our goal is to offer high-performance models, clear licensing terms, and well-aligned incentives to ensure that customers realize the value of our models, and that it directly translates to increased revenue for us and the agency. 4. The best way forward is a **modular Agency License** with four components: 1) API Access, 2) Dev Model Access, 3) Client-Hosted Add-On, and 4) Reseller Add-On. We will leverage minimum commits to capture value up-front, output caps to avoid losing value on scale, and rev shares/referral fees on efforts that require deeper partnership or commitment from BFL and the Agencies. ### 📊 Marketing Agency Landscape {toggle="true"} - The **Marketing Agencies** market size is estimated at \$453Bn in 2025, and is expected to reach USD 571.53 billion by 2030, at a CAGR of 4.8%. The key trends include **increased adoption of AI in creative development**, rapid scaling of performance-based pricing contracts, and cookie-less personalization technologies are reshaping how brands evaluate agency partnerships. [Source](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/global-marketing-agencies-market) - The key players continue to be fairly concentrated, with the top five groups: WPP, Omnicom, Publicis Groupe, Interpublic Group, and Dentsu, collectively accounting for a significant portion of 2024 billings. Omnicom’s planned merger with Interpublic, valued at over \$13Bn, is set to create the world’s largest holding entity and unlock substantial procurement and back-office synergies. **We collected feedback and use cases from both Omnicom and IPG (and a handful of their subsidiaries)**. WPP defends its leadership by funneling AI spend into its proprietary Open AI Studio that automates copy, imagery, and media-mix forecasting. **WPP has also expressed interest in our models, and we will be setting up time with them next week**. - **We’re already following through on inbound from some of the biggest Agency Holding Companies: **WPP, Omnicom, and IPG. Once we have these deals in place, we can approach the rest: Dentsu, Havas, and Stagwell, in addition to smaller creative agencies: *VML, TBWA, RAPP, Razorfish, Havas, Doner, Digitas, Huge, Publicis Sapient or* Media Agencies: Mindshare, Starcom, Magna, Carat, Assembly, OMD. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/6207aea2-e0c8-4aad-a666-8edeecdac89a/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466YUSMJ6K3%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095636Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIQD2b0seB7%2BZ6Rv4kZsjQw7p3zloyMdFfusByuFuPfjSsgIgIGJ1paZI7JF555WysyEetyOSOm%2B9F7R%2BIas5uNn0EAQq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDPPlWE5ZyLfOHBEYPyrcA4HVuELWJE3PwTrNFeQMtwUXljz7fmzSSI34u0Ho6El3ZGH9G%2F9scy4D8Fm1aRSjbbnixe9ffEOosj6kbjkak4Zt621WVaEdFPjS71fQbv7EnMLr00HmWeP6B8aPAxhGFl%2FHBfGWp9sEu1ZBjGvIoUUX%2FVYX1Fp5bjKJCQ4lWCvGiVtewXuBaK7rsB3T5NF2DnL0HmjHC536QptFP75z3Z859M7jAm81WJU6i%2B2JR28Kb3%2F26hAGk8%2BAYsvYl1cpPKOheH2d9iK1GEVS%2FHYfFtKlOX99ZwwYiQTLNYFbxNE1bDoevDvl7lYXFh559Tb3m223iBcziLryvmetn%2Bodg3t%2BhhLPIgPP4qa%2BJ21osx7j2NMTK2J5b32v49PUgsr2aQWvq%2Bskcfj%2BJoTShwYkDjZpSFUqsuB5R4jVFCbmWFdTXemqXSs2tkv4fW5FOmEPTNPA%2FEvMlQIL2nLIf4xApj998k%2FYkVeNBoyEKO0E61T7tPTfA0IhxuMGEvOg1SjvhStykbZqKWOFQGvVicremyUAVAjeXNn4O1%2FvyONfV7e3asxa5L4lz9TtpnzrYkSqDqhILY1LFdJeBT%2BAvqg2iYLbW0gyHtIR8FKnk%2BT047%2Fz4Vg%2BvI%2FPsbFdLnjWMKyvks8GOqUB06Qr%2BU5LAnCF6YDu9nHGsD2WSCQNBsN%2BTItVfKs18pgIXhiWQlsDet97OdDYQHhiajmXP4EeSpFRGcHOD77ZjtA9WPz5McrrdzcFHY0upoqVrPDArgL17TEFRf0n9LfB3MLomlV5DnqGba8WNuZvSogvwGVH25uZekHkg2hzJUgjc6UIFpo5%2BPJxJZNCeDmAAMEa6WXGJtjiVSoN2%2BhlUE%2FAdRPh&X-Amz-Signature=c0b468c27253a7cc8eb33ce38beccfa6a9ce74ee7e0bfc6237867cfc3cccf0af&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) View of Account & Partner Notes  # **1. How agencies are working w/ GenAI ** --- Feedback collected from: Omnicom (includes IPG, Craft, Grabarz, and PSG), Accenture, Havas (including Prose on Pixels), and Superside. *Upcoming calls: WPP* ### **AI is implemented in three layers across most Marketing Agencies / Large Professional Service Providers**
**1. Internal Creative Tools (employee-facing)** - Where most image requests originate (pitch decks, concepts, mockups, internal ideation). - BFL access typically embedded into internal platforms or plugins. **Internal tools mentioned:**
**Agency** **Internal Tool** **# Employees w/ access** **Tool Description**
**Omnicom **(includes IPG / Craft / McCann / Grabarz) **Omni platform + Omni Assist (gen-AI overlay); **AI OS across agencies \~20,000 active Omni users today, up to 75,000 possible - everyone “touching client work”). Assuming this refers to IPG merger.

\~55,000 at IPG (but innovation team small; unclear how many will use the tool)		 Omni created as a cross-agency data/marketing/insights/activation platform. Omni Assist, introduced 2023, adds generative-AI: a virtual assistant for audience insights, media planning, campaign workflows, measurement, optimization. ([Omnicom Group](https://www.omnicomgroup.com/newsroom/with-omni-assist-omnicom-leverages-first-mover-access-to-open-ai-to-accelerate-the-timeline-from-insights-to-outcomes/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
According to recent reporting, Omnicom is using a network of AI agents (powered by Omni data + gen-AI) to simulate focus groups, generate personalized content, run real-time optimization, dynamic content creation, and more. ([Digiday](https://digiday.com/marketing/ai-is-reshaping-omnicoms-workflow-its-revenue-model-may-be-next/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
**Accenture** **Song AI Tool** Initial cohort \~20,000; broad rollout to anyone touching client work (\~40k–60k) Accenture Song is a suite of AI-enabled capabilities built into Song’s offering: creative, data, analytics, customer-experience, content generation, commerce, and media automation.
**Havas** **Vermeer **(part of Converged.AI)**; **Prose on Pixels is the **innovation lab**, that is leading the integration of models within Vermeer) 23,000 global Havas employees Described as “next-gen video production platform” for agencies; uses generative-AI to produce video + creative content at scale. ([havas.com](https://www.havas.com/press_release/havas-accelerates-transformation-and-pivots-to-become-an-ai-driven-organization-fueled-by-human-ingenuity/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
**Superside** **Figma-based Superside plugin** \~500–1,000 internal (but used across all client accounts; no broad employee access) Superside advertises that they combine “AI-certified creative talent + custom AI workflows + latest AI tools” to deliver creative at scale. ([Superside](https://www.superside.com/ai-creative?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
**2. Client Delivery Workflows (service layer)** This is the **primary revenue engine** for agencies, and the unique differentiator when it comes to AI: - Training LoRAs or fine-tune models - Creating brand datasets - Using Flux for product imagery, portraits, packaging, lifestyle scenes - Rendering concept-to-production assets for campaigns, e-commerce, automotive - Building pipelines (often Unreal, C4D, or custom rendering stacks)
**3. Client-Hosted Deployments (emerging trend)** From Accenture, IPG, and the new agency call: - Agencies want to **install Dev Models inside client infra** (cloud or on-prem). - This is used for: 1) Regulated clients, 2) Automotive, 3) Global consumer brands with strict compliance, and 4)Data-sensitive or proprietary image systems **Important:** This is NOT resale; agencies are not trying to resell the model. They want a **right to deploy** as part of a service engagement.
# 2. How BFL can structure our terms to create joint incentives --- These are the different components we would need for an “Agency Sku”. - **Crawl (Accenture & Omnicom): **We are running the first “COMBO” pilot with Accenture, including API + Dev Access for 6 months at a \$500K minimum commit. The intent is to then include both the “client hosting” and “reseller add-ons” once we have a better understanding of their usage, and the number of clients they serve. Simultaneously, we are pitching a 6-month API only agreement w/ Omnicom, and from here we will add Dev. - **Walk: **Expand COMBO model to a small number of additional agencies (e.g., WPP). During this stage, we also begin piloting per-client deployment fees and structured reseller/referral pathways with agencies who deploy Flux inside client environments. - **Run:** Launch a dedicated **Agency SKU** on our website that clearly packages API access, Dev Model access, client-hosted rights, and optional reseller terms. We then introduce a tiered **Agency Partner Program** that recognizes and rewards top agencies, featuring them on our site with co-branded case studies and partner badges. For advanced partners, we offer joint FDE motions focused on complex, high-value workflows like client-hosted deployments. We also publish a directory of certified resellers and model integrators, ensuring only vetted partners can deploy or customize Flux models for clients. Together, this ecosystem positions Flux as the preferred model across the agency landscape, while scaling revenue through structured licensing, minimum commits, and partner incentives. *“Sub-license” is defined as re-selling access to our API and/or creating and selling a service/API powered by our dev model.*
**DEAL TYPE:** API ONLY DEV ONLY COMBO CLIENT HOSTING ADD-ON RESELLER ADD-ON
**Current
Challenges**		 • Agencies can switch away easily
• Difficult to attribute client-level usage without strict key hierarchy
• Hard to surface high-value use cases without visibility into workloads		 • Black box: no telemetry inside partner infra
• Hard to price fairly without knowing volumes

 • Agencies blend workloads across API and Dev, making billing opaque • Ideally we own the relationship with the client
• Hard to track deployments across client clouds
• Model updates and patching become operationally heavy		 • Agencies have low incentive to resell API (they profit more from FDE and creative services)
• Agencies may attempt to “bundle” our model under their own brand
• If agencies start selling model access via internal tools, BFL must capture value proportionally
**Proposals** • Introduce per-key reporting and audit rights.
• Incentivize usage via volume-based tiers.
• Provide upgrade paths to Dev License or Reseller.		 • Mandate monthly usage logs / callback endpoints and periodic audits.
• Add a per-client activation fee for each new deployment.
• Offer FDE onboarding packages to get visibility and ensure correct setup.
 • Set a combo minimum commit to ensure flexibility of use across API + Dev, but also prevent negotiation based on usage
• Predictable costs for Agencies
• Enforce workload separation via API key trees + Dev environment tagging.		 • Set a minimum commit or base fee for Agency-hosted; then a variable cost for every client
• Require mandatory client acknowledgment of BFL terms (DPA, IP, safety).
• Conduct joint onboarding calls to secure the BFL→Client relationship.
• Offer optional FDE add-on for infra validation and upgrades.		 • Introduce three structured reseller paths with clear economics:
1) Referral (10% referral fee): client signs directly with BFL.
2) Internal Tools (per client access fee): agencies sell fine-tuned model access via proprietary tools.
3) Client Deployments (rev share): agency installs in client infra with a per-client BFL license.
• Set agency-wide minimum commits, then per-client tenant fees.
• Require reseller certification (technical + compliance).
• Provide co-branded reseller badges and listing on BFL website.
• Offer joint GTM for qualified partners, but gatekeep resale rights.
**Governing Terms** **API License Agreement
**• Standard ToS and DPA apply directly between BFL & Agency
• No right to sublicense APIs without BFL approval
 **Developer License Agreement**
• Hosting rights limited to Agency’s secured infra
• No right to sublicense or redistribute model access
• Output rights defined
• Audit + security provisions for self-hosting		 **API + Dev (Platform License)**
• No right to sublicense APIs without BFL approval		 **Client Hosting Addendum**
• No right to sublicense APIs without BFL approval
 **Reseller Agreement**
### Scratchpad {toggle="true"} **How do we get & give value in each of these scenarios (are they balanced):**
Client of Agency Independent Agency Subsidiary Holding company
Outputs only - Highly transactional
UI
API - Stricter security requirements
 - Cost based on consumption - Cost based on consumption - Min Commit for BFL and cost based on consumption
Dev - Cost based on projects (not capacity) - Higher risk of abusing dev
- Cost based on projects (not capacity)
Service Layer
FDE/Support		 - What are all the collab efforts possible here?
**Open Questions:** - What opportunities exist w/ Agencies to optimize deployment/setup or API integration (e.g., custom moderation controls, RAG) - How do we disconnect from projects or transactions? → maybe brand kits, character vault, presets - How do we get our foot in the door? - Free Support to set up brand kits? - Free PG license w/ rev share on brand kits? ### Single Agency (Subsidiary) Commercial Weights License **Use case:** Agency produces work for clients using BFL models. No resale. No client access to weights or stand-alone APIs.
**Baseline Price** **Example (20 clients)**
**Per model pricing**
- Price based per model
- Includes the first **3 clients**		 • **Flux.2 Dev:** \$8,000 per month
• **Flux.2 \[klein\]:** \$4,000 per month
**→ Base total:** **\$12,000 per month**		 Base total: \$12,000 per month
**Per client activation pricing**
- Variable licensing fees for 4+ clients		 • Clients 1–3: included
• Clients 4+: **\$200 per client per month**		 17 additional clients × \$200 = \$3,400
For up to 100,000 images. **\$0.05** per generated image above 100,000 **Total monthly fee:** **\$15,400

*Optional support package.***
*This dev pricing breaks even with API pricing at \~100,000 images per month at \$0.15 per image***


What the license allows** - Self-host model weights on agency-controlled infrastructure. - Generate outputs for commercial client work. - Create internal derivatives, including fine-tunes, for agency use only. - Deliver outputs to clients without restriction on their commercial use. - Build internal tools and workflows using the models. **Operational and legal guardrails** - **Number of clients list** required, updated quarterly. - **Usage reporting** required on a monthly basis. **Holding Company Upsell:
** ## Onboarding Needs & Setup Requirements (WIP) --- 1. Usage Reporting 1. API + Self-reporting for Dev 2. Usage audits 2. Dev Setup 1. Parent & child keys 3. Billing 1. Agency fees vs. per client fees 2. Rev share, referral fees, etc. 4. Support 1. What does this look like for the Agency vs. Client 2. SLAs + channels that they can reach us 3. Scaled Moderation offering (e.g., Custom end-points) 4. Joint-custom models # Archive {toggle="true"} # **Agency X BFL Collabs**
Type of Agency Agency Offering Details Joint Opportunity (FDE/Monetization) Considerations
Creative Agency (Brand / Ideation)
***ToolofNA, IPG, Pieter Schmidt Group***		 - Project based
- Low volume
- Customization
- Fine-tuning/LoRAs		 - Joint FDE, we have relationship with client as well (billed as support hours or rev share on the project); ***needs to be further defined and is our strongest pref***
- Reseller of our fine-tune (3D, virtual try on, etc.)?
- ENT Playground w/ custom workflows (for indie agencies)

- Dev + Support (not our preference unless high volume)		 - If we start offering “curated image bundles” for customers, we would compete
- If we set up a rev share we may need to share accounts for better joint business
- Need to run a price per image analysis (what can bake into per image cost for different use cases)
Performance Marketing
***Omnicom, Havas***		 - Brand Kits / Variants
- High volume
- Campaign billing (ROI)		 - API out of the box
- Private end-points (for speed, moderation, etc.)
- (Explore) Presets based on campaign targeting info (upsampling, post-training)
- Dev + Support (not our preference unless high volume)
Professional Services
***Accenture, PWC***		 - Automation
- White-glover service
- Project based		 - API out of the box
- Private end-points (for speed, moderation, etc.)		 **

2. What Agencies Actually Do (Their Value)**
### **A. Agencies provide the “Brand Interpretation Layer”** They do things BFL should *not* do: - Create brand-specific datasets - Train LoRAs / fine-tunes - Build structured prompt templates - Define brand-safe constraints (colors, lenses, styling rules, cameras, copy tone) - Build plugins/UI layers in Figma, Comfy, Omni, Vermeer - Guide clients through brand alignment, representation, and safety - Do final post-production (retouching, compositing, layout) **This is the actual value clients pay agencies for.** BFL is the **model provider**, not the brand interpreter. ### **B. Agencies do NOT want to become model vendors** Consistent across all calls: - They **do not want to resell models** - They do not want the burden of: - Pricing - Billing - Model distribution - Model support - They only want the ability to **deploy** models into client environments. ### **C. Agencies want model capabilities that help them deliver:** - Realism, physics, coherence - Multi-reference + collage inputs - Editing and iterative refinements - Structured JSON prompting - World knowledge - Text in images - Brand consistency Flux.2 hits these needs *very directly*. ## ❓** Open Questions** {toggle="true"} **Open Questions:** 1. How do agencies bill customers or pass through consumption fees? 2. What are agencies appetite for spend? What kind of deals have they signed w/ other LLM providers? 3. What are the possible scenarios w/ Agencies? **Examples of Resell today:** - **Pro Dev License: **The only partner that hosts and resells the pro w/ Rev share is MSFT (MSFT gets 58% of deal, but if customers are using credits there is a chance MSFT doesn’t report on this rev share) - **Host public Dev models + their own API endpoint**: The rev share here is they keep 70% of revenue - Cloudflare, TogetherAI - **API: **The other resellers that don’t host our models, but pass through to API (Fal, Replicate) - Fal, Replicate: These players have volume discount but there is no rev share in place ### Feedback from Agencies on Needs ---

Typically, our work involves creating and optimizing training data, training LoRAs or fine-tunes, and supporting the implementation of AI applications within the client’s infrastructure. **Google** ### **Imagen (Text-to-Image AI)** - Back in early 2024, Google integrated **Imagen 2** into its **Performance Max** campaigns, enabling advertisers to generate realistic images—including of people—in ads across Search, YouTube, Gmail, and more. [digitalposition.com](https://www.digitalposition.com/resources/blog/ppc/google-ads-can-now-generate-humans-in-ai-ad-creative/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - These AI-generated images are being integrated into Google Ads’ creative tools/assets. To serve them, BFL should offer a modular Agency License, API access, dev models, client-hosted rights, and optional reseller terms, anchored in clear licensing and meaningful minimum commits. ## Summary --- 1. Marketing Agencies mainly want AI **to make campaigns faster, cheaper, and more effective;** creating content automatically, updating it in real time, and moving away from slow manual work and hourly fees toward results-driven production. 2. To achieve this, these companies are rapidly re-organizing around by: - Creating **dedicated innovation labs** and **technical teams** that blend creatives, engineers, and data experts. - They are also building **internal AI platforms** that sit across the entire organization, giving thousands of employees access to generative tools inside unified systems (e.g., Omnicom’s “Omni”, Havas’s “Vermeer”, Accenture’s “Song AI”, etc.). - Agencies also aksi **shifting their business models** toward high-velocity, on-brand, AI-assisted production, focusing on workflows like iterative editing, brand-specific generation, and automated content pipelines instead of traditional handcrafted creative. 3. As a result, **Agencies need a flexible AI offering** that allows for API access for thousands of employees, dev models for technical labs to customize and fine-tune, and client-hosted rights for delivery work. Agencies are uniquely positioned to provide brand interpretation and workflow expertise, which would be challenging for BFL to replicate at scale. Our goal is to offer high-performance models, clear licensing terms, and well-aligned incentives to ensure that customers realize the value of our models, and that it directly translates to increased revenue for us and the agency. 4. The best way forward is a **modular Agency License** with four components: 1) API Access, 2) Dev Model Access, 3) Client-Hosted Add-On, and 4) Reseller Add-On. We will leverage minimum commits to capture value up-front, output caps to avoid losing value on scale, and rev shares/referral fees on efforts that require deeper partnership or commitment from BFL and the Agencies. ### 📊 Marketing Agency Landscape {toggle="true"} - The **Marketing Agencies** market size is estimated at \$453Bn in 2025, and is expected to reach USD 571.53 billion by 2030, at a CAGR of 4.8%. The key trends include **increased adoption of AI in creative development**, rapid scaling of performance-based pricing contracts, and cookie-less personalization technologies are reshaping how brands evaluate agency partnerships. [Source](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/global-marketing-agencies-market) - The key players continue to be fairly concentrated, with the top five groups: WPP, Omnicom, Publicis Groupe, Interpublic Group, and Dentsu, collectively accounting for a significant portion of 2024 billings. Omnicom’s planned merger with Interpublic, valued at over \$13Bn, is set to create the world’s largest holding entity and unlock substantial procurement and back-office synergies. **We collected feedback and use cases from both Omnicom and IPG (and a handful of their subsidiaries)**. WPP defends its leadership by funneling AI spend into its proprietary Open AI Studio that automates copy, imagery, and media-mix forecasting. **WPP has also expressed interest in our models, and we will be setting up time with them next week**. - **We’re already following through on inbound from some of the biggest Agency Holding Companies: **WPP, Omnicom, and IPG. Once we have these deals in place, we can approach the rest: Dentsu, Havas, and Stagwell, in addition to smaller creative agencies: *VML, TBWA, RAPP, Razorfish, Havas, Doner, Digitas, Huge, Publicis Sapient or* Media Agencies: Mindshare, Starcom, Magna, Carat, Assembly, OMD. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/6207aea2-e0c8-4aad-a666-8edeecdac89a/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466YUSMJ6K3%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095636Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIQD2b0seB7%2BZ6Rv4kZsjQw7p3zloyMdFfusByuFuPfjSsgIgIGJ1paZI7JF555WysyEetyOSOm%2B9F7R%2BIas5uNn0EAQq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDPPlWE5ZyLfOHBEYPyrcA4HVuELWJE3PwTrNFeQMtwUXljz7fmzSSI34u0Ho6El3ZGH9G%2F9scy4D8Fm1aRSjbbnixe9ffEOosj6kbjkak4Zt621WVaEdFPjS71fQbv7EnMLr00HmWeP6B8aPAxhGFl%2FHBfGWp9sEu1ZBjGvIoUUX%2FVYX1Fp5bjKJCQ4lWCvGiVtewXuBaK7rsB3T5NF2DnL0HmjHC536QptFP75z3Z859M7jAm81WJU6i%2B2JR28Kb3%2F26hAGk8%2BAYsvYl1cpPKOheH2d9iK1GEVS%2FHYfFtKlOX99ZwwYiQTLNYFbxNE1bDoevDvl7lYXFh559Tb3m223iBcziLryvmetn%2Bodg3t%2BhhLPIgPP4qa%2BJ21osx7j2NMTK2J5b32v49PUgsr2aQWvq%2Bskcfj%2BJoTShwYkDjZpSFUqsuB5R4jVFCbmWFdTXemqXSs2tkv4fW5FOmEPTNPA%2FEvMlQIL2nLIf4xApj998k%2FYkVeNBoyEKO0E61T7tPTfA0IhxuMGEvOg1SjvhStykbZqKWOFQGvVicremyUAVAjeXNn4O1%2FvyONfV7e3asxa5L4lz9TtpnzrYkSqDqhILY1LFdJeBT%2BAvqg2iYLbW0gyHtIR8FKnk%2BT047%2Fz4Vg%2BvI%2FPsbFdLnjWMKyvks8GOqUB06Qr%2BU5LAnCF6YDu9nHGsD2WSCQNBsN%2BTItVfKs18pgIXhiWQlsDet97OdDYQHhiajmXP4EeSpFRGcHOD77ZjtA9WPz5McrrdzcFHY0upoqVrPDArgL17TEFRf0n9LfB3MLomlV5DnqGba8WNuZvSogvwGVH25uZekHkg2hzJUgjc6UIFpo5%2BPJxJZNCeDmAAMEa6WXGJtjiVSoN2%2BhlUE%2FAdRPh&X-Amz-Signature=c0b468c27253a7cc8eb33ce38beccfa6a9ce74ee7e0bfc6237867cfc3cccf0af&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) View of Account & Partner Notes  # **1. How agencies are working w/ GenAI ** --- Feedback collected from: Omnicom (includes IPG, Craft, Grabarz, and PSG), Accenture, Havas (including Prose on Pixels), and Superside. *Upcoming calls: WPP* ### **AI is implemented in three layers across most Marketing Agencies / Large Professional Service Providers**
**1. Internal Creative Tools (employee-facing)** - Where most image requests originate (pitch decks, concepts, mockups, internal ideation). - BFL access typically embedded into internal platforms or plugins. **Internal tools mentioned:**
**Agency** **Internal Tool** **# Employees w/ access** **Tool Description**
**Omnicom **(includes IPG / Craft / McCann / Grabarz) **Omni platform + Omni Assist (gen-AI overlay); **AI OS across agencies \~20,000 active Omni users today, up to 75,000 possible - everyone “touching client work”). Assuming this refers to IPG merger.

\~55,000 at IPG (but innovation team small; unclear how many will use the tool)		 Omni created as a cross-agency data/marketing/insights/activation platform. Omni Assist, introduced 2023, adds generative-AI: a virtual assistant for audience insights, media planning, campaign workflows, measurement, optimization. ([Omnicom Group](https://www.omnicomgroup.com/newsroom/with-omni-assist-omnicom-leverages-first-mover-access-to-open-ai-to-accelerate-the-timeline-from-insights-to-outcomes/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
According to recent reporting, Omnicom is using a network of AI agents (powered by Omni data + gen-AI) to simulate focus groups, generate personalized content, run real-time optimization, dynamic content creation, and more. ([Digiday](https://digiday.com/marketing/ai-is-reshaping-omnicoms-workflow-its-revenue-model-may-be-next/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
**Accenture** **Song AI Tool** Initial cohort \~20,000; broad rollout to anyone touching client work (\~40k–60k) Accenture Song is a suite of AI-enabled capabilities built into Song’s offering: creative, data, analytics, customer-experience, content generation, commerce, and media automation.
**Havas** **Vermeer **(part of Converged.AI)**; **Prose on Pixels is the **innovation lab**, that is leading the integration of models within Vermeer) 23,000 global Havas employees Described as “next-gen video production platform” for agencies; uses generative-AI to produce video + creative content at scale. ([havas.com](https://www.havas.com/press_release/havas-accelerates-transformation-and-pivots-to-become-an-ai-driven-organization-fueled-by-human-ingenuity/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
**Superside** **Figma-based Superside plugin** \~500–1,000 internal (but used across all client accounts; no broad employee access) Superside advertises that they combine “AI-certified creative talent + custom AI workflows + latest AI tools” to deliver creative at scale. ([Superside](https://www.superside.com/ai-creative?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
**2. Client Delivery Workflows (service layer)** This is the **primary revenue engine** for agencies, and the unique differentiator when it comes to AI: - Training LoRAs or fine-tune models - Creating brand datasets - Using Flux for product imagery, portraits, packaging, lifestyle scenes - Rendering concept-to-production assets for campaigns, e-commerce, automotive - Building pipelines (often Unreal, C4D, or custom rendering stacks)
**3. Client-Hosted Deployments (emerging trend)** From Accenture, IPG, and the new agency call: - Agencies want to **install Dev Models inside client infra** (cloud or on-prem). - This is used for: 1) Regulated clients, 2) Automotive, 3) Global consumer brands with strict compliance, and 4)Data-sensitive or proprietary image systems **Important:** This is NOT resale; agencies are not trying to resell the model. They want a **right to deploy** as part of a service engagement.
# 2. How BFL can structure our terms to create joint incentives --- These are the different components we would need for an “Agency Sku”. - **Crawl (Accenture & Omnicom): **We are running the first “COMBO” pilot with Accenture, including API + Dev Access for 6 months at a \$500K minimum commit. The intent is to then include both the “client hosting” and “reseller add-ons” once we have a better understanding of their usage, and the number of clients they serve. Simultaneously, we are pitching a 6-month API only agreement w/ Omnicom, and from here we will add Dev. - **Walk: **Expand COMBO model to a small number of additional agencies (e.g., WPP). During this stage, we also begin piloting per-client deployment fees and structured reseller/referral pathways with agencies who deploy Flux inside client environments. - **Run:** Launch a dedicated **Agency SKU** on our website that clearly packages API access, Dev Model access, client-hosted rights, and optional reseller terms. We then introduce a tiered **Agency Partner Program** that recognizes and rewards top agencies, featuring them on our site with co-branded case studies and partner badges. For advanced partners, we offer joint FDE motions focused on complex, high-value workflows like client-hosted deployments. We also publish a directory of certified resellers and model integrators, ensuring only vetted partners can deploy or customize Flux models for clients. Together, this ecosystem positions Flux as the preferred model across the agency landscape, while scaling revenue through structured licensing, minimum commits, and partner incentives. *“Sub-license” is defined as re-selling access to our API and/or creating and selling a service/API powered by our dev model.*
**DEAL TYPE:** API ONLY DEV ONLY COMBO CLIENT HOSTING ADD-ON RESELLER ADD-ON
**Current
Challenges**		 • Agencies can switch away easily
• Difficult to attribute client-level usage without strict key hierarchy
• Hard to surface high-value use cases without visibility into workloads		 • Black box: no telemetry inside partner infra
• Hard to price fairly without knowing volumes

 • Agencies blend workloads across API and Dev, making billing opaque • Ideally we own the relationship with the client
• Hard to track deployments across client clouds
• Model updates and patching become operationally heavy		 • Agencies have low incentive to resell API (they profit more from FDE and creative services)
• Agencies may attempt to “bundle” our model under their own brand
• If agencies start selling model access via internal tools, BFL must capture value proportionally
**Proposals** • Introduce per-key reporting and audit rights.
• Incentivize usage via volume-based tiers.
• Provide upgrade paths to Dev License or Reseller.		 • Mandate monthly usage logs / callback endpoints and periodic audits.
• Add a per-client activation fee for each new deployment.
• Offer FDE onboarding packages to get visibility and ensure correct setup.
 • Set a combo minimum commit to ensure flexibility of use across API + Dev, but also prevent negotiation based on usage
• Predictable costs for Agencies
• Enforce workload separation via API key trees + Dev environment tagging.		 • Set a minimum commit or base fee for Agency-hosted; then a variable cost for every client
• Require mandatory client acknowledgment of BFL terms (DPA, IP, safety).
• Conduct joint onboarding calls to secure the BFL→Client relationship.
• Offer optional FDE add-on for infra validation and upgrades.		 • Introduce three structured reseller paths with clear economics:
1) Referral (10% referral fee): client signs directly with BFL.
2) Internal Tools (per client access fee): agencies sell fine-tuned model access via proprietary tools.
3) Client Deployments (rev share): agency installs in client infra with a per-client BFL license.
• Set agency-wide minimum commits, then per-client tenant fees.
• Require reseller certification (technical + compliance).
• Provide co-branded reseller badges and listing on BFL website.
• Offer joint GTM for qualified partners, but gatekeep resale rights.
**Governing Terms** **API License Agreement
**• Standard ToS and DPA apply directly between BFL & Agency
• No right to sublicense APIs without BFL approval
 **Developer License Agreement**
• Hosting rights limited to Agency’s secured infra
• No right to sublicense or redistribute model access
• Output rights defined
• Audit + security provisions for self-hosting		 **API + Dev (Platform License)**
• No right to sublicense APIs without BFL approval		 **Client Hosting Addendum**
• No right to sublicense APIs without BFL approval
 **Reseller Agreement**

2. What Agencies Actually Do (Their Value)**
### **A. Agencies provide the “Brand Interpretation Layer”** They do things BFL should *not* do: - Create brand-specific datasets - Train LoRAs / fine-tunes - Build structured prompt templates - Define brand-safe constraints (colors, lenses, styling rules, cameras, copy tone) - Build plugins/UI layers in Figma, Comfy, Omni, Vermeer - Guide clients through brand alignment, representation, and safety - Do final post-production (retouching, compositing, layout) **This is the actual value clients pay agencies for.** BFL is the **model provider**, not the brand interpreter. ### **B. Agencies do NOT want to become model vendors** Consistent across all calls: - They **do not want to resell models** - They do not want the burden of: - Pricing - Billing - Model distribution - Model support - They only want the ability to **deploy** models into client environments. ### **C. Agencies want model capabilities that help them deliver:** - Realism, physics, coherence - Multi-reference + collage inputs - Editing and iterative refinements - Structured JSON prompting - World knowledge - Text in images - Brand consistency Flux.2 hits these needs *very directly*. ## ❓** Open Questions** {toggle="true"} **Open Questions:** 1. Investor updates set a growth narrative; app-led pricing suggests **seat/tenant + usage**; enterprise SOWs where custom integrations are needed. ([Stagwell](https://www.stagwellglobal.com/stagwell-stgw-will-host-2025-virtual-investor-day-and-announce-5-billion-revenue-target-by-end-of-fy29/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
### Let’s start by defining which Agencies we’re talking about
Category Core Focus / Value Proposition Why BFL Might Want to Partner Typical Clients / Scale
**Management & Strategy Consulting** Big-picture transformation, operating models, tech strategy, change management BFL can plug into AI / data strategy, serve as “tech arm” of consulting projects, co-deliver AI POCs Large enterprises, governments, regulated sectors
**Digital / Technology Consulting / Systems Integrators** Implementation, data pipelines, systems integration, architecture, AI/ML engineering BFL can act as innovation partner / accelerant, helping agencies handle AI model layers or experimentation Mid-large enterprises, digital transformation clients
**Creative / Advertising / Media Agencies (Holding Companies and Independents)** Marketing, brand, campaign execution, content, media buying BFL can help these agencies embed generative/AI capabilities (e.g. content automation, agentic systems, personalization) Consumer brands, enterprise B2B, digital advertisers
**Performance / Growth / Marketing Agencies** Demand generation, paid media, direct response, analytics BFL can bring AI-driven predictive, optimization, attribution, real-time feedback loops High-growth startups, mid-market, DTC, SaaS
**Public Relations / Communications / Reputation Agencies** Messaging, media strategy, narrative building, stakeholder relations BFL can add AI for sentiment analysis, generative drafting, media-monitoring, “share of model” (how much your brand gets cited in AI outputs) Corporates, NGOs, tech companies
**Specialist / Vertical-Niche Agencies** e.g. life sciences marketing, retail tech, experiential, data science boutiques These may be more agile and open to partnerships; BFL can offer deep AI stacks Clients with complex domain needs
**Platform / Martech / Data Platforms** (adjacent to agencies) Tools that agencies use or embed (CDPs, analytics, campaign platforms) BFL could integrate as a feature, or co-develop modules Agencies + brands adopting new stacks
**Ads Market Dynamics** - **Dominance of Major Platforms: **Google, Meta, and Amazon collectively control over half of the global ad market. - **Growth of Video Advertising: **Advertisers are increasingly investing in video, with content-rich video formats like social video, outstream, and AVOD (Advertising Video On Demand) gaining significant traction. - **AI Integration: **AI is playing a crucial role in ad performance, with product integrations for creative development, ad placement, and performance optimization benefiting major platforms. - At the highest level, 72% companies still see themselves in the experimental/
pilot stage with AI (32%) or having deployed it for limited use in specific
workflows (40%). [Source pg38](https://content.martechday.com/state-of-martech-2025.pdf) - B2B companies are proportionally using AI more in data enrichment, email
personalization, and sales enablement and engagement. B2C businesses are
more likely to use it for testing and optimization in campaigns and web/app
experiences. pg78 - Most of the acceleration and automation that AI is enabling is in production and
analysis. It’s getting easier, faster, and cheaper to produce the creative ideas
we conceive of and analyze their outcomes. A campaign that used to take
weeks to implement with multiple, specialized contributors might now only
take days, or even hours, for a marketing generalist augmented with state-ofthe-art AI tools. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/83931d36-1685-4d85-a920-57994b9007e4/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466YUSMJ6K3%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095636Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIQD2b0seB7%2BZ6Rv4kZsjQw7p3zloyMdFfusByuFuPfjSsgIgIGJ1paZI7JF555WysyEetyOSOm%2B9F7R%2BIas5uNn0EAQq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDPPlWE5ZyLfOHBEYPyrcA4HVuELWJE3PwTrNFeQMtwUXljz7fmzSSI34u0Ho6El3ZGH9G%2F9scy4D8Fm1aRSjbbnixe9ffEOosj6kbjkak4Zt621WVaEdFPjS71fQbv7EnMLr00HmWeP6B8aPAxhGFl%2FHBfGWp9sEu1ZBjGvIoUUX%2FVYX1Fp5bjKJCQ4lWCvGiVtewXuBaK7rsB3T5NF2DnL0HmjHC536QptFP75z3Z859M7jAm81WJU6i%2B2JR28Kb3%2F26hAGk8%2BAYsvYl1cpPKOheH2d9iK1GEVS%2FHYfFtKlOX99ZwwYiQTLNYFbxNE1bDoevDvl7lYXFh559Tb3m223iBcziLryvmetn%2Bodg3t%2BhhLPIgPP4qa%2BJ21osx7j2NMTK2J5b32v49PUgsr2aQWvq%2Bskcfj%2BJoTShwYkDjZpSFUqsuB5R4jVFCbmWFdTXemqXSs2tkv4fW5FOmEPTNPA%2FEvMlQIL2nLIf4xApj998k%2FYkVeNBoyEKO0E61T7tPTfA0IhxuMGEvOg1SjvhStykbZqKWOFQGvVicremyUAVAjeXNn4O1%2FvyONfV7e3asxa5L4lz9TtpnzrYkSqDqhILY1LFdJeBT%2BAvqg2iYLbW0gyHtIR8FKnk%2BT047%2Fz4Vg%2BvI%2FPsbFdLnjWMKyvks8GOqUB06Qr%2BU5LAnCF6YDu9nHGsD2WSCQNBsN%2BTItVfKs18pgIXhiWQlsDet97OdDYQHhiajmXP4EeSpFRGcHOD77ZjtA9WPz5McrrdzcFHY0upoqVrPDArgL17TEFRf0n9LfB3MLomlV5DnqGba8WNuZvSogvwGVH25uZekHkg2hzJUgjc6UIFpo5%2BPJxJZNCeDmAAMEa6WXGJtjiVSoN2%2BhlUE%2FAdRPh&X-Amz-Signature=a78deee29ce6b7c48ca8d471af6b8087c4ef53d3fb8ea9db06332605cf38f80d&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) **AD PLATFORMS:**
**Google** ### **Imagen (Text-to-Image AI)** - Back in early 2024, Google integrated **Imagen 2** into its **Performance Max** campaigns, enabling advertisers to generate realistic images—including of people—in ads across Search, YouTube, Gmail, and more. These AI images are watermark-protected to indicate they're synthetic, helping avoid misuse.[Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/technology/google-upgrades-ai-product-advertisers-with-gemini-models-2024-02-22/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - Through **Google Ads' AI Image Editor**, brands can now pull product imagery from the Merchant Center feed and apply AI-powered enhancements or generate fresh visuals. These go into the Asset Library for use in Performance Max campaigns.[Google Help](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/15205259?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com) - More recently, Google released features that let advertisers generate images directly within **Ads** and **Merchant Center**, showing products in action or stylized creative scenes. This functionality is rolling out and will soon be accessible via the upcoming **Asset Studio**, centralizing these creative tools.[blog.google](https://blog.google/products/ads-commerce/google-ai-ads-creative/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - Google’s AI help documentation confirms these capabilities: Asset Studio (coming soon) and the ability to do **image-to-video transformations** using both **Veo and Imagen**, already available in Ads and Merchant Center.[Google Help](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13580022?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com) --- ### **Veo (AI Video Generation)** - Announced in late 2024 as part of **Vertex AI**, **Veo** allows business users to generate high-quality videos from text or image prompts, with consistent visuals and built-in watermarking safeguards.[The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/2024/12/4/24312938/google-veo-generative-ai-video-model-available-preview?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - Since May 2025, Google has started pushing **image-to-video transformation** features powered by Veo—initially available in Merchant Center, with a rollout to Google Ads forthcoming.[blog.google](https://blog.google/products/ads-commerce/google-ai-ads-creative/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - Independent reports highlight **Veo 3**, the latest iteration showcased at Google I/O 2025, which adds **native audio generation** (dialogue, ambient noise, music) to high-definition video outputs—greatly streamlining ad production workflows.[ValueX2](https://www.valuex2.com/how-google-veo-3-will-make-your-ads-go-viral/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)[Syllaby](https://syllaby.io/blog/how-to-create-ads-in-google-veo-3/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) --- ### What Google *has* announced / is enabling for programmatic 1. **Veo 3 Fast** - Google recently released *Veo 3 Fast*, a cost- & speed-optimized version of the Veo 3 video generation model. It supports *text-to-video* and *image-to-video* modalities. [Google Developers Blog](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/veo-3-fast-image-to-video-capabilities-now-available-gemini-api/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - In the announcement, Google explicitly calls out *programmatic advertising* as a “use case” for Veo 3 Fast: “Powering backend services that automatically generate ad creatives” is listed among the ideal choices. So they anticipate Veo 3 / Veo 3 Fast being used in automated/large-scale ad creative generation. [Google Developers Blog](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/veo-3-fast-image-to-video-capabilities-now-available-gemini-api/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) 2. **Imagen for generating “humans in ad creative”** - Google has added the ability for advertisers to generate human imagery using **Imagen 3** for ad creative — e.g. for Performance Max, Demand Gen, Display, or App campaigns. This lets brands generate images of people (with demographic / attribute control) without doing a photoshoot. [digitalposition.com](https://www.digitalposition.com/resources/blog/ppc/google-ads-can-now-generate-humans-in-ai-ad-creative/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - These AI-generated images are being integrated into Google Ads’ creative tools/assets. This suggests they are usable in a programmatic/automated way, since many Google campaigns are at least semi-automated (assets are chosen dynamically). [digitalposition.com](https://www.digitalposition.com/resources/blog/ppc/google-ads-can-now-generate-humans-in-ai-ad-creative/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

# Meeting Summary: Austin's Anthropic Growth Marketing Journey + Lessons for Black Forest Labs
**Date:** Feb 12, 2026
**Participants:** Owais (Black Forest Labs) + Austin (Growth Marketing Lead at Anthropic)
---
## Austin's Complete Journey at Anthropic
### The Starting Point (When He Joined)
- **Team size:** 500 people total, but only **5-6 people in marketing**
- **Marketing structure at the time:**
	- Kevin (Head of Product Marketing) - basically solo
	- Sandy (Led overall marketing)
	- 1 person in partner marketing (handling AWS/Google relationships)
	- 1 person on events
	- Austin (hired to build ALL of growth marketing from zero)
### Phase 1: The Foundation Building (First 8 Months)
**Austin literally did every growth marketing job that exists at Notion today:**
- **Performance Marketing:** Built from scratch 
- **Lifecycle/Email:** Onboarded all tooling, built first email drips, set up entire infrastructure
- **SEO:** Started first iterations
- **Mobile App Store:** Worked on getting listings up
- **Paid Social:** Built and managed campaigns
**The Reality of Early Days:**
- "There was literally nothing here" - had to onboard vendors, build processes, figure out procurement
- Worked with skeleton cross-functional teams:
	- Few people in product marketing for copy
	- One designer (it was literally her first day) to figure out email templates
	- Brand new hire on data infrastructure to set up ETL for lifecycle drips
	- Two mobile engineers to get first App Store listing live
- **Pure execution mode** - no strategy docs, no inherited playbooks, just building and moving fast
- "Very draining and very stressful" but also fun
### Phase 2: The Overwhelming Period (January-February Last Year)
**The crisis point:**
- Started questioning his decision: "Dude, maybe I made a mistake"
	- Anthropic had 500 people vs. Notion had more
	- ARR was way lower than Notion's
	- Valuation was DOUBLE Notion's
	- "Did I make a mistake?"
**Then everything changed:**
- By end of year, traction really picked up momentum
- New year brought new team members BUT Austin was still solo executor
- Now had a Growth PM to work with
- Company pushing hard on consumer and student initiatives
- **Still the only person executing** on growth marketing side
**What "overwhelmed" actually meant:**
- Looped into "insane number of meetings"
- Operational overhead: Slides, prep work, mobile strategy docs
- Plus doing ALL the execution work himself
- Got so bad his manager assigned him a TPM (Technical Program Manager) just to support him
- "Really, really painful for a few months"
- Being pulled in so many different directions simultaneously
### Phase 3: How He Survived - The Prioritization Framework
**His Core Philosophy:**
> "Every day was a deep prioritization exercise"
**His Process:**
1. **Started with objectives:** What are we actually trying to achieve?
	- For consumer Claude: New user acquisition + Pro monetization
	- Only two products existed: API and Claude Pro
2. **Worked backwards:** Which channels ladder up to these goals?
	- Picked exactly TWO: Performance marketing + Lifecycle
	- Why? Could execute with minimal cross-functional dependencies
3. **Ruthlessly deprioritized:**
	- **SEO got completely cut** despite being "very important"
	- Reasoning: Needed too much web development support they didn't have
	- Performance marketing only needed one engineer to get a pixel up
	- Then could run Google Ads independently (doesn't even require creative)
**His Strong Recommendation:**
> "What I would really recommend you don't do is try to do a little bit of everything. Instead, hedge your bets and try to do like two things really, really well to get very strong signal whether or not they work for you."
### Phase 4: Scale & Growth (Recent Months)
**The team transformation:**
- Started: Austin reporting directly to Kevin (Head of Product Marketing) because team was tiny
- Then: Rolled up to Sandy (Kevin's boss) for a bit
- Then: Hired his direct manager
- Multiple reorgs later: "Lot more middle managers now" - team went more vertical
- Marketing overall: From \~6 people to pushing 130-140 people
**What finally got resources:**
- **Social strategy:** Didn't exist a year ago
	- Last year at this time: Had secured @anthropic handles, could post model announcements, but no real strategy
	- Recent shift: Spun up separate Claude AI handles to differentiate from Anthropic
	- Last 3 months: Consistent posting across every channel
	- Results:
		- Twitter: 0 → \~400K followers
		- Instagram: 0 → \~250K followers
		- "In a matter of a couple months because we were very consistent"
---
## Austin's Advice Applied to Black Forest Labs
### Our Context
- Strong revenue traction, 60 people, 3 in marketing (similar early stage to his start)
- Revenue from: Third-party tools (Krea, Figma, Adobe), aggregators (Fal), enterprise deals (Meta, movie studios)
- Challenge: Strong model usage, low brand awareness
- Goals: Quality awareness + direct API usage
### What Austin Said We Should Do
### Priority 1: Social Strategy ✅
**Why it works for us:**
- Our audience (technical AI creatives) lives on Twitter/Instagram
- We're visual/image generation - Instagram is natural fit
- Reference example: Krea got 8M views on controlled edits using OUR models, gave us zero credit
**Austin's Critical Warnings:**
- "You need to be very intentional what you post on social. Very, very intentional."
- Build editorial calendar
- Be clear about what you DO post vs. DON'T post
- Example of what NOT to do: Meme accounts that post every few hours
	- At first funny, then annoying, just "clogging up my feed"
	- "The value actually diminishes"
- Focus on UGC: Showcase what people build with our models
**His experience:**
- Anthropic had no social strategy a year ago
- Now posting consistently = massive growth in months
- Separated Claude AI brand from Anthropic (see branding section below)
### Priority 2: LinkedIn Ads (His Strong Suggestion)
**His reasoning:**
- We're targeting creative directors, decision makers, pro-level creatives
- LinkedIn is where they are (not Facebook/consumer platforms)
- **Our unique advantage:** "You guys are literally creative"
	- Can generate all our ad creative with our own models
	- Not bottlenecked by creative production
	- Ads ARE the product demonstration
**What to skip:**
- Paid social (Facebook, Instagram ads) - "very much a consumer play"
### What to Deprioritize Now
**Lifecycle/Email:**
- Austin's calculation: "What does volume look like?"
- If we're getting \~1,000 contact form submissions/day = 30K/month
- "That's very low" - don't spend 2 months building lifecycle infrastructure
- His recommendation: Basic hygiene only
	- Monthly release emails when we ship models
	- Use our own models to make "really, really beautiful email templates"
	- Wait until self-serve API launches and volume actually exists
**Dev Rel Content (YouTube, How-to's):**
- "I view that as something that comes a little bit later"
- Reasoning: "Amount of effort that needs to go in vs. perceived impact"
- Takes huge effort before anything ships
- Distribution problem: Who actually sees it?
- Audience problem: Will attract general consumers interested in image gen, but they'll realize "I can't really use this, it's API-only"
- Ends up being "cool tech demo" not growth driver
**Discord Community:**
- Only becomes priority IF/WHEN we launch self-serve API
- Developers expect it (MidJourney is Discord-only, does great)
- But without self-serve product, premature
**Sales Outbound:**
- Austin mentioned this but noted "doesn't live under your umbrella"
- Question for us: Do we have SDRs doing outbound?
- Should be separate consideration from marketing channels
---
## The Big Branding Question: Black Forest Labs vs. Flux
### The Anthropic/Claude Split Story
**What happened:**
- Started unified, then "it was kind of painful when we had to finally recognize we need to separate these two"
- Had to:
	- Stand up Claude.com domain (separate from Anthropic.com)
	- Create new social accounts for Claude AI separate from Anthropic
	- Split positioning: Research goes on Anthropic.com, product announcements on Claude.com
**Why they did it:**
- "All these frontier labs" do this: OpenAI/ChatGPT, Google/Gemini, Meta/Llama
- Two distinct brands because two different audiences:
	- People who care about the lab and research
	- People who just want to use the product ("I do not care about Black Forest Labs, but I care about the model")
**Austin's strong point:**
> "You want to think through if these two different - if the lab and the model want to represent different things and they also want to be able to have a channel in order to share that stuff."
### Our Situation & Austin's Validation
**My reasoning (which Austin agreed with):**
- Right now Flux is better known than Black Forest Labs
- "Cold start problem" - we have near-zero awareness for either
- Better to build unified awareness first: "Any attention for Flux by Black Forest Labs is a good start"
- Let people discover: "Oh what's this Black Forest Labs? Oh they build these Flux models"
- Wait for natural pull-based demand, then separate brands
- "I would almost rather do that and suffer the consequences"
**Austin's response:** "Yeah, okay, that's good."
---
## Austin's Key Principles (Direct Quotes)
1. **On prioritization:**
	- "You can't possibly do everything. I need to pick the few areas that I can actually dedicate some time to."
	- "You need to be very ruthless in terms of prioritization"
2. **On betting strategy:**
	- Don't do "a little bit of everything"
	- "Hedge your bets and try to do two things really, really well"
	- Get "very strong signal whether or not they work"
3. **On effort vs. impact:**
	- Constantly asked: "What is the amount of effort that needs to go in vs. perceived impact?"
	- "What is sort of the North Star objective" then "what are the channels that ladder up to that?"
4. **On one-to-many motions:**
	- When volume is low, focus on channels that reach many people at once
	- Social works, website works
	- Lifecycle doesn't make sense until you have the volume to justify the infrastructure

# Meeting Summary: Austin's Anthropic Growth Marketing Journey + Lessons for Black Forest Labs
**Date:** Feb 12, 2026
**Participants:** Owais (Black Forest Labs) + Austin (Growth Marketing Lead at Anthropic)
---
## Austin's Complete Journey at Anthropic
### The Starting Point (When He Joined)
- **Team size:** 500 people total, but only **5-6 people in marketing**
- **Marketing structure at the time:**
	- Kevin (Head of Product Marketing) - basically solo
	- Sandy (Led overall marketing)
	- 1 person in partner marketing (handling AWS/Google relationships)
	- 1 person on events
	- Austin (hired to build ALL of growth marketing from zero)
### Phase 1: The Foundation Building (First 8 Months)
**Austin literally did every growth marketing job that exists at Notion today:**
- **Performance Marketing:** Built from scratch 
- **Lifecycle/Email:** Onboarded all tooling, built first email drips, set up entire infrastructure
- **SEO:** Started first iterations
- **Mobile App Store:** Worked on getting listings up
- **Paid Social:** Built and managed campaigns
**The Reality of Early Days:**
- "There was literally nothing here" - had to onboard vendors, build processes, figure out procurement
- Worked with skeleton cross-functional teams:
	- Few people in product marketing for copy
	- One designer (it was literally her first day) to figure out email templates
	- Brand new hire on data infrastructure to set up ETL for lifecycle drips
	- Two mobile engineers to get first App Store listing live
- **Pure execution mode** - no strategy docs, no inherited playbooks, just building and moving fast
- "Very draining and very stressful" but also fun
### Phase 2: The Overwhelming Period (January-February Last Year)
**The crisis point:**
- Started questioning his decision: "Dude, maybe I made a mistake"
	- Anthropic had 500 people vs. Notion had more
	- ARR was way lower than Notion's
	- Valuation was DOUBLE Notion's
	- "Did I make a mistake?"
**Then everything changed:**
- By end of year, traction really picked up momentum
- New year brought new team members BUT Austin was still solo executor
- Now had a Growth PM to work with
- Company pushing hard on consumer and student initiatives
- **Still the only person executing** on growth marketing side
**What "overwhelmed" actually meant:**
- Looped into "insane number of meetings"
- Operational overhead: Slides, prep work, mobile strategy docs
- Plus doing ALL the execution work himself
- Got so bad his manager assigned him a TPM (Technical Program Manager) just to support him
- "Really, really painful for a few months"
- Being pulled in so many different directions simultaneously
### Phase 3: How He Survived - The Prioritization Framework
**His Core Philosophy:**
> "Every day was a deep prioritization exercise"
**His Process:**
1. **Started with objectives:** What are we actually trying to achieve?
	- For consumer Claude: New user acquisition + Pro monetization
	- Only two products existed: API and Claude Pro
2. **Worked backwards:** Which channels ladder up to these goals?
	- Picked exactly TWO: Performance marketing + Lifecycle
	- Why? Could execute with minimal cross-functional dependencies
3. **Ruthlessly deprioritized:**
	- **SEO got completely cut** despite being "very important"
	- Reasoning: Needed too much web development support they didn't have
	- Performance marketing only needed one engineer to get a pixel up
	- Then could run Google Ads independently (doesn't even require creative)
**His Strong Recommendation:**
> "What I would really recommend you don't do is try to do a little bit of everything. Instead, hedge your bets and try to do like two things really, really well to get very strong signal whether or not they work for you."
### Phase 4: Scale & Growth (Recent Months)
**The team transformation:**
- Started: Austin reporting directly to Kevin (Head of Product Marketing) because team was tiny
- Then: Rolled up to Sandy (Kevin's boss) for a bit
- Then: Hired his direct manager
- Multiple reorgs later: "Lot more middle managers now" - team went more vertical
- Marketing overall: From \~6 people to pushing 130-140 people
**What finally got resources:**
- **Social strategy:** Didn't exist a year ago
	- Last year at this time: Had secured @anthropic handles, could post model announcements, but no real strategy
	- Recent shift: Spun up separate Claude AI handles to differentiate from Anthropic
	- Last 3 months: Consistent posting across every channel
	- Results:
		- Twitter: 0 → \~400K followers
		- Instagram: 0 → \~250K followers
		- "In a matter of a couple months because we were very consistent"
---
## Austin's Advice Applied to Black Forest Labs
### Our Context
- Strong revenue traction, 60 people, 3 in marketing (similar early stage to his start)
- Revenue from: Third-party tools (Krea, Figma, Adobe), aggregators (Fal), enterprise deals (Meta, movie studios)
- Challenge: Strong model usage, low brand awareness
- Goals: Quality awareness + direct API usage
### What Austin Said We Should Do
### Priority 1: Social Strategy ✅
**Why it works for us:**
- Our audience (technical AI creatives) lives on Twitter/Instagram
- We're visual/image generation - Instagram is natural fit
- Reference example: Krea got 8M views on controlled edits using OUR models, gave us zero credit
**Austin's Critical Warnings:**
- "You need to be very intentional what you post on social. Very, very intentional."
- Build editorial calendar
- Be clear about what you DO post vs. DON'T post
- Example of what NOT to do: Meme accounts that post every few hours
	- At first funny, then annoying, just "clogging up my feed"
	- "The value actually diminishes"
- Focus on UGC: Showcase what people build with our models
**His experience:**
- Anthropic had no social strategy a year ago
- Now posting consistently = massive growth in months
- Separated Claude AI brand from Anthropic (see branding section below)
### Priority 2: LinkedIn Ads (His Strong Suggestion)
**His reasoning:**
- We're targeting creative directors, decision makers, pro-level creatives
- LinkedIn is where they are (not Facebook/consumer platforms)
- **Our unique advantage:** "You guys are literally creative"
	- Can generate all our ad creative with our own models
	- Not bottlenecked by creative production
	- Ads ARE the product demonstration
**What to skip:**
- Paid social (Facebook, Instagram ads) - "very much a consumer play"
### What to Deprioritize Now
**Lifecycle/Email:**
- Austin's calculation: "What does volume look like?"
- If we're getting \~1,000 contact form submissions/day = 30K/month
- "That's very low" - don't spend 2 months building lifecycle infrastructure
- His recommendation: Basic hygiene only
	- Monthly release emails when we ship models
	- Use our own models to make "really, really beautiful email templates"
	- Wait until self-serve API launches and volume actually exists
**Dev Rel Content (YouTube, How-to's):**
- "I view that as something that comes a little bit later"
- Reasoning: "Amount of effort that needs to go in vs. perceived impact"
- Takes huge effort before anything ships
- Distribution problem: Who actually sees it?
- Audience problem: Will attract general consumers interested in image gen, but they'll realize "I can't really use this, it's API-only"
- Ends up being "cool tech demo" not growth driver
**Discord Community:**
- Only becomes priority IF/WHEN we launch self-serve API
- Developers expect it (MidJourney is Discord-only, does great)
- But without self-serve product, premature
**Sales Outbound:**
- Austin mentioned this but noted "doesn't live under your umbrella"
- Question for us: Do we have SDRs doing outbound?
- Should be separate consideration from marketing channels
---
## The Big Branding Question: Black Forest Labs vs. Flux
### The Anthropic/Claude Split Story
**What happened:**
- Started unified, then "it was kind of painful when we had to finally recognize we need to separate these two"
- Had to:
	- Stand up Claude.com domain (separate from Anthropic.com)
	- Create new social accounts for Claude AI separate from Anthropic
	- Split positioning: Research goes on Anthropic.com, product announcements on Claude.com
**Why they did it:**
- "All these frontier labs" do this: OpenAI/ChatGPT, Google/Gemini, Meta/Llama
- Two distinct brands because two different audiences:
	- People who care about the lab and research
	- People who just want to use the product ("I do not care about Black Forest Labs, but I care about the model")
**Austin's strong point:**
> "You want to think through if these two different - if the lab and the model want to represent different things and they also want to be able to have a channel in order to share that stuff."
### Our Situation & Austin's Validation
**My reasoning (which Austin agreed with):**
- Right now Flux is better known than Black Forest Labs
- "Cold start problem" - we have near-zero awareness for either
- Better to build unified awareness first: "Any attention for Flux by Black Forest Labs is a good start"
- Let people discover: "Oh what's this Black Forest Labs? Oh they build these Flux models"
- Wait for natural pull-based demand, then separate brands
- "I would almost rather do that and suffer the consequences"
**Austin's response:** "Yeah, okay, that's good."
---
## Austin's Key Principles (Direct Quotes)
1. **On prioritization:**
	- "You can't possibly do everything. I need to pick the few areas that I can actually dedicate some time to."
	- "You need to be very ruthless in terms of prioritization"
2. **On betting strategy:**
	- Don't do "a little bit of everything"
	- "Hedge your bets and try to do two things really, really well"
	- Get "very strong signal whether or not they work"
3. **On effort vs. impact:**
	- Constantly asked: "What is the amount of effort that needs to go in vs. perceived impact?"
	- "What is sort of the North Star objective" then "what are the channels that ladder up to that?"
4. **On one-to-many motions:**
	- When volume is low, focus on channels that reach many people at once
	- Social works, website works
	- Lifecycle doesn't make sense until you have the volume to justify the infrastructure
