2bcc3702-22d5-805d-869b-e207d7bbd022.title: Adobe Pro Proposal
2bcc3702-22d5-805d-869b-e207d7bbd022.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2bcc370222d5805d869be207d7bbd022 as of 2026-04-17T13:55:58.070Z: {"title":"Adobe Pro Proposal"} --- **Context:** A summary of a deal for Adobe to license our Flex model (external proposal linked below) specifically for use with Enterprise customers within Foundry. 💡***What has been added: non-negotiables and commercial tiers based on their desired terms.*** ## **A. Overall Value & Risks**
Opportunities Risks
BFL • Adobe is one of a small handful of companies where BFL can strike a large closed-weights deal.
• There is strong product-market fit between Flux models and Adobe's product surfaces, and given industry trends Adobe is in a highly likely position to pay a substantial fee for frontier model weights.
• BFL cannot efficiently serve Adobe's end-customer base directly at scale, so a single high-value agreement with Adobe allows BFL to capture that market through one commercial relationship rather than fragmenting across thousands of ENT accounts.		 • Adobe products still hold significant market share in creative tooling. While usage of traditional creative software is at risk as image and video models get better, there is a substantial lag in market adoption of models that could give Adobe a durable advantage if allowed to distribute fine-tuned versions of our models.
• Given Adobe's penetration of the ENT customer segment (some that directly overlap with BFL's current and target base) allowing broad distribution of Pro model derivates could cut off a large portion of both BFL's commercial licensing and API business).
• The scope restrictions in this deal exist specifically to prevent this outcome.
Adobe • Allows Adobe to fine-tune a SOTA model on ENT customer data to deliver on key Foundry workflows.
• Adobe already has existing ENT customers and relationships, and this deal allows them to deliver: 1) a differentiated, brand-safe generative capability on top of those accounts, 2) post-training and fine-tuning flexibility that no API-only arrangement provides, and 3) ENT customer brand customization at scale, which is the core commercial promise of Foundry.		 • Dependence on a 3P model for a flagship ENT product surface creates continuity and roadmap risk.
• Adobe also needs attribution flexibility to market Foundry as a proprietary product, which creates tension with our interest in brand visibility.
• And the scope of what Adobe can do with distribution, derivatives, white-labeling needs to be permissive enough for Adobe to build and market a real product.
## **B. Adobe’s Feedback & Our Recommendations** **Current Status:** They have continued to stress the urgency of the deal, although we’re not sure what is driving this (e.g., turning our draft in a matter of days, which is unusual). They have positioned this deal as a "Strategic Partnership" designation alongside Google, Runway, Microsoft, and OpenAI, but this is not reflected in their changes to the agreement. ***⚠️ The latest from my call w/ Ersin last night (April 9th)*** ---
**Deal-blockers** ** • White-labeling: **Despite Adobe legal scrapping all co-marketing commitments, he said he'll do joint PR, publicly position Foundry as collaborating with Black Forest Labs, and even offer BFL-labeled base models alongside white-labeled derivatives for customers who want them. ***He specifically wants fine-tuned models built on customer data to be white-labeled, ***since he views those as containing Adobe and customer IP, not just BFL's.

** • Distribution: **Adobe legal removed our language limiting distribution, and Ersin himself admitted that “Foundry” is just a construct. **"Foundry-only" is enterprise-private, not product-surface-limited.** Ersin's understanding of Foundry scope = private to specific enterprise customers, not accessible to the general subscriber base. But ***he can't commit to limiting which Adobe application surfaces an enterprise customer uses to access their endpoint*** (e.g., a Photoshop panel for that specific enterprise). Amanda pushed back that powering multiple workflows across multiple products for a single customer is still distribution — even at 50 seats. Ersin acknowledged the distinction and agreed to tier that separately.
***Nice-to-haves*** ** • Beyond Foundry Distribution & Internal Use: He proactively proposed a second tier for GA consumer surfaces.** Without much prompting, Ersin suggested structuring the agreement with a base enterprise tier (Foundry/derivatives, white-label + co-marketing) and an optional second tier that kicks in if any Adobe product team wants to deploy a derivative in consumer-facing GA products (CC apps, Firefly subscriber base, etc.). He acknowledged this would reach hundreds of millions of users and warrants meaningfully higher commercials. He even suggested measuring it by number of deployed model instances as a scale limiter.
**Other clarifications** ** • He's only interested in derivatives for Foundry, not hosted-as-is.** Ersin confirmed he will not host \[Flex\] as-is, whether labeled or white-labeled. This agreement is exclusively about creating and deploying fine-tuned derivatives for ENT Foundry customers.

• **Derivative destruction is solvable.** Despite Adobe legal adding more favorable terms around their control, distribution, and post-expiry rights for derivatives, Ersin confirmed Adobe would destroy derivatives at end of term with documentation. His ask is a wind-down/cool-down period so existing enterprise customer agreements can run out naturally, he doesn't want to pull back a live deployment from a paying customer mid-term. He framed this as a legal timing issue, not ownership.		 • The derivative wind-down period should be added as a standard term across all tiers (something like a 12-month cool-down where no new customer agreements can be signed post-expiry, but existing live deployments can run to their natural end) - Ersin signaled he's ready to agree to this.
## Our Recommendation --- ### Non-Negotiables
Term Status
On-prem deployment for their customers ❌ Not permitted
Distillation / Reverse-engineering ❌ Not permitted
Using models for AI-training workflows ❌ Not permitted
Standalone APIs ❌ Not permitted
Less than \$8M in Year 1 for white-labeling and distribution ❌ Not permitted
LoRAs / Fine-tunes ✅ Permitted (expire when contract expires)
Derivatives ✅ Permitted (expire when contract expires)
### Commercial Tiers & Our Recommendation The current tiers need to shift, because the call fundamentally changed two things: (1) white-labeling is no longer a premium add-on, and (2) the distribution distinction is now enterprise-private-multi-surface vs. GA consumer, not Foundry vs. everything else.
Commercial Tier Terms Internal Comments
**(Current Adobe anchor - what we proposed)**
\$4M / year		 Flex only · Foundry surface only · No white-labeling · No internal Adobe use · Models labeled "Flux" ***None-starter for Adobe***
**Tier 1 (Floor): Enterprise Foundry with white-labeling + co-marketing**

**\$8M in year 1, \$16M in year 2**
\*Alternative is \$4M trial for 6 months

OR

\$XM floor + variable (options: #images, #derivatives instances per customer)

*\*\*At \$500K selling price to their customers they will break even at 16 ENT customers in year 1.*
 • Flex only
• Private end-points exposed in Adobe ecosystem/products for ENT Foundry customers only
• NO standalone end-points
• White-labeling
• No internal Adobe services use		 • This captures table-stakes distribution and white-labeling
• ENT Foundry customers access their derivative model through multiple Adobe product surfaces (a Photoshop panel, a GenStudio workflow, etc.) rather than a single private API endpoint.
• Premium for removing BFL attribution; enables Adobe to sell \[Flex\] as proprietary. The co-marketing commitments should be explicitly baked in as conditions of this tier, not optionals (joint press release, Foundry x BFL public positioning, BFL-labeled base models available alongside derivatives).
**Tier 2: Broader Distribution** + **White-Labeling **
\$20M in year 1; \$30M year 2

*\*\* They could see it as a 8% R&D cost on what we believe is \$120M in annual ENT Firefly revenue.
This would cannibalize the current API spend of \$1.2M per year (primarily driven by Photoshop and Firefly), and also allow Adobe to use Flux for Brand-Brain (their B2B tool for Marketers to create on brand assets).
*		 Tier 1
+ distribution across other Adobe Customer segments (not just ENT Foundry)
+ use of Flex across Adobe internal services		 • This becomes pan-Adobe deal, and reflects platform-level embed in an \$18B+ product ecosystem (across DME + DX).
• This is what Ersin proactively proposed for CC apps, Firefly subscriber base, general public-facing products. Frame it as an option that can be exercised during the license term (his suggestion), not something Adobe has to commit to upfront.
• For this type of deal we would need to involve **Ely Greenfield** (CTO, Digital Media) and **Varun Parmar** (GM for ENT Firefly and Gen Studio).
## Recommendation w/ Variable Components {toggle="true"} ## Final Proposal for Adobe: ***Non-negotiables:*** - No on-prem deployment on behalf of clients - No distillation / reverse-engineering - No using models for AI-training workflows - No standalone APIs; however, derivatives can be integrated into Adobe products - \$8M flat fee per year - Some co-marketing commitments (PR, Placement, etc.) **Year 1** - \$8M flat fee **Year 2** Full sensitivity analysis [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/10bjVD05MliEiEmKo4y9XbyrtO9Z_3X80/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=100040495989598506312&rtpof=true&sd=true). - \$8M flat fee continues - **Foundry Customers:** - Variable per instance cost at waterfall per customer, and potentially waterfall per instance - If 1-2 instance on avg. per customer then pricing would be: - \$100K per instance for 1-10 customers - \$75K per instance for 11-20 customers (\$50K backup) - \$50K per instance beyond 20 customers (\$10K backup) - Renegotiation cap at 200 absolute instances - *Anchored in both our per image list price and ENT licensing fees since this is our opportunity cost - both the per image is below our average list price and the total per customer amount is below our ENT ACV.* - \*The per-image equivalent of the \$100K instance fee ***~~at 70% utilization~~*** works out to \$0.068/image, above our \$0.06 list price. The total \$100K is also below our annual ENT contract value for open weights licensing, which are \[dev\] / less good models. - GA / Consumer Customers: - Variable per image cost \$0.062 (list price would be \$0.09) up to 200M images per year, then it goes down to \$***0.038 ***per image after that ## Path 1: Lower cost on Foundry, and pricing GA/other segments for scale {toggle="true"} --- ***BFL Fee Assumptions*** - Fixed: \$8M /year - Variable (Foundry): Each P5 instance setup fee per customer is \$20K (first 10 customers), then \$15K (customers 11-50), and \$10K (51+ customers). - Variable (GA/Consumer Segment): Waterfall pricing, \$0.062 per image up to 200M images/year, then as low as \$0.038 per image ### 1. Conservative Case ***Only 10 Foundry customers in both years, and 20M images across their consumer segment (cannibilizing all direct API spend from Adobe today).***
Year 1 Year 2 2-Year Total
Adobe Deal \$8.0M \$9.44M **\$17.44M**
Direct API (same demand @ \$0.09) \$3.12M \$3.12M **\$6.25M**
Open Weights (\$10K/customer/month) \$1.2M \$1.2M **\$2.4M**
**Our POV: **This is a very good deal for us. Over two years, we earn \$17–17.4M versus \$6.25M if we'd served the same demand through direct API; roughly a **\$10.7–11.2M premium**. - Open weights at this scale isn't scaling fully; the deal earns 7× what we'd make on OW licenses alone (assuming each customer won’t go over 2M images per year). The \$8M flat fee is driving most of our value. - We would need to charge \$0.062 per image for their consumer segments for up to 20M images to safe-guard the current API revenue we get from them. We would also recommend to start waterfall pricing at 200M images per year and above. **Adobe's POV:** Potentially comfortable. They're paying \$8M to access FLUX derivatives across their Foundry platform, white-labeled and distribution-ready. On the GA images they process, they're paying \$0.038–\$0.062 versus the \$0.09 they'd pay BFL directly, saving them **\$560K at the high price** in Year 2 versus equivalent direct access. The deal saves them money relative to every alternative. --- ### 2. Realistic Case: ***20 Foundry customers Year 2, and doubling current image count to 40M GA/Consumer images***
Year 1 Year 2 2-Year Total
Adobe Deal \$8.0M \$10.83M **\$18.83M**
Direct API (same demand @ \$0.09) \$3.12M \$6.25M **\$9.37M**
Open Weights (\$10K/cust/month) \$1.2M \$2.4M **\$3.6M**
**BFL's POV:** Still a strong deal at **\$8.5–9.5M premium over direct API** across two years. - The Foundry per instance component starts to become a bit more meaningful (\$350K at 20 customers), though it's still modest. - The GA/Consumer per image side at 40M images looks good: net GA contribution of **\$1.28M **after cannibalization of \$1.2M. **Adobe's POV:** - 20 Foundry customers is a natural growth trajectory. For them, the deal at 40M GA images (doubling their current # images via direct API) costs \$10.83M vs. \$11.95M if they paid BFL's direct fine-tuned rate for everything (\$0.09). They're **saving \$1.12M**. That saving grows as volume grows, so Adobe is incentivized to push more volume through the licensed model rather than through direct API calls. It’s the cost we pay for distribution, even if we have to sell it to them at a discount. --- ## Breakevens 1. **ENT customers: Scenario 1 (no GA variable):** The deal beats direct API up to approximately **68 Foundry customers**. Below 68, the flat fee structure wins decisively. Above 68, BFL would have earned more serving those customers directly at \$0.09/image. In practice, whether BFL could realistically service 68+ enterprise Foundry customers directly is a different question — the distribution value of the Adobe deal is real even above the breakeven. 2. **GA image volume:** At a **lower per-image price (\$0.038):** direct API becomes more valuable once GA images exceed **\~132M per year**. That's a 6.6× multiple on current baseline demand, plausible if Firefly consumer usage scales meaningfully, but not a near-term concern if we believe they will run 20–40M images. At a **higher per-image price (recommendation is \$0.062):** the breakeven pushes all the way to **\~246M images**. At 100M images, the deal at high price still outperforms direct API by about \$4M. Again, we would have to believe that we could achieve that scale on our own, which isn’t necessarily as feasible. The only way this becomes unfavorable for us is if Foundry scales to 70+ enterprise customers *and* GA volumes cross 130–250M images *simultaneously*. ## Path 2: Higher cost on Foundry, and pricing GA/other segments for scale {toggle="true"} --- ***BFL Fee Assumptions*** - Fixed: \$8M /year - Variable (Foundry): Each P5 instance setup fee per customer is \$100K (first 10 customers), then \$90K (customers 11-50), and \$80K (51+ customers). - Variable (GA/Consumer Segment): Waterfall pricing, \$0.062 per image up to 200M images/year, then as low as \$0.038 per image ### 1. Conservative Case: ***Only 10 Foundry customers in both years, and 20M images across their consumer segment (cannibilizing all direct API spend from Adobe today).***
Year 1 Year 2 2-Year Total
Adobe Deal \$8.0M \$10.24M **\$18.24M**
Direct API (same demand @ \$0.09) \$3.12M \$3.12M **\$6.25M**
Open Weights (\$10K/cust/month) \$1.2M \$1.2M **\$2.4M**
**BFL's POV:** Over two years we earn \$17.76–18.24M versus \$6.25M if we were to serve customers directly via our API(a **\$11.5–12M premium)**. \$1M of the Year 2 revenue is coming from 10 instance fees. If the GA variable underperforms, the instance fees carry the slack. - The per-image equivalent of the \$100K instance fee at 70% utilization works out to **\$0.068/image,** above our \$0.06 list price. This means the Foundry instance pricing is now more aggressive on a per-image basis than our public API rate. **Adobe's POV:** Adobe's total per-instance cost would be **\$240K/year** (\$140K P5 compute + \$100K BFL fee), 71% above raw compute cost. Adobe will likely push back given the large flat fee, but our argument is that \$100K per instance is **17% below our ENT rate for open weights** (\$120K/year per customer). Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2bcc370222d5805d869be207d7bbd022 as of 2026-04-17T13:55:58.070Z: {"title":"Adobe Pro Proposal"} --- **Context:** A summary of a deal for Adobe to license our Flex model (external proposal linked below) specifically for use with Enterprise customers within Foundry. 💡***What has been added: non-negotiables and commercial tiers based on their desired terms.*** ## **A. Overall Value & Risks**
Opportunities Risks
BFL • Adobe is one of a small handful of companies where BFL can strike a large closed-weights deal.
• There is strong product-market fit between Flux models and Adobe's product surfaces, and given industry trends Adobe is in a highly likely position to pay a substantial fee for frontier model weights.
• BFL cannot efficiently serve Adobe's end-customer base directly at scale, so a single high-value agreement with Adobe allows BFL to capture that market through one commercial relationship rather than fragmenting across thousands of ENT accounts.		 • Adobe products still hold significant market share in creative tooling. While usage of traditional creative software is at risk as image and video models get better, there is a substantial lag in market adoption of models that could give Adobe a durable advantage if allowed to distribute fine-tuned versions of our models.
• Given Adobe's penetration of the ENT customer segment (some that directly overlap with BFL's current and target base) allowing broad distribution of Pro model derivates could cut off a large portion of both BFL's commercial licensing and API business).
• The scope restrictions in this deal exist specifically to prevent this outcome.
Adobe • Allows Adobe to fine-tune a SOTA model on ENT customer data to deliver on key Foundry workflows.
• Adobe already has existing ENT customers and relationships, and this deal allows them to deliver: 1) a differentiated, brand-safe generative capability on top of those accounts, 2) post-training and fine-tuning flexibility that no API-only arrangement provides, and 3) ENT customer brand customization at scale, which is the core commercial promise of Foundry.		 • Dependence on a 3P model for a flagship ENT product surface creates continuity and roadmap risk.
• Adobe also needs attribution flexibility to market Foundry as a proprietary product, which creates tension with our interest in brand visibility.
• And the scope of what Adobe can do with distribution, derivatives, white-labeling needs to be permissive enough for Adobe to build and market a real product.
## **B. Adobe’s Feedback & Our Recommendations** **Current Status:** They have continued to stress the urgency of the deal, although we’re not sure what is driving this (e.g., turning our draft in a matter of days, which is unusual). They have positioned this deal as a "Strategic Partnership" designation alongside Google, Runway, Microsoft, and OpenAI, but this is not reflected in their changes to the agreement. ***⚠️ The latest from my call w/ Ersin last night (April 9th)*** ---
**Deal-blockers** ** • White-labeling: **Despite Adobe legal scrapping all co-marketing commitments, he said he'll do joint PR, publicly position Foundry as collaborating with Black Forest Labs, and even offer BFL-labeled base models alongside white-labeled derivatives for customers who want them. ***He specifically wants fine-tuned models built on customer data to be white-labeled, ***since he views those as containing Adobe and customer IP, not just BFL's.

** • Distribution: **Adobe legal removed our language limiting distribution, and Ersin himself admitted that “Foundry” is just a construct. **"Foundry-only" is enterprise-private, not product-surface-limited.** Ersin's understanding of Foundry scope = private to specific enterprise customers, not accessible to the general subscriber base. But ***he can't commit to limiting which Adobe application surfaces an enterprise customer uses to access their endpoint*** (e.g., a Photoshop panel for that specific enterprise). Amanda pushed back that powering multiple workflows across multiple products for a single customer is still distribution — even at 50 seats. Ersin acknowledged the distinction and agreed to tier that separately.
***Nice-to-haves*** ** • Beyond Foundry Distribution & Internal Use: He proactively proposed a second tier for GA consumer surfaces.** Without much prompting, Ersin suggested structuring the agreement with a base enterprise tier (Foundry/derivatives, white-label + co-marketing) and an optional second tier that kicks in if any Adobe product team wants to deploy a derivative in consumer-facing GA products (CC apps, Firefly subscriber base, etc.). He acknowledged this would reach hundreds of millions of users and warrants meaningfully higher commercials. He even suggested measuring it by number of deployed model instances as a scale limiter.
**Other clarifications** ** • He's only interested in derivatives for Foundry, not hosted-as-is.** Ersin confirmed he will not host \[Flex\] as-is, whether labeled or white-labeled. This agreement is exclusively about creating and deploying fine-tuned derivatives for ENT Foundry customers.

• **Derivative destruction is solvable.** Despite Adobe legal adding more favorable terms around their control, distribution, and post-expiry rights for derivatives, Ersin confirmed Adobe would destroy derivatives at end of term with documentation. His ask is a wind-down/cool-down period so existing enterprise customer agreements can run out naturally, he doesn't want to pull back a live deployment from a paying customer mid-term. He framed this as a legal timing issue, not ownership.		 • The derivative wind-down period should be added as a standard term across all tiers (something like a 12-month cool-down where no new customer agreements can be signed post-expiry, but existing live deployments can run to their natural end) - Ersin signaled he's ready to agree to this.
## Our Recommendation --- ### Non-Negotiables
Term Status
On-prem deployment for their customers ❌ Not permitted
Distillation / Reverse-engineering ❌ Not permitted
Using models for AI-training workflows ❌ Not permitted
Standalone APIs ❌ Not permitted
Less than \$8M in Year 1 for white-labeling and distribution ❌ Not permitted
LoRAs / Fine-tunes ✅ Permitted (expire when contract expires)
Derivatives ✅ Permitted (expire when contract expires)
### Commercial Tiers & Our Recommendation The current tiers need to shift, because the call fundamentally changed two things: (1) white-labeling is no longer a premium add-on, and (2) the distribution distinction is now enterprise-private-multi-surface vs. GA consumer, not Foundry vs. everything else.
Commercial Tier Terms Internal Comments
**(Current Adobe anchor - what we proposed)**
\$4M / year		 Flex only · Foundry surface only · No white-labeling · No internal Adobe use · Models labeled "Flux" ***None-starter for Adobe***
**Tier 1 (Floor): Enterprise Foundry with white-labeling + co-marketing**

**\$8M in year 1, \$16M in year 2**
\*Alternative is \$4M trial for 6 months

OR

\$XM floor + variable (options: #images, #derivatives instances per customer)

*\*\*At \$500K selling price to their customers they will break even at 16 ENT customers in year 1.*
 • Flex only
• Private end-points exposed in Adobe ecosystem/products for ENT Foundry customers only
• NO standalone end-points
• White-labeling
• No internal Adobe services use		 • This captures table-stakes distribution and white-labeling
• ENT Foundry customers access their derivative model through multiple Adobe product surfaces (a Photoshop panel, a GenStudio workflow, etc.) rather than a single private API endpoint.
• Premium for removing BFL attribution; enables Adobe to sell \[Flex\] as proprietary. The co-marketing commitments should be explicitly baked in as conditions of this tier, not optionals (joint press release, Foundry x BFL public positioning, BFL-labeled base models available alongside derivatives).
**Tier 2: Broader Distribution** + **White-Labeling **
\$20M in year 1; \$30M year 2

*\*\* They could see it as a 8% R&D cost on what we believe is \$120M in annual ENT Firefly revenue.
This would cannibalize the current API spend of \$1.2M per year (primarily driven by Photoshop and Firefly), and also allow Adobe to use Flux for Brand-Brain (their B2B tool for Marketers to create on brand assets).
*		 Tier 1
+ distribution across other Adobe Customer segments (not just ENT Foundry)
+ use of Flex across Adobe internal services		 • This becomes pan-Adobe deal, and reflects platform-level embed in an \$18B+ product ecosystem (across DME + DX).
• This is what Ersin proactively proposed for CC apps, Firefly subscriber base, general public-facing products. Frame it as an option that can be exercised during the license term (his suggestion), not something Adobe has to commit to upfront.
• For this type of deal we would need to involve **Ely Greenfield** (CTO, Digital Media) and **Varun Parmar** (GM for ENT Firefly and Gen Studio).
## Recommendation w/ Variable Components {toggle="true"} ## Final Proposal for Adobe: ***Non-negotiables:*** - No on-prem deployment on behalf of clients - No distillation / reverse-engineering - No using models for AI-training workflows - No standalone APIs; however, derivatives can be integrated into Adobe products - \$8M flat fee per year - Some co-marketing commitments (PR, Placement, etc.) **Year 1** - \$8M flat fee **Year 2** Full sensitivity analysis [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/10bjVD05MliEiEmKo4y9XbyrtO9Z_3X80/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=100040495989598506312&rtpof=true&sd=true). - \$8M flat fee continues - **Foundry Customers:** - Variable per instance cost at waterfall per customer, and potentially waterfall per instance - If 1-2 instance on avg. per customer then pricing would be: - \$100K per instance for 1-10 customers - \$75K per instance for 11-20 customers (\$50K backup) - \$50K per instance beyond 20 customers (\$10K backup) - Renegotiation cap at 200 absolute instances - *Anchored in both our per image list price and ENT licensing fees since this is our opportunity cost - both the per image is below our average list price and the total per customer amount is below our ENT ACV.* - \*The per-image equivalent of the \$100K instance fee ***~~at 70% utilization~~*** works out to \$0.068/image, above our \$0.06 list price. The total \$100K is also below our annual ENT contract value for open weights licensing, which are \[dev\] / less good models. - GA / Consumer Customers: - Variable per image cost \$0.062 (list price would be \$0.09) up to 200M images per year, then it goes down to \$***0.038 ***per image after that ## Path 1: Lower cost on Foundry, and pricing GA/other segments for scale {toggle="true"} --- ***BFL Fee Assumptions*** - Fixed: \$8M /year - Variable (Foundry): Each P5 instance setup fee per customer is \$20K (first 10 customers), then \$15K (customers 11-50), and \$10K (51+ customers). - Variable (GA/Consumer Segment): Waterfall pricing, \$0.062 per image up to 200M images/year, then as low as \$0.038 per image ### 1. Conservative Case ***Only 10 Foundry customers in both years, and 20M images across their consumer segment (cannibilizing all direct API spend from Adobe today).***
Year 1 Year 2 2-Year Total
Adobe Deal \$8.0M \$9.44M **\$17.44M**
Direct API (same demand @ \$0.09) \$3.12M \$3.12M **\$6.25M**
Open Weights (\$10K/customer/month) \$1.2M \$1.2M **\$2.4M**
**Our POV: **This is a very good deal for us. Over two years, we earn \$17–17.4M versus \$6.25M if we'd served the same demand through direct API; roughly a **\$10.7–11.2M premium**. - Open weights at this scale isn't scaling fully; the deal earns 7× what we'd make on OW licenses alone (assuming each customer won’t go over 2M images per year). The \$8M flat fee is driving most of our value. - We would need to charge \$0.062 per image for their consumer segments for up to 20M images to safe-guard the current API revenue we get from them. We would also recommend to start waterfall pricing at 200M images per year and above. **Adobe's POV:** Potentially comfortable. They're paying \$8M to access FLUX derivatives across their Foundry platform, white-labeled and distribution-ready. On the GA images they process, they're paying \$0.038–\$0.062 versus the \$0.09 they'd pay BFL directly, saving them **\$560K at the high price** in Year 2 versus equivalent direct access. For them, the deal at 40M GA images (doubling their current # images via direct API) costs \$10.83M vs. \$11.95M if they paid BFL's direct fine-tuned rate for everything (\$0.09). They're **saving \$1.12M**. That saving grows as volume grows, so Adobe is incentivized to push more volume through the licensed model rather than through direct API calls. It’s the cost we pay for distribution, even if we have to sell it to them at a discount. --- ## Breakevens 1. **ENT customers: Scenario 1 (no GA variable):** The deal beats direct API up to approximately **68 Foundry customers**. Below 68, the flat fee structure wins decisively. Above 68, BFL would have earned more serving those customers directly at \$0.09/image. In practice, whether BFL could realistically service 68+ enterprise Foundry customers directly is a different question — the distribution value of the Adobe deal is real even above the breakeven. 2. **GA image volume:** At a **lower per-image price (\$0.038):** direct API becomes more valuable once GA images exceed **\~132M per year**. At a **higher per-image price (recommendation is \$0.062):** the breakeven pushes all the way to **\~246M images**. At 100M images, the deal at high price still outperforms direct API by about \$4M. Again, we would have to believe that we could achieve that scale on our own, which isn’t necessarily as feasible. The only way this becomes unfavorable for us is if Foundry scales to 70+ enterprise customers *and* GA volumes cross 130–250M images *simultaneously*. ## Path 2: Higher cost on Foundry, and pricing GA/other segments for scale {toggle="true"} --- ***BFL Fee Assumptions*** - Fixed: \$8M /year - Variable (Foundry): Each P5 instance setup fee per customer is \$100K (first 10 customers), then \$90K (customers 11-50), and \$80K (51+ customers). - Variable (GA/Consumer Segment): Waterfall pricing, \$0.062 per image up to 200M images/year, then as low as \$0.038 per image ### 1. If the GA variable underperforms, the instance fees carry the slack. - The per-image equivalent of the \$100K instance fee at 70% utilization works out to **\$0.068/image,** above our \$0.06 list price. This means the Foundry instance pricing is now more aggressive on a per-image basis than our public API rate. **Adobe's POV:** Adobe's total per-instance cost would be **\$240K/year** (\$140K P5 compute + \$100K BFL fee), 71% above raw compute cost. Adobe will likely push back given the large flat fee, but our argument is that \$100K per instance is **17% below our ENT rate for open weights** (\$120K/year per customer). They get a closed-weights model, white-label rights, and Foundry integration for less than a bare OW license per customer. This is where FLUX is integrated. - [How Amazon is using AI to dominate streaming TV ads - Fast Company](https://www.fastcompany.com/91435813/amazon-dominating-streaming-tv-ads-ai) - [How Amazon is using AI to dominate streaming TV ads - Fast Company](https://archive.ph/20251111151129/https://www.fastcompany.com/91435813/amazon-dominating-streaming-tv-ads-ai) - [Amazon is about to be flooded with AI-generated video ads](https://www.theverge.com/news/685160/amazon-ads-ai-video-generator-us-launch-availability) - [Amazon has a new creative agent to help your business build its own ads](https://www.techradar.com/pro/amazon-has-a-new-creative-agent-to-help-your-business-build-its-own-ads) - [AWS re:Invent 2025 - Amazon Ads Creative Agent uses AWS to democratize ad creation (IND3335)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EPRE8_FHGdQ) **Alexa+ ** - [Introducing Alexa.com, a completely new way to interact with Alexa+](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/alexa-plus-web-ai-assistant) > You can use [Alexa.com](http://alexa.com/) to get quick answers, explore complex topics, create content, plan trip itineraries, and get help with homework. But Alexa+ doesn't just provide information, it’s designed to take action. It can help you complete countless tasks: managing your to-do list, updating your family calendar, controlling your smart home, making reservations, and so much more. It also provides persistent context and continuity, allowing you to access Alexa on whichever device or interface best serves the task at hand, with all previous chats, preferences, and personalization seamlessly carrying over. - [Expedia, Yelp, Angi, and Square to build new agentic experiences for Alexa+](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/alexa-plus-voice-booking-integrations) **Prime Video** **Amazon MGM Studios** - [Exclusive: Amazon plans to use AI to speed up TV and film production](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/amazon-plans-use-ai-speed-up-tv-film-production-2026-02-04/) ### Customizations {toggle="true"} Amazon Product Photo Dataset \[EXT SVEN\] Product Photography Alexa Deal — Pending Items ## Meeting Notes --- ### \| Matt / Augustine {toggle="true"} **Attendees:** - BFL: Matt - Amazon: Augustine ### Call Prep ### Opening (2 min) "Hey Augustine, appreciate the time. I read through your latest draft and your comments. I want to use this call to understand what's actually blocking us, not to negotiate, because I think Monday will be more productive if we go in knowing where the real gaps are." "Augustine, I appreciate the time. I want to be direct with you before Monday.
We've now moved our positions twice in your favor. On SLAs, on commercial terms, on structure. Your latest draft came back more complex and more restrictive than the one before it. That's not the direction we need to be moving.
We have a shared goal of launching to customers in 10 days. That means a signed contract by next Friday. I want to hit that. But the way we get there isn't another round of redlines. It's getting the right people in a room early next week who can actually make decisions.
So here's what I need from this call. One, who on your technical team is driving the SLA requirements? I want them on a call with Ian before Monday. Two, who has the authority on your side to close on training restrictions and the minimum commit? Those are the two issues where we're genuinely stuck, and I haven't been able to get resolution through you. That's not a criticism, it's just a recognition that we probably need to escalate on both sides to get this done.
If we can get the right people in the room Monday with a mandate to close, I'm confident we can get there. If we go into Monday the same way we've gone into the last few calls, we're going to miss the launch window. I don't think either of us wants that." --- ### Signal 1: Who's Driving the SLA Complexity? (8 min) "Your team came back with more metrics, not fewer. P50, P90, a separate uptime SLA. Help me understand, is that coming from your engineering team, legal, or somewhere else?" *What you're listening for: does he name someone, or deflect?* If he names an engineer: "Great. Can we get that person on a call with Ian today or tomorrow? I think there's a genuine technical misunderstanding here that a 30-minute conversation can resolve." If he says "I'm not technical": "I know, so who are you relying on for the technical input? I want to connect them with Ian directly before Monday so we're not debating this in a big room." If he deflects entirely: he either doesn't have engineering backing or is being told to hold the line regardless of technical merit. That's your signal. --- ### Signal 2: Is the Training Restriction a Policy or a Position? (8 min) "You mentioned yesterday that other teams share your sentiment on training restrictions. I want to understand that better. Is this an Amazon data policy that prevents you from making this commitment in writing, or is this the Alexa team's view?" *What you're listening for:* - "It's Amazon policy" = you need a different person in the room, not Augustine. - "We just don't think it's necessary" = negotiating position, moveable. - Deflection or "we'll address it later" = same non-answer as before, signals he doesn't have authority to resolve it. Follow-up if he deflects: "You've said you'd be open to revisiting this a few times now, but it hasn't gone anywhere. If you're genuinely open to it, who on your side has the authority to agree to language? That's who I need on Monday's call." --- ### Signal 3: The Minimum Commit Binary (8 min) "Your comment in the doc is pretty clear: unlimited termination for convenience or no minimum. I want to understand if that's your personal read or a position that's been signed off above you. Because those two things together don't work for us, but I think there's a middle ground on the wind-down structure that might." *What you're listening for:* - "That's my position" = he has room to move, probe on what the wind-down could look like. - "That's what our team needs" = someone above him set this. Ask who. - "We can talk about it" = good signal, flag for Monday. #### The Asymmetry
Amazon's ask BFL's reality
Walk away with 60 days notice BFL has long-term compute contracts it cannot exit in 60 days
Pay only accrued usage fees BFL pays compute costs whether Amazon uses it or not
Receive 60 days of transition support BFL absorbs transition cost on top of stranded compute
No minimum if T4C is unconstrained Minimum exists to recover compute cost, not to generate margin
The minimum and the T4C are not independent levers. They are two sides of the same equation. Amazon framing them as a binary choice ("pick one") misses the point entirely, whether intentionally or not. --- ### Closing (4 min) "Here's what I need to know going into Monday. On SLAs: can you get your technical lead on a call with Ian before then? On training: who has the authority to actually agree to language, and can they be on Monday's call? On the minimum commit: is there a wind-down structure that works for both sides, or is this a hard no?" Pause. Let him respond to all three. If he's vague on decision-makers: "Augustine, I want to be straight with you. We've moved twice. The draft got more complex, not simpler. I don't want to spend Monday going in circles. If there are people on your side who need to be in the room for us to actually close this, let's make sure they're there." ### \| Amazon Redlines Review {toggle="true"} [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1f45OfaTd9fo3otYbjks1ToQ8kO9MBiz1/edit](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1f45OfaTd9fo3otYbjks1ToQ8kO9MBiz1/edit) :docs: Alexa+ \| Service Order #5 Redline Tracker → Reasoning for the focus on Latency SLA vs Uptime ### \| Mohan / Matt - Debrief {toggle="true"} **Attendees:** - BFL: Matt / Mohan **Notes** - Get Anthony’s perspective - Half acknowledged - Seems like the resolution is: 1. Connect us with the team that can negotiate this. 2. Add some language to the contract saying that we will revisit this. - Risk: - They continue to not address this or negotiate in good faith - ### \| Alexa / BFL - Training {toggle="true"} **Attendees:** - BFL: Matt, Mohan - Amazon: - Augustine, Sarah Kelley, Jonathan Abrams **Context / Agenda** Training Data Dispute - Separately, Amazon's push back on the inclusion of this language has **commercial conflict**: - Amazon's AGI team wanted to **train output moderation models on BFL-generated images** - BFL's hard line: **no pipeline from Flux directly into training a competitive image model** - Open to discussion on safety/moderation model training specifically - This became a major sticking point in contract negotiations — Amazon argued BFL couldn't renegotiate core terms retroactively - BFL's position: pricing was set for image generation for their product, not for training **Notes** - \[Augustine\] Understand where BFL is coming from. - Not resistant to incorporating the language. Want to keep it separate from this agreement. - Want to decouple the training discussion to avoid this being a launch blocker. - No issue on Amazon’s end to ensure they don’t train on our data. But Alexa+ doesn't just provide information, it’s designed to take action. It can help you complete countless tasks: managing your to-do list, updating your family calendar, controlling your smart home, making reservations, and so much more. It also provides persistent context and continuity, allowing you to access Alexa on whichever device or interface best serves the task at hand, with all previous chats, preferences, and personalization seamlessly carrying over. - [Expedia, Yelp, Angi, and Square to build new agentic experiences for Alexa+](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/alexa-plus-voice-booking-integrations) **Prime Video** **Amazon MGM Studios** - [Exclusive: Amazon plans to use AI to speed up TV and film production](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/amazon-plans-use-ai-speed-up-tv-film-production-2026-02-04/) ### Customizations {toggle="true"} Amazon Product Photo Dataset \[EXT SVEN\] Product Photography Alexa Deal — Pending Items ## Meeting Notes --- ### \| Matt / Augustine {toggle="true"} **Attendees:** - BFL: Matt - Amazon: Augustine ### Call Prep ### Opening (2 min) "Hey Augustine, appreciate the time. I read through your latest draft and your comments. I want to use this call to understand what's actually blocking us, not to negotiate, because I think Monday will be more productive if we go in knowing where the real gaps are." "Augustine, I appreciate the time. I want to be direct with you before Monday.
We've now moved our positions twice in your favor. On SLAs, on commercial terms, on structure. Your latest draft came back more complex and more restrictive than the one before it. That's not the direction we need to be moving.
We have a shared goal of launching to customers in 10 days. That means a signed contract by next Friday. I want to hit that. But the way we get there isn't another round of redlines. It's getting the right people in a room early next week who can actually make decisions.
So here's what I need from this call. One, who on your technical team is driving the SLA requirements? I want them on a call with Ian before Monday. Two, who has the authority on your side to close on training restrictions and the minimum commit? Those are the two issues where we're genuinely stuck, and I haven't been able to get resolution through you. That's not a criticism, it's just a recognition that we probably need to escalate on both sides to get this done.
If we can get the right people in the room Monday with a mandate to close, I'm confident we can get there. If we go into Monday the same way we've gone into the last few calls, we're going to miss the launch window. I don't think either of us wants that." --- ### Signal 1: Who's Driving the SLA Complexity? (8 min) "Your team came back with more metrics, not fewer. P50, P90, a separate uptime SLA. Help me understand, is that coming from your engineering team, legal, or somewhere else?" *What you're listening for: does he name someone, or deflect?* If he names an engineer: "Great. Can we get that person on a call with Ian today or tomorrow? I think there's a genuine technical misunderstanding here that a 30-minute conversation can resolve." If he says "I'm not technical": "I know, so who are you relying on for the technical input? I want to connect them with Ian directly before Monday so we're not debating this in a big room." If he deflects entirely: he either doesn't have engineering backing or is being told to hold the line regardless of technical merit. That's your signal. --- ### Signal 2: Is the Training Restriction a Policy or a Position? (8 min) "You mentioned yesterday that other teams share your sentiment on training restrictions. I want to understand that better. Is this an Amazon data policy that prevents you from making this commitment in writing, or is this the Alexa team's view?" *What you're listening for:* - "It's Amazon policy" = you need a different person in the room, not Augustine. - "We just don't think it's necessary" = negotiating position, moveable. - Deflection or "we'll address it later" = same non-answer as before, signals he doesn't have authority to resolve it. Follow-up if he deflects: "You've said you'd be open to revisiting this a few times now, but it hasn't gone anywhere. If you're genuinely open to it, who on your side has the authority to agree to language? That's who I need on Monday's call." --- ### Signal 3: The Minimum Commit Binary (8 min) "Your comment in the doc is pretty clear: unlimited termination for convenience or no minimum. I want to understand if that's your personal read or a position that's been signed off above you. Because those two things together don't work for us, but I think there's a middle ground on the wind-down structure that might." *What you're listening for:* - "That's my position" = he has room to move, probe on what the wind-down could look like. - "That's what our team needs" = someone above him set this. Ask who. - "We can talk about it" = good signal, flag for Monday. #### The Asymmetry
Amazon's ask BFL's reality
Walk away with 60 days notice BFL has long-term compute contracts it cannot exit in 60 days
Pay only accrued usage fees BFL pays compute costs whether Amazon uses it or not
Receive 60 days of transition support BFL absorbs transition cost on top of stranded compute
No minimum if T4C is unconstrained Minimum exists to recover compute cost, not to generate margin
The minimum and the T4C are not independent levers. They are two sides of the same equation. Amazon framing them as a binary choice ("pick one") misses the point entirely, whether intentionally or not. --- ### Closing (4 min) "Here's what I need to know going into Monday. On SLAs: can you get your technical lead on a call with Ian before then? On training: who has the authority to actually agree to language, and can they be on Monday's call? On the minimum commit: is there a wind-down structure that works for both sides, or is this a hard no?" Pause. Let him respond to all three. If he's vague on decision-makers: "Augustine, I want to be straight with you. We've moved twice. The draft got more complex, not simpler. I don't want to spend Monday going in circles. If there are people on your side who need to be in the room for us to actually close this, let's make sure they're there." ### \| Amazon Redlines Review {toggle="true"} [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1f45OfaTd9fo3otYbjks1ToQ8kO9MBiz1/edit](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1f45OfaTd9fo3otYbjks1ToQ8kO9MBiz1/edit) :docs: Alexa+ \| Service Order #5 Redline Tracker → Reasoning for the focus on Latency SLA vs Uptime ### \| Mohan / Matt - Debrief {toggle="true"} **Attendees:** - BFL: Matt / Mohan **Notes** - Get Anthony’s perspective - Half acknowledged - Seems like the resolution is: 1. Connect us with the team that can negotiate this. 2. Add some language to the contract saying that we will revisit this. - Risk: - They continue to not address this or negotiate in good faith - ### \| Alexa / BFL - Training {toggle="true"} **Attendees:** - BFL: Matt, Mohan - Amazon: - Augustine, Sarah Kelley, Jonathan Abrams **Context / Agenda** Training Data Dispute - Separately, Amazon's push back on the inclusion of this language has **commercial conflict**: - Amazon's AGI team wanted to **train output moderation models on BFL-generated images** - BFL's hard line: **no pipeline from Flux directly into training a competitive image model** - Open to discussion on safety/moderation model training specifically - This became a major sticking point in contract negotiations — Amazon argued BFL couldn't renegotiate core terms retroactively - BFL's position: pricing was set for image generation for their product, not for training **Notes** - \[Augustine\] Understand where BFL is coming from. - Not resistant to incorporating the language. Want to keep it separate from this agreement. - Want to decouple the training discussion to avoid this being a launch blocker. - No issue on Amazon’s end to ensure they don’t train on our data. The issue is that this team is not the one that is responsible for the eng changes. - Acknowledge our concerns but want to table it for now. - \[Mohan\] Question for Legal: - Which team would be responsible for implementing the restriction on training or add an amendment or order form? - What would the timing be? - Happy to have this discussion on an immediate basis - \[Augustine\] Amazon’s stance is that this is a valid concern. The issue is this potentially blocking or delaying launch. - \[Sarah\] Expect that this will take a lot of time to negotiate. The goal is to unblock the ACE team. **Action Items** - \[Sarah\] Will get back to Matt on who will lead this discussion on training from Amazon’s perspective. - \[Matt\] From my perspective if we can kick off this call in parallel that will create a lot more comfort in striking in this Service Order Form #5. - Helps BFL understand that we aren’t just kicking the can down the road. - We need to understand the who, what, and timelines - \[Augustine\] Share redlines back to BFL. ### \| Matt / Mohan - Sync {toggle="true"} **Attendees:** - BFL: Matt, Mohan **Agenda** **C2PA - Under review by Amazon ** Request to incorporate this: Please send over one consolidated quote. It will be helpful if the quote could include: 1. The \$50 for the 1K beta test images 2. A tiered table around the cost for load testing by batch. Here is a template; just need you to fill out the yellow rows and include it in the quote:
Load test image count BFL cost
50K \$2,500
100K \$4,500
150K \$6,500
200K \$9,000
**Indemnification Carve-Outs** **Training on FLUX outputs** ## Alexa Minimum Commit Framework {toggle="true"} ### Context Setting - Based on Amazon's TPS forecasts, BFL needs to acquire additional compute to meet peak demand. - Acquiring that compute creates real fixed cost exposure. To manage that risk responsibly, we need to introduce a monthly minimum commitment structure. - Our goal is to keep it simple and fair for both sides. ### Mechanics - **Monthly minimum.** Amazon pays a monthly floor based on a percentage of peak TPS, multiplied by image volume and price. Any usage above the minimum is invoiced within 30 days of month end. - **Prepayment.** Monthly minimum is prepaid at the start of each billing period. - **Minimum set quarterly.** Each quarter's minimum is derived from prior actual usage and Amazon's forecasted volume for the next quarter. - **30-day notice requirement.** Amazon must provide at least 30 days written notice ahead of any material change to expected volume so BFL can plan compute procurement accordingly. - **Quarterly ratchet mechanism.** At least 15 days prior to the end of each quarter, BFL and Amazon review actual usage together and reset the committed TPS for the next quarter. - Amazon can reduce their committed TPS by up to 20% quarter-over-quarter. - No cap on upward adjustments. - Protects BFL from cliff-drop scenarios without locking Amazon into a fixed annual number. - Contract term: 12 months. ### Rate Limiting - BFL reserves the right to technically enforce the committed TPS ceiling via API rate limiting. - To increase committed TPS, Amazon must provide 30 days written notice, subject to BFL's written approval. - This is a capacity planning mechanism, not a punitive one. It ensures BFL can provision correctly before absorbing demand spikes. ### SLAs - BFL's SLA obligations apply up to the committed TPS threshold only. - No SLA credits or remedies apply to usage above committed TPS. - Above-commit usage is best-effort. Reliability above threshold is a function of notice and approval process, not a default guarantee. ### \| \[Email\] **Quick Clarification: Data Handling Requirements Under our Agreement** {toggle="true"} From Roshni Hi Matt and Augustine, Quick question on our end as we work through some internal privacy data pipeline planning. Under our current agreement with Black Forest Labs, are there any contractual restrictions on how Amazon Alexa can use the generated outputs (i.e., the images returned via your API), specifically around whether those outputs can be included in data workflows such as internal model improvements (e.g., moderation models). As we discussed earlier this week, we are asking this because if there is a hard requirement around this from Black Forest Labs, we’d need to scope some engineering work on our side to ensure those outputs are tagged and handled appropriately in our systems. We want to make sure we are setup correctly. Thanks, Roshni ### \| \[Email\] **Re: Alexa + BFL: Cost Discussion** {toggle="true"} [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1tTq4LFwTqLmBxzwJ_xcoZbC_6EZ2Jtp7/view?usp=drive_link](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1tTq4LFwTqLmBxzwJ_xcoZbC_6EZ2Jtp7/view?usp=drive_link) From Roshni: Hi team - My apologies for the delay in summarizing this meeting. Thank you for the productive discussion yesterday. I wanted to summarize where we landed and provide additional context on the volume estimates.**Volume Breakdown for Launch**: Our estimates are organized into two phases - - Development: This includes load testing (with 1 hour of soak time) and beta testing with internal participants. - \[Ian: our tech team flagged me today that your calculations did not reflect soak time - so lets connect tomorrow in tech session\] - Production: Estimated traffic from March through June, based on realistic usage expectations for our current scope. This includes Alexa+ Core Agent experience on Echo, Web, Mobile. **Why the Estimates Are Lower Than Previously Shared** I want to be upfront about this. The change has nothing to do with the model upgrade project itself. Two features that were originally planned to launch alongside this upgrade have been pushed - one to next month and one to May - due to technical readiness issues within those respective projects. Those teams are working through their timelines independently, and we expect to have clearer line of sight soon. Once those features are ready, they will add approximately 20 to 25 TPS of additional volume toward the end of the Q2 quarter or early Q3 quarter which we will evaluate capacity and cost once we have a better signal on readiness of those programs. **Our Approach** Our intention is to make the switch in the core agent workflow first (and fast pending all the internal Amazon launch ceremonies that are non-negotiable), within the next 2 weeks, rather than waiting until every downstream feature workflow is ready. Once the core integration is live, we will continue layering in additional features as they become available through the quarter. We want to make sure we are scaled appropriately to support this initial switch as soon as possible. Hence the volume estimates shared matched are most realistic expectation at this first launch. **Next Steps** - Load testing: Targeting start date of March 23rd. - Beta unblock: Augustine is working to unblock beta through direct payments to BFL. - C2PA compliance: Tracking toward completion next week, required before launch. Matt is tracking from BFL - BFL action item: BFL to revert with any clarifications on the requirements we've shared. - Pricing: We need to finalize pricing that accounts for pan-Amazon-wide usage at launch. Sarah/Augustine to co-ordinate. I want to be transparent with how and why things are moving. We want to be in it for the long-run. We’ll keep you updated as the feature timelines firm up and share similar capacity assessments. Best, Roshni ### \| Provider Safety Infrastructure and Contractual Protections {toggle="true"} Shared with Amazon on March 19th: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zIx48UcejLemsSnHWA37t-lTSxtNt7iu9GXvTeae_3Q/edit?tab=t.0](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zIx48UcejLemsSnHWA37t-lTSxtNt7iu9GXvTeae_3Q/edit?tab=t.0) 🟢 From Amazon's Privacy Team on our two responses around Safety Infra and Contractual Protections. ### \| \[Meeting Name\] {toggle="true"} Slack Update EOD Update Attached is the doc shared with us today. Volumes - As Ian alluded to above, the volume estimates shared today being materially lower than what was shared yesterday. We are still aiming to drive more clarity here on expected volumes. This ultimately ties into the pricing and minimums Minimum Commit - Amazon pushed back on this but seemed to be understanding of our position. Once we share the framework as part of the order form, it should be more clear. - They requested that if a minimum were to exist they would want some sort of rollover of unused commit. - No major questions or pushback on the proposed volume tiers or discounts. Pan-Amazon Deal / Combined Pricing - There was a request to combine all usage at Amazon under a single agreement and single tiering structure to hit higher tiers faster. Conversations are already underway with Ads, Prime Video and two other teams at Amazon. - Open Questions / Next Steps - Purchase Order: Two questions: 1. Would we be open to a PO to allow for testing rather than a Service Order. Amazon is confirming on their end. 2. Would we be open to an agreement that goes through June to cover the first 3 months of usage while we negotiate a pan-Amazon deal? - Training on output images: Would we consider allowing Amazon to train on output images? They specifically wanted to train better safety filters. - 2-hour deletion SLA: Can we agree to this? cc: - Requirements: Can you confirm the requirements listed are all on your radar? - C2PA Draft: Any updates on the adjustments to the draft? **Minimum Commit / TPS** - Amazon explicitly pushed back on contractual volume commitments. Roshni's framing: "I haven't seen Amazon sign up to volume guarantees." Augustine acknowledged the risk-sharing logic and will take it back internally. - Anthony handled the framing well: quarterly ratchet, flexible vs. typical annual commit, shared risk narrative. Amazon seemed to accept the logic even if not ready to sign. - Sarah flagged a hard requirement: any unused committed spend must roll over, not expire. 30fc3702-22d5-81c6-adfc-cf72c1c263a2.title: BFL Creator/Influencer Program Version 1
30fc3702-22d5-81c6-adfc-cf72c1c263a2.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/30fc370222d581c6adfccf72c1c263a2 as of 2026-04-16T14:35:07.628Z: {"title":"BFL Creator/Influencer Program Version 1"} ## The Problem Professional creatives use tools like Krea, Figma, and Flora but they don't often know which model to pick and why. They often default to Nano Banana because of name recognition. The creator program can be our demo layer until a destination product from BFL exists. Goal: build quality awareness that drives frontier devs to prefer building on FLUX and professional creatives to pick FLUX as their preferred model within tools they use (Krea, Flora, Adobe, Figma Weavy). --- ## The Approach Don't talk to "creatives" as one blob. Everything in the program — who we recruit, what we ask for, which channels we use flows from user segments (eg Instagram/LinkedIn for the e-comm world. Twitter/X for dev creatives. Focus on 3 segments to start: **1. Fashion & E-Commerce** *Why:* Large creative vertical by deal volume. Zalando (62K videos, +40% page-to-cart), Hugo Boss (customer story in draft), Schwarz (\$100K virtual try-on), Envato (\$4M renewal), Photoroom. Goal across the segment: eliminate physical photo shoots entirely. - Fashion photographers/retouchers going AI-augmented - E-commerce creative directors at DTC brands - Virtual try-on / digital fashion creators - Fashion-tech content creators bridging style + technology **2. Film/TV/Entertainment Production** *Why:* Logos for credibility signaling. Disney (company-wide license in motion across ILM, Pixar, Marvel, Imagineering), Warner Bros (custom training infrastructure), Amazon Prime Video (FLUX-powered NBA replays already airing live), Netflix, NBC, SKY, Meta Creative X (450-person agency onboarded). Influential people here may have small social presences but enormous industry pull. - VFX supervisors and concept artists at major studios - Commercial directors doing AI-augmented production - Post-production pros (editors, compositors) exploring AI - Virtual production / pre-viz artists - AI filmmaking community leaders (Machine Cinema network) **3. Product Design & 3D Visualization** *Why:* might be underserved. Schmidt Group doing 500K kitchen renders/month, Hyundai and Mercedes design teams on FLUX, AVATR using ComfyUI + FLUX Depth for car design, 3DCloud targeting millions of furniture renders/month. - Industrial/product designers using 3D → AI rendering workflows - Automotive design visualization specialists - Architectural visualization artists - Interior design creators (kitchen/furniture/real estate renders) - ComfyUI power users specializing in ControlNet + 3D pipelines
**Tier 2 segments to consider in the future** **4. Game Development** *Why:* Epic Games integrating FLUX into Fab/Unreal Engine with free credits to millions of developers. 2K Games/Take-Two evaluating across all studios. Meta Horizon Worlds ramping to 1–2M generations/month. - Unreal Engine content creators and technical artists - Game environment artists using AI-assisted asset creation - Indie devs using AI for concept art and prototyping **5. Creative Tool Power Users** *Why:* Multiplier segment. These creators drive adoption into adjacent communities. Gamma (\$2M+ deal), VSCO (co-marketing assets live), Lightricks, Flora.ai, Picsart all integrating FLUX. - Tool reviewers / "workflow" content creators (YouTube/TikTok) - Graphic designers showcasing AI-augmented processes - Presentation design creators (Gamma ecosystem) **6. Brand & Marketing** *Why:* Adobe Brand Brain partnership active, ERGO enterprise playground, Meta Creative X using Playground for brand campaigns. - Agency creative directors exploring AI - Brand designers at tech companies - Marketing creative leads using AI in campaign workflows - Agency founders building AI-native studios
--- ## Phase 1 — Find the nodes (Month 1–2) Hand-pick **5-10 creators** across the three segments. The most respected practitioners whose audiences are other practitioners. BFL's own social channels start publishing in parallel. Content that speaks the specific language of each segment, not generic "cool image" posts. **Outreach is personal and done by us, not an agency.** Show we've actually looked at their work. Lead with what they get. **The offer:** - Free API credits covered - Early access to new fine-tuned model variants - Direct line to our team (this is our differentiator. No one else offers this) - Co-promotion when they make something great **What we ask for:** authentic use and honest feedback. --- ## Phase 2 — Prove the format (Month 2–3) The content that moves this market isn't "look what I made" — it's **"here's how I replaced a real workflow."** eg Zalando eliminating shoots, Schmidt rendering 500K kitchens, Prime Video airing live replays. Work with initial creators to co-produce 3–5 anchor pieces that each show a complete production workflow in a specific segment. Fashion photographer going from product sample → FLUX → final campaign asset. Product designer going from 3D model → FLUX render → client deliverable. (Internal) \[Klein\] Samples and initial comp to Z-image 💡 ** **See** **[**here**](/2e2c370222d5803e9f63d452e9dee0ff?pvs=25)** **for \[klein\] samples and initial feedback from Can based on generating at 1440×2048 pixels and without PUP: - The Prompt adherence, flexibility, aesthetic and variance in the seeds is really amazing for a 9b Model - Z-Image performs better in terms of raw realism, but Klein is way more flexible than any other model in this size range. Also, in comparison Qwen and Z-Image have extremely poor seed variance. - Seems better than flex/pro with non-photo styles, especially amazing at Anime. Colors and sharpness are great, way better than any other Flux Model so far. - One of the weaknesses is anatomy - hands, fingers, and anatomy are sometimes not so good in complex poses. - Seems like medium length prompts work better than the long prompts that the up-sampler produces
### **Launch Partner Tracker ** {toggle="true"} Launch Partners/Customers ### Partner Comms {toggle="true"}
**(Phase 1): **Message to share with dev partners for the klein models (external, but limited to phase 1 partners). Hi friends,
We are planning to release new FLUX.2 models (4B/9B), step-distilled and base model.
The base models are not guidance distilled. These models also use a new text encoder. You will find an attachment that includes an extension of [https://github.com/black-forest-labs/flux2](https://github.com/black-forest-labs/flux2) which implements the new base models.
***Please note***: the step distilled models are not yet part of the code/weights package - these will be shared at a later point in time. Additionally, all model names might still be subject to change. To run inference with the base models in the shared repo, just follow the FLUX.2 setup instructions in the README and set the following variables: ```javascript export KLEIN4B_MODEL_PATH=/blob/raw/checkpoints/production/flux2-klein-4b.safetensors export KLEIN9B_MODEL_PATH=/blob/raw/checkpoints/production/flux2-klein-9b.safetensors ```
Please share your feedback on the model. We will follow up with more information about the release dates and licenses soon. **Links to model weights** 4b base: [https://bflexternalmodels.blob.core.windows.net/flux2-klein/flux2-klein-4b.safetensors?sp=r&st=2026-01-10T17:09:27Z&se=2026-01-18T01:24:27Z&spr=https&sv=2024-11-04&sr=b&sig=RTiiFH7NdA7Jk8%2B%2FoDfbbYXaOUTtxVQ%2FYSgku1owsLo%3D](https://bflexternalmodels.blob.core.windows.net/flux2-klein/flux2-klein-4b.safetensors?sp=r&st=2026-01-10T17:09:27Z&se=2026-01-18T01:24:27Z&spr=https&sv=2024-11-04&sr=b&sig=RTiiFH7NdA7Jk8%2B%2FoDfbbYXaOUTtxVQ%2FYSgku1owsLo%3D) 9b base: [https://bflexternalmodels.blob.core.windows.net/flux2-klein/flux2-klein-9b.safetensors?sp=r&st=2026-01-10T17:13:21Z&se=2026-01-18T01:28:21Z&spr=https&sv=2024-11-04&sr=b&sig=z8A3OqRcZ2LRQLu0PfCMBAMyrgkvNlebo32bscDDf%2BU%3D](https://bflexternalmodels.blob.core.windows.net/flux2-klein/flux2-klein-9b.safetensors?sp=r&st=2026-01-10T17:13:21Z&se=2026-01-18T01:28:21Z&spr=https&sv=2024-11-04&sr=b&sig=z8A3OqRcZ2LRQLu0PfCMBAMyrgkvNlebo32bscDDf%2BU%3D) **Link to repo**

2f3c3702-22d5-80b5-b4c0-df3ce1845d67.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2f3c370222d580b5b4c0df3ce1845d67 as of 2026-04-17T07:54:45.913Z: {"Verification":"verified","title":"BFL AI Solutions Strategy"} World-class model do not automatically translate into business value!

AI Solutions inserts a highly technical, commercially minded layer between research & GTM to: - Unblock revenue - Build solutions that create value around our models - Protect & inform core eng, product and research **AI Solutions Offering Overview Presentation (internal):** # Why AI Solutions Team? ## Stakeholder Challenges & Hypotheses ### **Customers & Partners…** - … do not (yet) know the value they can get out of BFL models - … have ad hoc questions that should not require involvement from research or eng - … need customized models to solve specific use cases - … need a customized platform with workflows and UI to make FLUX accessible to their organizations - … need help with deployment of BFL models on their premises ### **BFL Sales & Partnership…** - … busy with negotiation on contract terms, no time to discuss use cases in detail - … missing technical knowledge to handhold customers through implementation - … missing hands on view on strengths and limitations of our models & products ### **BFL Research, Product & Eng…** - … missing feedback on what users want & need - … need to set the focus on research and maintenance of our systems ### **BFL Leadership ** - BFL revenue currently highly coupled with model releases - Our offerings lack stickiness - partners can switch out endpoints easily when a better base model comes out - We fail to capture the value in low volume deals (e.g. marketing campaigns with few but high quality images) - we have no clear feedback loop from customers use cases and challenges to the research teams —\> need someone to establish this ## The AI Solutions Team solves the challenges above by… - … becoming *the* point of contact on how to make flux useful, automated & at scale - …collecting and sharing feedback and novel use cases build around our tech with research & product teams - … customizing playground UI & image generation workflows for enterprises at scale - … driving up the price BFL charges per image for high value use cases by owning further parts of the media generation value chain ## What the AI Solutions motion should NOT do for us (risks!) - Turning BFL into a service business → *consultification* of BFL - Creating hundreds of slightly unique PG deployments that become unbearable to manage - Developing the same feature for multiple customers multiple times without reusability - Handle sales on their own and negotiate with large partners without sales/partnerships teams involvement ### Reading material on FDE: [The Palantir-ization of everything](https://www.a16z.news/p/the-palantirization-of-everything?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=13145&post_id=184727331&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=yfr2&triedRedirect=true&utm_medium=email) [Palantir: Inside the category of one – forward deployed software engineers - Everest Group Research Portal](https://www.everestgrp.com/palantir-inside-the-category-of-one-forward-deployed-software-engineers-blog/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) # Strategic Pillars for success ## 2026 Targets - 20+ case studies out that show BFL’s success as a solutions provider - 30M\$ revenue (ACV) through customization - this is not clearly measurable as most revenue will still be license & api, even if it’s a customized solution - generally activities/deals heavily driven by customization - Revenue decoupling from launches ## Bets & Pillars ### Pillar 1: Build Knowledge, Documentation & Feedback loop We need to become the best in the world when it comes to solving real world problems with BFL tech. Every customization and solution builds on deep knowledge of our own technology and how it is used effectively. Thus collecting knowledge about is a core success factor for the AI Solutions team.
**Initiatives:** Internal Knowledge management & Documentation \[\] - FLUX Use Cases ( & ) - Light-House Solution Reports (e.g. ) - Conceptual Education Material on Diffusion Models for GTM External Knowledge Spreading \[\] - Customer Success Stories - Blog Posts - Use Case Show Cases - Domain Use Case Decks Internal Tooling - API & Playground Customer analysis (prompt clustering, request parameter extraction based on task id, …) - Build tools that allow us to iterate faster and know more Feedback Loop with Product, Eng & Research \[\] - Collect customer feedback across the team - Define & maintain structured process to make sure our challenge cases are graduated into future model versions External Representation & Marketing \[\] - AI Solutions will support dev rel to represent BFL at events, hackathons & similar - ~~Building intern program to scale solution dev effort & make BFL popular among talent ()~~
### Pillar 2: Unblock & Close Deals The AI Solutions Team closes the gap between tech and customer. We need to act as point of contact for all strategic and ad-hoc technical questions of our focus customers. We need to solve all technical deal blockers.
**Initiatives:** Ongoing Customer Work \[everyone\] - everyone is owning customer engagement AI Solutions Account Ownership - Strategic & ad hoc technical & best practice support - We handle this as best effort support via Slack and meetings at the moment Customer Onboarding \[\] - We need a “structured” customer quick start & onboarding format - Format is open, onsite and/or remote - *“How do we reduce the time from first contact to first use case solved?”* Model Containers & Delivery \[\] - offer & maintain model serving containers to partners - Standardize model delivery & versioning
### Pillar 3: Embed & Create Applied Domain Value The AI Solutions Team radically embeds into our high potential customers workflows and systems. We aim to deeply understand their use cases and offer customized solutions that extend our value creation beyond a model call. It is *not* our aim to become the next Accenture, building thousands of unique solutions. We aim for customization through generalization. That means, understand useful primitives, build one platform around them, and customize by orchestrating primitives.
**Initiatives:** BFL Enterprise Studio \[ & \] - Enterprise PG Biz Model & GTM () - Tech & implementation Lead \[ \] ~~BFL Studio SDK \[\]~~ - ~~BFL Studio SDK & Plugin system ()~~ LoRA Finetuning Dataset Library \[\] - Assessment of relevant use cases we need to solve now & in the future - Evaluation and tracking of dataset requirements for these use cases - Streamlined dataset acquisition pipeline that is documented and available for the team - Transparent index of available highest quality dataset for the identified use cases Customized Workflow/Model Endpoints - Endpoint with customized pre / post processing ( )\[ \] - Endpoint with LoRA \[ \] - Open question: - How do we price this ()? \[ \] Hosting 3rd party models \[ & \] - we are exploring the possibilities / usefulness of hosting 3rd party models via our public api - e.g. segmentation model, upscaler & more LoRA factory \[\] - - How do we set up a standard fine tuning process for FDEs? \[ \] Demo Factory (Showcases) \[ \] - A minimalistic & reusable demo platform with thin auth layer - It should not take longer than a few hours to vibe a demo UI around e.g. a custom endpoint and share it publicly or with a specific customer - Platform to rapidly host demo UIs - Easy and secure sharing with selected customers - Lined out road to production if showcases fit into the product roadmap Open to closed source LoRa funnel \[\] - - We want to become market leader in offering LoRA for FLUX open source models, currently this market is dominated by fal - [https://huggingface.co/fal/flux-2-klein-4B-outpaint-lora](https://huggingface.co/fal/flux-2-klein-4B-outpaint-lora) - [fal/flux-2-klein-4B-object-remove-lora · Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/fal/flux-2-klein-4B-object-remove-lora) - [https://huggingface.co/fal/flux-2-klein-4B-zoom-lora](https://huggingface.co/fal/flux-2-klein-4B-zoom-lora) - [https://huggingface.co/fal/flux-klein-9b-virtual-tryon-lora](https://huggingface.co/fal/flux-klein-9b-virtual-tryon-lora) - We want to build out open source lora leadership as acquisition funnel into custom endpoints with LoRAs on our private source models - same LoRAs as improved versions for private source models Support Packages with dev licenses \[\] - Tiered Success Packages that guarantee access to FDE expertise, architecture reviews, and priority routing. - Billing FDE hours for general support & co-working ~~Agency Motion \[\]~~ - ~~Agency support model, how do we enable agencies & motivate them to use FLUX as default model ( )~~ - ~~Asset generation for select customers for selected campaigns ( )~~ - ~~LoRA Service for Customers - they bring data, we train for them~~
*Archive:* Near term SE/FDE motion for BFL
