304c3702-22d5-802f-b407-da495ea60413.title: Our Open Weights Opportunity
304c3702-22d5-802f-b407-da495ea60413.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/304c370222d5802fb407da495ea60413 as of 2026-04-16T15:37:31.031Z: {"title":"Our Open Weights Opportunity"} **TL/DR: **Open weights licensing is BFL’s structural moat, and there is room to better frame this value. It represents the primary frontier image model enterprises can ***own***, ***customize***, and ***self-host*** without security, IP, jurisdiction, or supply chain risk. Our previous self-serve price anchors did not fully reflect the strategic upside of ownership and infrastructure control, and we can articulate more clearly why that control carries a premium. The opportunity lies in 1) clarifying the enterprise value narrative, 2) aligning pricing with demonstrated willingness to pay, and 3) building tighter processes to convert high intent enterprise inbound, and 4) automating the long tail of startups and hobbyists so the team stays focused on high impact deals and strategic partnerships.
☑️** Next Steps: Decisions Needed** *Before this strategy is ready to execute, we need alignment on the following:* **🗳 Vote on the following: ** - **Price point per tier:** **Are these the right anchors, or do they need to move? **We have good early validation on the Professional SKU at \$8K/month. We need a decision on Builder (\$500/month) and Platform (\$3,000/month). - **Volume caps per tier:** **Do these caps create the right upgrade pressure, or are they too aggressive / too generous for the segments we're targeting? **The current proposal is 10K/month at Builder, 100K/month at Platform and Professional, and bespoke bands at Enterprise. - **Add-on menu: Are there other add-ons worth building in? **The current menu covers fine-tuning/LoRA rights, additional models, additional domains, resell rights, and priority support. (e.g., on-prem deployment rights as a standalone add-on, evaluation license for prospects, fine-tuning compute credits) - **Definition of "ENT": What should that threshold be?** We need a working definition of Enterprise that lets us route inbound and prioritize sales effort without ambiguity. Proposal: any company with projected open weights ARR above \$200K/year qualifies for ENT level support and engagement. Anything below goes through the Platform or Professional path. **💬 Input needed from the FDE team on Support tiers.** Before the add-on menu is final, we need the FDE team's input on what's actually deliverable at each support level, and whether there are any hard limits (e.g., number of supported tickets/month, response window by issue type) we should bake into the tier definitions before they're customer-facing.
## Our Strategy --- 📊 **A quick look at our Open Weights business** --- BFL's [open weights models](https://bfl.ai/licensing) are distributed for free, but they generate direct commercial value by funneling developers into commercial licenses. Today, BFL offers two commercial licenses: 1) The **Enterprise Commercial License **(via contacting our sales team);** **which brings in \$20M in annual revenue (not including Meta). This allows customers to host and fine-tune our models, and includes some ENT terms (e.g., indemnification). ENT customers are highly concentrated (80% of minimum commit comes from top 10 customers). ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/508dd818-505e-40b4-b2ef-1e6b7e2a27be/0c9e13b1-8f2d-40c4-b4e5-37fb77a2e3bc.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466UUAYNJDR%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095750Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIB%2FUDGJ7VSVMU1UbRztCeA6BK%2BUuS%2BS1uOLMQUsAGQl4AiACqa0enH%2BjyAF4MXg2vn7fiQ4Hg5Who%2BN5qV2fzff84Cr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMqCsotjCmK4cOlTv2KtwDyKLSR41Df%2F%2BieVXRduVBQcukRFP2HCyTr2EcvocUd7wuyX87OaDUsR%2BBK9K58xFsdBT7s3FSfpU%2FUPjblwu9jXp1lwafgz2eUTnZ0zGgmIgGAdrM5d5gQz3CxbkvHBniTfijfUPT%2Bx2NjIKkOuWCdYC9qROO5fawFuPg1BFQD%2BKaNN7SHCyDYvKXQ1GJ%2F2dIcGlvziZEwcIfX2%2F7PmLaZ9Q%2BVKTKr7RoA%2B8l%2FaEtwAniwR69Ps5vRNErNPZxIKWwDpVafvNQpmhSPD6EWMWnDRnQckewK%2FipN6ognUKYD5zj6C1UO%2BiSX1FV68kBt2uva64cH0v8iqTNbLxZsOWbM6IzFjB1YBodnp%2FtIDAOAnj1rdCdh5%2BDxZLYFfxmCQbcbF%2BV%2BBw9ug7Nal0CuGY4hUKnbJOtW9UA5L2H%2FbP3mvBzhhGOxygZdBo8FLhlzSNta%2BxhpyyI8Ko7LtAtYfmGchKS6kOsjqjubVZw663nsheQ7nA%2Fn4yNANC6B7Mg%2F%2FJad8wjjhTUtd2WY7BrpUkLpwiBJaoyI%2Bk0k5Kt1%2BjXifT0ho%2BTaKN1jyF85Ja9sCmZvzr6I5hYBVFNfetA5MfS%2BNNqJUsOHqtUlj80mt0cOOLU6%2Bh%2BlOqgz3Y6zcIwuq%2BSzwY6pgGA6%2F9EZz%2BiyDqFKHcg1DioWIIE%2BJsaiuiVnfB%2Bl%2FzEQ356T203nnMeKMpAnrTUbSlpVzA7vPfszk78d%2F0TPRLpOc0OpMi00VfQ0lCpRxh3hBeYogkPcvM3I83txojXP80yC33VTePmrSQ1mElLqnB7uKEvMRAkqDlauxFqb9s9yyRkvTV4%2BP9nE2rFBKwn5QXW07UY9fb61wI71zlTiLn6SUOYS1wG&X-Amz-Signature=d5ccc7f18acb2a538a730701ccdb5fee472c09b4d739d37b8701d02ea3d4db3d&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) 2) The **Self-serve Commercial License **(via our click through terms and subscribing on our website); which brings in** **roughly** **\~\$700K in annual revenue. Self-Serve customers range from hobbyists, startups, and there are some ENT customers as well. ✨** We need to position open weights as a Strategic Enterprise Offering** --- BFL has a structural advantage the market is demonstrably willing to pay for. The ability to self-host and customize a frontier-quality image model is genuinely differentiated: Google and OpenAI are strongly incentivized against releasing frontier open weights, as doing so would cannibalize their API businesses; open-source community models offer weights but not commercial clarity, consistent quality leadership, or enterprise support. Simultaneously, the rise of inference-providers like FAL and the preference from ENT customers for vendor flexibility is impacting margins across the API tier and making pure API positioning increasingly difficult to defend. Our opportunity lies in meeting the ENT customer intent directly: infrastructure ownership, deployment flexibility, customization control, and commercial/IP clarity that no competing closed source provider or API reseller can match.
**💡 The industry trends and internal signals that support this** - **We need to calibrate pricing to the market.** Enterprises already run a median of 14 models per production deployment, and they're allocating meaningful budget across a multi-model stack. 58% cite cost optimization as their primary infrastructure criterion, meaning they think precisely about value-per-output. Based on the avg. We could unlock \~\$5M open weights ARR if the long tail of ENT weights customers** **increased their ARR to the current average of \$3000/month based on higher monthly licensing fees, which would also help us reduce concentration. - **BFL may be the only credible Western open-weights frontier model, and that window is time-limited.** Chinese open-source labs are making substantial quality gains, but for enterprises with compliance requirements, data sovereignty concerns, or geopolitical exposure, those models aren't viable regardless of quality. BFL has a structural tailwind in regulated industries that most AI products don't, but it only holds while the capability lead does. - **The ownership value prop has never been more relevant.** "When you need brand consistency or product fidelity across millions of assets, fine-tuning on your own data isn't optional, it's the whole game ([A16Z report](https://a16z.com/the-state-of-generative-media-2026/)). Closed APIs generally don't allow that." That's possible through our weights product. With an FDE team now in place, we can finally put the narrative in front of the right buyers. - **The pipeline is there, but the process isn't.** The three verticals flagged as moving the fastest (gaming, advertising, & e-commerce) map to our self-serve and inbound: Nero, Ubisoft, Hyundai, Tommy Hilfiger, Duolingo, Zillow. Now that we have sunset our self-serve offering, and we’re actively getting more information from leads there are easy steps we can take to qualify these deals and route them to sales faster.
🔧** Fixing this requires us to do three things at once:** --- 1. **Value Positioning**: Rather than presenting a menu of model weights, we should organize our offering around the outcomes or workflows customers are trying to achieve within key verticals where we already have strong model-market fit (e.g., e-commerce, advertising, and design), with a focus on the three things they care most about: **flexibility**, **optimization**, and **customization**. 2. **Tiered Pricing**: Standardized tiers that match customer segments, create clear upgrade triggers, and capture the right willingness to pay (without self-serve anchors that undervalue customization and infrastructure control). We need to ensure pricing also aligns with commercial terms, indemnification and support offerings. 3. **Clear Prioritization**: Build the operational infrastructure to convert ENT and Agency inbound quickly. Qualification at the top of funnel, a defined response SLA, and an automation path that handles the long tail without consuming sales resources. ## Value Positioning --- ⚖️** The true value of open weights:** ---
**Against closed APIs (including our own public APIs)** The economic case should be that a self-hosted FLUX deployment runs materially cheaper than per-image API pricing. Closed models also offer zero customization: no fine-tuning, no data sovereignty, and perpetual exposure to unilateral price changes. For regulated verticals (government/defence, finance, healthcare), closed cloud APIs are frequently not viable at all.
**Against open-source alternatives** Against open-source alternatives, the question is not “can I get weights for free?” but “what is the total cost of running an unlicensed model?” The answer includes IP exposure, no quality improvement path, no support, and no commercial indemnification. Every enterprise team that self-hosts a community model is carrying silent risk. BFL’s licensed weights give customers the control of open source with the commercial standing of an enterprise product.
**BFL Open Weights** **Closed APIs
***Google, OpenAI, MSFT, Midjourney, Runway, ByteDance*		 **Open Source
***Stable Diffusion, Qwen, Wan*
Frontier image quality ✅ ✅ Varies
Fine-tune on proprietary data ✅ ❌ ✅
Infrastructure control ✅ ❌ ✅
Predictable unit economics at scale ✅ ❌ ✅
Commercial legal clarity ✅ ✅ ❌
IP indemnification ✅ ✅ ❌
Support + SLA ✅ ✅ ❌
**🔄 The framing shift we need** --- Instead of a la carte model weights access, we need to start selling “workflow outcomes.” Every major vertical has a specific workflow that FLUX can accelerate. Below is the packaging framework for each vertical, with recommended models and the commercial angle. A few high-level examples: - ***Retail / E-commerce***: when you need product shots, lifestyle imagery, and seasonal creative across thousands of SKUs, generative media turns what used to require a team of photographers, weeks of shoots, and long editing cycles into a few prompts and a library of production-ready assets. - ***Advertising***: campaigns that once took weeks of production now spin up hundreds of personalized variations in hours. It’s changing the economics of creative testing and spawning entirely new startup categories. - ***Gaming***: studios are using generative models to prototype concept art, populate environments, and produce in-game assets at a pace traditional pipelines can’t touch.
✨** How we tell a story about “Flux, purpose built for your workflow”**
Vertical Workflow Flux Value Recommended Models Volume Key Accounts/Inbound

## Tiered Pricing --- ⚙️ **Our weights offering needs to serve a variety of end users** ---
⚠️ **Previous weights pricing** → Self-serve allowed companies to “subscribe” to any model a la carte, with prices ranging from \$199/month for a starter klein license - \$1999/month for a \[dev\] license. Companies had full commercial rights, but no indemnification. → ENT pricing was completely custom, with no framework around minimum commitments, support costs, etc.
Rather than selling model access à la carte, we've proposed tiers around the workflows and scale of each customer segment, with a clear path from first license to enterprise commit as usage grows. Each tier is grounded in the specific group or “bundle” of models we believe will fit the average use case, and has a volume cap to ensure there are upgrade paths as companies grow their usage. **The new framework is designed around two variables: ** 1. *What you're building* (which determines the right model bundle) 2. *How much you're generating* (which determines the right tier and whether add-ons apply)
**Upgrade triggers: **Customers move up tiers when they hit volume ceilings, need models not in their current bundle, or require more substantial commercial terms, like multi-domain rights for agencies, or indemnification, that are only available at higher tiers.
📈** Scenarios that trigger a plan upgrade** - **Volume:** Builder caps at 10K images/month; Platform and Professional cap at 100K. Once a customer is consistently hitting their ceiling, the economics of staying on overage pricing should tip in favor of upgrading. - **Model access:** Builder only includes klein models. Customers who need \[dev\]-quality have to move to Platform or above. - **Client work:** Serving more than one domain (i.e., building for multiple clients or deploying across multiple products) requires either the multi-domain add-on or an upgrade to Professional, which includes 3 domains by default. - **Commercial terms:** Certain indemnification and resell rights aren't available at the Builder level. As customers move toward production and legal review, the commercial terms they need can also lead to the need for a higher tier. - **Scale:** Customers projecting sustained volume above 100K/month, or needing API + weights in a single agreement, move to Enterprise, where pricing is structured as a minimum commit rather than a usage meter.
**Add-ons: **exist for needs that **don't warrant a full tier upgrade**; an additional model, an extra client domain, or priority support can be layered onto an existing plan rather than forcing a premature step up. Enterprise replaces the per-image model entirely with a minimum commit, unlimited weights access, and bespoke volume bands negotiated at signing. **Open Weights Option Summary:** --- - **B****uilder (\$500/month)** FLUX.2 \[klein\] 9B + FLUX.2 \[klein\] 4B, 10K images/month. Sized for startups and hobbyists who are evaluating or building lightweight integrations. The klein models are the right cost-quality tradeoff at low volume; the 10K cap creates a natural upgrade trigger once they move toward production. Onboarding is self-serve via dev portal. - **Platform (or TBD Name)**** (\$3,000/month)** FLUX.2 \[klein\] 9B + FLUX.2 \[dev\] + FLUX.1 Kontext \[dev\], 100K images/month. Designed for growth-stage companies embedding FLUX into a product at scale. This bundle covers both high-volume generation \[klein\] and the editing/identity-preservation workflows that make FLUX sticky once it's inside a product. - **Professional (\$8,000/month)** FLUX.2 \[dev\] as the hero model, 100K images/month, up to 3 domains. Built for PSPs, agencies, and studios who are producing on behalf of clients. The 3-domain allowance is the defining commercial feature here, and everything else is either included or available as an add-on, and while the upgrade trigger is volume or additional client domains, the ENT plan will likely make the most sense if multiple subsidiaries have distinct licenses and they’re looking to consolidate to optimize for cost. - **Enterprise (\$10K+ minimum commit)** All 7 models including new releases, bespoke volume bands. The minimum commit replaces the per-image overage model entirely; ENT customers get unlimited weights access and negotiate volume based on projected generation.

## Clear Prioritization --- The pipeline is there, but the process isn't. Of the 147 inbound requests we received in the six weeks, especially after replacing self-serve with a contact sales button, only 17% represented real commercial pipeline (17 ENT and 8 Agency leads). The remainder were a mix of startups worth nurturing (42), hobbyists to route to a dev portal (64), and outright spam (16). All of them landed in the same queue, which means the highest-value leads are competing for attention with billing questions and affiliate spam.
**Fixing this requires two structural changes:** --- 1. **Qualify at the top of the funnel:** 1. **Additional questions in contact form: **Before any submission reaches the team, we need an additional two or three routing questions: company size, projected monthly generation volume, and whether the use case is commercial or internal. Surfacing this upfront gives us better context to filter for ENT and Agency requests before they get buried. 2. **Appending 3rd party data based on domain or email: ** 1. We should consider email domain enrichment via **Clearbit, Apollo, or ZoomInfo**. When someone submits a request using their work email, we’d get company size, industry vertical, funding stage, annual revenue estimate, and location. 2. Adding UTM source to further qualify interest (e.g., LinkedIn or direct = more commercial; Reddit or HuggingFace = hobbyist/developer) 3. Gated repos or resources on HuggingFace / Github to match emails: If we can match the email in the form to a registration for resources via a HF account, we can see if they're building something real with FLUX or just exploring. 2. **Automate the bottom of the funnel:** 1. **Dev Portal for both API + Weights Registration/Access: **Hobbyists and smaller startups should be handled via the dev portal with click-through commercial terms (that are much more restricted than our current terms today), hard generation caps, and predetermined upgrade triggers. This would not be a public self-serve offering, it's a contained, automated path that keeps the long tail out of the manual queue. ***The goal is to make the upgrade to a prope r license seamless when they hit the cap, not to create a new free tier.*** The opportunity is also bigger than just ENT and Agency: Five high-signal startups from our inbound (e.g., Gendo, Customix, Structure Studios, Snuggle Lens, and UPF) came with concrete volume data when we followed up over email. Gendo alone is projecting 1M images/month. A structured startup path with a low entry price and a volume ratchet would convert a meaningful portion of this segment without taking up too much of our time. *In the meantime, will be responsible for qualifying inbound weights requests via the *[*contact form*](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1yHSTXvQ619vlC4pc-Mnt98aalBxgHTDqsRPVXZlio4Q/edit?gid=0#gid=0)*, and will be responsible for qualifying API requests. The goal is to make the upgrade path to a proper license frictionless when they hit the cap, not to create a new free tier. **C. Guiding Principles (Informed by Industry Trends)** --- 1. **The unit of work isn’t one model, it’s a workflow**: The tier strategy should be anchored in 1) audience and 2) workflow instead of based on which models. 2. **We want our messaging to be grounded in customiZation**, and we want to optimize for flexibility or a la carte bundles based on objective. *Informed by: C*ustomers need to orchestrate multi-step pipelines with low cumulative latency, manage dependencies between steps, and make it easy to swap in new models as the frontier moves. 3. **We want open weights licensing to be complimentary to API usage** to ensure there’s a unified experience or interface across workflows and customer needs. *Informed by: *The orchestration layer matters as much as the models themselves, and it’s a big part of why infrastructure like Fal’s is so critical to take models from prototyping to production. 4. **We need model pricing positioning based on what you’re generating *and* at what scale.** *Informed by: *If you’re producing huge volumes of small, utilitarian images (e.g. product thumbnails or feed assets) you bias toward models that are fast and cheap, because the marginal value of perfection is low and the marginal cost compounds fast. 5. **Provide the best support and guidance for cost optimization on model infra for our models.** *Informed by: *58% of organizations identified cost optimization as their ***primary*** criterion when selecting model infrastructure, ahead of factors like model availability and generation speed. Competition is happening at two layers simultaneously: between infra providers racing to offer the most cost-effective run of a given model, and between models along the cost-quality frontier where the right choice depends on traffic scale and tolerance for imperfection. 6. Ensure the pricing works for 1) ENT (incuding key verticals like studios, gaming, advertising, and e-commerce), 2) hobbyists/small business, and 3) service scalers (Agencies). In advertising, the shift is dramatic – campaigns that once took weeks of production now spin up hundreds of personalized variations in hours. It’s changing the economics of creative testing and spawning entirely new startup categories. And in e-commerce, the case almost makes itself: when you need product shots, lifestyle imagery, and seasonal creative across thousands of SKUs, generative media turns what used to require a team of photographers, weeks of shoots, and long editing cycles into a few prompts and a library of production-ready assets. ### Additional Resources Open Weights Inbound Recap ---

It represents the primary frontier image model enterprises can ***own***, ***customize***, and ***self-host*** without security, IP, jurisdiction, or supply chain risk. Our previous self-serve price anchors did not fully reflect the strategic upside of ownership and infrastructure control, and we can articulate more clearly why that control carries a premium. The opportunity lies in 1) clarifying the enterprise value narrative, 2) aligning pricing with demonstrated willingness to pay, and 3) building tighter processes to convert high intent enterprise inbound, and 4) automating the long tail of startups and hobbyists so the team stays focused on high impact deals and strategic partnerships.

Proposal: any company with projected open weights ARR above \$200K/year qualifies for ENT level support and engagement. Anything below goes through the Platform or Professional path. **💬 Input needed from the FDE team on Support tiers.** Before the add-on menu is final, we need the FDE team's input on what's actually deliverable at each support level, and whether there are any hard limits (e.g., number of supported tickets/month, response window by issue type) we should bake into the tier definitions before they're customer-facing.

Self-Serve customers range from hobbyists, startups, and there are some ENT customers as well. ✨** We need to position open weights as a Strategic Enterprise Offering** --- BFL has a structural advantage the market is demonstrably willing to pay for. The ability to self-host and customize a frontier-quality image model is genuinely differentiated: Google and OpenAI are strongly incentivized against releasing frontier open weights, as doing so would cannibalize their API businesses; open-source community models offer weights but not commercial clarity, consistent quality leadership, or enterprise support. Simultaneously, the rise of inference-providers like FAL and the preference from ENT customers for vendor flexibility is impacting margins across the API tier and making pure API positioning increasingly difficult to defend. Our opportunity lies in meeting the ENT customer intent directly: infrastructure ownership, deployment flexibility, customization control, and commercial/IP clarity that no competing closed source provider or API reseller can match.
**💡 The industry trends and internal signals that support this** - **We need to calibrate pricing to the market.** Enterprises already run a median of 14 models per production deployment, and they're allocating meaningful budget across a multi-model stack. 58% cite cost optimization as their primary infrastructure criterion, meaning they think precisely about value-per-output. Based on the avg. We could unlock \~\$5M open weights ARR if the long tail of ENT weights customers** **increased their ARR to the current average of \$3000/month based on higher monthly licensing fees, which would also help us reduce concentration. - **BFL may be the only credible Western open-weights frontier model, and that window is time-limited.** Chinese open-source labs are making substantial quality gains, but for enterprises with compliance requirements, data sovereignty concerns, or geopolitical exposure, those models aren't viable regardless of quality. BFL has a structural tailwind in regulated industries that most AI products don't, but it only holds while the capability lead does. - **The ownership value prop has never been more relevant.** "When you need brand consistency or product fidelity across millions of assets, fine-tuning on your own data isn't optional, it's the whole game ([A16Z report](https://a16z.com/the-state-of-generative-media-2026/)). Closed APIs generally don't allow that." That's possible through our weights product. With an FDE team now in place, we can finally put the narrative in front of the right buyers. - **The pipeline is there, but the process isn't.** The three verticals flagged as moving the fastest (gaming, advertising, & e-commerce) map to our self-serve and inbound: Nero, Ubisoft, Hyundai, Tommy Hilfiger, Duolingo, Zillow. Now that we have sunset our self-serve offering, and we’re actively getting more information from leads there are easy steps we can take to qualify these deals and route them to sales faster.
🔧** Fixing this requires us to do three things at once:** --- 1. **Value Positioning**: Rather than presenting a menu of model weights, we should organize our offering around the outcomes or workflows customers are trying to achieve within key verticals where we already have strong model-market fit (e.g., e-commerce, advertising, and design), with a focus on the three things they care most about: **flexibility**, **optimization**, and **customization**. 2. **Tiered Pricing**: Standardized tiers that match customer segments, create clear upgrade triggers, and capture the right willingness to pay (without self-serve anchors that undervalue customization and infrastructure control). We need to ensure pricing also aligns with commercial terms, indemnification and support offerings. 3. **Clear Prioritization**: Build the operational infrastructure to convert ENT and Agency inbound quickly. Qualification at the top of funnel, a defined response SLA, and an automation path that handles the long tail without consuming sales resources. ## Value Positioning --- ⚖️** The true value of open weights:** ---
**Against closed APIs (including our own public APIs)** The economic case should be that a self-hosted FLUX deployment runs materially cheaper than per-image API pricing. Closed models also offer zero customization: no fine-tuning, no data sovereignty, and perpetual exposure to unilateral price changes. For regulated verticals (government/defence, finance, healthcare), closed cloud APIs are frequently not viable at all.
**Against open-source alternatives** Against open-source alternatives, the question is not “can I get weights for free?” but “what is the total cost of running an unlicensed model?” The answer includes IP exposure, no quality improvement path, no support, and no commercial indemnification. Every enterprise team that self-hosts a community model is carrying silent risk. BFL’s licensed weights give customers the control of open source with the commercial standing of an enterprise product.

Adding UTM source to further qualify interest (e.g., LinkedIn or direct = more commercial; Reddit or HuggingFace = hobbyist/developer) 3. Gated repos or resources on HuggingFace / Github to match emails: If we can match the email in the form to a registration for resources via a HF account, we can see if they're building something real with FLUX or just exploring. 2. **Automate the bottom of the funnel:** 1. **Dev Portal for both API + Weights Registration/Access: **Hobbyists and smaller startups should be handled via the dev portal with click-through commercial terms (that are much more restricted than our current terms today), hard generation caps, and predetermined upgrade triggers. A structured startup path with a low entry price and a volume ratchet would convert a meaningful portion of this segment without taking up too much of our time. *In the meantime, will be responsible for qualifying inbound weights requests via the *[*contact form*](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1yHSTXvQ619vlC4pc-Mnt98aalBxgHTDqsRPVXZlio4Q/edit?gid=0#gid=0)*, and will be responsible for qualifying API requests. **B. Inbound Requests for Weights** --- We replaced our “subscribe” with a contact sales button and analyzed entries from the last 6 weeks. 147 entries came in over the last six weeks. Only 17% represented real commercial pipeline (17 ENT and 8 Agencies) and have been prioritized. The ENT list includes Zillow, Duolingo, Hyundai, Tommy Hilfiger/PVH, and Shinhan Bank. The remaining entries are a mix of startups worth nurturing (42), hobbyists to route to self-serve (64), and outright spam (16). [Analysis here](/312c370222d5809798a5fda5196a7023?pvs=25) - The current form is functioning as a catch-all: billing issues, support tickets, affiliate spam, and genuine enterprise inquiries all land in the same queue. This creates two problems: 1) It obscures high-value leads, and 2) It requires manual triage on a volume that will only grow. - **The opportunity is bigger than ENT/Agency alone.** When we followed up over email, we found five high-signal startups (Gendo, Customix, Structure Studios, Snuggle Lens, UPF) with concrete volume data. Gendo alone is projecting 1M images/month. These companies are building FLUX into customer-facing products, not testing it. A structured startup path with a low entry price with a volume ratchet would convert a meaningful portion of the 42-company startup segment without requiring manual sales attention. - **Two actions needed: 1) Qualify at the top of the funnel.** Add two or three questions upfront re. company size, projected monthly generation volume, and whether the use case is commercial or internal before the submission is routed to anyone. This alone would surface ENT and Agency requests before they get buried, and would give the sales team the context they need for first calls (volume in particular is almost entirely absent from ENT submissions today, which makes deal sizing impossible); and 2) **Automate the bottom of the funnel.** Hobbyists and smaller startups should be handled via the dev portal with click-through commercial terms, hard generation caps, and predetermined upgrade triggers (***not a public self-serve offering***, but a contained, automated path that keeps these users out of the manual queue entirely). The goal is to make the upgrade path to a proper license frictionless when they hit the cap, not to create a new free tier. **C. Guiding Principles (Informed by Industry Trends)** --- 1. **The unit of work isn’t one model, it’s a workflow**: The tier strategy should be anchored in 1) audience and 2) workflow instead of based on which models. 2. **We want our messaging to be grounded in customiZation**, and we want to optimize for flexibility or a la carte bundles based on objective. *Informed by: C*ustomers need to orchestrate multi-step pipelines with low cumulative latency, manage dependencies between steps, and make it easy to swap in new models as the frontier moves. 3. **We want open weights licensing to be complimentary to API usage** to ensure there’s a unified experience or interface across workflows and customer needs. *Informed by: *The orchestration layer matters as much as the models themselves, and it’s a big part of why infrastructure like Fal’s is so critical to take models from prototyping to production. 4. **We need model pricing positioning based on what you’re generating *and* at what scale.** *Informed by: *If you’re producing huge volumes of small, utilitarian images (e.g. product thumbnails or feed assets) you bias toward models that are fast and cheap, because the marginal value of perfection is low and the marginal cost compounds fast. 5. **Provide the best support and guidance for cost optimization on model infra for our models.** *Informed by: *58% of organizations identified cost optimization as their ***primary*** criterion when selecting model infrastructure, ahead of factors like model availability and generation speed. Competition is happening at two layers simultaneously: between infra providers racing to offer the most cost-effective run of a given model, and between models along the cost-quality frontier where the right choice depends on traffic scale and tolerance for imperfection. 6. Ensure the pricing works for 1) ENT (incuding key verticals like studios, gaming, advertising, and e-commerce), 2) hobbyists/small business, and 3) service scalers (Agencies). In advertising, the shift is dramatic – campaigns that once took weeks of production now spin up hundreds of personalized variations in hours. It’s changing the economics of creative testing and spawning entirely new startup categories. And in e-commerce, the case almost makes itself: when you need product shots, lifestyle imagery, and seasonal creative across thousands of SKUs, generative media turns what used to require a team of photographers, weeks of shoots, and long editing cycles into a few prompts and a library of production-ready assets. ### Additional Resources Open Weights Inbound Recap ---

# Time off Philosophy
Our time off policy is flexible time off, in the sense that you can take what you need. Like work, we approach our time off with high ownership, and want to acknowledge that everyone is working hard to make BFL successful. 
We offer flexible paid time off, with the expectation that everyone takes **at least **the statutory allowance shown in your Rippling profile. 
<empty-block/>
**Note **
- This policy applies globally. 
- In Rippling, under **My Time**, you see your total holiday balance, which aligns with local statutory requirements. Make sure to use it all and have your balance at **0 or negative by the end of the year. **You can go into negative balance without any impact, all submitted time off days are paid. 
- All balances reset at the start of the year, no days accrue. 
- All leave is tracked through Rippling. Submit all your leave days include PTO, Sick Day, Child Sick day, Special leave, etc. through Rippling. 
- Please also log any public holidays you take in Rippling, so our teams across different countries stay aligned. These will **not **be deducted from your total holiday balance.
<callout icon="☝" color="gray_bg">
	For people hired through [Remote.com](http://Remote.com) - Please log in all your leave days on the Remote portal. 
</callout>
# **Standard Operating Procedure **
When you take time off, do the following: 
**Plan**
- Notify your team at minimum 2x the length of planned leave in advance
- For 2+consecutive weeks outside of the Christmas period, please ask your team lead 
- Submit requests through Rippling, once you have used your statutory days, your balance will go into negative 
- Ensure no conflicts with team deliverables like new releases or key meetings like offsites 
**Prepare**
- **Block your calendar using "Out of Office" instead of Event in your calendar. This automatically updates Slack so people are aware you’re away.**
- Ensure nothing will be blocked on you during this time. Either close out or delegate ongoing items and ensure there is an escalation path. Create a handover document for any ongoing projects if needed. 
- Enable email auto-response if you won’t check your email 
# Global vacation, public holiday & birthday calendar 
Get visibility into when someone might be off. 
Click on "+" next to "other calendars" and add URL.

190c3702-22d5-80fc-9f41-fffb4fa2a0e7.title: Technical Questions
190c3702-22d5-80fc-9f41-fffb4fa2a0e7.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/190c370222d580fc9f41fffb4fa2a0e7 as of 2026-04-13T08:20:40.849Z: {"title":"Technical Questions"} **New questions: ** - Are we planning to include additional natural representations in our pre-training (in particular those representations that are already used in robotics, e.g. LiDAR, echolocation, sonar or those on invisible spectrum of light)? For anything that can be measured with sensors, there are probably datasets that we could acquire and then train on, right? While this might not have any immediate effect on visual outputs, it could expand “visual” intelligence to “physical” intelligence and expand robotics use cases? (Seb) - How can we compete with OS models - apart from quality, more on an architecture level? What can we offer that others don’t have? - How are we prioritizing on the F3 development when it comes to “features” like resolution, aspect ratio, etc.? - Did Flux.1 Fill actually inpaint without changing things outside of the mask? - How is Video to Video coming along? Realistic for F.3? - Could tensor RT help with speed but also releasing pressure on the shortage of GPUs for inference? --- --- How are we doing with FLUX.3???? #### **How are we prioritizing on the F3 development when it comes to “features” like resolution, aspect ratio, etc.?** {toggle="true"} - some features like different aspect ratios are quite easy to get into the model with e.g packing or bucketing. So low hanging fruits should absolutely be collected. - longer durations than 5s are important so we will want to support these with rolling out generations. - Very high res is kind of painful to train on and thus we have not really prioritized it, due to lack of signal that this would induce a lot of demand. But maybe we need to rethink this one at some point when it becomes the industry standard. ### For video models, seems understanding movement is a problem as labeling data is an issue. Why can’t we use videogame engines as a fix? Some engine have super precise animations and physics, and can output labeling data to train the VLM to follow up what’s up on screen. Seems a bit farfetch, but for robots we used a lot simulations to train recognition, so I was wondering if we could do the same for video models. :D {toggle="true"} Yes! Very much! {toggle="true"} **Max (Flux2 Pro Max workflow)** - Goal: “Highest possible quality & robustness” on top of Flux2 Pro. - Intended for: - Users who care more about reliability/leaderboard quality than cost. - Avoiding catastrophic failures (missing objects, broken text, etc.) by generating multiple candidates and picking the best. - Customers who want the “top” model on public leaderboards and don’t mind higher price/latency. **Klein** - Goal: “Efficient, open-source, photoreal workhorse.” - Intended for: - People who want an Apache-licensed, relatively small model they can self-host. - Use cases that skew heavily to photorealism (what most people actually prompt). - Directly competing in the ZImage / “small-but-good” open-source segment. **Schnell** - Goal: “Real-time editing experience.” - Intended for: - Extremely fast image edits (latency-first, ‘fun’ UX, slider/brush style workflows). - Interactive tools where users want to see changes live as they move controls. - Difference vs Klein: - Klein: general text-to-image + edit, optimized for quality/photoreal and efficient serving. - Schnell: aggressively distilled for *speed*, focused on edit latency rather than absolute quality; more experimental/novel (no real competitor today doing proper real-time editing). **Flux 2.5** - Goal: “Solid, iterative upgrade of Flux 2 while big research runs on 3.x / multimodal.” - Intended for: - General improvement over Flex/Pro in: robustness, text, editing, and overall quality. - Keeping us competitive while multi‑modal/video/audio research cooks. - Likely also setting up a better teacher for future distillations (Klein/Schnell-type models). ### How should they compare to each other and the competition? {toggle="true"} - **Max** - Internal stack: “best quality” offering on top of Pro, for customers who want maximum consistency and can pay more. - External: designed to rank clearly above “vanilla” Pro/Flex and close the gap vs top-tier models on T2I Arena (e.g. Gemini, Hunyuan) by +15–20 Elo. - Positioning: more expensive than Pro, but still cheaper/faster than some competitor “ultra” workflows (e.g. multi-pass banana/nano-banana equivalents). - **Klein** - Internal: small Apache model that’s good enough for many production workloads, especially photoreal. - External: direct answer to ZImage (6B) and similar open models; slightly larger (\~9B) but still “normal hardware friendly.” - Positioning: more general than ZImage (which is very photoreal-focused), but still tuned so photoreal use cases feel great. - **Schnell** - Internal: “new category” – real-time editing, not just faster T2I. - External: almost no serious real-time editing competitor; this can differentiate UX (live sliders/brushes) more than raw leaderboard Elo. - Positioning: not necessarily leaderboard king on static T2I benchmarks, but unique product story: *“you move a slider and the image changes instantly.”* - **Flux 2.5** - Internal: upgraded Flex 2 pipeline; better data, better training, larger model. - External: general Elo bump vs current Flex/Pro, narrowing gaps vs top proprietary models. - Positioning: “default recommendation” for quality vs cost; 2.x “LTS line” while 3.x research explores multimodal, video, etc. ### What technical steps are taken in the background to build them? {toggle="true"} **Max** - Built as a *workflow* on top of Flux2 Pro (2.4.2): 1. Generate multiple candidates (e.g. 4 images) for a given prompt (and possibly mix Flex/Pro generations depending on final workflow). 2. Score/rank the candidates with internal metrics/judgers (text alignment, visual quality, text legibility, etc.). 3. Return the best-ranked image. - Effect: same base model, but much lower probability of catastrophic failures; improves leaderboard Elo with no change to the underlying Pro weights. **Klein** - Technical recipe: classic teacher–student distillation. 1. Start from the large 32B “dev”/teacher model. 2. Train a smaller \~9B student model to mimic the teacher (distillation). 3. Replace the big \~24B text encoder with a much smaller text encoder. 4. (Likely) release *undistilled by guidance* first (no guidance distillation yet). - Result: a much smaller Apache-licensed model that retains most of the teacher’s capabilities, especially in photoreal generation, at far lower serving cost. **Schnell** - Technical recipe: “aggressive distillation + editing.” 1. Take Klein / 4B / 9B family as starting points. 2. Distill them very aggressively for speed (few steps, highly optimized sampling). 3. Train with strong *image editing* supervision so the model can apply targeted edits extremely fast. - Result: a tiny, highly distilled model specialized for real-time editing (plus T2I), trading a bit of absolute quality for latency. **Flux 2.5** - Technical recipe: “run the proved Flex2 pipeline again, but better.” - **Mid-training**: - Add more/image-editing-style data *earlier* in training rather than just at the very end. - Use larger, scaled-up datasets that took time to build (especially for editing). - **Post-training**: - With more stable compute (no constant job crashes), run more/bigger post-training ablations. - What previously took \~2 weeks due to instability can now be done in \~1 day. - **Model size**: - Likely bigger base model (e.g. 72B teacher for 2.5) to maximize what can later be distilled down. - Plus: improvements on serving/edit cost (e.g. ideas to make editing cost \~equal to T2I). ### Why should a customer use Pro vs Flex? {toggle="true"} **Flex** - \~50 denoising steps (longer sampler). - More “knobs” (e.g. guidance scale) → more controllable for power users. - Tends to be better for **text**: - Long/complex text benefits from more iterative refinement. - If text is important and customers are willing to tweak params, Flex is usually best. **Pro** - \~16 steps (shorter sampler; not visible to users, but impacts speed/cost). - Trained with an **adversarial discriminator** (“is this AI or real?”) → better “natural blending.” - Often more harmonized images. - Humans can look more realistic / slightly “sweaty” – some people love that photoreal punch. - Typically better when: - You want a strong, realistic look with less parameter fiddling. - You care about natural blending/compositing more than perfect long-text rendering. **Rule of thumb:** - Text-heavy / fine control / power-user knobs → **Flex**. - Photoreal, natural blending, “click and get something that pops” → **Pro**. - **Max** on top when customers want *even more* reliability and price is secondary. ### What is an autoencoder, why and where do we use it, and why/how is it good to sell? {toggle="true"} **What is an autoencoder?** - A neural network that: - **Encodes** an image from pixel space into a *lower-dimensional latent space* (compressed representation). - **Decodes** that latent back to pixels. - In Flux, this is mostly a convolutional network + a bit of attention, not a traditional JPEG/MPEG-style codec. **Why do we use it?** - Directly modeling pixels is too expensive. - Autoencoder lets us: - Work in a much lower-dimensional latent space (cheaper compute, faster training/serving). - Preserve spatial structure (top-left in pixels ≈ top-left in latents). - Maintain high reconstruction quality: decoding the latents gives you a sharp, faithful image. - There’s a big research focus on “learnability”: certain latent spaces make it *easier* for diffusion models to learn good generative behavior. Flux 2’s autoencoder is tuned to be on a good Pareto frontier between: - Reconstruction quality and - How easy it is to learn a generative model in that space. **Where do we use it?** - Every time we: - **Train** diffusion models (we train in latent space, not pixels). - **Generate**: - Sample latents with the diffusion model. - Decode them with the autoencoder into final images. - **Edit**: - Encode existing images to latents. - Edit in latent space. - Decode back. **Why/how is it good to sell?** - In principle: - A strong autoencoder gives other teams **better training efficiency** (cheaper training) and **better learnability** (higher quality for a given compute budget). - That’s real value to model builders. - In practice (current decision): - We previously released the autoencoder for free; selling it later can feel odd to customers. - It’s also hard to *visibly* demonstrate its value to non-research buyers (you see the benefit only when you train your own model). - So for now, we focus on selling the full image-generation stack rather than the AE as a standalone product, even though the AE is still absolutely central to why the pipeline works well. > **Claude said:** An **autoencoder** is a neural network architecture that learns to compress data into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and then reconstruct it back to the original form (decoding). It consists of: - **Encoder**: Compresses input into a compact latent representation - **Latent space**: The compressed representation (bottleneck) - **Decoder**: Reconstructs the original data from the latent representation ## Why You Need It in Diffusion Models Modern diffusion models like FLUX, Stable Diffusion, and DALL-E use **Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)** or similar architectures for a crucial reason: **computational efficiency**. **The problem**: Running diffusion directly in pixel space is prohibitively expensive. For a 1024×1024 RGB image, you're working with \~3 million dimensions. The denoising process requires many iterative steps, making this computationally intractable. **The solution**: Use a VAE to work in **latent space** instead: 1. The encoder compresses a 1024×1024×3 image down to something like 128×128×4 (a \~64x reduction in dimensions) 2. The diffusion process operates in this compressed latent space 3. The decoder upsamples the final latent back to full resolution This approach, called **Latent Diffusion Models (LDM)**, reduces compute requirements dramatically while maintaining perceptual quality because the VAE is trained to preserve perceptually important features. ## Where It's Used **Training**: - Images → VAE Encoder → Latents (training data for the diffusion model) - Noise is added to these latents during training **Inference**: - Start with random noise in latent space - Denoise iteratively using the diffusion model - VAE Decoder → Final image The VAE is typically **frozen** during diffusion model training - you train it separately first, then use it as a fixed component for encoding/decoding. **A complete, turnkey solution**: They can generate images immediately without needing to: - Source a compatible VAE separately - Train their own VAE (extremely expensive - requires massive datasets and compute) - Debug compatibility issues between different components - Worry about quality mismatches ## How They Did It Before With **Stable Diffusion**, customers typically: - Used the open-source VAE that came bundled with the model - Sometimes swapped in alternative VAEs (like the "MSE VAE" or "EMA VAE") to improve quality - Had to deal with version compatibility issues - Occasionally trained custom VAEs for specific use cases (rare, due to cost) ## The FLUX Advantage For **FLUX dev/pro customers**, bundling the autoencoder means: 1. **Optimized performance**: The VAE is specifically trained and tuned to work with FLUX's diffusion model architecture 2. **Consistent quality**: You've validated the end-to-end pipeline 3. **Reduced complexity**: One less component to manage or worry about 4. **Competitive moat**: Your VAE architecture and training approach are part of your IP 5. **Support simplification**: You only need to support one known-good configuration It's basically the difference between selling "assembly required" vs. "plug and play." Enterprise customers especially value this because it reduces their time-to-production and technical risk. They're paying for the integrated system, not just the diffusion weights. ### How can we use data from Inditex for virtual try-on? {toggle="true"} Data quality is key here, as in ideally we can build an amazing dataset by applying some logic to the metadata only, and can be sure that the same garnment/person is present and well visible for example. (Kontext Max) {toggle="true"} ITS stands for Inference Time scaling. The idea is that you want to have a mechanism during inference that allows you to get better result when putting more time/compute into the inference. This got popular in the LLM world with “thinking” modes, solving this very elegantly for LLMs and greatly improving the answers of LLMs especially on hard problems.
[https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)

Ideally we also have such a mechanism for image generation. One approach, based on the observation that some results in a batch of n images are better than others, is to generate multiple images and post hoc pick the best result. This is what we are currently doing with max. It has shown to help for text to image and image to image tasks, especially when evaluating prompt following. We pick the best sample with a lightweight model that associates a score with each image on how good it thinks the image is.
This approach is n times more expensive than generating only one image but can get peak performance, and such approaches will dominate the benchmark leaderboards in the end.

Side note. Image gpt is also doing a sort of Inference time scaling with their image generation pipeline, however it is very different. It seems that they are able to predict a different number of tokens to describe an image (they are generating autoregressively) in that way they can generate a different number tokens for the same area of image leading to more detailed images at the cost of more inference time compute. This ensures the model is not memorizing the training data.
For e.g classification tasks this is quite easy, we can just classify on the validation set and get our validation accuracy. Or we can calculate the loss (our training objective) on the validation set and see how that improves. With Diffusion/Flow models things are a bit trickier. The task of the model is to predict, given some noised image X, a text conditioning c and a timestep t signaling how much noise was added to the image, what the unnoised image/the path towards the unnoised image would look like. This task can be more or less difficult depending on how much noise we add to the image. (That is also why we spend a lot of the training compute on high noise, this is very crucial and a big research question on how to distribute the compute based on the timestep)
If we would simply calculate the average loss we do not really get an idea where/if the model is improving. For example that is why the loss looks like it is not improving if we just sample random timesteps: ## What are we doing in final training distribution ablations? {toggle="true"} In final training distribution ablations we are trying to determine the final “data mix”. Our training data for e.g. bagel consists of multiple datasets each covering certain tasks (e.g. one is for style one for inplace editing one for character reference etc). Before investing a lot into a large final run, we do a few smaller runs with less compute and different data mixed, to determine how much of to put into the final run. This is generally hard to determine perfectly and in the end these ablations mainly give us a better informed estimate of what to put in the final mix. ## Can you explain two stage training? {toggle="true"} two stage training means that we train a model not in one go on the same data with the same optimization objective but instead alter the optimization objective or data at some point.
A multi stage approach is typically being used in model development if we were to start from scratch. We typically have a pretraining phase that will take the longest/most compute/most data. Followed by this can be multiple further stages of finetuning the model on highly aesthetic / hand curated datasets and aligning the model with human preference e.g. via DPO. ## How do we do DPO? {toggle="true"} DPO and other Preference Optimization techniques leverage either paired signals (image a is better than b, both had the prompt “XXX”) (DPO falls into this category) or single signals (I like image a, and dislike image b, they are completely independent and have different prompts) This is typically the last stage of training where one want to align the model with user preference. This can also be used as a kind of do “this instead of this”.
We do not need as much data for this stage, the difficulty is getting good pairs that guide the model in the right direction/have clear differences between images. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/0735fe5c-62a3-45b3-abf8-2b4109906fa5/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466SP4WP6QV%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095752Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIFhxCz8i7lz4PRkyAkyy0%2Bk4yMR9Co6QUtaBzCbIE4V3AiAuB8Pni4oNYqvO389vmdX8L%2FK7YDfeqPYUxhI1U%2FS6LCr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMKRHHL8Zy%2FILI0nIYKtwDRogUM1YA%2BQ%2FsGMZiGaaGA9gV%2BSC85eOPrQ9M0Cxyd%2Bf%2FSTgDghOQLmtM9ZNOXbtvvmxBCWRyK3hw6CWmOyuJO8b5LXaWCgz9aU0jNQ1zLWc1LhWvioBJspn1XpwBgH96MMX4blKWXxa%2FrtFwHD7rzCHbc2XOg1IqZS8Klpyn3Qef4eaRWWNfSVMaC3KFAKFNzEOzr2J0g58nkHRINF11ZCgTkepREmr%2BrSlgWTIDzfUkME12elXtmZuSzZZCeu7lgHCbneq2PzOZns6DHeyoMEz6khXzyRp4ajjZTtgWj36UNHa89OLHuWZDvaR6ObzswLONblbw5qxguqKu%2FtP3xNVJiGEXVF9uykvFTH%2FA7Aj50aC8LhgQWzJl%2FnIaPUCsRohpkxVHoXOZNv9cwhbFArsasRxqa320yIfk8JmIA978%2B7rM7BGMqq1UKcZ0PJQTljHzxQdlpDAJWGzrwwueVddluQmGvWuO4reil%2FGYSuK5boGcA494vcGk6%2FunCttwxq0ALwzboIiY0M%2BUeslhCiyGHdPcMU8I9LIAZxxTpTZmvLVTvIDpaBLx3bqlE9DAsmD8xCPQLh0Z%2BO5IiVCxwg7vLiGs4EdVJmmw7c104uXHe0s3CbBItmnfIFIwh66SzwY6pgF9y1ltUCWsLue0CGwIrdENt3WqW%2FMp4sRbDCrOitiY%2BcuQKl13RUc%2B7I2iFFgLTMmk4a8NufKtTWFxYMZyXppm6jByOEsu%2FBEES60zrsvUWg%2FZebeO6BQS4pG45zIR%2FrF1ZPe5%2BEKhFLoB7XnJ3iLuvgsJLwvZmtVePQMQ%2BxTFbeKeJmrnpdAn7cBGmHDB3qsN94oiCV07osZckb1pQopD%2FTB1HLmI&X-Amz-Signature=aefb95995a9e38999a6d4eba32ca10661800a28d575d2813b2f1b3045a4e94f9&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) reference: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12908](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12908) ## long answer: we train a trigger word into the model by mentioning a relatively uncommon text sequence (such as “TOK” or “mycustom bike” etc.) which the model can associate with the images shown, without having too much “baked” in knowledge about what that text should look like. (in contrast to just using “dog” and hope the finetune learns to always generate my dog).
In theory we could add a token that the model has never seen before by introducing a new mapping e.g. x12876zyh → to a new embedding that the model has 100% never seen before (we can add this programmatically) This would then be a “true” trigger word. We do not do this, mainly for complexity vs benefits reasons. ## Can you explain prompt upsampling? {toggle="true"} We train our text to image model with captions from a vlm in different verbosities
i.e. a very detailed caption, a long one a short one a one word caption.
The model learns this distribution/mapping between these captions and images.
However people prompt in all kinds of ways that the model has never seen. (for example, “a woman that is not smiling”, “please make me an image of …”, “ein Hund”)

Prompt upsampling loops in a LLM to turn the freeform prompt into a prompt that is more aligned with our training prompts + more detailed which can help the model to generate more interesting images. e.g.:
Ein Hund → “This is a photograph of a dog walking towards the camera. His fur is black and he is wearing a blue dog collar”

A symptom of not running prompt upsampling per default is that FLUX score a lot worse on user prompts compared to english only prompts in the LM Arena (which has a significant amount of non-English prompts)

This is in the engineering backlog currently. ## What happens behind the scenes when doing finetunes via our API? What about LoRa? {toggle="true"} These are the steps happening in the background: 1. check that the data is clean (as in no attack), that there are images in the uploaded folder, potentially also text descriptions, not too many, not too large files etc. 2. Run moderation on all images. 3. Caption the images if captioning: true 4. encode the images and text to be ready for training 5. run the training loop, here either only the LoRa weights (see LoRa section below) will be trained or all weights 6. Save the LoRa weights or if all weights were trained, calculate the difference between the model now vs the original model and convert the difference into a LoRA 7. The weights are stored in the cluster and can now be referenced for inference ## What’s a VLM? {toggle="true"} VLM stands for Vision Language Model. It integrates both visual and textual understanding. It is designed to process and generate outputs based on both image and text inputs. They are typically very similar to LLMs (Large Language Models) but have a dedicated part that will extract high level features from images which are then fed into the model. ## Why no finetune for Pro 1.1? {toggle="true"} As mentioned in the distillation section, distilled models ## **What is this guidance thing? ** {toggle="true"} Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is a technique used in diffusion models to improve the quality of generated images. It works by balancing the trade-off between sample quality and diversity. Here's how it works: During the sampling process, CFG combines two predictions: 1. A conditional prediction (guided by the text prompt or other conditioning) 2. An unconditional prediction (with no guidance)
- Higher guidance values produce images that more closely follow the prompt but may be less diverse or creative. Too much guidance can lead to the “bakey”/artificial look that we want to avoid. - Lower guidance values produce more diverse and raw looking outputs but may follow the prompt less strictly. At very low guidance values, structures can fall apart.
CFG essentially amplifies the difference between conditional and unconditional models, strengthening the influence of the conditioning signal while maintaining the core image generation capabilities. These are combined using a guidance scale parameter Resources:
[https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598)
[https://theaisummer.com/classifier-free-guidance/](https://theaisummer.com/classifier-free-guidance/) ## What is a distilled model? {toggle="true"} A distilled diffusion model is a model that needs less forward passes to produce a sample, increasing efficiency at the cost of quality and flexibility. ### 1. **Speeding Up Inference** - Diffusion models require multiple forward passes to produce a sample:
our default for pro-1.0 is 50 steps with 2 forward passes per step due to guidance computation - Distillation techniques (e.g., **guidance distillation**, **direct step distillation**, or **teacher-student approaches**) help train a smaller, more efficient model that can generate high-quality samples in fewer steps. ### 2. **Reducing Computational Costs** - Running diffusion models at scale is expensive → by reducing the number of forward passes needed to generate a sample we drastically reduce the cost per generation. - Pro-1.1 for example only takes 6 steps instead 50 and is guidance distilled, meaning we only do one forward pass per step → 100 forward passes vs 6 forward passes at \$0.05 vs \$0.04 → drastic margin increase ### 3. Making the model less flexible - Distillation can also be used to “hide” certain aspects of the sampling processsuch as the concrete guidance method by distilling them into the model - With distillation we typically use some flexibility/capability when trying to finetune the model further. → Distilled models can be good candidates for open source models, as they offer less flexibility than the base model
**Resources:
**[https://sander.ai/2024/02/28/paradox.html](https://sander.ai/2024/02/28/paradox.html) [https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17042](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17042)
[https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12015](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12015) ## What’s the difference between Pro 1.1, dev and schnell? {toggle="true"} Overview of our distilled models: **FLUX.1 dev: ** - guidance distilled (the guidance value can still be controlled via a vector), needing only one forward pass per step instead of two, still needs the same amount of steps to produce good images. - small level of distillation, and still good to finetune - Non-commercial license **FLUX.1 schnell: ** - guidance distilled + step distilled to generate samples in 2-4 steps - Heavy distillation and extremely hard to finetune, also significant quality degradation vs pro - Apache 2.0 licensed **FLUX.1.1 pro:** - guidance distilled + step distilled to produce samples in 1-50 steps - The distillation method was improved between schnell and 1.1 and the number of steps we use for 1.1 is 6 which significantly improves over the limited 2-4 steps. - Heavy distillation makes it hard to finetune - Closed, as it outperforms pro-1.0 ## Why should you use Pro 1.1 and not schnell {toggle="true"} - Benchmarks 🙂 - It generally does better across the board, is a lot better in realism and spelling ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/e2dfee3a-4bb8-41d5-aa27-6e5699d3fb1e/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466SP4WP6QV%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095752Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIFhxCz8i7lz4PRkyAkyy0%2Bk4yMR9Co6QUtaBzCbIE4V3AiAuB8Pni4oNYqvO389vmdX8L%2FK7YDfeqPYUxhI1U%2FS6LCr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMKRHHL8Zy%2FILI0nIYKtwDRogUM1YA%2BQ%2FsGMZiGaaGA9gV%2BSC85eOPrQ9M0Cxyd%2Bf%2FSTgDghOQLmtM9ZNOXbtvvmxBCWRyK3hw6CWmOyuJO8b5LXaWCgz9aU0jNQ1zLWc1LhWvioBJspn1XpwBgH96MMX4blKWXxa%2FrtFwHD7rzCHbc2XOg1IqZS8Klpyn3Qef4eaRWWNfSVMaC3KFAKFNzEOzr2J0g58nkHRINF11ZCgTkepREmr%2BrSlgWTIDzfUkME12elXtmZuSzZZCeu7lgHCbneq2PzOZns6DHeyoMEz6khXzyRp4ajjZTtgWj36UNHa89OLHuWZDvaR6ObzswLONblbw5qxguqKu%2FtP3xNVJiGEXVF9uykvFTH%2FA7Aj50aC8LhgQWzJl%2FnIaPUCsRohpkxVHoXOZNv9cwhbFArsasRxqa320yIfk8JmIA978%2B7rM7BGMqq1UKcZ0PJQTljHzxQdlpDAJWGzrwwueVddluQmGvWuO4reil%2FGYSuK5boGcA494vcGk6%2FunCttwxq0ALwzboIiY0M%2BUeslhCiyGHdPcMU8I9LIAZxxTpTZmvLVTvIDpaBLx3bqlE9DAsmD8xCPQLh0Z%2BO5IiVCxwg7vLiGs4EdVJmmw7c104uXHe0s3CbBItmnfIFIwh66SzwY6pgF9y1ltUCWsLue0CGwIrdENt3WqW%2FMp4sRbDCrOitiY%2BcuQKl13RUc%2B7I2iFFgLTMmk4a8NufKtTWFxYMZyXppm6jByOEsu%2FBEES60zrsvUWg%2FZebeO6BQS4pG45zIR%2FrF1ZPe5%2BEKhFLoB7XnJ3iLuvgsJLwvZmtVePQMQ%2BxTFbeKeJmrnpdAn7cBGmHDB3qsN94oiCV07osZckb1pQopD%2FTB1HLmI&X-Amz-Signature=3932f14e8959757f5c2626819f533832b55ebdcf0d21e7e4e0d313e104081b38&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) ## What’s LoRa? {toggle="true"} LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a technique for fine-tuning large neural networks, in a way that significantly reduces memory and computational costs. It works by injecting trainable low-rank matrices into specific layers of a pre-trained model instead of modifying all model weights. It gained large popularity in the Stable Diffusion community as this enabled people to train custom models on consumer GPUs. (They have around 100x less parameters than the full model) ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/b60ad7fb-0830-4bc6-9696-857e339daed8/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466SP4WP6QV%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095752Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIFhxCz8i7lz4PRkyAkyy0%2Bk4yMR9Co6QUtaBzCbIE4V3AiAuB8Pni4oNYqvO389vmdX8L%2FK7YDfeqPYUxhI1U%2FS6LCr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMKRHHL8Zy%2FILI0nIYKtwDRogUM1YA%2BQ%2FsGMZiGaaGA9gV%2BSC85eOPrQ9M0Cxyd%2Bf%2FSTgDghOQLmtM9ZNOXbtvvmxBCWRyK3hw6CWmOyuJO8b5LXaWCgz9aU0jNQ1zLWc1LhWvioBJspn1XpwBgH96MMX4blKWXxa%2FrtFwHD7rzCHbc2XOg1IqZS8Klpyn3Qef4eaRWWNfSVMaC3KFAKFNzEOzr2J0g58nkHRINF11ZCgTkepREmr%2BrSlgWTIDzfUkME12elXtmZuSzZZCeu7lgHCbneq2PzOZns6DHeyoMEz6khXzyRp4ajjZTtgWj36UNHa89OLHuWZDvaR6ObzswLONblbw5qxguqKu%2FtP3xNVJiGEXVF9uykvFTH%2FA7Aj50aC8LhgQWzJl%2FnIaPUCsRohpkxVHoXOZNv9cwhbFArsasRxqa320yIfk8JmIA978%2B7rM7BGMqq1UKcZ0PJQTljHzxQdlpDAJWGzrwwueVddluQmGvWuO4reil%2FGYSuK5boGcA494vcGk6%2FunCttwxq0ALwzboIiY0M%2BUeslhCiyGHdPcMU8I9LIAZxxTpTZmvLVTvIDpaBLx3bqlE9DAsmD8xCPQLh0Z%2BO5IiVCxwg7vLiGs4EdVJmmw7c104uXHe0s3CbBItmnfIFIwh66SzwY6pgF9y1ltUCWsLue0CGwIrdENt3WqW%2FMp4sRbDCrOitiY%2BcuQKl13RUc%2B7I2iFFgLTMmk4a8NufKtTWFxYMZyXppm6jByOEsu%2FBEES60zrsvUWg%2FZebeO6BQS4pG45zIR%2FrF1ZPe5%2BEKhFLoB7XnJ3iLuvgsJLwvZmtVePQMQ%2BxTFbeKeJmrnpdAn7cBGmHDB3qsN94oiCV07osZckb1pQopD%2FTB1HLmI&X-Amz-Signature=244ff06ed7ae18652780e07121c41d8c4f0c8006e8cac8160f648a8d671dde1c&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) **Resources: **
[https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685) ## What’s controlnets? {toggle="true"} ControlNet extends diffusion models by incorporating **conditioning inputs** that "control" the generation process in a more structured way. Popular ones are: ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/1c87b074-79c0-4661-b603-37e5c7932e61/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466SP4WP6QV%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095752Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIFhxCz8i7lz4PRkyAkyy0%2Bk4yMR9Co6QUtaBzCbIE4V3AiAuB8Pni4oNYqvO389vmdX8L%2FK7YDfeqPYUxhI1U%2FS6LCr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMKRHHL8Zy%2FILI0nIYKtwDRogUM1YA%2BQ%2FsGMZiGaaGA9gV%2BSC85eOPrQ9M0Cxyd%2Bf%2FSTgDghOQLmtM9ZNOXbtvvmxBCWRyK3hw6CWmOyuJO8b5LXaWCgz9aU0jNQ1zLWc1LhWvioBJspn1XpwBgH96MMX4blKWXxa%2FrtFwHD7rzCHbc2XOg1IqZS8Klpyn3Qef4eaRWWNfSVMaC3KFAKFNzEOzr2J0g58nkHRINF11ZCgTkepREmr%2BrSlgWTIDzfUkME12elXtmZuSzZZCeu7lgHCbneq2PzOZns6DHeyoMEz6khXzyRp4ajjZTtgWj36UNHa89OLHuWZDvaR6ObzswLONblbw5qxguqKu%2FtP3xNVJiGEXVF9uykvFTH%2FA7Aj50aC8LhgQWzJl%2FnIaPUCsRohpkxVHoXOZNv9cwhbFArsasRxqa320yIfk8JmIA978%2B7rM7BGMqq1UKcZ0PJQTljHzxQdlpDAJWGzrwwueVddluQmGvWuO4reil%2FGYSuK5boGcA494vcGk6%2FunCttwxq0ALwzboIiY0M%2BUeslhCiyGHdPcMU8I9LIAZxxTpTZmvLVTvIDpaBLx3bqlE9DAsmD8xCPQLh0Z%2BO5IiVCxwg7vLiGs4EdVJmmw7c104uXHe0s3CbBItmnfIFIwh66SzwY6pgF9y1ltUCWsLue0CGwIrdENt3WqW%2FMp4sRbDCrOitiY%2BcuQKl13RUc%2B7I2iFFgLTMmk4a8NufKtTWFxYMZyXppm6jByOEsu%2FBEES60zrsvUWg%2FZebeO6BQS4pG45zIR%2FrF1ZPe5%2BEKhFLoB7XnJ3iLuvgsJLwvZmtVePQMQ%2BxTFbeKeJmrnpdAn7cBGmHDB3qsN94oiCV07osZckb1pQopD%2FTB1HLmI&X-Amz-Signature=20b9ee489a22d1040db96f23558bf59ae76001d91d78f42549f4d2999358af13&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) Resources: [https://github.com/lllyasviel/ControlNet](https://github.com/lllyasviel/ControlNet) ## What’s comfy UI? {toggle="true"} ComfyUI is a **graph-based, node-based** interface for ML models, starting with Stable Diffusion designed to give users more control over the AI image generation process. Unlike traditional prompt-based interfaces, it lets you visually connect nodes representing different steps in the image generation pipeline (e.g., model selection, image processing, control net inputs, etc.). ### **Key Features of ComfyUI** - **Fully customizable workflows**: Users can create intricate pipelines by connecting nodes for different Stable Diffusion operations. - **Flexible control**: Users can tweak denoising, samplers, latents, conditioning, and more. - **Efficiency**: Saves workflows, making reproducibility and iteration easier. Also a lot optimization happening under the hood to make it work on consumer hardware. - **Extensible**: Supports extensions and plugins, allowing further customization. It’s great for **power users** who want precise control over image generation but can have a steep learning curve compared to simpler UI options like **AUTOMATIC1111**. Resources:
[https://docs.comfy.org/get_started/introduction](https://docs.comfy.org/get_started/introduction)
[https://stable-diffusion-art.com/comfyui/](https://stable-diffusion-art.com/comfyui/) ## How do you fine-tune dev locally? What are you doing and what can you achieve? What do you need to be able to fine-tune it? {toggle="true"} Fine-tuning FLUX (or any **text-to-image** model) locally requires a solid setup, depending on **your goals, hardware, and dataset**. --- ## **1. What Are You Doing?** Fine-tuning a **diffusion model** means adjusting its weights using custom datasets to specialize it for: - **Style transfer** (mimicking a specific artist’s style) - **Custom character training** (making the model generate a specific person/character) - **Domain-specific tuning** (e.g., medical images, anime, architectural designs) - **Better prompt understanding** (enhancing how well the model interprets prompts) Fine-tuning modifies the **entire model**, unlike LoRAs or embeddings (which are lightweight modifications). --- ## **2. What Can You Achieve?** - **More personalized generations** – The model learns nuances from a dataset, producing more consistent results. - **Domain-specific knowledge** – It can generate images tailored to niche areas (e.g., fashion design, industrial design, historical accuracy). - **Reduce prompt engineering struggles** – No need to fight with prompts to get what you want. - **Improve coherence** – Helps maintain subject consistency across multiple generations. There a re a multiple of repositories that provide the necessary software. e.g.:
[https://github.com/ostris/ai-toolkit](https://github.com/ostris/ai-toolkit)
[https://github.com/bmaltais/kohya_ss](https://github.com/bmaltais/kohya_ss) ## What is upscaling {toggle="true"} - The process of turning a low resolution image or video into higher resolution image or video - It is one of the most popular “real life” use cases of generative media. (e.g. Krea’s most used tool is upscaling by far) There are a lot of decent upscalers out there, it gets tricky when the upscaler should work on any data you put into it. - Most upscalers are trained by artifically corrupting (adding jpeg artifacts, downsampling, adding noise etc)“clean high res” images and then training on the reverse process. If not all possible modes of bad data are covered here, this can lead to bad results during inference. - As the task is somewhat easier than text to image gneration, smaller networks or less network evaluations can be enough to achieve good results - Example: [https://videogigagan.github.io](https://videogigagan.github.io/) [https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-x4-upscaler](https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-x4-upscaler)

Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/190c370222d580fc9f41fffb4fa2a0e7 as of 2026-04-13T08:20:40.849Z: {"title":"Technical Questions"} **New questions: ** - Are we planning to include additional natural representations in our pre-training (in particular those representations that are already used in robotics, e.g. LiDAR, echolocation, sonar or those on invisible spectrum of light)? For anything that can be measured with sensors, there are probably datasets that we could acquire and then train on, right? While this might not have any immediate effect on visual outputs, it could expand “visual” intelligence to “physical” intelligence and expand robotics use cases? (Seb) - How can we compete with OS models - apart from quality, more on an architecture level? What can we offer that others don’t have? - How are we prioritizing on the F3 development when it comes to “features” like resolution, aspect ratio, etc.? - Did Flux.1 Fill actually inpaint without changing things outside of the mask? - How is Video to Video coming along? Realistic for F.3? - Could tensor RT help with speed but also releasing pressure on the shortage of GPUs for inference? --- --- How are we doing with FLUX.3???? #### **How are we prioritizing on the F3 development when it comes to “features” like resolution, aspect ratio, etc.?** {toggle="true"} - some features like different aspect ratios are quite easy to get into the model with e.g packing or bucketing. So low hanging fruits should absolutely be collected. - longer durations than 5s are important so we will want to support these with rolling out generations. - Very high res is kind of painful to train on and thus we have not really prioritized it, due to lack of signal that this would induce a lot of demand. But maybe we need to rethink this one at some point when it becomes the industry standard. ### For video models, seems understanding movement is a problem as labeling data is an issue. Why can’t we use videogame engines as a fix? Some engine have super precise animations and physics, and can output labeling data to train the VLM to follow up what’s up on screen. Seems a bit farfetch, but for robots we used a lot simulations to train recognition, so I was wondering if we could do the same for video models. :D {toggle="true"} Yes! Very much! We do not have an effort as of now to run these but are actively planning.
