{toggle="true"} **Max (Flux2 Pro Max workflow)** - Goal: “Highest possible quality & robustness” on top of Flux2 Pro. - Intended for: - Users who care more about reliability/leaderboard quality than cost. - Avoiding catastrophic failures (missing objects, broken text, etc.) by generating multiple candidates and picking the best. - Customers who want the “top” model on public leaderboards and don’t mind higher price/latency. **Klein** - Goal: “Efficient, open-source, photoreal workhorse.” - Intended for: - People who want an Apache-licensed, relatively small model they can self-host. - Use cases that skew heavily to photorealism (what most people actually prompt). - Directly competing in the ZImage / “small-but-good” open-source segment. **Schnell** - Goal: “Real-time editing experience.” - Intended for: - Extremely fast image edits (latency-first, ‘fun’ UX, slider/brush style workflows). - Interactive tools where users want to see changes live as they move controls. - Difference vs Klein: - Klein: general text-to-image + edit, optimized for quality/photoreal and efficient serving. - Schnell: aggressively distilled for *speed*, focused on edit latency rather than absolute quality; more experimental/novel (no real competitor today doing proper real-time editing). **Flux 2.5** - Goal: “Solid, iterative upgrade of Flux 2 while big research runs on 3.x / multimodal.” - Intended for: - General improvement over Flex/Pro in: robustness, text, editing, and overall quality. - Keeping us competitive while multi‑modal/video/audio research cooks. - Likely also setting up a better teacher for future distillations (Klein/Schnell-type models). ### How should they compare to each other and the competition? {toggle="true"} - **Max** - Internal stack: “best quality” offering on top of Pro, for customers who want maximum consistency and can pay more. - External: designed to rank clearly above “vanilla” Pro/Flex and close the gap vs top-tier models on T2I Arena (e.g. Gemini, Hunyuan) by +15–20 Elo. - Positioning: more expensive than Pro, but still cheaper/faster than some competitor “ultra” workflows (e.g. multi-pass banana/nano-banana equivalents). - **Klein** - Internal: small Apache model that’s good enough for many production workloads, especially photoreal. - External: direct answer to ZImage (6B) and similar open models; slightly larger (\~9B) but still “normal hardware friendly.” - Positioning: more general than ZImage (which is very photoreal-focused), but still tuned so photoreal use cases feel great. - **Schnell** - Internal: “new category” – real-time editing, not just faster T2I. - External: almost no serious real-time editing competitor; this can differentiate UX (live sliders/brushes) more than raw leaderboard Elo. - Positioning: not necessarily leaderboard king on static T2I benchmarks, but unique product story: *“you move a slider and the image changes instantly.”* - **Flux 2.5** - Internal: upgraded Flex 2 pipeline; better data, better training, larger model. - External: general Elo bump vs current Flex/Pro, narrowing gaps vs top proprietary models. - Positioning: “default recommendation” for quality vs cost; 2.x “LTS line” while 3.x research explores multimodal, video, etc. ### What technical steps are taken in the background to build them? {toggle="true"} **Max** - Built as a *workflow* on top of Flux2 Pro (2.4.2): 1. Generate multiple candidates (e.g. 4 images) for a given prompt (and possibly mix Flex/Pro generations depending on final workflow). 2. Score/rank the candidates with internal metrics/judgers (text alignment, visual quality, text legibility, etc.). 3. Return the best-ranked image. - Effect: same base model, but much lower probability of catastrophic failures; improves leaderboard Elo with no change to the underlying Pro weights. **Klein** - Technical recipe: classic teacher–student distillation. 1. Start from the large 32B “dev”/teacher model. 2. Train a smaller \~9B student model to mimic the teacher (distillation). 3. Replace the big \~24B text encoder with a much smaller text encoder. 4. (Likely) release *undistilled by guidance* first (no guidance distillation yet). - Result: a much smaller Apache-licensed model that retains most of the teacher’s capabilities, especially in photoreal generation, at far lower serving cost. **Schnell** - Technical recipe: “aggressive distillation + editing.” 1. Take Klein / 4B / 9B family as starting points. 2. Distill them very aggressively for speed (few steps, highly optimized sampling). 3. Train with strong *image editing* supervision so the model can apply targeted edits extremely fast. - Result: a tiny, highly distilled model specialized for real-time editing (plus T2I), trading a bit of absolute quality for latency. **Flux 2.5** - Technical recipe: “run the proved Flex2 pipeline again, but better.” - **Mid-training**: - Add more/image-editing-style data *earlier* in training rather than just at the very end. - Use larger, scaled-up datasets that took time to build (especially for editing). - **Post-training**: - With more stable compute (no constant job crashes), run more/bigger post-training ablations. - What previously took \~2 weeks due to instability can now be done in \~1 day. - **Model size**: - Likely bigger base model (e.g. 72B teacher for 2.5) to maximize what can later be distilled down. - Plus: improvements on serving/edit cost (e.g. ideas to make editing cost \~equal to T2I). ### Why should a customer use Pro vs Flex? {toggle="true"} **Flex** - \~50 denoising steps (longer sampler). - More “knobs” (e.g. guidance scale) → more controllable for power users. - Tends to be better for **text**: - Long/complex text benefits from more iterative refinement. - If text is important and customers are willing to tweak params, Flex is usually best. **Pro** - \~16 steps (shorter sampler; not visible to users, but impacts speed/cost). - Trained with an **adversarial discriminator** (“is this AI or real?”) → better “natural blending.” - Often more harmonized images. - Humans can look more realistic / slightly “sweaty” – some people love that photoreal punch. - Typically better when: - You want a strong, realistic look with less parameter fiddling. - You care about natural blending/compositing more than perfect long-text rendering. **Rule of thumb:** - Text-heavy / fine control / power-user knobs → **Flex**. - Photoreal, natural blending, “click and get something that pops” → **Pro**. - **Max** on top when customers want *even more* reliability and price is secondary. ### What is an autoencoder, why and where do we use it, and why/how is it good to sell? {toggle="true"} **What is an autoencoder?** - A neural network that: - **Encodes** an image from pixel space into a *lower-dimensional latent space* (compressed representation). - **Decodes** that latent back to pixels. - In Flux, this is mostly a convolutional network + a bit of attention, not a traditional JPEG/MPEG-style codec. **Why do we use it?** - Directly modeling pixels is too expensive. - Autoencoder lets us: - Work in a much lower-dimensional latent space (cheaper compute, faster training/serving). - Preserve spatial structure (top-left in pixels ≈ top-left in latents). - Maintain high reconstruction quality: decoding the latents gives you a sharp, faithful image. - There’s a big research focus on “learnability”: certain latent spaces make it *easier* for diffusion models to learn good generative behavior. Flux 2’s autoencoder is tuned to be on a good Pareto frontier between: - Reconstruction quality and - How easy it is to learn a generative model in that space. **Where do we use it?** - Every time we: - **Train** diffusion models (we train in latent space, not pixels). - **Generate**: - Sample latents with the diffusion model. - Decode them with the autoencoder into final images. - **Edit**: - Encode existing images to latents. - Edit in latent space. - Decode back. **Why/how is it good to sell?** - In principle: - A strong autoencoder gives other teams **better training efficiency** (cheaper training) and **better learnability** (higher quality for a given compute budget). - That’s real value to model builders. - In practice (current decision): - We previously released the autoencoder for free; selling it later can feel odd to customers. - It’s also hard to *visibly* demonstrate its value to non-research buyers (you see the benefit only when you train your own model). - So for now, we focus on selling the full image-generation stack rather than the AE as a standalone product, even though the AE is still absolutely central to why the pipeline works well. > **Claude said:** An **autoencoder** is a neural network architecture that learns to compress data into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and then reconstruct it back to the original form (decoding). It consists of: - **Encoder**: Compresses input into a compact latent representation - **Latent space**: The compressed representation (bottleneck) - **Decoder**: Reconstructs the original data from the latent representation ## Why You Need It in Diffusion Models Modern diffusion models like FLUX, Stable Diffusion, and DALL-E use **Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)** or similar architectures for a crucial reason: **computational efficiency**. **The problem**: Running diffusion directly in pixel space is prohibitively expensive. For a 1024×1024 RGB image, you're working with \~3 million dimensions. The denoising process requires many iterative steps, making this computationally intractable. **The solution**: Use a VAE to work in **latent space** instead: 1. The encoder compresses a 1024×1024×3 image down to something like 128×128×4 (a \~64x reduction in dimensions) 2. The diffusion process operates in this compressed latent space 3. The decoder upsamples the final latent back to full resolution This approach, called **Latent Diffusion Models (LDM)**, reduces compute requirements dramatically while maintaining perceptual quality because the VAE is trained to preserve perceptually important features. ## Where It's Used **Training**: - Images → VAE Encoder → Latents (training data for the diffusion model) - Noise is added to these latents during training **Inference**: - Start with random noise in latent space - Denoise iteratively using the diffusion model - VAE Decoder → Final image The VAE is typically **frozen** during diffusion model training - you train it separately first, then use it as a fixed component for encoding/decoding. **A complete, turnkey solution**: They can generate images immediately without needing to: - Source a compatible VAE separately - Train their own VAE (extremely expensive - requires massive datasets and compute) - Debug compatibility issues between different components - Worry about quality mismatches ## How They Did It Before With **Stable Diffusion**, customers typically: - Used the open-source VAE that came bundled with the model - Sometimes swapped in alternative VAEs (like the "MSE VAE" or "EMA VAE") to improve quality - Had to deal with version compatibility issues - Occasionally trained custom VAEs for specific use cases (rare, due to cost) ## The FLUX Advantage For **FLUX dev/pro customers**, bundling the autoencoder means: 1. **Optimized performance**: The VAE is specifically trained and tuned to work with FLUX's diffusion model architecture 2. **Consistent quality**: You've validated the end-to-end pipeline 3. **Reduced complexity**: One less component to manage or worry about 4. **Competitive moat**: Your VAE architecture and training approach are part of your IP 5. **Support simplification**: You only need to support one known-good configuration It's basically the difference between selling "assembly required" vs. "plug and play." Enterprise customers especially value this because it reduces their time-to-production and technical risk. They're paying for the integrated system, not just the diffusion weights. ### How can we use data from Inditex for virtual try-on? {toggle="true"} Data quality is key here, as in ideally we can build an amazing dataset by applying some logic to the metadata only, and can be sure that the same garnment/person is present and well visible for example. (Kontext Max) {toggle="true"} ITS stands for Inference Time scaling. The idea is that you want to have a mechanism during inference that allows you to get better result when putting more time/compute into the inference. This got popular in the LLM world with “thinking” modes, solving this very elegantly for LLMs and greatly improving the answers of LLMs especially on hard problems.
[https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)

Ideally we also have such a mechanism for image generation. One approach, based on the observation that some results in a batch of n images are better than others, is to generate multiple images and post hoc pick the best result. This is what we are currently doing with max. It has shown to help for text to image and image to image tasks, especially when evaluating prompt following. We pick the best sample with a lightweight model that associates a score with each image on how good it thinks the image is.
This approach is n times more expensive than generating only one image but can get peak performance, and such approaches will dominate the benchmark leaderboards in the end.

Side note. Image gpt is also doing a sort of Inference time scaling with their image generation pipeline, however it is very different. It seems that they are able to predict a different number of tokens to describe an image (they are generating autoregressively) in that way they can generate a different number tokens for the same area of image leading to more detailed images at the cost of more inference time compute. It is mainly a question of focus at this point in time. ## What about these loss curves? {toggle="true"} Generally when we train ML models we want to observe how our training objective improves. We can do this on the training data itself, but most of the time one has a validation set, that stem from the same distribution as the training data, but is never explicitely trained on. For e.g classification tasks this is quite easy, we can just classify on the validation set and get our validation accuracy. Or we can calculate the loss (our training objective) on the validation set and see how that improves. With Diffusion/Flow models things are a bit trickier. The task of the model is to predict, given some noised image X, a text conditioning c and a timestep t signaling how much noise was added to the image, what the unnoised image/the path towards the unnoised image would look like. This task can be more or less difficult depending on how much noise we add to the image. (That is also why we spend a lot of the training compute on high noise, this is very crucial and a big research question on how to distribute the compute based on the timestep)
If we would simply calculate the average loss we do not really get an idea where/if the model is improving. For example that is why the loss looks like it is not improving if we just sample random timesteps: ## What are we doing in final training distribution ablations? {toggle="true"} In final training distribution ablations we are trying to determine the final “data mix”. Our training data for e.g. bagel consists of multiple datasets each covering certain tasks (e.g. one is for style one for inplace editing one for character reference etc). Before investing a lot into a large final run, we do a few smaller runs with less compute and different data mixed, to determine how much of to put into the final run. This is generally hard to determine perfectly and in the end these ablations mainly give us a better informed estimate of what to put in the final mix. ## Can you explain two stage training? {toggle="true"} two stage training means that we train a model not in one go on the same data with the same optimization objective but instead alter the optimization objective or data at some point.
A multi stage approach is typically being used in model development if we were to start from scratch. We typically have a pretraining phase that will take the longest/most compute/most data. Followed by this can be multiple further stages of finetuning the model on highly aesthetic / hand curated datasets and aligning the model with human preference e.g. via DPO. ## How do we do DPO? {toggle="true"} DPO and other Preference Optimization techniques leverage either paired signals (image a is better than b, both had the prompt “XXX”) (DPO falls into this category) or single signals (I like image a, and dislike image b, they are completely independent and have different prompts) This is typically the last stage of training where one want to align the model with user preference. This can also be used as a kind of do “this instead of this”.
We do not need as much data for this stage, the difficulty is getting good pairs that guide the model in the right direction/have clear differences between images. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/0735fe5c-62a3-45b3-abf8-2b4109906fa5/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466SP4WP6QV%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095752Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIFhxCz8i7lz4PRkyAkyy0%2Bk4yMR9Co6QUtaBzCbIE4V3AiAuB8Pni4oNYqvO389vmdX8L%2FK7YDfeqPYUxhI1U%2FS6LCr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMKRHHL8Zy%2FILI0nIYKtwDRogUM1YA%2BQ%2FsGMZiGaaGA9gV%2BSC85eOPrQ9M0Cxyd%2Bf%2FSTgDghOQLmtM9ZNOXbtvvmxBCWRyK3hw6CWmOyuJO8b5LXaWCgz9aU0jNQ1zLWc1LhWvioBJspn1XpwBgH96MMX4blKWXxa%2FrtFwHD7rzCHbc2XOg1IqZS8Klpyn3Qef4eaRWWNfSVMaC3KFAKFNzEOzr2J0g58nkHRINF11ZCgTkepREmr%2BrSlgWTIDzfUkME12elXtmZuSzZZCeu7lgHCbneq2PzOZns6DHeyoMEz6khXzyRp4ajjZTtgWj36UNHa89OLHuWZDvaR6ObzswLONblbw5qxguqKu%2FtP3xNVJiGEXVF9uykvFTH%2FA7Aj50aC8LhgQWzJl%2FnIaPUCsRohpkxVHoXOZNv9cwhbFArsasRxqa320yIfk8JmIA978%2B7rM7BGMqq1UKcZ0PJQTljHzxQdlpDAJWGzrwwueVddluQmGvWuO4reil%2FGYSuK5boGcA494vcGk6%2FunCttwxq0ALwzboIiY0M%2BUeslhCiyGHdPcMU8I9LIAZxxTpTZmvLVTvIDpaBLx3bqlE9DAsmD8xCPQLh0Z%2BO5IiVCxwg7vLiGs4EdVJmmw7c104uXHe0s3CbBItmnfIFIwh66SzwY6pgF9y1ltUCWsLue0CGwIrdENt3WqW%2FMp4sRbDCrOitiY%2BcuQKl13RUc%2B7I2iFFgLTMmk4a8NufKtTWFxYMZyXppm6jByOEsu%2FBEES60zrsvUWg%2FZebeO6BQS4pG45zIR%2FrF1ZPe5%2BEKhFLoB7XnJ3iLuvgsJLwvZmtVePQMQ%2BxTFbeKeJmrnpdAn7cBGmHDB3qsN94oiCV07osZckb1pQopD%2FTB1HLmI&X-Amz-Signature=aefb95995a9e38999a6d4eba32ca10661800a28d575d2813b2f1b3045a4e94f9&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) reference: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12908](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12908) ## long answer: we train a trigger word into the model by mentioning a relatively uncommon text sequence (such as “TOK” or “mycustom bike” etc.) which the model can associate with the images shown, without having too much “baked” in knowledge about what that text should look like. (in contrast to just using “dog” and hope the finetune learns to always generate my dog).
In theory we could add a token that the model has never seen before by introducing a new mapping e.g. x12876zyh → to a new embedding that the model has 100% never seen before (we can add this programmatically) This would then be a “true” trigger word. We do not do this, mainly for complexity vs benefits reasons. ## Can you explain prompt upsampling? {toggle="true"} We train our text to image model with captions from a vlm in different verbosities
i.e. a very detailed caption, a long one a short one a one word caption.
The model learns this distribution/mapping between these captions and images.
However people prompt in all kinds of ways that the model has never seen. (for example, “a woman that is not smiling”, “please make me an image of …”, “ein Hund”)

Prompt upsampling loops in a LLM to turn the freeform prompt into a prompt that is more aligned with our training prompts + more detailed which can help the model to generate more interesting images. e.g.:
Ein Hund → “This is a photograph of a dog walking towards the camera. His fur is black and he is wearing a blue dog collar”

A symptom of not running prompt upsampling per default is that FLUX score a lot worse on user prompts compared to english only prompts in the LM Arena (which has a significant amount of non-English prompts)

This is in the engineering backlog currently. ## What happens behind the scenes when doing finetunes via our API? What about LoRa? {toggle="true"} These are the steps happening in the background: 1. check that the data is clean (as in no attack), that there are images in the uploaded folder, potentially also text descriptions, not too many, not too large files etc. 2. Run moderation on all images. 3. Caption the images if captioning: true 4. encode the images and text to be ready for training 5. run the training loop, here either only the LoRa weights (see LoRa section below) will be trained or all weights 6. Save the LoRa weights or if all weights were trained, calculate the difference between the model now vs the original model and convert the difference into a LoRA 7. The weights are stored in the cluster and can now be referenced for inference ## What’s a VLM? {toggle="true"} VLM stands for Vision Language Model. It integrates both visual and textual understanding. It is designed to process and generate outputs based on both image and text inputs. They are typically very similar to LLMs (Large Language Models) but have a dedicated part that will extract high level features from images which are then fed into the model. ## Why no finetune for Pro 1.1? {toggle="true"} As mentioned in the distillation section, distilled models ## **What is this guidance thing? ** {toggle="true"} Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is a technique used in diffusion models to improve the quality of generated images. It works by balancing the trade-off between sample quality and diversity. Here's how it works: During the sampling process, CFG combines two predictions: 1. A conditional prediction (guided by the text prompt or other conditioning) 2. An unconditional prediction (with no guidance)
- Higher guidance values produce images that more closely follow the prompt but may be less diverse or creative. Too much guidance can lead to the “bakey”/artificial look that we want to avoid. - Lower guidance values produce more diverse and raw looking outputs but may follow the prompt less strictly. At very low guidance values, structures can fall apart.
CFG essentially amplifies the difference between conditional and unconditional models, strengthening the influence of the conditioning signal while maintaining the core image generation capabilities. These are combined using a guidance scale parameter Resources:
[https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598)
[https://theaisummer.com/classifier-free-guidance/](https://theaisummer.com/classifier-free-guidance/) ## What is a distilled model? {toggle="true"} A distilled diffusion model is a model that needs less forward passes to produce a sample, increasing efficiency at the cost of quality and flexibility. ### 1. **Speeding Up Inference** - Diffusion models require multiple forward passes to produce a sample:
our default for pro-1.0 is 50 steps with 2 forward passes per step due to guidance computation - Distillation techniques (e.g., **guidance distillation**, **direct step distillation**, or **teacher-student approaches**) help train a smaller, more efficient model that can generate high-quality samples in fewer steps. ### 2. **Reducing Computational Costs** - Running diffusion models at scale is expensive → by reducing the number of forward passes needed to generate a sample we drastically reduce the cost per generation. - Pro-1.1 for example only takes 6 steps instead 50 and is guidance distilled, meaning we only do one forward pass per step → 100 forward passes vs 6 forward passes at \$0.05 vs \$0.04 → drastic margin increase ### 3. Making the model less flexible - Distillation can also be used to “hide” certain aspects of the sampling processsuch as the concrete guidance method by distilling them into the model - With distillation we typically use some flexibility/capability when trying to finetune the model further. → Distilled models can be good candidates for open source models, as they offer less flexibility than the base model
**Resources:
**[https://sander.ai/2024/02/28/paradox.html](https://sander.ai/2024/02/28/paradox.html) [https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17042](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17042)
[https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12015](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12015) ## What’s the difference between Pro 1.1, dev and schnell? {toggle="true"} Overview of our distilled models: **FLUX.1 dev: ** - guidance distilled (the guidance value can still be controlled via a vector), needing only one forward pass per step instead of two, still needs the same amount of steps to produce good images. - small level of distillation, and still good to finetune - Non-commercial license **FLUX.1 schnell: ** - guidance distilled + step distilled to generate samples in 2-4 steps - Heavy distillation and extremely hard to finetune, also significant quality degradation vs pro - Apache 2.0 licensed **FLUX.1.1 pro:** - guidance distilled + step distilled to produce samples in 1-50 steps - The distillation method was improved between schnell and 1.1 and the number of steps we use for 1.1 is 6 which significantly improves over the limited 2-4 steps. - Heavy distillation makes it hard to finetune - Closed, as it outperforms pro-1.0 ## Why should you use Pro 1.1 and not schnell {toggle="true"} - Benchmarks 🙂 - It generally does better across the board, is a lot better in realism and spelling ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/e2dfee3a-4bb8-41d5-aa27-6e5699d3fb1e/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466SP4WP6QV%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095752Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIFhxCz8i7lz4PRkyAkyy0%2Bk4yMR9Co6QUtaBzCbIE4V3AiAuB8Pni4oNYqvO389vmdX8L%2FK7YDfeqPYUxhI1U%2FS6LCr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMKRHHL8Zy%2FILI0nIYKtwDRogUM1YA%2BQ%2FsGMZiGaaGA9gV%2BSC85eOPrQ9M0Cxyd%2Bf%2FSTgDghOQLmtM9ZNOXbtvvmxBCWRyK3hw6CWmOyuJO8b5LXaWCgz9aU0jNQ1zLWc1LhWvioBJspn1XpwBgH96MMX4blKWXxa%2FrtFwHD7rzCHbc2XOg1IqZS8Klpyn3Qef4eaRWWNfSVMaC3KFAKFNzEOzr2J0g58nkHRINF11ZCgTkepREmr%2BrSlgWTIDzfUkME12elXtmZuSzZZCeu7lgHCbneq2PzOZns6DHeyoMEz6khXzyRp4ajjZTtgWj36UNHa89OLHuWZDvaR6ObzswLONblbw5qxguqKu%2FtP3xNVJiGEXVF9uykvFTH%2FA7Aj50aC8LhgQWzJl%2FnIaPUCsRohpkxVHoXOZNv9cwhbFArsasRxqa320yIfk8JmIA978%2B7rM7BGMqq1UKcZ0PJQTljHzxQdlpDAJWGzrwwueVddluQmGvWuO4reil%2FGYSuK5boGcA494vcGk6%2FunCttwxq0ALwzboIiY0M%2BUeslhCiyGHdPcMU8I9LIAZxxTpTZmvLVTvIDpaBLx3bqlE9DAsmD8xCPQLh0Z%2BO5IiVCxwg7vLiGs4EdVJmmw7c104uXHe0s3CbBItmnfIFIwh66SzwY6pgF9y1ltUCWsLue0CGwIrdENt3WqW%2FMp4sRbDCrOitiY%2BcuQKl13RUc%2B7I2iFFgLTMmk4a8NufKtTWFxYMZyXppm6jByOEsu%2FBEES60zrsvUWg%2FZebeO6BQS4pG45zIR%2FrF1ZPe5%2BEKhFLoB7XnJ3iLuvgsJLwvZmtVePQMQ%2BxTFbeKeJmrnpdAn7cBGmHDB3qsN94oiCV07osZckb1pQopD%2FTB1HLmI&X-Amz-Signature=3932f14e8959757f5c2626819f533832b55ebdcf0d21e7e4e0d313e104081b38&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) ## What’s LoRa? {toggle="true"} LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a technique for fine-tuning large neural networks, in a way that significantly reduces memory and computational costs. It works by injecting trainable low-rank matrices into specific layers of a pre-trained model instead of modifying all model weights. It gained large popularity in the Stable Diffusion community as this enabled people to train custom models on consumer GPUs. (They have around 100x less parameters than the full model) ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/b60ad7fb-0830-4bc6-9696-857e339daed8/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466SP4WP6QV%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095752Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIFhxCz8i7lz4PRkyAkyy0%2Bk4yMR9Co6QUtaBzCbIE4V3AiAuB8Pni4oNYqvO389vmdX8L%2FK7YDfeqPYUxhI1U%2FS6LCr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMKRHHL8Zy%2FILI0nIYKtwDRogUM1YA%2BQ%2FsGMZiGaaGA9gV%2BSC85eOPrQ9M0Cxyd%2Bf%2FSTgDghOQLmtM9ZNOXbtvvmxBCWRyK3hw6CWmOyuJO8b5LXaWCgz9aU0jNQ1zLWc1LhWvioBJspn1XpwBgH96MMX4blKWXxa%2FrtFwHD7rzCHbc2XOg1IqZS8Klpyn3Qef4eaRWWNfSVMaC3KFAKFNzEOzr2J0g58nkHRINF11ZCgTkepREmr%2BrSlgWTIDzfUkME12elXtmZuSzZZCeu7lgHCbneq2PzOZns6DHeyoMEz6khXzyRp4ajjZTtgWj36UNHa89OLHuWZDvaR6ObzswLONblbw5qxguqKu%2FtP3xNVJiGEXVF9uykvFTH%2FA7Aj50aC8LhgQWzJl%2FnIaPUCsRohpkxVHoXOZNv9cwhbFArsasRxqa320yIfk8JmIA978%2B7rM7BGMqq1UKcZ0PJQTljHzxQdlpDAJWGzrwwueVddluQmGvWuO4reil%2FGYSuK5boGcA494vcGk6%2FunCttwxq0ALwzboIiY0M%2BUeslhCiyGHdPcMU8I9LIAZxxTpTZmvLVTvIDpaBLx3bqlE9DAsmD8xCPQLh0Z%2BO5IiVCxwg7vLiGs4EdVJmmw7c104uXHe0s3CbBItmnfIFIwh66SzwY6pgF9y1ltUCWsLue0CGwIrdENt3WqW%2FMp4sRbDCrOitiY%2BcuQKl13RUc%2B7I2iFFgLTMmk4a8NufKtTWFxYMZyXppm6jByOEsu%2FBEES60zrsvUWg%2FZebeO6BQS4pG45zIR%2FrF1ZPe5%2BEKhFLoB7XnJ3iLuvgsJLwvZmtVePQMQ%2BxTFbeKeJmrnpdAn7cBGmHDB3qsN94oiCV07osZckb1pQopD%2FTB1HLmI&X-Amz-Signature=244ff06ed7ae18652780e07121c41d8c4f0c8006e8cac8160f648a8d671dde1c&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) **Resources: **
[https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685) ## What’s controlnets? {toggle="true"} ControlNet extends diffusion models by incorporating **conditioning inputs** that "control" the generation process in a more structured way. Popular ones are: ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/1c87b074-79c0-4661-b603-37e5c7932e61/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466SP4WP6QV%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095752Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIFhxCz8i7lz4PRkyAkyy0%2Bk4yMR9Co6QUtaBzCbIE4V3AiAuB8Pni4oNYqvO389vmdX8L%2FK7YDfeqPYUxhI1U%2FS6LCr%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMKRHHL8Zy%2FILI0nIYKtwDRogUM1YA%2BQ%2FsGMZiGaaGA9gV%2BSC85eOPrQ9M0Cxyd%2Bf%2FSTgDghOQLmtM9ZNOXbtvvmxBCWRyK3hw6CWmOyuJO8b5LXaWCgz9aU0jNQ1zLWc1LhWvioBJspn1XpwBgH96MMX4blKWXxa%2FrtFwHD7rzCHbc2XOg1IqZS8Klpyn3Qef4eaRWWNfSVMaC3KFAKFNzEOzr2J0g58nkHRINF11ZCgTkepREmr%2BrSlgWTIDzfUkME12elXtmZuSzZZCeu7lgHCbneq2PzOZns6DHeyoMEz6khXzyRp4ajjZTtgWj36UNHa89OLHuWZDvaR6ObzswLONblbw5qxguqKu%2FtP3xNVJiGEXVF9uykvFTH%2FA7Aj50aC8LhgQWzJl%2FnIaPUCsRohpkxVHoXOZNv9cwhbFArsasRxqa320yIfk8JmIA978%2B7rM7BGMqq1UKcZ0PJQTljHzxQdlpDAJWGzrwwueVddluQmGvWuO4reil%2FGYSuK5boGcA494vcGk6%2FunCttwxq0ALwzboIiY0M%2BUeslhCiyGHdPcMU8I9LIAZxxTpTZmvLVTvIDpaBLx3bqlE9DAsmD8xCPQLh0Z%2BO5IiVCxwg7vLiGs4EdVJmmw7c104uXHe0s3CbBItmnfIFIwh66SzwY6pgF9y1ltUCWsLue0CGwIrdENt3WqW%2FMp4sRbDCrOitiY%2BcuQKl13RUc%2B7I2iFFgLTMmk4a8NufKtTWFxYMZyXppm6jByOEsu%2FBEES60zrsvUWg%2FZebeO6BQS4pG45zIR%2FrF1ZPe5%2BEKhFLoB7XnJ3iLuvgsJLwvZmtVePQMQ%2BxTFbeKeJmrnpdAn7cBGmHDB3qsN94oiCV07osZckb1pQopD%2FTB1HLmI&X-Amz-Signature=20b9ee489a22d1040db96f23558bf59ae76001d91d78f42549f4d2999358af13&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) Resources: [https://github.com/lllyasviel/ControlNet](https://github.com/lllyasviel/ControlNet) ## What’s comfy UI? {toggle="true"} ComfyUI is a **graph-based, node-based** interface for ML models, starting with Stable Diffusion designed to give users more control over the AI image generation process. Unlike traditional prompt-based interfaces, it lets you visually connect nodes representing different steps in the image generation pipeline (e.g., model selection, image processing, control net inputs, etc.). ### **Key Features of ComfyUI** - **Fully customizable workflows**: Users can create intricate pipelines by connecting nodes for different Stable Diffusion operations. - **Flexible control**: Users can tweak denoising, samplers, latents, conditioning, and more. - **Efficiency**: Saves workflows, making reproducibility and iteration easier. Also a lot optimization happening under the hood to make it work on consumer hardware. - **Extensible**: Supports extensions and plugins, allowing further customization. It’s great for **power users** who want precise control over image generation but can have a steep learning curve compared to simpler UI options like **AUTOMATIC1111**. Resources:
[https://docs.comfy.org/get_started/introduction](https://docs.comfy.org/get_started/introduction)
[https://stable-diffusion-art.com/comfyui/](https://stable-diffusion-art.com/comfyui/) ## How do you fine-tune dev locally? What are you doing and what can you achieve? What do you need to be able to fine-tune it? {toggle="true"} Fine-tuning FLUX (or any **text-to-image** model) locally requires a solid setup, depending on **your goals, hardware, and dataset**. --- ## **1. What Are You Doing?** Fine-tuning a **diffusion model** means adjusting its weights using custom datasets to specialize it for: - **Style transfer** (mimicking a specific artist’s style) - **Custom character training** (making the model generate a specific person/character) - **Domain-specific tuning** (e.g., medical images, anime, architectural designs) - **Better prompt understanding** (enhancing how well the model interprets prompts) Fine-tuning modifies the **entire model**, unlike LoRAs or embeddings (which are lightweight modifications). --- ## **2. What Can You Achieve?** - **More personalized generations** – The model learns nuances from a dataset, producing more consistent results. - **Domain-specific knowledge** – It can generate images tailored to niche areas (e.g., fashion design, industrial design, historical accuracy). - **Reduce prompt engineering struggles** – No need to fight with prompts to get what you want. - **Improve coherence** – Helps maintain subject consistency across multiple generations. There a re a multiple of repositories that provide the necessary software. e.g.:
[https://github.com/ostris/ai-toolkit](https://github.com/ostris/ai-toolkit)
[https://github.com/bmaltais/kohya_ss](https://github.com/bmaltais/kohya_ss) ## What is upscaling {toggle="true"} - The process of turning a low resolution image or video into higher resolution image or video - It is one of the most popular “real life” use cases of generative media. (e.g. Krea’s most used tool is upscaling by far) There are a lot of decent upscalers out there, it gets tricky when the upscaler should work on any data you put into it. - Most upscalers are trained by artifically corrupting (adding jpeg artifacts, downsampling, adding noise etc)“clean high res” images and then training on the reverse process. If not all possible modes of bad data are covered here, this can lead to bad results during inference. - As the task is somewhat easier than text to image gneration, smaller networks or less network evaluations can be enough to achieve good results - Example: [https://videogigagan.github.io](https://videogigagan.github.io/) [https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-x4-upscaler](https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-x4-upscaler)

313c3702-22d5-81ac-89de-eab10b6a5fd9.text:

<page url="https://www.notion.so/313c370222d581ac89deeab10b6a5fd9">
<ancestor-path>
<parent-page url="https://www.notion.so/312c370222d580a6841fc2a6312f0ed1" title="Shop proposals"/>
<ancestor-2-page url="https://www.notion.so/13ec370222d5801f82e4e449987adf58" title="Research"/>
<ancestor-3-page url="https://www.notion.so/21bc370222d580cab1aae5ec0f8cac31" title=""/>
<ancestor-4-page url="https://www.notion.so/21bc370222d5808facd7c952b579a4cd" title=""/>
<ancestor-5-database url="https://www.notion.so/11ec370222d58020ad93e98fe0cc4607" title="Company Home"/>
</ancestor-path>
<properties>
{"title":"Reasoning Flux"}
</properties>
<content>
# TL;DR
Give flux reasoning tokens in the style of Tiny Recursive Models ([https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04871](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04871)). 
Already shows improved stratified losses vs parameter matched baselines.
<unknown url="https://www.notion.so/313c370222d581ac89deeab10b6a5fd9#329c370222d580719999db1d38679107" alt="external_object_instance"/>
# Motivation
The iterative reasoning approach (or inference-time-scaling) has led to major strides in quality in LLMs and reasoning benchmarks like ARC-AGI. A core property of reasoning-based approaches is allowing the model to re-iterate and refine its own predictions using a scratchpad that is not part of the final answer.
We can see different instantiations of this shared idea in prior works:
- **Reasoning in LLMs**: Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022 \[1\]) and scratchpad-based approaches let models iteratively refine their output without increasing model size. This idea has been scaled further in models like OpenAI o1 \[2\] and DeepSeek-R1 \[3\], where extended reasoning chains at inference time yield large gains on hard benchmarks.
- **Reasoning in small models (HRM, TRM)**: HRM \[4\] and TRM \[5\] demonstrate that a small model iterated many times can match the performance of much larger models. TRM, a 2-layer, 7M-parameter network with recursive forward passes, achieves 40% on ARC-AGI-1, competitive with models orders of magnitude larger (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro Thinking with 41.0%, Claude Opus 4 Thinking w/ 35.7%).
So far, reasoning approaches in diffusion models have largely explored:
- **LLM-based prompt reasoning**: Using LLMs to reason about a prompt before generation, e.g. to produce intermediate layout representations (bounding boxes, scene graphs) that condition a diffusion model. Representative work: LLM-grounded Diffusion (Lian et al., 2023 \[6\]).
- **Agentic iterative editing**: Using a vision-language model as an agent that generates an image, evaluates it, and iteratively applies edits via tool use. Representative work: Idea2Img (Yang et al., 2023 \[7\]), which uses GPT-4V in a self-refinement loop over a T2I model.
However, we believe a more fundamental reasoning scratchpad-based approach, integrated into the diffusion process itself, can help diffusion models at a deeper level. As one core example, while diffusion models are iterative by nature, key structural decisions (global layout, composition) are made in early denoising steps and are hard to revise. Reasoning tokens embedded in the model itself could give it a mechanism to correct these early-step decisions *within* a single forward pass cycle, rather than from the outside via agent loops.
# Core Idea
**TRM: iterating a small model to match larger ones**
The Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) transforms a standard single-pass model `f(x)` into a recurrent one `f(x, a, r)`, where `x` is the input query, `a` is the most up-to-date answer (initialized to a learned value), and `r` is a set of reasoning tokens (a learned scratchpad). The model iterates, updating `r` and `a` before committing to a final answer:
<columns>
	<column>
		```python
# TRM forward pass
a = init_answer()
r = init_reasoning_tokens()

# All but the last answer update cycle: no gradients
with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(Y - 1):       # early answer update steps
        for _ in range(X):       # reasoning steps
            r = f(x, a, r).reasoning
        a = f(x, a, r).answer

# Final answer update cycle: backprop through reasoning + answer pass
for _ in range(X):               # reasoning steps (with gradient)
    r = f(x, a, r).reasoning
a = f(x, a, r).answer

# Loss on final answer
loss = criterion(a, target)
		```
	</column>
	<column>
		![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/731accae-ef97-4929-8ae5-78570728a938/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466WCRIBDK5%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095800Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIQCsbMtrWnlXdAoFk86SgOFezT8b8xIv45dMSThQTv267AIgW2G6lz50nYJHReDUmWfh9%2B%2FRfMloAWYAEPqDhG18LLYq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDHWEywvb2Hj6PO9F5ircA8PKfNtGC2p%2FOKlhoRs9fpJHjXxXYAl4OjUlNhdnUijuagQDWxU%2BQWLaqVrvhMkjtKrv5VMD3KdwuzmGcZ3m%2Fuq6me3xQvy8VOBufaJ1AZ5C3vi1nYCoAx3LPeMpsCEIgnEWMGHuTavq4gL1T9tIqHeK87ucMgNGWZiEA8Ig%2FT%2BNjXDVIVDAoYKA4qtsltsKTpLJT%2FBSgTcf9uphVbpG%2BvqmEqET9iiQ7QZyfhpMTqwt2IWRus4PHdWwPPcIe%2B0oKLtQpHrzj8WXmWF9idehutejHirBvSwRI%2BaUqlr0k8BeGN819FxBmmo%2FJIhVEg5D4UupCDOKM%2F8ahQk2sk4c6%2B8KZWog7GsjIn8Gk8eofEeOiFviLEJ9s233QL6PpQavbi6Bc%2FaE0z8OIYdVZqY1PuCfE9pLJJ%2BweAqQKjWPR5scXl0zoqGguqKrxpUEZ7IgmVgMdyvvwAnMNKymNuSAHkQOe20RaCI5YRZ0FesF2sLkKn01Wy5UVRLuWnzbTfkJ1R7knufYx0rEL8ISxlUkAEONfG8l7CQwlhChfvwh5dgmH5n6C82OGGfAqkF9K4EHFTJuhtN%2BND81FfVvo65djPvfdpwob58JD%2BSHFB4j081tM48vnUdWs%2F%2BSQjjjMJavks8GOqUBxxEvCZWld5susBnuwaP4QI1d9Wz%2FcjyKPpWGgX9KIrXgBHbIhEJapI%2FyR6LI8IByFKvlCRMwX6sH4d%2FhlBAj1iGs8bRXJ33bc%2BCCO7V5FM3bH07okGae5QT%2B6%2BV%2BZ9u3X5fmVFIy%2BMwmbs6WdUpJ1CmZjsudtQJnZwHqAje8VxHmo%2BV3B%2FczlZTANHR2sxd0hSPYdfQD1D43shCemXtZG9WZ5Y7w&X-Amz-Signature=486ff335629b886fa17d30033c7a4a730ca4424e40032d6a05a18bd7d2145c6b&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject)
	</column>
</columns>
**Applying TRM-style reasoning to diffusion**
We map this idea onto a diffusion denoising step. A standard step computes a v-prediction as `v = f(z_t, c, t)`, where `z_t` is the noisy latent, `c` is the text condition, and `t` is the timestep. We extend this to `f(z_t, c, t, v, r)`, where `v` is the current best v-prediction (the "answer") and `r` is a set of reasoning tokens (the scratchpad):
```python
# Reasoning Diffusion forward pass for one denoising timestep
v = init_v_prediction()
r = init_reasoning_tokens()

# All but the last answer update cycle: no gradients
with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(Y - 1):       # early answer update steps
        for _ in range(X):
            r = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).reasoning
        v = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).v_prediction

# Final answer update cycle: backprop through all X reasoning steps + answer pass
for _ in range(X):               # reasoning steps (with gradient)
    r = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).reasoning
v = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).v_prediction

# Flow matching loss on final v-prediction
loss = flow_matching_loss(v, v_target)
loss.backward()
```
This gives the model multiple "thinking" iterations per denoising step, with gradients flowing through the entire final answer update cycle (both its reasoning steps and the answer pass) for memory efficiency across the Y−1 earlier cycles.
# Initial Experiments
We extend Flux's double-stream transformer (image + text tokens) with a **third reasoning stream** of learned tokens, each with their own QKV projections, layer norms, MLPs, and modulation. All three streams participate in joint multi-head attention. 
# Preliminary Results
Initial experiments (typical config: 5 reasoning steps, 3 answer steps, 512 reasoning tokens) show the reasoning model **outperforms a parameter-matched non-reasoning baseline on Stratified Loss**. The gap between 2.7B with reasoning (size of a 2B model after a DoubleStream→TripleStream change) vs. 2.7B without reasoning (5.8e-3 at 150k steps) is significantly larger (\~6.85x) than the gap between a 2.7B and a 2B non-reasoning model (8.5e-4).

- Improved global structure in generated images
- Benefits are **concentrated in early denoising steps**, consistent with the hypothesis that reasoning helps resolve high-level layout decisions

# Potential Benefits and Outcomes
**Community impact - GPU-poor models**: A small reasoning model may match the quality of a much larger standard model, providing a strong option for users with limited VRAM.
**Distillation path**: Train a large reasoning model (e.g., 32B) that benefits from extended test-time compute, then distill back into fewer steps. This is speculative but could yield a very capable compact model.
**Post-training / RLHF axis**: The reasoning token stream opens a natural path for optimizing information retention across diffusion timesteps using post-training objectives (e.g., GRPO).
**Test-time compute scaling**: Provides an additional axis for test-time scaling in Max-style models, complementing parallel generation + best-of-N selection with depth-based scaling.
**Sister project — Visual reasoning across frames**: A parallel direction applies this unrolling approach across frames generated autoregressively by a multimodal model, where consecutive frames serve as "updated answers." This would be a form of visual-space reasoning for image editing or generation. However, this feels better to explore once we have an autoregressive Flux.3 variant.
# Downsides & Risks
- **Slower training and inference**: The multi-pass forward loop significantly increases compute per training step and per denoising step.
- **Memory intensive during training**: Back-propagating gradients through multiple forward passes can create scaling challenges.
- **Limited API model benefit**: For large API models where we can already run bigger networks, the VRAM vs step trade-off may not be beneficial.
# Compute Needs
- Unrolling multiple steps is VRAM hungry. Even small runs need to be sharded across \~4 nodes on the GB200.
- Minimum viable: 10 Nodes
- Ideal: 24 Nodes
# Open Questions & Next Research Steps
- [ ] Can this reasoning ability be **fine-tuned into a pre-trained model** in post-training (without training from scratch)?
- [ ] Evaluate on downstream metrics: **FID**, **CLIP Score**, human preference evals
- [ ] How does this compare to other test-time compute extensions, such as **more diffusion steps** or **repeated denoising steps **(initial visual comparisons suggest its better, but not finalized)?
- [ ] Can we distill the reasoning model into a standard forward-pass model?
- [ ] Investigate optimal reasoning/answer step ratios (X reasoning steps, Y answer updates)

\[4\] Wang et al. (2025). *Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM).* arXiv:2506.21734. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21734](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21734)
\[5\] Jolicoeur-Martineau, A. (2025). *Tiny Recursive Model (TRM).* arXiv:2510.04871. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04871](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04871)
\[6\] Lian, L. et al. (2023). *LLM-grounded Diffusion: Enhancing Prompt Understanding of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Large Language Models.* TMLR 2024. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13655](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13655)

# TL;DR
Give flux reasoning tokens in the style of Tiny Recursive Models ([https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04871](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04871)). 
Already shows improved stratified losses vs parameter matched baselines.
<unknown url="https://www.notion.so/313c370222d581ac89deeab10b6a5fd9#329c370222d580719999db1d38679107" alt="external_object_instance"/>
# Motivation
The iterative reasoning approach (or inference-time-scaling) has led to major strides in quality in LLMs and reasoning benchmarks like ARC-AGI. A core property of reasoning-based approaches is allowing the model to re-iterate and refine its own predictions using a scratchpad that is not part of the final answer.
We can see different instantiations of this shared idea in prior works:
- **Reasoning in LLMs**: Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022 \[1\]) and scratchpad-based approaches let models iteratively refine their output without increasing model size. This idea has been scaled further in models like OpenAI o1 \[2\] and DeepSeek-R1 \[3\], where extended reasoning chains at inference time yield large gains on hard benchmarks.
- **Reasoning in small models (HRM, TRM)**: HRM \[4\] and TRM \[5\] demonstrate that a small model iterated many times can match the performance of much larger models. TRM, a 2-layer, 7M-parameter network with recursive forward passes, achieves 40% on ARC-AGI-1, competitive with models orders of magnitude larger (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro Thinking with 41.0%, Claude Opus 4 Thinking w/ 35.7%).
So far, reasoning approaches in diffusion models have largely explored:
- **LLM-based prompt reasoning**: Using LLMs to reason about a prompt before generation, e.g. to produce intermediate layout representations (bounding boxes, scene graphs) that condition a diffusion model. Representative work: LLM-grounded Diffusion (Lian et al., 2023 \[6\]).
- **Agentic iterative editing**: Using a vision-language model as an agent that generates an image, evaluates it, and iteratively applies edits via tool use. Representative work: Idea2Img (Yang et al., 2023 \[7\]), which uses GPT-4V in a self-refinement loop over a T2I model.
However, we believe a more fundamental reasoning scratchpad-based approach, integrated into the diffusion process itself, can help diffusion models at a deeper level. As one core example, while diffusion models are iterative by nature, key structural decisions (global layout, composition) are made in early denoising steps and are hard to revise. Reasoning tokens embedded in the model itself could give it a mechanism to correct these early-step decisions *within* a single forward pass cycle, rather than from the outside via agent loops.
# Core Idea
**TRM: iterating a small model to match larger ones**
The Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) transforms a standard single-pass model `f(x)` into a recurrent one `f(x, a, r)`, where `x` is the input query, `a` is the most up-to-date answer (initialized to a learned value), and `r` is a set of reasoning tokens (a learned scratchpad). The model iterates, updating `r` and `a` before committing to a final answer:
<columns>
	<column>
		```python
# TRM forward pass
a = init_answer()
r = init_reasoning_tokens()

# All but the last answer update cycle: no gradients
with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(Y - 1):       # early answer update steps
        for _ in range(X):       # reasoning steps
            r = f(x, a, r).reasoning
        a = f(x, a, r).answer

# Final answer update cycle: backprop through reasoning + answer pass
for _ in range(X):               # reasoning steps (with gradient)
    r = f(x, a, r).reasoning
a = f(x, a, r).answer

# Loss on final answer
loss = criterion(a, target)
		```
	</column>
	<column>
		![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/731accae-ef97-4929-8ae5-78570728a938/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466WCRIBDK5%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095800Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIQCsbMtrWnlXdAoFk86SgOFezT8b8xIv45dMSThQTv267AIgW2G6lz50nYJHReDUmWfh9%2B%2FRfMloAWYAEPqDhG18LLYq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDHWEywvb2Hj6PO9F5ircA8PKfNtGC2p%2FOKlhoRs9fpJHjXxXYAl4OjUlNhdnUijuagQDWxU%2BQWLaqVrvhMkjtKrv5VMD3KdwuzmGcZ3m%2Fuq6me3xQvy8VOBufaJ1AZ5C3vi1nYCoAx3LPeMpsCEIgnEWMGHuTavq4gL1T9tIqHeK87ucMgNGWZiEA8Ig%2FT%2BNjXDVIVDAoYKA4qtsltsKTpLJT%2FBSgTcf9uphVbpG%2BvqmEqET9iiQ7QZyfhpMTqwt2IWRus4PHdWwPPcIe%2B0oKLtQpHrzj8WXmWF9idehutejHirBvSwRI%2BaUqlr0k8BeGN819FxBmmo%2FJIhVEg5D4UupCDOKM%2F8ahQk2sk4c6%2B8KZWog7GsjIn8Gk8eofEeOiFviLEJ9s233QL6PpQavbi6Bc%2FaE0z8OIYdVZqY1PuCfE9pLJJ%2BweAqQKjWPR5scXl0zoqGguqKrxpUEZ7IgmVgMdyvvwAnMNKymNuSAHkQOe20RaCI5YRZ0FesF2sLkKn01Wy5UVRLuWnzbTfkJ1R7knufYx0rEL8ISxlUkAEONfG8l7CQwlhChfvwh5dgmH5n6C82OGGfAqkF9K4EHFTJuhtN%2BND81FfVvo65djPvfdpwob58JD%2BSHFB4j081tM48vnUdWs%2F%2BSQjjjMJavks8GOqUBxxEvCZWld5susBnuwaP4QI1d9Wz%2FcjyKPpWGgX9KIrXgBHbIhEJapI%2FyR6LI8IByFKvlCRMwX6sH4d%2FhlBAj1iGs8bRXJ33bc%2BCCO7V5FM3bH07okGae5QT%2B6%2BV%2BZ9u3X5fmVFIy%2BMwmbs6WdUpJ1CmZjsudtQJnZwHqAje8VxHmo%2BV3B%2FczlZTANHR2sxd0hSPYdfQD1D43shCemXtZG9WZ5Y7w&X-Amz-Signature=486ff335629b886fa17d30033c7a4a730ca4424e40032d6a05a18bd7d2145c6b&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject)
	</column>
</columns>
**Applying TRM-style reasoning to diffusion**
We map this idea onto a diffusion denoising step. A standard step computes a v-prediction as `v = f(z_t, c, t)`, where `z_t` is the noisy latent, `c` is the text condition, and `t` is the timestep. We extend this to `f(z_t, c, t, v, r)`, where `v` is the current best v-prediction (the "answer") and `r` is a set of reasoning tokens (the scratchpad):
```python
# Reasoning Diffusion forward pass for one denoising timestep
v = init_v_prediction()
r = init_reasoning_tokens()

# All but the last answer update cycle: no gradients
with torch.no_grad():
    for _ in range(Y - 1):       # early answer update steps
        for _ in range(X):
            r = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).reasoning
        v = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).v_prediction

# Final answer update cycle: backprop through all X reasoning steps + answer pass
for _ in range(X):               # reasoning steps (with gradient)
    r = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).reasoning
v = f(z_t, c, t, v, r).v_prediction

# Flow matching loss on final v-prediction
loss = flow_matching_loss(v, v_target)
loss.backward()
```
This gives the model multiple "thinking" iterations per denoising step, with gradients flowing through the entire final answer update cycle (both its reasoning steps and the answer pass) for memory efficiency across the Y−1 earlier cycles.
# Initial Experiments
We extend Flux's double-stream transformer (image + text tokens) with a **third reasoning stream** of learned tokens, each with their own QKV projections, layer norms, MLPs, and modulation. All three streams participate in joint multi-head attention. 
# Preliminary Results
Initial experiments (typical config: 5 reasoning steps, 3 answer steps, 512 reasoning tokens) show the reasoning model **outperforms a parameter-matched non-reasoning baseline on Stratified Loss**. The gap between 2.7B with reasoning (size of a 2B model after a DoubleStream→TripleStream change) vs. 2.7B without reasoning (5.8e-3 at 150k steps) is significantly larger (\~6.85x) than the gap between a 2.7B and a 2B non-reasoning model (8.5e-4).
Key observations:
- Improved global structure in generated images
- Benefits are **concentrated in early denoising steps**, consistent with the hypothesis that reasoning helps resolve high-level layout decisions

# Potential Benefits and Outcomes
**Community impact - GPU-poor models**: A small reasoning model may match the quality of a much larger standard model, providing a strong option for users with limited VRAM.
**Distillation path**: Train a large reasoning model (e.g., 32B) that benefits from extended test-time compute, then distill back into fewer steps. This is speculative but could yield a very capable compact model.
**Post-training / RLHF axis**: The reasoning token stream opens a natural path for optimizing information retention across diffusion timesteps using post-training objectives (e.g., GRPO).
**Test-time compute scaling**: Provides an additional axis for test-time scaling in Max-style models, complementing parallel generation + best-of-N selection with depth-based scaling.
**Sister project — Visual reasoning across frames**: A parallel direction applies this unrolling approach across frames generated autoregressively by a multimodal model, where consecutive frames serve as "updated answers." This would be a form of visual-space reasoning for image editing or generation. However, this feels better to explore once we have an autoregressive Flux.3 variant.
# Downsides & Risks
- **Slower training and inference**: The multi-pass forward loop significantly increases compute per training step and per denoising step.
- **Memory intensive during training**: Back-propagating gradients through multiple forward passes can create scaling challenges.
- **Limited API model benefit**: For large API models where we can already run bigger networks, the VRAM vs step trade-off may not be beneficial.
# Compute Needs
- Unrolling multiple steps is VRAM hungry. Even small runs need to be sharded across \~4 nodes on the GB200.
- Minimum viable: 10 Nodes
- Ideal: 24 Nodes
# Open Questions & Next Research Steps
- [ ] Can this reasoning ability be **fine-tuned into a pre-trained model** in post-training (without training from scratch)?
- [ ] Evaluate on downstream metrics: **FID**, **CLIP Score**, human preference evals
- [ ] How does this compare to other test-time compute extensions, such as **more diffusion steps** or **repeated denoising steps **(initial visual comparisons suggest its better, but not finalized)?
- [ ] Can we distill the reasoning model into a standard forward-pass model?
- [ ] Investigate optimal reasoning/answer step ratios (X reasoning steps, Y answer updates)
# References
\[1\] Wei, J. et al. (2022). *Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models.* NeurIPS 2022. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)
\[2\] OpenAI (2024). *OpenAI o1 System Card.* [https://openai.com/index/openai-o1-system-card/](https://openai.com/index/openai-o1-system-card/)
\[3\] DeepSeek-AI (2025). *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning.* [https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)
\[4\] Wang et al. (2025). *Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM).* arXiv:2506.21734. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21734](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21734)
\[5\] Jolicoeur-Martineau, A. (2025). *Tiny Recursive Model (TRM).* arXiv:2510.04871. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04871](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04871)
\[6\] Lian, L. et al. (2023). *LLM-grounded Diffusion: Enhancing Prompt Understanding of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Large Language Models.* TMLR 2024. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13655](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13655)

Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/33cc370222d58123910fd469ee0d959e as of 2026-04-08T17:21:49.866Z: {"title":"RL Research Shop Presentation (8th Apr) — Slides"} --- # Motivation & Background Three levels of training frontier models, with increasing supervision. - Despite impressive task generalization from pretraining, **in-domain specialization is still dominated by supervised methods**. - We all share the same internet → "convergent evolution" of pretraining. **Post-training is where differentiation happens.** **Post-training** — RLHF, RLAIF, DPO — closes the loop with user feedback **Mid-training / CPT** — Supervised fine-tuning, domain-specific corpora **Pretraining / SSL** — Self-supervised — tokens + compute + scale *Supervision increases from bottom to top* --- # RLAIF: Replace Humans with a VLM Judge Remove the human from the loop and replace with an aligned VLM to zero-shot predict preferences. **Motivation:** Why does Flux 2 Max rank higher than Pro on LMArena when both are the same base model? The difference is post-training. 📎 `lmarena_leaderboard.png` — Max (1166) \> Flex (1158) ≥ Pro (1158) **Online RLAIF Feedback Loop:** Model $`\pi_\theta`$ → Generate $`G`$ images/prompt → VLM Judge (GPT-5, 0-shot) → Pref Pairs $`(y_w, y_l)`$ → DPO Train → ↻
VLM Judge System Prompt (I2I best/worst mode) ```javascript You are an objective and precise evaluator for image quality comparison. Evaluate across: Realism, Consistency, Semantic consistency, Aesthetics, Authenticity, Edit fidelity, Identity preservation, Detail, Background preservation, Spatial/anatomical coherence, Lighting/shadow consistency, Text rendering, Scale/perspective Respond with JSON: {"best": "B", "worst": "D", "confidence": 1-5, "reasoning": "..."} ```
### Example 1: CAD Drawing *Prompt: "Convert this image into a precise 2D CAD drawing"* 📎 `edd358f9a04c_input.png` (input) + `rlaif_i2i_edd358f9a04c_g0-g4.png` (A–E) Best = C (ref), Worst = D (policy) **GPT-5 Reasoning (conf 4/5):** "Image C is the closest: overhead view with clear line work and tile grid. D is the weakest: awkward cropping, inconsistent annotations." ### Example 2: Enhance & Smoothen *Prompt: "Enhance, smoothen, keep facial and body features, place her hands on her hips"* 📎 `dc20f2bdbf6e_input.png` (input) + `rlaif_i2i_dc20f2bdbf6e_g0-g4.png` (A–E) Best = D (policy), Worst = B (policy), Ref = A (mid-ranked) **GPT-5 Reasoning:** "D is the most natural: realistic skin, coherent fingers. B is the worst: heavy airbrushing, plastic sheen." **Pros** - **Very close to on-policy** - Much cheaper than human evals - Scales much better with compute - Easy to "train" a new reward model (just change the prompt) - Easily configurable to be "multi-reward" - Exploits inter-sample differences (no external model necessary) **Cons** - Biased estimator (e.g., positional bias) - Limited external supervisory signal - Not the most compute-efficient algorithm --- # Can GPT-5 Replace Human Annotators? 500 I2I pairs evaluated by three independent raters with the same anonymized A/B assignment. *Source: RLHF Plan — Agreement Study*
Comparison All conf ≥ 3 conf ≥ 4 conf = 5
**Prolific vs GPT-5** **73.6%** **73.3%** **75.0%** **94.6%**
Prolific vs GPT-5.4 66.8% 68.9% 71.9% 88.0%
Prolific vs Playground 62.4% 62.3% 65.1% 74.3%
GPT-5 vs Playground 64.4% 64.4% 65.9% 77.9%
GPT-5 vs GPT-5.4 74.6% 75.8% 78.5% 94.1%
**GPT-5 is the best proxy for Prolific** — 73.6% overall, **94.6%** at conf=5. Better than GPT-5.4 despite being \~4× cheaper. Chosen for production scoring. --- # Iterative RLAIF: Sample → Score → Train → Repeat Each iteration: sample → score → train → evaluate. Repeat 5–10×. **Phase 1: Sample** (SLURM GPU) — Generate $`G`$ images per prompt from $`\pi_\theta`$ ↓ **Phase 2: Score** (CPU) — GPT-5, 5-way best/worst → `preferences.parquet` **Phase 2b+2c: External** — nbp2 + seedream4 via FAL → 3-way GPT comparison ↓ **Phase 3a/3b: DPO Train** on internal / external data ↓ **Phase 4: Evaluate** — lmarena_bench SxS vs previous + baseline ↓ back to Phase 1 ↻ --- # Building the I2I DPO Dataset: 298K → 42K
Stage Filter Out Drop
1 Model filter (Flux 2 pro/max/flex-pg) 219,870 -26%
3 Prompt dedup 150,125 -10%
**5-6** **Hard quality filters** **56,450** **-62%**
**9-10** **Confidence filter (≥4) + packing** **\~42K** **-25%**
*Source: * --- # RLAIF Iter-0: Does It Work? Iter-0 DPO checkpoints vs base model, scored by paid Prolific annotators on lmarena-bench. 📎 `rlaif_result_1.png` — Elo statistics table 📎 `rlaif_result_2.png` through `rlaif_result_5.png` — Sample comparisons (shoes, plate, helmet, t-shirt) --- # How DPO Learns from Preferences $$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)} \left[ \log \sigma\!\left( \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)} \right) \right] $$ **Implicit Reward:** $`r_\theta(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}`$ The policy *is* the reward model. **Implicit Accuracy:** $`\text{acc} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}[r_\theta(x,y_w) > r_\theta(x,y_l)]]`$ Starts \~0.5, should rise to \~0.6–0.7. --- # Likelihood Displacement: When DPO Forgets *(Razin et al., 2024 — arXiv:2410.08847)* 📎 `likelihood_displacement_1.png` — Concept diagram (benign vs catastrophic) 📎 `likelihood_displacement_2.png` — Table from paper 📎 `likelihood_displacement_3.png` — train/loss (decreasing) 📎 `likelihood_displacement_4.png` — train/raw_model_loss (increasing) **The paradox:** DPO loss goes down (learns preferences), but raw flow-matching loss goes up (forgets how to generate). The policy learns *which* output is preferred but loses the ability to *produce* good outputs. --- # Flow GRPO: Policy Gradients for Diffusion $$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}} = -\mathbb{E} \left[ \frac{1}{G} \sum_{i=1}^{G} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left( \min\!\left( \rho_t^{(i)} \hat{A}_i, \text{clip}(\rho_t^{(i)}, 1{-}\epsilon, 1{+}\epsilon) \hat{A}_i \right) - \beta D_{\text{KL}} \right) \right] $$ **Group-Relative Advantage:** $`\hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \bar{r}_G}{\sigma_{r_G}}`$ Normalize within group of $`G`$ samples. No value network. **Importance Ratio:** $`\rho_t^{(i)} = \frac{\pi_\theta(x_t | x_{t-1}, c)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(x_t | x_{t-1}, c)}`$ Off-policy correction per denoising step. **Key difference from LLM GRPO:** per-timestep over continuous latent trajectories, not per-token. Reward is scalar per image. --- # GRPO System: Actor, Reward, Learner **ACTOR — 64B:** Old Policy (Flux2 · 32B · eval) + Ref Policy (Flux2 · 32B · frozen KL) ↓ **1.** $`G`$ images per prompt **REWARD — 8B:** UnifiedReward (Qwen3-VL · 8B · vLLM · KV cache) ↓ **2.** per-image scores → group-relative advantages **LEARNER — 96B:** Current Policy (Flux2 + LoRA · 32B) + Optimizer State (AdamW · 64B · fp32) **3.** off-policy corrected ∇θ → AdamW step **4.** sync weights ↰ back to Actor ↻ \~168B parameters in memory. FSDP shards each Flux2-32B across all GPUs. --- # KL Regularization: Schulman's k1, k2, k3 Three KL estimators for flow-matching. Where \$r = log(pi_theta / pi_\{text\{old\}\})\$. **k1:** $`\hat{D}_{\text{KL}}^{(k1)} = \mathbb{E}[-r]`$ — negative log ratio mean. Unbiased but high variance. **Complete collapse.** **k2:** $`\hat{D}_{\text{KL}}^{(k2)} = \mathbb{E}[r^2/2]`$ — Taylor expansion. **Works reasonably well.** **k3:** $`\hat{D}_{\text{KL}}^{(k3)} = \mathbb{E}[(e^r - 1) - r]`$ — ratio trick. Non-negative, low variance. **Best reward.** 📎 `kl_ablation_chart.png` — KL estimator comparison (k1 collapses, k3 best) 📎 `kl_results.png` — Prolific results with regularization
Model Elo Win Rate
baseline 986.7 47.5%
📎 `positive_result_1-3.png` — Visual comparisons **GRPO works:** 55.5% win rate, Elo 1025 — significantly above baseline. HPSv3 reward produces measurably better images per Prolific annotators. --- # OCR Reward: +12% on Dense Text Rendering

Worse Images HPSv3 over-optimization → saturated colors, exaggerated contrast, loss of realism. 📎 `hacking_wandb.png` — HPSv3 reward curve 📎 Before/after pairs: - `banaue_step0.png` → Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/33cc370222d58123910fd469ee0d959e as of 2026-04-08T17:21:49.866Z: {"title":"RL Research Shop Presentation (8th Apr) — Slides"} --- # Motivation & Background Three levels of training frontier models, with increasing supervision. - Despite impressive task generalization from pretraining, **in-domain specialization is still dominated by supervised methods**. - We all share the same internet → "convergent evolution" of pretraining. **Post-training is where differentiation happens.** **Post-training** — RLHF, RLAIF, DPO — closes the loop with user feedback **Mid-training / CPT** — Supervised fine-tuning, domain-specific corpora **Pretraining / SSL** — Self-supervised — tokens + compute + scale *Supervision increases from bottom to top* --- # RLAIF: Replace Humans with a VLM Judge Remove the human from the loop and replace with an aligned VLM to zero-shot predict preferences. **Motivation:** Why does Flux 2 Max rank higher than Pro on LMArena when both are the same base model? The difference is post-training. 📎 `lmarena_leaderboard.png` — Max (1166) \> Flex (1158) ≥ Pro (1158) **Online RLAIF Feedback Loop:** Model $`\pi_\theta`$ → Generate $`G`$ images/prompt → VLM Judge (GPT-5, 0-shot) → Pref Pairs $`(y_w, y_l)`$ → DPO Train → ↻
VLM Judge System Prompt (I2I best/worst mode) ```javascript You are an objective and precise evaluator for image quality comparison. Evaluate across: Realism, Consistency, Semantic consistency, Aesthetics, Authenticity, Edit fidelity, Identity preservation, Detail, Background preservation, Spatial/anatomical coherence, Lighting/shadow consistency, Text rendering, Scale/perspective Respond with JSON: {"best": "B", "worst": "D", "confidence": 1-5, "reasoning": "..."} ```
### Example 1: CAD Drawing *Prompt: "Convert this image into a precise 2D CAD drawing"* 📎 `edd358f9a04c_input.png` (input) + `rlaif_i2i_edd358f9a04c_g0-g4.png` (A–E) Best = C (ref), Worst = D (policy) **GPT-5 Reasoning (conf 4/5):** "Image C is the closest: overhead view with clear line work and tile grid. D is the weakest: awkward cropping, inconsistent annotations." ### Example 2: Enhance & Smoothen *Prompt: "Enhance, smoothen, keep facial and body features, place her hands on her hips"* 📎 `dc20f2bdbf6e_input.png` (input) + `rlaif_i2i_dc20f2bdbf6e_g0-g4.png` (A–E) Best = D (policy), Worst = B (policy), Ref = A (mid-ranked) **GPT-5 Reasoning:** "D is the most natural: realistic skin, coherent fingers. B is the worst: heavy airbrushing, plastic sheen." **Pros** - **Very close to on-policy** - Much cheaper than human evals - Scales much better with compute - Easy to "train" a new reward model (just change the prompt) - Easily configurable to be "multi-reward" - Exploits inter-sample differences (no external model necessary) **Cons** - Biased estimator (e.g., positional bias) - Limited external supervisory signal - Not the most compute-efficient algorithm --- # Can GPT-5 Replace Human Annotators? 500 I2I pairs evaluated by three independent raters with the same anonymized A/B assignment. *Source: RLHF Plan — Agreement Study*
Comparison All conf ≥ 3 conf ≥ 4 conf = 5
**Prolific vs GPT-5** **73.6%** **73.3%** **75.0%** **94.6%**
Prolific vs GPT-5.4 66.8% 68.9% 71.9% 88.0%
Prolific vs Playground 62.4% 62.3% 65.1% 74.3%
GPT-5 vs Playground 64.4% 64.4% 65.9% 77.9%
GPT-5 vs GPT-5.4 74.6% 75.8% 78.5% 94.1%
**GPT-5 is the best proxy for Prolific** — 73.6% overall, **94.6%** at conf=5. Better than GPT-5.4 despite being \~4× cheaper. Chosen for production scoring. --- # Iterative RLAIF: Sample → Score → Train → Repeat Each iteration: sample → score → train → evaluate. Repeat 5–10×. **Phase 1: Sample** (SLURM GPU) — Generate $`G`$ images per prompt from $`\pi_\theta`$ ↓ **Phase 2: Score** (CPU) — GPT-5, 5-way best/worst → `preferences.parquet` **Phase 2b+2c: External** — nbp2 + seedream4 via FAL → 3-way GPT comparison ↓ **Phase 3a/3b: DPO Train** on internal / external data ↓ **Phase 4: Evaluate** — lmarena_bench SxS vs previous + baseline ↓ back to Phase 1 ↻ --- # Building the I2I DPO Dataset: 298K → 42K
Stage Filter Out Drop
1 Model filter (Flux 2 pro/max/flex-pg) 219,870 -26%
3 Prompt dedup 150,125 -10%

Iter-0 DPO checkpoints vs base model, scored by paid Prolific annotators on lmarena-bench. 📎 `rlaif_result_1.png` — Elo statistics table 📎 `rlaif_result_2.png` through `rlaif_result_5.png` — Sample comparisons (shoes, plate, helmet, t-shirt) --- # How DPO Learns from Preferences $$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)} \left[ \log \sigma\!\left( \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)} \right) \right] $$ **Implicit Reward:** $`r_\theta(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}`$ The policy *is* the reward model. **Implicit Accuracy:** $`\text{acc} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}[r_\theta(x,y_w) > r_\theta(x,y_l)]]`$ Starts \~0.5, should rise to \~0.6–0.7. --- # Likelihood Displacement: When DPO Forgets *(Razin et al., 2024 — arXiv:2410.08847)* 📎 `likelihood_displacement_1.png` — Concept diagram (benign vs catastrophic) 📎 `likelihood_displacement_2.png` — Table from paper 📎 `likelihood_displacement_3.png` — train/loss (decreasing) 📎 `likelihood_displacement_4.png` — train/raw_model_loss (increasing) **The paradox:** DPO loss goes down (learns preferences), but raw flow-matching loss goes up (forgets how to generate). The policy learns *which* output is preferred but loses the ability to *produce* good outputs. --- # Flow GRPO: Policy Gradients for Diffusion $$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}} = -\mathbb{E} \left[ \frac{1}{G} \sum_{i=1}^{G} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left( \min\!\left( \rho_t^{(i)} \hat{A}_i, \text{clip}(\rho_t^{(i)}, 1{-}\epsilon, 1{+}\epsilon) \hat{A}_i \right) - \beta D_{\text{KL}} \right) \right] $$ **Group-Relative Advantage:** $`\hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \bar{r}_G}{\sigma_{r_G}}`$ Normalize within group of $`G`$ samples. No value network. **Importance Ratio:** $`\rho_t^{(i)} = \frac{\pi_\theta(x_t | x_{t-1}, c)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(x_t | x_{t-1}, c)}`$ Off-policy correction per denoising step. **Key difference from LLM GRPO:** per-timestep over continuous latent trajectories, not per-token. Reward is scalar per image. --- # GRPO System: Actor, Reward, Learner **ACTOR — 64B:** Old Policy (Flux2 · 32B · eval) + Ref Policy (Flux2 · 32B · frozen KL) ↓ **1.** $`G`$ images per prompt **REWARD — 8B:** UnifiedReward (Qwen3-VL · 8B · vLLM · KV cache) ↓ **2.** per-image scores → group-relative advantages **LEARNER — 96B:** Current Policy (Flux2 + LoRA · 32B) + Optimizer State (AdamW · 64B · fp32) **3.** off-policy corrected ∇θ → AdamW step **4.** sync weights ↰ back to Actor ↻ \~168B parameters in memory. FSDP shards each Flux2-32B across all GPUs. --- # KL Regularization: Schulman's k1, k2, k3 Three KL estimators for flow-matching. Where \$r = log(pi_theta / pi_\{text\{old\}\})\$. **k1:** $`\hat{D}_{\text{KL}}^{(k1)} = \mathbb{E}[-r]`$ — negative log ratio mean. Unbiased but high variance. **Complete collapse.** **k2:** $`\hat{D}_{\text{KL}}^{(k2)} = \mathbb{E}[r^2/2]`$ — Taylor expansion. **Works reasonably well.** **k3:** $`\hat{D}_{\text{KL}}^{(k3)} = \mathbb{E}[(e^r - 1) - r]`$ — ratio trick. Non-negative, low variance. **Best reward.** 📎 `kl_ablation_chart.png` — KL estimator comparison (k1 collapses, k3 best) 📎 `kl_results.png` — Prolific results with regularization

2e1c3702-22d5-8069-a95d-ca87c30720f4.text: Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2e1c370222d58069a95dca87c30720f4 as of 2026-03-16T21:25:11.452Z: {"title":"Email for Revenue Share/Usage Reporting"} **Important Notes** The lists of customers shared here are reflecting the customer base as of January 2026 and may be updated from time to time. Please consider this. The date needs to be updated each month, see comments (I’m sure we can easily automate this). Other than that this email remains static. So also probably good to automate this. # Usage Based Customers ### Email Subject Monthly Usage Reporting 2025/12 ### Email Body Dear Customer, This is a reminder to report your usage data and applicable fees for the BFL open weights models for the past month. We need it to generate your invoice accurately. Please take a moment to enter your usage details in the form linked below. **Action Required** Kindly submit your usage data for 2025/12 by following [this link](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfXM7pqA55EmRsgWbV01yYcgOitbW_vsNpTH2QwWBLMi41T1Q/viewform?usp=sf_link). **Please only submit one form per model for the model type/types that is/are included in your contract. The model types are FLUX.1 \[dev\], FLUX.1Tools \[dev\] (you can bulk report for all FLUX.1 Tools \[dev\] models together), FLUX.1 Kontext \[dev\], FLUX.1 Krea \[dev\] and FLUX.2 \[dev\].** **Example 1:** **If you have a contract for FLUX.1 \[dev\] only, fill out one form for FLUX.1 \[dev\] for the corresponding month and select the respective model in the model dropdown menu.** **Example 2:** **If you have a contract for both FLUX.1 \[dev\] and FLUX.1 Kontext \[dev\], please fill out one form for each model for the corresponding month and select the respective model in the model dropdown menu.** The data you provide will allow us to finalize and issue your invoice promptly. If you have any questions or need assistance, please feel free to reach out to [requests@blackforestlabs.ai](mailto:requests@blackforestlabs.ai). Please note that you have to report this within 30 days after the end of the reported month. Thank you for your cooperation and timely response. The BFL team ### Customer Emails # Revenue Share Based Customers ### Email Subject Monthly Revenue Reporting 2025/12 ### Email Body Dear Customer, This is a reminder to report your revenue from the FLUX dev models for the past month. We need it to generate your invoice accurately. Please take a moment to enter your revenue details for the past month in the form linked below. **Action Required** Kindly submit your revenue data for 2025/12 by following [this link](https://forms.gle/SWJ9yDraas44vLfq5). The data you provide will allow us to finalize and issue your invoice promptly. If you have any questions or need assistance, please feel free to reach out. Please note that you have to report this within 30 days after the end of the reported month. Thank you for your cooperation and timely response. The BFL team ### Customer Emails
