It is optimized for low latency and is currently available to approved partner organizations. You can try it out directly here: [Black Forest Labs - Frontier AI Lab](https://showcase-vto.preview.bfl.ai/) Your domain should be already whitelisted, but in case that you do not have access to the app: please let us know! ## Before / After examples ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/4c6dc6ab-0a98-4845-94a2-af6b47c76abc/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB4662QZOE5L3%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095825Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCICGknLlsw6TttDU%2FnmtpanbF9ZBq%2F2uXkuSwVq%2BSGEplAiEAtmrM2tttmRjKcjRLOZV5tebNpVFjCmr0fMGjhNAugSIq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDBkh%2F4u9wHVPMlvJOCrcAzbvXedWARBhcmbzAMwmoUr51hjZtCw%2FOyyiOoOLi6uMOirtGk292CgJVBYryitd%2BuBGctaWsaQzAU%2BOLfd%2F239JKc5BNrgMaC9UhePetDiCImdpOY8v5ErcHY5g8Waf04pVuQicfbngoyW8rhVt4j6icSCOBGS7XIPZcxUVxO4VoLeRHWvskNwA17tkDNvHXfh8HRYk2qLiK0fupmHJzEsC0rHhm9yZTuioC8zdJ7zJsEorC2mCzCGrO0nxm%2FyUpa1pOaGlq5gB%2FQ9syQ9rlwpdmOs0KqJU%2F9%2BxWLyuR15%2FpBYUQ2t2VSipy2wTVuLTBKEkUQxZSuXIFfkX5tNlmRQXsKA8MkLDCLuOXiB%2B2VkfPnvuf6zw6f2GwtjaoTTYcr3eyFJ%2FVP%2BOijxfVhEw82LxKIM098SopbUfQiNxXxdJHI1BqL%2BM8E80ptMredVRLuH4S38X8ypudCr852rQF8lN%2F8uiEbUPDHdpHMFRJIIMReSaOyfJlw9NbqyB7r3GCqmoZaicLYF62bpayr5yElClrkF83kz0KP1BujszDPX%2B%2F73BaPykmC6iau2vO3DYRohKrROZBM3BSi270%2FHkL9ZAISYOj0wUpQ8Z11uMnXsBUyNVL2AJyQM2yLUdMLmvks8GOqUBx77I4WdCT2A6yU65v5j9krkHXzKSZpA2Lj4LRqJQxmsPB0hMvAXLhlqzankwQMsjBYTulr3CrLCxpnaCy01enfBHCC0Sevxa4MdrsgFg2xxEAhi6A6GHupLow%2BOGLiYT2RnJPdH06G8xlj%2Bq%2FC86FUXz6NodEZy%2FsfVSJdaHPY2%2BYrl85OpoVmSAdBCwW8bOh0UmckCAlz5KbVOrK0sH%2BdQwxaAG&X-Amz-Signature=aec781259d3f16426568619510cd1f69b80a9fdaf028cbb72a5beaca198f97aa&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) --- ## Get started in 30 seconds **1. Get access + API key** You need: - an approved API key - organization access to the VTO route If you are not sure your project is allowlisted, contact the BFL team. **2. Submit a VTO request** ```bash PERSON_B64="$(base64 < /path/to/person.png | tr -d '\n')" GARMENT_B64="$(base64 < /path/to/garment_top.png | tr -d '\n')" # Optional second garment (for bottom, jacket layer, etc.) GARMENT2_B64="$(base64 < /path/to/garment_bottom.png | tr -d '\n')" jq -n \ --arg person "$PERSON_B64" \ --arg garment "$GARMENT_B64" \ '{ prompt: "model is wearing the provided garments, realistic studio lighting, clean background", person: $person, garment: $garment, garment_2: (if $garment2 == "" then null else $garment2 end), width: 1024, height: 1024, output_format: "png" }' > /tmp/vto_request.json curl -sS -X POST "https://labs.eu2.bfl.ai/v1/flux-try-on" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-Key: $BFL_API_KEY" \ --data-binary @/tmp/vto_request.json ``` Response: ```json {"id":"xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx","polling_url":"..."} ``` **3. Poll for your result** ```bash curl -sS "https://labs.eu2.bfl.ai/v1/get_result?id=YOUR_TASK_ID" \ -H "X-Key: $BFL_API_KEY" ``` When `status` is `"Ready"`, use `result.sample`. --- ## Performance tip If you want to send 2 or more garment images, we recommend merging them into a single canvas first to keep latency down. In our testing, we could not notice any quality degradation from doing this. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/ca070cd9-81da-4dfc-af0d-3fdc829da054/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB4662QZOE5L3%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095825Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCICGknLlsw6TttDU%2FnmtpanbF9ZBq%2F2uXkuSwVq%2BSGEplAiEAtmrM2tttmRjKcjRLOZV5tebNpVFjCmr0fMGjhNAugSIq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDBkh%2F4u9wHVPMlvJOCrcAzbvXedWARBhcmbzAMwmoUr51hjZtCw%2FOyyiOoOLi6uMOirtGk292CgJVBYryitd%2BuBGctaWsaQzAU%2BOLfd%2F239JKc5BNrgMaC9UhePetDiCImdpOY8v5ErcHY5g8Waf04pVuQicfbngoyW8rhVt4j6icSCOBGS7XIPZcxUVxO4VoLeRHWvskNwA17tkDNvHXfh8HRYk2qLiK0fupmHJzEsC0rHhm9yZTuioC8zdJ7zJsEorC2mCzCGrO0nxm%2FyUpa1pOaGlq5gB%2FQ9syQ9rlwpdmOs0KqJU%2F9%2BxWLyuR15%2FpBYUQ2t2VSipy2wTVuLTBKEkUQxZSuXIFfkX5tNlmRQXsKA8MkLDCLuOXiB%2B2VkfPnvuf6zw6f2GwtjaoTTYcr3eyFJ%2FVP%2BOijxfVhEw82LxKIM098SopbUfQiNxXxdJHI1BqL%2BM8E80ptMredVRLuH4S38X8ypudCr852rQF8lN%2F8uiEbUPDHdpHMFRJIIMReSaOyfJlw9NbqyB7r3GCqmoZaicLYF62bpayr5yElClrkF83kz0KP1BujszDPX%2B%2F73BaPykmC6iau2vO3DYRohKrROZBM3BSi270%2FHkL9ZAISYOj0wUpQ8Z11uMnXsBUyNVL2AJyQM2yLUdMLmvks8GOqUBx77I4WdCT2A6yU65v5j9krkHXzKSZpA2Lj4LRqJQxmsPB0hMvAXLhlqzankwQMsjBYTulr3CrLCxpnaCy01enfBHCC0Sevxa4MdrsgFg2xxEAhi6A6GHupLow%2BOGLiYT2RnJPdH06G8xlj%2Bq%2FC86FUXz6NodEZy%2FsfVSJdaHPY2%2BYrl85OpoVmSAdBCwW8bOh0UmckCAlz5KbVOrK0sH%2BdQwxaAG&X-Amz-Signature=e94227315d9205d72a2adbdb6daf67c149c7a321de5c094a068399d3f3000ea7&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) --- ## Python quick start ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import base64 import os import time import requests API_KEY = os.environ["BFL_API_KEY"] BASE = "https://labs.us2.bfl.ai" HEADERS = {"X-Key": API_KEY, "Content-Type": "application/json"} PROMPT = "model is wearing the provided garments, realistic fabric detail" PERSON_PATH = "/path/to/person.png" GARMENT_PATH = "/path/to/garment_top.png" GARMENT2_PATH = None # optional with open(PERSON_PATH, "rb") as f: person_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() with open(GARMENT_PATH, "rb") as f: garment_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() payload = { "prompt": PROMPT, "person": person_b64, "garment": garment_b64, "width": 1024, "height": 1024, "steps": 2, "output_format": "png", } if GARMENT2_PATH: with open(GARMENT2_PATH, "rb") as f: payload["garment_2"] = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() submit = requests.post(f"{BASE}/v1/flux-try-on", headers=HEADERS, json=payload) submit.raise_for_status() meta = submit.json() task_id = meta["id"] poll_url = meta.get("polling_url", f"{BASE}/v1/get_result?id={task_id}") while True: r = requests.get(poll_url, headers={"X-Key": API_KEY}) r.raise_for_status() result = r.json() status = result.get("status") if status == "Ready": print("Result URL:", result["result"]["sample"]) break if status in {"Error", "Request Moderated", "Content Moderated", "Task not found"}: raise RuntimeError(f"VTO failed with status: {status} | payload: {result}") time.sleep(1) ``` --- ## Input fields Use `person` + `garment` as the minimum payload.
Field Type Required Notes
--- --- ---: ---
`prompt` string yes Natural-language styling instruction
`person` base64 string no\* Person image (mapped to `input_image`)
`garment` base64 string no\* Garment reference/references (mapped to `input_image_2`)
`width` int no `>=64`, max total output 4MP
`height` int no `>=64`, max total output 4MP
`steps` int no `1-4`, defaults to 4
`seed` int no For reproducibility
`output_format` string no `jpeg` (default), `png`, `webp`
`webhook_url` URL no Async callback
`webhook_secret` string no Signature secret
- In practice, provide at least `person` and `garment` for useful try-on behavior. --- ## Prompting tips - Keep prompts focused on fit, pose consistency, lighting, and material realism. - Mention garment category and desired drape, for example: denim jacket, oversized tee, tailored trousers. - If identity preservation matters, explicitly ask to preserve face, hairstyle, and body proportions. Example prompts: - `person wearing provided bomber jacket, preserve face and pose, realistic fabric wrinkles` - `swap upper body garment only, preserve lower body clothing and background` - `fit provided top and bottom garments, full body fashion photo, clean studio lighting` --- ## Key details
**Endpoint** `POST https://labs.us2.bfl.ai/v1/flux-try-on`
**Auth** `X-Key: $BFL_API_KEY`
**Result polling** `GET https://labs.us2.bfl.ai/v1/get_result?id=`
**Access** Restricted allowlist (partner orgs + internal)
--- ## Troubleshooting - `403 Forbidden`: your project or org is not allowlisted for VTO. - `422`/validation errors: check base64 encoding and field types. - Poor garment transfer: tighten prompt wording and ensure garment reference is clean and well-lit.

You can try it out directly here: [Black Forest Labs - Frontier AI Lab](https://showcase-vto.preview.bfl.ai/) Your domain should be already whitelisted, but in case that you do not have access to the app: please let us know! ## Before / After examples ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/4c6dc6ab-0a98-4845-94a2-af6b47c76abc/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB4662QZOE5L3%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095825Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCICGknLlsw6TttDU%2FnmtpanbF9ZBq%2F2uXkuSwVq%2BSGEplAiEAtmrM2tttmRjKcjRLOZV5tebNpVFjCmr0fMGjhNAugSIq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDBkh%2F4u9wHVPMlvJOCrcAzbvXedWARBhcmbzAMwmoUr51hjZtCw%2FOyyiOoOLi6uMOirtGk292CgJVBYryitd%2BuBGctaWsaQzAU%2BOLfd%2F239JKc5BNrgMaC9UhePetDiCImdpOY8v5ErcHY5g8Waf04pVuQicfbngoyW8rhVt4j6icSCOBGS7XIPZcxUVxO4VoLeRHWvskNwA17tkDNvHXfh8HRYk2qLiK0fupmHJzEsC0rHhm9yZTuioC8zdJ7zJsEorC2mCzCGrO0nxm%2FyUpa1pOaGlq5gB%2FQ9syQ9rlwpdmOs0KqJU%2F9%2BxWLyuR15%2FpBYUQ2t2VSipy2wTVuLTBKEkUQxZSuXIFfkX5tNlmRQXsKA8MkLDCLuOXiB%2B2VkfPnvuf6zw6f2GwtjaoTTYcr3eyFJ%2FVP%2BOijxfVhEw82LxKIM098SopbUfQiNxXxdJHI1BqL%2BM8E80ptMredVRLuH4S38X8ypudCr852rQF8lN%2F8uiEbUPDHdpHMFRJIIMReSaOyfJlw9NbqyB7r3GCqmoZaicLYF62bpayr5yElClrkF83kz0KP1BujszDPX%2B%2F73BaPykmC6iau2vO3DYRohKrROZBM3BSi270%2FHkL9ZAISYOj0wUpQ8Z11uMnXsBUyNVL2AJyQM2yLUdMLmvks8GOqUBx77I4WdCT2A6yU65v5j9krkHXzKSZpA2Lj4LRqJQxmsPB0hMvAXLhlqzankwQMsjBYTulr3CrLCxpnaCy01enfBHCC0Sevxa4MdrsgFg2xxEAhi6A6GHupLow%2BOGLiYT2RnJPdH06G8xlj%2Bq%2FC86FUXz6NodEZy%2FsfVSJdaHPY2%2BYrl85OpoVmSAdBCwW8bOh0UmckCAlz5KbVOrK0sH%2BdQwxaAG&X-Amz-Signature=aec781259d3f16426568619510cd1f69b80a9fdaf028cbb72a5beaca198f97aa&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) --- ## Get started in 30 seconds **1. Get access + API key** You need: - an approved API key - organization access to the VTO route If you are not sure your project is allowlisted, contact the BFL team. **2. Submit a VTO request** ```bash PERSON_B64="$(base64 < /path/to/person.png | tr -d '\n')" GARMENT_B64="$(base64 < /path/to/garment_top.png | tr -d '\n')" # Optional second garment (for bottom, jacket layer, etc.) GARMENT2_B64="$(base64 < /path/to/garment_bottom.png | tr -d '\n')" jq -n \ --arg person "$PERSON_B64" \ --arg garment "$GARMENT_B64" \ '{ prompt: "model is wearing the provided garments, realistic studio lighting, clean background", person: $person, garment: $garment, garment_2: (if $garment2 == "" then null else $garment2 end), width: 1024, height: 1024, output_format: "png" }' > /tmp/vto_request.json curl -sS -X POST "https://labs.eu2.bfl.ai/v1/flux-try-on" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-Key: $BFL_API_KEY" \ --data-binary @/tmp/vto_request.json ``` Response: ```json {"id":"xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx","polling_url":"..."} ``` **3. Poll for your result** ```bash curl -sS "https://labs.eu2.bfl.ai/v1/get_result?id=YOUR_TASK_ID" \ -H "X-Key: $BFL_API_KEY" ``` When `status` is `"Ready"`, use `result.sample`. --- ## Performance tip If you want to send 2 or more garment images, we recommend merging them into a single canvas first to keep latency down. In our testing, we could not notice any quality degradation from doing this. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/ca070cd9-81da-4dfc-af0d-3fdc829da054/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB4662QZOE5L3%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095825Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCICGknLlsw6TttDU%2FnmtpanbF9ZBq%2F2uXkuSwVq%2BSGEplAiEAtmrM2tttmRjKcjRLOZV5tebNpVFjCmr0fMGjhNAugSIq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDBkh%2F4u9wHVPMlvJOCrcAzbvXedWARBhcmbzAMwmoUr51hjZtCw%2FOyyiOoOLi6uMOirtGk292CgJVBYryitd%2BuBGctaWsaQzAU%2BOLfd%2F239JKc5BNrgMaC9UhePetDiCImdpOY8v5ErcHY5g8Waf04pVuQicfbngoyW8rhVt4j6icSCOBGS7XIPZcxUVxO4VoLeRHWvskNwA17tkDNvHXfh8HRYk2qLiK0fupmHJzEsC0rHhm9yZTuioC8zdJ7zJsEorC2mCzCGrO0nxm%2FyUpa1pOaGlq5gB%2FQ9syQ9rlwpdmOs0KqJU%2F9%2BxWLyuR15%2FpBYUQ2t2VSipy2wTVuLTBKEkUQxZSuXIFfkX5tNlmRQXsKA8MkLDCLuOXiB%2B2VkfPnvuf6zw6f2GwtjaoTTYcr3eyFJ%2FVP%2BOijxfVhEw82LxKIM098SopbUfQiNxXxdJHI1BqL%2BM8E80ptMredVRLuH4S38X8ypudCr852rQF8lN%2F8uiEbUPDHdpHMFRJIIMReSaOyfJlw9NbqyB7r3GCqmoZaicLYF62bpayr5yElClrkF83kz0KP1BujszDPX%2B%2F73BaPykmC6iau2vO3DYRohKrROZBM3BSi270%2FHkL9ZAISYOj0wUpQ8Z11uMnXsBUyNVL2AJyQM2yLUdMLmvks8GOqUBx77I4WdCT2A6yU65v5j9krkHXzKSZpA2Lj4LRqJQxmsPB0hMvAXLhlqzankwQMsjBYTulr3CrLCxpnaCy01enfBHCC0Sevxa4MdrsgFg2xxEAhi6A6GHupLow%2BOGLiYT2RnJPdH06G8xlj%2Bq%2FC86FUXz6NodEZy%2FsfVSJdaHPY2%2BYrl85OpoVmSAdBCwW8bOh0UmckCAlz5KbVOrK0sH%2BdQwxaAG&X-Amz-Signature=e94227315d9205d72a2adbdb6daf67c149c7a321de5c094a068399d3f3000ea7&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) --- ## Python quick start ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import base64 import os import time import requests API_KEY = os.environ["BFL_API_KEY"] BASE = "https://labs.us2.bfl.ai" HEADERS = {"X-Key": API_KEY, "Content-Type": "application/json"} PROMPT = "model is wearing the provided garments, realistic fabric detail" PERSON_PATH = "/path/to/person.png" GARMENT_PATH = "/path/to/garment_top.png" GARMENT2_PATH = None # optional with open(PERSON_PATH, "rb") as f: person_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() with open(GARMENT_PATH, "rb") as f: garment_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() payload = { "prompt": PROMPT, "person": person_b64, "garment": garment_b64, "width": 1024, "height": 1024, "steps": 2, "output_format": "png", } if GARMENT2_PATH: with open(GARMENT2_PATH, "rb") as f: payload["garment_2"] = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() submit = requests.post(f"{BASE}/v1/flux-try-on", headers=HEADERS, json=payload) submit.raise_for_status() meta = submit.json() task_id = meta["id"] poll_url = meta.get("polling_url", f"{BASE}/v1/get_result?id={task_id}") while True: r = requests.get(poll_url, headers={"X-Key": API_KEY}) r.raise_for_status() result = r.json() status = result.get("status") if status == "Ready": print("Result URL:", result["result"]["sample"]) break if status in {"Error", "Request Moderated", "Content Moderated", "Task not found"}: raise RuntimeError(f"VTO failed with status: {status} | payload: {result}") time.sleep(1) ``` --- ## Input fields Use `person` + `garment` as the minimum payload.
Field Type Required Notes
--- --- ---: ---
`prompt` string yes Natural-language styling instruction
`person` base64 string no\* Person image (mapped to `input_image`)
`garment` base64 string no\* Garment reference/references (mapped to `input_image_2`)
`width` int no `>=64`, max total output 4MP
`height` int no `>=64`, max total output 4MP
`steps` int no `1-4`, defaults to 4
`seed` int no For reproducibility
`output_format` string no `jpeg` (default), `png`, `webp`
`webhook_url` URL no Async callback
`webhook_secret` string no Signature secret
- In practice, provide at least `person` and `garment` for useful try-on behavior. --- ## Prompting tips - Keep prompts focused on fit, pose consistency, lighting, and material realism. - Mention garment category and desired drape, for example: denim jacket, oversized tee, tailored trousers. - If identity preservation matters, explicitly ask to preserve face, hairstyle, and body proportions. Example prompts: - `person wearing provided bomber jacket, preserve face and pose, realistic fabric wrinkles` - `swap upper body garment only, preserve lower body clothing and background` - `fit provided top and bottom garments, full body fashion photo, clean studio lighting` --- ## Key details
**Endpoint** `POST https://labs.us2.bfl.ai/v1/flux-try-on`
**Auth** `X-Key: $BFL_API_KEY`
**Result polling** `GET https://labs.us2.bfl.ai/v1/get_result?id=`
**Access** Restricted allowlist (partner orgs + internal)
--- ## Troubleshooting - `403 Forbidden`: your project or org is not allowlisted for VTO. - `422`/validation errors: check base64 encoding and field types. - Poor garment transfer: tighten prompt wording and ensure garment reference is clean and well-lit.

326c3702-22d5-8012-87df-c12e8e0b85eb.title: Model versioning strategy
326c3702-22d5-8012-87df-c12e8e0b85eb.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/326c370222d5801287dfc12e8e0b85eb as of 2026-04-08T11:45:35.509Z: {"title":"Model versioning strategy"} ## **Motivation** Our current model naming is ad-hoc: `flux-2-pro`, `flux-2-pro-preview`, `flux-2-klein-9b-preview`, `flux-kontext-pro`, etc. There is no systematic way to distinguish between model generations, track when a model was released, communicate lifecycle status, or give customers a predictable deprecation timeline. We want to adopt a versioning model inspired by Anthropic's approach: **dated snapshot versions** for pinning, **aliases** for convenience, and a **formal lifecycle** with guaranteed notice periods. We propose to move to this new strategy starting Flux 3 and gradually phase out old endpoints. ## **1. Naming Convention** ### **1.1 Model Families** A model family is a product line that shares an architecture tier:
**Family** **Description** **Current equivalents**
`flux-pro` Flagship quality `flux-2-pro`, `flux-2-max`
`flux-klein` Fast, cost-efficient `flux-2-klein-9b`, `flux-2-klein-4b`
`flux-kontext` `flux-kontext-pro`, `flux-kontext-max`
`flux-flex` `flux-2-flex`
???
Family names are stable and do not change across generations. ### **1.2 Dated Versions (Snapshots)** Every model release gets a **dated identifier** using the format: `{family}-{generation}-{date}` - **generation**: major model generation (`2`, `3`, …) - **date**: release date as `YYYYMMDD` Examples:
**Dated version** **Description**
`flux-pro-2-20260401` FLUX Pro gen-2, released 2026-04-01
`flux-pro-2-20260715` Updated FLUX Pro gen-2 snapshot
`flux-klein-2-20260401` FLUX Klein gen-2, released 2026-04-01
`flux-kontext-2-20260401` FLUX Kontext gen-2, released 2026-04-01
Dated versions are **immutable**: once published, the model weights and behavior behind a dated version never change. ### **1.3 Aliases** Aliases are mutable pointers to the latest recommended dated version within a family and generation:
**Alias** **Points to (example)**
`flux-pro-2` `flux-pro-2-20260715`
`flux-klein-2` `flux-klein-2-20260401`
`flux-kontext-2` `flux-kontext-2-20260401`
When we release a new snapshot, the alias is updated. Customers using aliases get the latest model automatically. Customers using dated versions are unaffected. **Top-level aliases** (optional, for discovery):
**Alias** **Points to**
`flux-pro` `flux-pro-2` (latest generation)
`flux-klein` `flux-klein-2`
### **1.4 ****Quality Tiers**** Within a Family** Where a family has multiple quality levels (e.g., current `flux-2-pro` vs `flux-2-max`), encode the tier in the family name:
**New name** **Current equivalent**
`flux-pro-2-{date}` `flux-2-pro`
`flux-pro-max-2-{date}` `flux-2-max`
`flux-kontext-2-{date}` `flux-kontext-pro`
`flux-kontext-max-2-{date}` `flux-kontext-max`
## **2. Model Lifecycle** Every model passes through four states: `Active → Legacy (optional) → Deprecated → Retired`
**State** **Definition** **API behavior**
**Active** Fully supported and recommended Requests succeed normally
**Legacy** Still works, will not receive updates, may be deprecated in the future Requests succeed; response includes `X-Model-Status: legacy` header
**Deprecated** Retirement date assigned; not available to new customers Requests succeed for existing users; response includes `X-Model-Status: deprecated` and `X-Model-Retirement-Date` headers
**Retired** No longer available Requests return `410 Gone` with a JSON body containing the replacement model
### **2.1 Notice Periods** Model lifecycle transitions map to our API communication tiers:
**Transition** **Communication tier** **Minimum notice** **Recommended notice**
Active → Deprecated Tier 2 (Deprecation) 30 days 60 days
Deprecated → Retired Tier 1 (Breaking Change) 30 days 30 days
The combined timeline from deprecation notice to retirement is **at minimum 60 days** (30 + 30). ### **2.2 Deprecation Response Headers** When a model is deprecated or legacy, every successful response includes: `X-Model-Status: deprecated` `X-Model-Retirement-Date: 2026-09-01` `X-Model-Replacement: flux-pro-2-20260715` This allows automated monitoring — customers can alert on these headers without reading email. ### **2.3 ****Retired Model Response** ```javascript { "error": { "type": "model_retired", "message": "flux-pro-2-20260401 was retired on 2026-09-01. Use flux-pro-2-20260715 instead.", "replacement": "flux-pro-2-20260715" } } ``` HTTP status: `410 Gone`. ## **3. Migration from Current to New Naming** ### **3.1 New Models (FLUX 3+): Versioned from Day One** The new naming convention takes effect with **FLUX 3** onwards. Existing FLUX 1.x and FLUX 2 endpoints keep their current URLs and are not renamed. Instead, they receive lightweight deprecation headers through the lifecycle middleware when their replacements ship. Every FLUX 3 model launches under the new naming convention with dated snapshots, aliases, and full lifecycle management via the model registry. ### **3.2 Existing Models (FLUX 1.x, FLUX 2): Deprecation Headers Only** Existing endpoints (`/v1/flux-2-pro`, `/v1/flux-kontext-pro`, `/v1/flux-pro-1.1-ultra`, etc.) are **not renamed or moved into the versioned registry**. Their routing, cost calculation, worker dispatch, and handler code remain exactly as they are today. When a FLUX 3 replacement ships, the corresponding FLUX 2 / 1.x endpoint receives deprecation metadata by setting `request.state.model_version` in its existing handler or setup function. The `LifecycleHeadersMiddleware` reads this and injects headers automatically. Lifecycle progression for an existing endpoint:\*
When Status Response headers Handler change
Before FLUX 3 launches (unchanged) None None
FLUX 3 launches (Day 0) Legacy (where applicable) `X-Model-Status: legacy` Add one line in setup function
Deprecation notice (Day 0 of deprecation) Deprecated `X-Model-Status: deprecated` + `X-Model-Retirement-Date` + `X-Model-Replacement` Update lifecycle fields
Retirement (Day 60+) Retired `410 Gone` with replacement in body Replace handler body with 410 response
### **3.3 Implementation Changes** **Route Config Domain Model** Add lifecycle metadata to the route config: ```javascript class ModelLifecycle(BaseModel): status: Literal["active", "legacy", "deprecated", "retired"] deprecated_at: date | None = None retirement_date: date | None = None replacement: str | None = None class RouteConfig(BaseModel): # ... existing fields ... lifecycle: ModelLifecycle = ModelLifecycle(status="active") ``` **Alias Resolution** Add an alias registry that maps alias names to dated versions: ```javascript MODEL_ALIASES: dict[str, str] = { "flux-pro-2": "flux-pro-2-20260401", "flux-pro-max-2": "flux-pro-max-2-20260401", "flux-klein-2": "flux-klein-2-20260401", # ... } ``` The router resolves aliases before dispatching to setup functions. The resolved dated version is recorded in the request metadata for billing and analytics. **Response Middleware** Add middleware that inspects `RouteConfig.lifecycle` and injects the appropriate headers: ```javascript def add_lifecycle_headers(response: Response, config: RouteConfig) -> None: lifecycle = config.lifecycle if lifecycle.status in ("legacy", "deprecated"): response.headers["X-Model-Status"] = lifecycle.status if lifecycle.retirement_date: response.headers["X-Model-Retirement-Date"] = lifecycle.retirement_date.isoformat() if lifecycle.replacement: response.headers["X-Model-Replacement"] = lifecycle.replacement ``` **Retired Model Handler** ```javascript def retired_model_handler(config: RouteConfig) -> JSONResponse: return JSONResponse( status_code=410, content={ "error": { "type": "model_retired", "message": f"This model was retired on {config.lifecycle.retirement_date}. " f"Use {config.lifecycle.replacement} instead.", "replacement": config.lifecycle.replacement, } }, ) ``` ## **4. Customer Communication Plan** This section follows the API Communication Procedures framework. Model lifecycle transitions classify as follows:
**Event** **Tier** **Rationale**
New model version released Tier 3 (Non-Breaking) Additive — new endpoint, no removal
Model deprecated (notice) Tier 2 (Deprecation) Advance notice that an endpoint will be removed
Model retired (removal) Tier 1 (Breaking Change) Endpoint ceases to function
### **4.1 Communication Channels** **Primary channels** (required for Tier 1 and Tier 2):
**Channel** **Audience**
Email / Customer.io Account contacts with usage of the affected model
Slack Account contacts with usage of the affected model
Status page Public — scheduled maintenance entry for the retirement date
**Secondary channels** (used as appropriate):
**Channel** **Audience**
API response headers All API consumers (automated monitoring)
Developer documentation Public
In-dashboard banner All logged-in users
Direct outreach by GTM Enterprise customers
Blog post Public (for major model launches)
### **4.2 Communication Timeline** ```javascript Day 0 - Tier 2 — Deprecation Notice Model moves to Deprecated status. - Email + Slack: "{model} is deprecated, retiring on Day 60" - Status page: scheduled retirement event created - Dashboard banner appears - API headers: X-Model-Status: deprecated, X-Model-Retirement-Date - Documentation updated (endpoint marked deprecated) - GTM briefed; enterprise customer outreach begins Day 30 - Tier 1 — Breaking Change Reminder 30 days until removal. - Email + Slack: "30 days until {model} is removed — take action now" - Engineering checks usage of affected model by organization - GTM/Marketing aligned on additional comms if usage remains high Day 53 - Final Warning 7 days until removal. - Email + Slack: "{model} is being removed in 7 days" Day 60 - Tier 1 — Endpoint Removed Model moves to Retired status. - Requests return 410 Gone with replacement model in body - Email + Slack: "{model} has been retired" - Status page updated - Documentation: endpoint removed from schema ``` ### **4.3 Email Template Examples ** **Day 0 — Tier 2 Deprecation Notice** > *Subject: \[Action Required\] FLUX Pro 2 model **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** is being deprecated
We are releasing an improved version of FLUX Pro 2 (**`flux-pro-2-20260715`**).
The previous version **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** is now **deprecated** and will be **removed on \{retirement_date\}**.
**What you need to do:**
• If you use the alias **`flux-pro-2`**: no action needed — the alias already points to the new version.
• If you pin to **`flux-pro-2-20260401`**: update your integration to use **`flux-pro-2-20260715`** before \{retirement_date\}.
After removal, requests to **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** will return HTTP 410.
See our migration guide for details.* **Day 30 — Tier 1 Breaking Change Reminder** > *Subject: \[Action Required\] **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** is being removed in 30 days
Our records show you still have active usage of **`flux-pro-2-20260401`**. This endpoint will stop accepting requests on \{retirement_date\}.
Please migrate to **`flux-pro-2-20260715`** or use the **`flux-pro-2`** alias.* **Day 53 — Final Warning** > *Subject: \[Urgent\] **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** is being removed in 7 days
This model will stop accepting requests on \{retirement_date\}. Migrate now to avoid service disruption.* ### **4.4 Usage Audit** Before sending the Day 0 deprecation email and again at Day 30: 1. Query billing data for all API keys that have called the affected model in the last 30 days. 2. Group by organization. 3. Include volume (request count) and last-used timestamp. 4. Attach to the communication so customers know which of their API keys are affected. 5. Share the Day 30 audit with GTM for targeted enterprise outreach. ### **4.5 Tracking Checklist** For each deprecation/retirement cycle: - [ ] Change is tested and impact scoped by Engineering. Retirement date is defined. - [ ] Retirement event added to Maintenance Calendar. - [ ] Customer contact details verified in Customer.io / email system. - [ ] Customer-facing documentation updated and peer reviewed. - [ ] Day 0: Tier 2 emails and Slack messages sent (deprecation notice with dates and unambiguous actions). - [ ] Day 0: GTM and Marketing teams briefed. - [ ] Day 0: Enterprise customers contacted directly by GTM. - [ ] Day 30: Usage audit run. Tier 1 reminder emails and Slack messages sent. - [ ] Day 30: Engineering checks usage; GTM/Marketing aligned on additional comms if needed. - [ ] Day 30: Enterprise customer responses/acknowledgments tracked. - [ ] Day 53: Final warning emails and Slack messages sent. - [ ] Day 60: Endpoint retired. Confirmation communications sent. - [ ] Post-retirement: issues documented, retro scheduled if needed. ## **5. Finetuned Model Handling** Finetuned models follow their base model's lifecycle with an extended grace period: - When a base model is deprecated, finetuned endpoints built on it get an additional 30 days (90 days total from deprecation to retirement). - Customers are offered a migration path: re-finetune on the new base model with a discount or credit. - Finetuned model names include the base model date: `flux-pro-2-20260401:ft:{customer_id}:{finetune_id}`. ## **6. Internal and Partner Endpoints**
**Endpoint type** **Versioning** **Deprecation policy**
`-internal` Follow same naming, no public notice required Coordinate with internal teams via Slack
`-private` (org-allowlisted) Follow same naming Direct outreach to the partner org
`-pg` (playground) Follow alias only Update playground to use alias
`-vsco`, `-mistral` (partner) Follow same naming Per-partner SLA, minimum 60 days
## **7. API Schema and Documentation** ### **7.1 OpenAPI Spec** - Active models: listed in schema with full documentation. - Legacy models: listed in schema, marked with `deprecated: true` in the operation metadata. - Deprecated models: listed in schema, marked `deprecated: true`, description includes retirement date and replacement. - Retired models: removed from schema. The 410 handler is not documented in the public schema. ### **7.2 Model Discovery Endpoint** Add a `/v1/models` endpoint (or expand existing) that returns: ```javascript { "models": [ { "id": "flux-pro-2-20260715", "family": "flux-pro", "generation": 2, "status": "active", "aliases": ["flux-pro-2", "flux-pro"], "released": "2026-07-15", "retirement_date": null }, { "id": "flux-pro-2-20260401", "family": "flux-pro", "generation": 2, "status": "deprecated", "aliases": [], "released": "2026-04-01", "retirement_date": "2026-09-01", "replacement": "flux-pro-2-20260715" } ] } ``` ## **8. Success Criteria** - Every model version is identifiable by a unique, immutable dated name. - Customers using aliases experience seamless upgrades. - Customers pinning to dated versions get at least 60 days from Tier 2 deprecation notice to Tier 1 retirement. - Enterprise customers receive direct GTM outreach from Day 0 of the deprecation cycle. - Zero silent breakage: retired models return structured errors with the replacement. - Usage audit data is available before every deprecation email. - Response headers enable automated monitoring of model lifecycle status. ## **9. Open Questions** 1. **Generation numbering**: Start at 3 for FLUX 3. Existing endpoints keep their current names and are not back-numbered. 2. **Alias update cadence**: Immediate -- that is the alias contract. When a new snapshot ships, the alias points to it right away. 3. **Preview models**: Should preview/beta models have dated versions, or are they exempt since they carry no stability guarantee? 4. **FLUX 1.x / 2.x:** Not renamed. Receive deprecation headers via `LEGACY_DEPRECATIONS` when replacements ship. Retired via 410 after the standard notice period. 5. **Snapshot cadence:** No more than quarterly for mainline models to keep communication load manageable. 6. We need **a list of drop in replacements** - which model replaces which and keeps the quality/improves experience while offering the same quality (do we have this mentioned in the customer facing documentation already?)

raw.title: Model versioning strategy
raw.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/326c370222d5801287dfc12e8e0b85eb as of 2026-04-08T11:45:35.509Z: {"title":"Model versioning strategy"} ## **Motivation** Our current model naming is ad-hoc: `flux-2-pro`, `flux-2-pro-preview`, `flux-2-klein-9b-preview`, `flux-kontext-pro`, etc. There is no systematic way to distinguish between model generations, track when a model was released, communicate lifecycle status, or give customers a predictable deprecation timeline. We want to adopt a versioning model inspired by Anthropic's approach: **dated snapshot versions** for pinning, **aliases** for convenience, and a **formal lifecycle** with guaranteed notice periods. We propose to move to this new strategy starting Flux 3 and gradually phase out old endpoints. ## **1. Naming Convention** ### **1.1 Model Families** A model family is a product line that shares an architecture tier:
**Family** **Description** **Current equivalents**
`flux-pro` Flagship quality `flux-2-pro`, `flux-2-max`
`flux-klein` Fast, cost-efficient `flux-2-klein-9b`, `flux-2-klein-4b`
`flux-kontext` `flux-kontext-pro`, `flux-kontext-max`
`flux-flex` `flux-2-flex`
???
Family names are stable and do not change across generations. ### **1.2 Dated Versions (Snapshots)** Every model release gets a **dated identifier** using the format: `{family}-{generation}-{date}` - **generation**: major model generation (`2`, `3`, …) - **date**: release date as `YYYYMMDD` Examples:
**Dated version** **Description**
`flux-pro-2-20260401` FLUX Pro gen-2, released 2026-04-01
`flux-pro-2-20260715` Updated FLUX Pro gen-2 snapshot
`flux-klein-2-20260401` FLUX Klein gen-2, released 2026-04-01
`flux-kontext-2-20260401` FLUX Kontext gen-2, released 2026-04-01
Dated versions are **immutable**: once published, the model weights and behavior behind a dated version never change. ### **1.3 Aliases** Aliases are mutable pointers to the latest recommended dated version within a family and generation:
**Alias** **Points to (example)**
`flux-pro-2` `flux-pro-2-20260715`
`flux-klein-2` `flux-klein-2-20260401`
`flux-kontext-2` `flux-kontext-2-20260401`
When we release a new snapshot, the alias is updated. Customers using aliases get the latest model automatically. Customers using dated versions are unaffected. **Top-level aliases** (optional, for discovery):
**Alias** **Points to**
`flux-pro` `flux-pro-2` (latest generation)
`flux-klein` `flux-klein-2`
### **1.4 ****Quality Tiers**** Within a Family** Where a family has multiple quality levels (e.g., current `flux-2-pro` vs `flux-2-max`), encode the tier in the family name:
**New name** **Current equivalent**
`flux-pro-2-{date}` `flux-2-pro`
`flux-pro-max-2-{date}` `flux-2-max`
`flux-kontext-2-{date}` `flux-kontext-pro`
`flux-kontext-max-2-{date}` `flux-kontext-max`
## **2. Model Lifecycle** Every model passes through four states: `Active → Legacy (optional) → Deprecated → Retired`
**State** **Definition** **API behavior**
**Active** Fully supported and recommended Requests succeed normally
**Legacy** Still works, will not receive updates, may be deprecated in the future Requests succeed; response includes `X-Model-Status: legacy` header
**Deprecated** Retirement date assigned; not available to new customers Requests succeed for existing users; response includes `X-Model-Status: deprecated` and `X-Model-Retirement-Date` headers
**Retired** No longer available Requests return `410 Gone` with a JSON body containing the replacement model
### **2.1 Notice Periods** Model lifecycle transitions map to our API communication tiers:
**Transition** **Communication tier** **Minimum notice** **Recommended notice**
Active → Deprecated Tier 2 (Deprecation) 30 days 60 days
Deprecated → Retired Tier 1 (Breaking Change) 30 days 30 days
The combined timeline from deprecation notice to retirement is **at minimum 60 days** (30 + 30). ### **2.2 Deprecation Response Headers** When a model is deprecated or legacy, every successful response includes: `X-Model-Status: deprecated` `X-Model-Retirement-Date: 2026-09-01` `X-Model-Replacement: flux-pro-2-20260715` This allows automated monitoring — customers can alert on these headers without reading email. ### **2.3 ****Retired Model Response** ```javascript { "error": { "type": "model_retired", "message": "flux-pro-2-20260401 was retired on 2026-09-01. Use flux-pro-2-20260715 instead.", "replacement": "flux-pro-2-20260715" } } ``` HTTP status: `410 Gone`. ## **3. Migration from Current to New Naming** ### **3.1 New Models (FLUX 3+): Versioned from Day One** The new naming convention takes effect with **FLUX 3** onwards. Existing FLUX 1.x and FLUX 2 endpoints keep their current URLs and are not renamed. Instead, they receive lightweight deprecation headers through the lifecycle middleware when their replacements ship. Every FLUX 3 model launches under the new naming convention with dated snapshots, aliases, and full lifecycle management via the model registry. ### **3.2 Existing Models (FLUX 1.x, FLUX 2): Deprecation Headers Only** Existing endpoints (`/v1/flux-2-pro`, `/v1/flux-kontext-pro`, `/v1/flux-pro-1.1-ultra`, etc.) are **not renamed or moved into the versioned registry**. Their routing, cost calculation, worker dispatch, and handler code remain exactly as they are today. When a FLUX 3 replacement ships, the corresponding FLUX 2 / 1.x endpoint receives deprecation metadata by setting `request.state.model_version` in its existing handler or setup function. The `LifecycleHeadersMiddleware` reads this and injects headers automatically. Lifecycle progression for an existing endpoint:\*
When Status Response headers Handler change
Before FLUX 3 launches (unchanged) None None
FLUX 3 launches (Day 0) Legacy (where applicable) `X-Model-Status: legacy` Add one line in setup function
Deprecation notice (Day 0 of deprecation) Deprecated `X-Model-Status: deprecated` + `X-Model-Retirement-Date` + `X-Model-Replacement` Update lifecycle fields
Retirement (Day 60+) Retired `410 Gone` with replacement in body Replace handler body with 410 response
### **3.3 Implementation Changes** **Route Config Domain Model** Add lifecycle metadata to the route config: ```javascript class ModelLifecycle(BaseModel): status: Literal["active", "legacy", "deprecated", "retired"] deprecated_at: date | None = None retirement_date: date | None = None replacement: str | None = None class RouteConfig(BaseModel): # ... existing fields ... lifecycle: ModelLifecycle = ModelLifecycle(status="active") ``` **Alias Resolution** Add an alias registry that maps alias names to dated versions: ```javascript MODEL_ALIASES: dict[str, str] = { "flux-pro-2": "flux-pro-2-20260401", "flux-pro-max-2": "flux-pro-max-2-20260401", "flux-klein-2": "flux-klein-2-20260401", # ... } ``` The router resolves aliases before dispatching to setup functions. The resolved dated version is recorded in the request metadata for billing and analytics. **Response Middleware** Add middleware that inspects `RouteConfig.lifecycle` and injects the appropriate headers: ```javascript def add_lifecycle_headers(response: Response, config: RouteConfig) -> None: lifecycle = config.lifecycle if lifecycle.status in ("legacy", "deprecated"): response.headers["X-Model-Status"] = lifecycle.status if lifecycle.retirement_date: response.headers["X-Model-Retirement-Date"] = lifecycle.retirement_date.isoformat() if lifecycle.replacement: response.headers["X-Model-Replacement"] = lifecycle.replacement ``` **Retired Model Handler** ```javascript def retired_model_handler(config: RouteConfig) -> JSONResponse: return JSONResponse( status_code=410, content={ "error": { "type": "model_retired", "message": f"This model was retired on {config.lifecycle.retirement_date}. " f"Use {config.lifecycle.replacement} instead.", "replacement": config.lifecycle.replacement, } }, ) ``` ## **4. Customer Communication Plan** This section follows the API Communication Procedures framework. Model lifecycle transitions classify as follows:
**Event** **Tier** **Rationale**
New model version released Tier 3 (Non-Breaking) Additive — new endpoint, no removal
Model deprecated (notice) Tier 2 (Deprecation) Advance notice that an endpoint will be removed
Model retired (removal) Tier 1 (Breaking Change) Endpoint ceases to function
### **4.1 Communication Channels** **Primary channels** (required for Tier 1 and Tier 2):
**Channel** **Audience**
Email / Customer.io Account contacts with usage of the affected model
Slack Account contacts with usage of the affected model
Status page Public — scheduled maintenance entry for the retirement date
**Secondary channels** (used as appropriate):
**Channel** **Audience**
API response headers All API consumers (automated monitoring)
Developer documentation Public
In-dashboard banner All logged-in users
Direct outreach by GTM Enterprise customers
Blog post Public (for major model launches)
### **4.2 Communication Timeline** ```javascript Day 0 - Tier 2 — Deprecation Notice Model moves to Deprecated status. - Email + Slack: "{model} is deprecated, retiring on Day 60" - Status page: scheduled retirement event created - Dashboard banner appears - API headers: X-Model-Status: deprecated, X-Model-Retirement-Date - Documentation updated (endpoint marked deprecated) - GTM briefed; enterprise customer outreach begins Day 30 - Tier 1 — Breaking Change Reminder 30 days until removal. - Email + Slack: "30 days until {model} is removed — take action now" - Engineering checks usage of affected model by organization - GTM/Marketing aligned on additional comms if usage remains high Day 53 - Final Warning 7 days until removal. - Email + Slack: "{model} is being removed in 7 days" Day 60 - Tier 1 — Endpoint Removed Model moves to Retired status. - Requests return 410 Gone with replacement model in body - Email + Slack: "{model} has been retired" - Status page updated - Documentation: endpoint removed from schema ``` ### **4.3 Email Template Examples ** **Day 0 — Tier 2 Deprecation Notice** > *Subject: \[Action Required\] FLUX Pro 2 model **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** is being deprecated
We are releasing an improved version of FLUX Pro 2 (**`flux-pro-2-20260715`**).
The previous version **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** is now **deprecated** and will be **removed on \{retirement_date\}**.
**What you need to do:**
• If you use the alias **`flux-pro-2`**: no action needed — the alias already points to the new version.
• If you pin to **`flux-pro-2-20260401`**: update your integration to use **`flux-pro-2-20260715`** before \{retirement_date\}.
After removal, requests to **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** will return HTTP 410.
See our migration guide for details.* **Day 30 — Tier 1 Breaking Change Reminder** > *Subject: \[Action Required\] **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** is being removed in 30 days
Our records show you still have active usage of **`flux-pro-2-20260401`**. This endpoint will stop accepting requests on \{retirement_date\}.
Please migrate to **`flux-pro-2-20260715`** or use the **`flux-pro-2`** alias.* **Day 53 — Final Warning** > *Subject: \[Urgent\] **`flux-pro-2-20260401`** is being removed in 7 days
This model will stop accepting requests on \{retirement_date\}. Migrate now to avoid service disruption.* ### **4.4 Usage Audit** Before sending the Day 0 deprecation email and again at Day 30: 1. Query billing data for all API keys that have called the affected model in the last 30 days. 2. Group by organization. 3. Include volume (request count) and last-used timestamp. 4. Attach to the communication so customers know which of their API keys are affected. 5. Share the Day 30 audit with GTM for targeted enterprise outreach. ### **4.5 Tracking Checklist** For each deprecation/retirement cycle: - [ ] Change is tested and impact scoped by Engineering. Retirement date is defined. - [ ] Retirement event added to Maintenance Calendar. - [ ] Customer contact details verified in Customer.io / email system. - [ ] Customer-facing documentation updated and peer reviewed. - [ ] Day 0: Tier 2 emails and Slack messages sent (deprecation notice with dates and unambiguous actions). - [ ] Day 0: GTM and Marketing teams briefed. - [ ] Day 0: Enterprise customers contacted directly by GTM. - [ ] Day 30: Usage audit run. Tier 1 reminder emails and Slack messages sent. - [ ] Day 30: Engineering checks usage; GTM/Marketing aligned on additional comms if needed. - [ ] Day 30: Enterprise customer responses/acknowledgments tracked. - [ ] Day 53: Final warning emails and Slack messages sent. - [ ] Day 60: Endpoint retired. Confirmation communications sent. - [ ] Post-retirement: issues documented, retro scheduled if needed. ## **5. Finetuned Model Handling** Finetuned models follow their base model's lifecycle with an extended grace period: - When a base model is deprecated, finetuned endpoints built on it get an additional 30 days (90 days total from deprecation to retirement). - Customers are offered a migration path: re-finetune on the new base model with a discount or credit. - Finetuned model names include the base model date: `flux-pro-2-20260401:ft:{customer_id}:{finetune_id}`. ## **6. Internal and Partner Endpoints**
**Endpoint type** **Versioning** **Deprecation policy**
`-internal` Follow same naming, no public notice required Coordinate with internal teams via Slack
`-private` (org-allowlisted) Follow same naming Direct outreach to the partner org
`-pg` (playground) Follow alias only Update playground to use alias
`-vsco`, `-mistral` (partner) Follow same naming Per-partner SLA, minimum 60 days
## **7. API Schema and Documentation** ### **7.1 OpenAPI Spec** - Active models: listed in schema with full documentation. - Legacy models: listed in schema, marked with `deprecated: true` in the operation metadata. - Deprecated models: listed in schema, marked `deprecated: true`, description includes retirement date and replacement. - Retired models: removed from schema. The 410 handler is not documented in the public schema. ### **7.2 Model Discovery Endpoint** Add a `/v1/models` endpoint (or expand existing) that returns: ```javascript { "models": [ { "id": "flux-pro-2-20260715", "family": "flux-pro", "generation": 2, "status": "active", "aliases": ["flux-pro-2", "flux-pro"], "released": "2026-07-15", "retirement_date": null }, { "id": "flux-pro-2-20260401", "family": "flux-pro", "generation": 2, "status": "deprecated", "aliases": [], "released": "2026-04-01", "retirement_date": "2026-09-01", "replacement": "flux-pro-2-20260715" } ] } ``` ## **8. Success Criteria** - Every model version is identifiable by a unique, immutable dated name. - Customers using aliases experience seamless upgrades. - Customers pinning to dated versions get at least 60 days from Tier 2 deprecation notice to Tier 1 retirement. - Enterprise customers receive direct GTM outreach from Day 0 of the deprecation cycle. - Zero silent breakage: retired models return structured errors with the replacement. - Usage audit data is available before every deprecation email. - Response headers enable automated monitoring of model lifecycle status. ## **9. Open Questions** 1. **Generation numbering**: Start at 3 for FLUX 3. Existing endpoints keep their current names and are not back-numbered. 2. **Alias update cadence**: Immediate -- that is the alias contract. When a new snapshot ships, the alias points to it right away. 3. **Preview models**: Should preview/beta models have dated versions, or are they exempt since they carry no stability guarantee? 4. **FLUX 1.x / 2.x:** Not renamed. Receive deprecation headers via `LEGACY_DEPRECATIONS` when replacements ship. Retired via 410 after the standard notice period. 5. **Snapshot cadence:** No more than quarterly for mainline models to keep communication load manageable. 6. We need **a list of drop in replacements** - which model replaces which and keeps the quality/improves experience while offering the same quality (do we have this mentioned in the customer facing documentation already?)

336c3702-22d5-80c6-af9d-e408d1adeb0a.title: [WIP] BFL Data Strategy 2026
336c3702-22d5-80c6-af9d-e408d1adeb0a.text: Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/336c370222d580c6af9de408d1adeb0a as of 2026-04-14T18:18:31.496Z: {"title":"\\[WIP\\] BFL Data Strategy 2026"} --- ### Primer - The importance of data for generative modeling The goal of generative modeling is to approximate a data distribution and - in the case of current frontier AI models - to be able to sample from that distribution in order to create new datapoints from that distribution. The learning algorithm which is employed ensures that the model can approximate the true (and unknown) distribution of the data the model is trained on as good as possible and is therefore the first central cornerstone for training a frontier model. However, the second - and sometimes underestimated - component, is the dataset which is used to train the model. This dataset represents the data distribution the model is targeting learning. It’s easy to imagine that a model won’t be competitive even with the most powerful learning algorithm, if the data distribution it’s trained on (aka the training dataset) is containing low quality training examples - garbage in, garbage out. This is why training data acquisition and processing is strategically extremely important for every foundation model company. As a result of this, we need to treat data as a first class citizen at BFL as well. ### Use Cases vs. Model Capabilities - Separating the target distribution from the conditioning method **The difference between targets and the conditioning ** The training data for foundation models has two main interfaces with the learning algorithm during training, which are the following 1. The* target: *The target is the actual ‘training example’ and it’s used as a reference point to calculate how good the model is performing the task it’s trained to do. From the difference between the model output and the target, the loss is calculated and then backpropagated through the model to update the weights. In fact, for most probabilistic approaches, the target also gives rise to the model input at training time. In those cases, the model input is often a transformation of the target (e.g. a more noisy version of the training example in the case of diffusion models). 2. The* conditioning: *Under conditioning, we subsume all additional input signals that go into the model (at both training and inference), apart from the random variable, that the model learns to generate. These conditioning inputs are what make the model controllable in the end. So if we take e.g. text-to-image models, we want to be able to generate images based (or conditioned) on text prompts. That means that, at train time, we need to have text prompts for each training image we want to use. Note that the conditioning can be more than one additional inputs, e.g. in the case of image-to-video, where we both use a text prompt and an image as conditionings to create a video. (The name image-to-video is very unfortunate, since it’s actually text+image-to-video). From a data perspective, it’s important to separate these two interfaces from each other since they affect different aspects of what the model learns during training. 1. The targets define the visual properties, the data that the model learns to generate will follow. For instance, if a model was only trained on illustrated content, it would not understand photorealism and no matter if I would prompt for ‘a blue bird’, or ‘a photorealistic blue bird’, the model would always create images that would resemble illustrations 2. The conditioning defines how users can interact with the model and how they can apply control to the data that the model generates. For instance, if I only have a dataset of paired text prompts and images, and train a model to generate images conditioned on the text prompts, users cannot use that model for image editing, since training an image editing model would require to always have a set of images (e.g. two images showing the same person in different environments) and (one or more) text prompts describing how to arrive at one image based on one (or multiple) other image(s) in that set. In that sense, the conditioning define the set of tasks that the model is generally capable to do. The above separation is helpful to understand the dimensions along which we should be thinking when it comes to data acquisition. We need to understand what we need along both these dimensions in order to create a well suited dataset for training a state of the art model. Failure to do so will make it likely that we end up with sub-optimal decisions for data acquisition and will make blind spots in our data strategy more likely. **Separating use cases from model capabilities** Based on the above separation of the targets (or target distribution) and the conditioning, we make the following definitions. **Use Case** A *use case* describes the requirements for the targets that we would like to have in a training dataset. Understanding the *use cases* our models are used for will help us answer the question: *How should the target distribution look like, that the model learns to generate during training?* Example: If the use case would be film making, we would rather be looking to license data from movie studies and other types of data, e.g. ads, would not be super important. Note that this is independent of the conditioning and does not tell us something about the model capability that we need. For instance, one could look for image editing data based on this use case, but also every other task, e.g. text-to-video. **Model Capability** A *model capability* describes how users can interact with the model, i.e. it is directly connected to the conditioning information we need at training time. We need to be clear on the model capabilities we want in our model. After we know that, we can answer the question: *How well does our data support the conditioning we want to use to make sure we reach SOTA accuracy and controllability?* Example: If we want our model to be good at multi reference image editing, this tells us that we need training training examples which contain not only a text+image pair (as it would be the case for t2i), but also reference images, containing some visual aspects/objects/characters that are present in the target example as well. However this *doesn’t *tell us something about the the target distribution should look visually. **So what?** Making the distinction between use cases and model capability can help us to get data in a more targeted way and will reduce the probability of blind spots on the data acquisition side. - By selecting use cases we tailor the output distribution to what our customers actually need. - Listing und selecting certain model capabilities we ensure to not forget any interesting new applications that we could takle with a new model. especially for multimodal and general models, it’s important to be clear about which combinations of conditionings we want to support since the number of possibilities is a superlinear function of the number of conditionings. ### Who defines what data we need? There are many stakeholders giving input on which data we need within different time frames. The following picture maps out those stakeholders and connects them to the data acquisition function which is executing on the needs that are put forward from the different stakeholders. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/077b9bfd-2fd0-4ddb-9c4d-4efa44a81f1a/Screenshot_2026-02-20_at_10.09.47.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466VZHLAKPQ%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095848Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIGcjUPAIk6iiIOd6%2FH6DZOoLII4kRZ2hNZ1Buq3E9s3RAiEA1Yo%2FUwnJ3hh3WzOx5y1ADg8ttfK8qXwY19LDd6rrbc0q%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDDndpKl4WVc0fCEDkCrcA4PicMo4MjSCSNofu0GvAogfRU0mw9v0Jts2O6KzEujwsmewWIHZqa9UdCFxmAlUkAOokp7nosCC8vYfFBeH6dZCcTLHcBSrmnziz4kED9LmsfXuXy3%2BLDb0jiRiLYKDezukTcTRuxe6xv1XHhQtwt3mo3Yvrg7cpIvkWpJldfw7kSamxWnd3q4CxgXMS5n0qtqqIAZQ5onm%2Bf3Dj7QRw5UNemdpsL04jyLGPKTs6N1UqQfsChuzgztCFRzwisf2MPfU5Bmgxl0ZQY5aF64WNBgkLWGJT6JYvgKwx31GXdvPwinXhs9YqYegvydoCGVjP24RTxtbJR1zqJJhRVpUvG0IzNMNIbCnK8W2Kb8p4cjF4QKtwZS67wuHdBMstnE8KgjyDfgwt8p95F4FsKne6GVOXwwV%2B%2FZtTaLVf4hZQLmZ7%2BK8HmDHXuby6xumGGsPub0yt2PABee3p%2Fz803TJg5%2BgspR%2BQ3I3AW4rzeqYBoeSKFurGdK4rvFUJKbhrR2TlVxGNHre2qPdWp0QSa4%2FV7sNs0Lv4I1CwTBSo2cH46yBDOjlmDR5fSyEPIKTqoxVaBUTA7BO%2FFXvP1ZHO2yhraNCr8oDlGRo3UTub0B7wXgGSt%2B2HD1fRT9s%2F9ONMPatks8GOqUBJeXLDYHgI3CxlhkU4VSXbYsPHDpMwUltyQGq1Us8ML4E%2BlkTQQ9BNByAM4faMD0qOGFzawcAAQydCfh5WRuh5JvozItQE1gFaS6bnzsDVKj3jZusFAVcVp8pBeca0Nl27hg%2BLsjhNqJfTQH2blckFtS5JCo0gpF%2BBL%2FvVO7BRq3XATLNSGgfeHnkPtUsMet6CSAtO%2BtSAH9e2cnTSVKP8w0KbfpR&X-Amz-Signature=fc99a10192394154b750ab3406d059d23358ac457d7991af712033096f8acb34&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) Some further explanation on how the interaction looks like: - Product: - Short/mid term needs - Communicates customer feedback, which define the reactive bets we - **Important: **customer feedback is most often a bit more noisy and here it’s highly important to explain the difference between use cases and capability (see above). - Research (input/datasets needs collected [here](/329c370222d580e8b37fc360fc2b191f?pvs=25)): - Task Force: - Short/mid term needs - defined by proactive bets on model capabilities and use cases - Research Shops: - short/mid term needs - the vast majority of shop research should be doable using open source datasets/benchmarks, but if needed - Research Leads: - Long term needs - defined by research direction Inputs from the research and products will be defined on a rolling basis. - For research ⇒ data needs, there’s the weekly research council sync where data needs are discussed. - For product → data needs: Will be discussed and re-defined on a frequent basis and needs will be updated accordingly. In the beginning, Andi and Morgan will discuss this and set up a tracker ### How to understand the best way to acquire a dataset We have various options on how to acquire a dataset supporting certain capabilities and use cases. raw.title: [WIP] BFL Data Strategy 2026
raw.text: Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/336c370222d580c6af9de408d1adeb0a as of 2026-04-14T18:18:31.496Z: {"title":"\\[WIP\\] BFL Data Strategy 2026"} --- ### Primer - The importance of data for generative modeling The goal of generative modeling is to approximate a data distribution and - in the case of current frontier AI models - to be able to sample from that distribution in order to create new datapoints from that distribution. The learning algorithm which is employed ensures that the model can approximate the true (and unknown) distribution of the data the model is trained on as good as possible and is therefore the first central cornerstone for training a frontier model. However, the second - and sometimes underestimated - component, is the dataset which is used to train the model. This dataset represents the data distribution the model is targeting learning. It’s easy to imagine that a model won’t be competitive even with the most powerful learning algorithm, if the data distribution it’s trained on (aka the training dataset) is containing low quality training examples - garbage in, garbage out. This is why training data acquisition and processing is strategically extremely important for every foundation model company. As a result of this, we need to treat data as a first class citizen at BFL as well. ### Use Cases vs. Model Capabilities - Separating the target distribution from the conditioning method **The difference between targets and the conditioning ** The training data for foundation models has two main interfaces with the learning algorithm during training, which are the following 1. The* target: *The target is the actual ‘training example’ and it’s used as a reference point to calculate how good the model is performing the task it’s trained to do. From the difference between the model output and the target, the loss is calculated and then backpropagated through the model to update the weights. In fact, for most probabilistic approaches, the target also gives rise to the model input at training time. In those cases, the model input is often a transformation of the target (e.g. a more noisy version of the training example in the case of diffusion models). 2. The* conditioning: *Under conditioning, we subsume all additional input signals that go into the model (at both training and inference), apart from the random variable, that the model learns to generate. These conditioning inputs are what make the model controllable in the end. So if we take e.g. text-to-image models, we want to be able to generate images based (or conditioned) on text prompts. That means that, at train time, we need to have text prompts for each training image we want to use. Note that the conditioning can be more than one additional inputs, e.g. in the case of image-to-video, where we both use a text prompt and an image as conditionings to create a video. (The name image-to-video is very unfortunate, since it’s actually text+image-to-video). From a data perspective, it’s important to separate these two interfaces from each other since they affect different aspects of what the model learns during training. 1. The targets define the visual properties, the data that the model learns to generate will follow. For instance, if a model was only trained on illustrated content, it would not understand photorealism and no matter if I would prompt for ‘a blue bird’, or ‘a photorealistic blue bird’, the model would always create images that would resemble illustrations 2. The conditioning defines how users can interact with the model and how they can apply control to the data that the model generates. For instance, if I only have a dataset of paired text prompts and images, and train a model to generate images conditioned on the text prompts, users cannot use that model for image editing, since training an image editing model would require to always have a set of images (e.g. two images showing the same person in different environments) and (one or more) text prompts describing how to arrive at one image based on one (or multiple) other image(s) in that set. In that sense, the conditioning define the set of tasks that the model is generally capable to do. The above separation is helpful to understand the dimensions along which we should be thinking when it comes to data acquisition. We need to understand what we need along both these dimensions in order to create a well suited dataset for training a state of the art model. Failure to do so will make it likely that we end up with sub-optimal decisions for data acquisition and will make blind spots in our data strategy more likely. **Separating use cases from model capabilities** Based on the above separation of the targets (or target distribution) and the conditioning, we make the following definitions. **Use Case** A *use case* describes the requirements for the targets that we would like to have in a training dataset. Understanding the *use cases* our models are used for will help us answer the question: *How should the target distribution look like, that the model learns to generate during training?* Example: If the use case would be film making, we would rather be looking to license data from movie studies and other types of data, e.g. ads, would not be super important. Note that this is independent of the conditioning and does not tell us something about the model capability that we need. For instance, one could look for image editing data based on this use case, but also every other task, e.g. text-to-video. **Model Capability** A *model capability* describes how users can interact with the model, i.e. it is directly connected to the conditioning information we need at training time. We need to be clear on the model capabilities we want in our model. After we know that, we can answer the question: *How well does our data support the conditioning we want to use to make sure we reach SOTA accuracy and controllability?* Example: If we want our model to be good at multi reference image editing, this tells us that we need training training examples which contain not only a text+image pair (as it would be the case for t2i), but also reference images, containing some visual aspects/objects/characters that are present in the target example as well. However this *doesn’t *tell us something about the the target distribution should look visually. **So what?** Making the distinction between use cases and model capability can help us to get data in a more targeted way and will reduce the probability of blind spots on the data acquisition side. - By selecting use cases we tailor the output distribution to what our customers actually need. - Listing und selecting certain model capabilities we ensure to not forget any interesting new applications that we could takle with a new model. especially for multimodal and general models, it’s important to be clear about which combinations of conditionings we want to support since the number of possibilities is a superlinear function of the number of conditionings. ### Who defines what data we need? There are many stakeholders giving input on which data we need within different time frames. The following picture maps out those stakeholders and connects them to the data acquisition function which is executing on the needs that are put forward from the different stakeholders. ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/077b9bfd-2fd0-4ddb-9c4d-4efa44a81f1a/Screenshot_2026-02-20_at_10.09.47.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB466VZHLAKPQ%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095848Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIGcjUPAIk6iiIOd6%2FH6DZOoLII4kRZ2hNZ1Buq3E9s3RAiEA1Yo%2FUwnJ3hh3WzOx5y1ADg8ttfK8qXwY19LDd6rrbc0q%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDDndpKl4WVc0fCEDkCrcA4PicMo4MjSCSNofu0GvAogfRU0mw9v0Jts2O6KzEujwsmewWIHZqa9UdCFxmAlUkAOokp7nosCC8vYfFBeH6dZCcTLHcBSrmnziz4kED9LmsfXuXy3%2BLDb0jiRiLYKDezukTcTRuxe6xv1XHhQtwt3mo3Yvrg7cpIvkWpJldfw7kSamxWnd3q4CxgXMS5n0qtqqIAZQ5onm%2Bf3Dj7QRw5UNemdpsL04jyLGPKTs6N1UqQfsChuzgztCFRzwisf2MPfU5Bmgxl0ZQY5aF64WNBgkLWGJT6JYvgKwx31GXdvPwinXhs9YqYegvydoCGVjP24RTxtbJR1zqJJhRVpUvG0IzNMNIbCnK8W2Kb8p4cjF4QKtwZS67wuHdBMstnE8KgjyDfgwt8p95F4FsKne6GVOXwwV%2B%2FZtTaLVf4hZQLmZ7%2BK8HmDHXuby6xumGGsPub0yt2PABee3p%2Fz803TJg5%2BgspR%2BQ3I3AW4rzeqYBoeSKFurGdK4rvFUJKbhrR2TlVxGNHre2qPdWp0QSa4%2FV7sNs0Lv4I1CwTBSo2cH46yBDOjlmDR5fSyEPIKTqoxVaBUTA7BO%2FFXvP1ZHO2yhraNCr8oDlGRo3UTub0B7wXgGSt%2B2HD1fRT9s%2F9ONMPatks8GOqUBJeXLDYHgI3CxlhkU4VSXbYsPHDpMwUltyQGq1Us8ML4E%2BlkTQQ9BNByAM4faMD0qOGFzawcAAQydCfh5WRuh5JvozItQE1gFaS6bnzsDVKj3jZusFAVcVp8pBeca0Nl27hg%2BLsjhNqJfTQH2blckFtS5JCo0gpF%2BBL%2FvVO7BRq3XATLNSGgfeHnkPtUsMet6CSAtO%2BtSAH9e2cnTSVKP8w0KbfpR&X-Amz-Signature=fc99a10192394154b750ab3406d059d23358ac457d7991af712033096f8acb34&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) Some further explanation on how the interaction looks like: - This serves as a chance-level baseline for comparison with trained checkpoints. - **Model**: LeAE-B (default config), random weights - **Encoder output**: 64-dim embeddings, 5 CLS tokens/sec (200ms hop) - **Sample rate**: 24kHz - **Evaluation**: Linear probe (MLP) + k-NN on 22 public tasks - **Date**: 2026-03-27 --- ## Results

**Weighted Average MLP: 0.127 — KNN: 0.189** --- ## Notes - ASV2015 (0.95) is inflated due to class imbalance in spoof detection (binary task, mostly one class) - LibriSpeech-MF (0.49) is \~chance for binary gender classification - Tasks with "—" for KNN: those tasks don't support KNN evaluation in X-ARES (e.g. frame-level, contrastive, or ASR tasks) - 5 tasks skipped: 2 private (subway_broadcast, inside_outside_car), 3 disabled (finger_snap, key_scratching, liveenv) --- ## Reproducibility ```shell # Install uv pip install -e ".[eval]" # Run benchmark (random init, no checkpoint) python -m xares.run ssl_ae/eval/xares_encoder.py xares_tasks/*.py --max-jobs 1 # With a trained checkpoint: LEAE_CHECKPOINT=/path/to/step_100000.pt \ python -m xares.run ssl_ae/eval/xares_encoder.py xares_tasks/*.py --max-jobs 1 ``` Datasets stored at `/mnt/data/gaetan/xares/` (426 GB total).

Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/330c370222d581afb759eb90062d26dc as of 2026-03-27T12:57:09.631Z: {"title":"X-ARES Benchmark — LeAE (random init)"} ## Summary X-ARES evaluation of **LeAE encoder with random initialization** (no training). This serves as a chance-level baseline for comparison with trained checkpoints. - **Model**: LeAE-B (default config), random weights - **Encoder output**: 64-dim embeddings, 5 CLS tokens/sec (200ms hop) - **Sample rate**: 24kHz - **Evaluation**: Linear probe (MLP) + k-NN on 22 public tasks - **Date**: 2026-03-27 --- ## Results
Dataset MLP Score KNN Score

LibriSpeech-MF 0.491 0.501

**Weighted Average MLP: 0.127 — KNN: 0.189** --- ## Notes - ASV2015 (0.95) is inflated due to class imbalance in spoof detection (binary task, mostly one class) - LibriSpeech-MF (0.49) is \~chance for binary gender classification - Tasks with "—" for KNN: those tasks don't support KNN evaluation in X-ARES (e.g. frame-level, contrastive, or ASR tasks) - 5 tasks skipped: 2 private (subway_broadcast, inside_outside_car), 3 disabled (finger_snap, key_scratching, liveenv) --- ## Reproducibility ```shell # Install uv pip install -e ".[eval]" # Run benchmark (random init, no checkpoint) python -m xares.run ssl_ae/eval/xares_encoder.py xares_tasks/*.py --max-jobs 1 # With a trained checkpoint: LEAE_CHECKPOINT=/path/to/step_100000.pt \ python -m xares.run ssl_ae/eval/xares_encoder.py xares_tasks/*.py --max-jobs 1 ``` Datasets stored at `/mnt/data/gaetan/xares/` (426 GB total).

**Stadtgarten**

	</column>
	<column>
		- Take the tram (Schlossbergbahn) or walk up to the Schloßberg for a view of Freiburg and the Black Forest + see some castle ruins (from the year 1091 🤯)
		- From here there are access points into the Forest for a variety of trails
		- After, take the pedestrian foot bridge to cross over to Altstadt
	</column>
</columns>

	<column>
		- The market on the Münsterplatz is open everyday but Sunday until 2pm. Grab some fresh fruit, a sausage, or some souvenirs to take home
			- Order a Lange Rote (literally ‘long red’ - pork sausage)
			- find Stefan’s (bright yellow van) for Freiburg’s famous cheesecake
	</column>

- Go inside the Münster - construction on Freiburg’s cathedral started in 1120. [Organ concerts](https://www.muensterorgelkonzerte.de/) happen nearly each week!
- Climb to the top of the Münster to see the bells - the cathedral holds 19 bells 🔔 altogether 25 tonnes, making it one of the largest peals in Germany.

	</column>
	<column>
		- Rathausplatz
		- Alexanderplatz
		- Martinstor
		- Schwabentor
	</column>
</columns>
<empty-block/>
### Activities {color="green"}
- Hike into the Black Forest (*see below for more hiking*)
- Cheer on [SC Freiburg](https://www.scfreiburg.com/en/stadium/europa-park-stadium/) at a Fußball match ⚽️ at the Europa-Park Stadium
- Take a soak/sauna at the [Keidel Mineral Thermal Bath](https://www.keideltherme.de/)
- Bike along the Dreisam River ([route inspo here](https://www.komoot.com/highlight/404674))
- Take [the cable car](https://www.schauinslandbahn.de/en/) up to the Schauinsland (stay/eat at [Die Halde](https://www.halde.com/) + more hiking if you like!)
- Go wine tasting in the Kaiserstuhl - Freiburg is best known for its white wine, if you’re lucky enough to be here in the Fall, try a glass of Neuer Süßer! 
<empty-block/>
### **Eating** {color="green"}
**Local Food:**
- Cafe Ruef
- Feierling Brauerei
- Martinsbräu
- Omas Küche
- Breisgauer Flammkuchen - SW German pizza
- Markthalle - variety of food options in a 19th century food hall
<empty-block/>
**More Delicious Food:**
- Primo Market - Italian
- Trattorio Cum Laude - Italian
- Chada Thai Nudelsuppe - by the Uni on Rempartstraße (there is another Chada Thai in the North part of town - also delicious but a much farther walk!!)
- Jeju Korean Bistro
- Umami Ramen 
- PIN Kitchen - Chinese
- Indian Curryhouse
- Bengal - Bangladeshi
- Lollo - brunch, burgers
<empty-block/>
**Cafes / Dessert:**
- Cafe Auszeit (right by the office, everyone’s go-to)
- Cafe Schmidt (down the street, with amazing cakes)
- Cafe Marcel (at the Stadtgarten, great coffee and croissants)
- Günter Coffee (grab a coffee - and a bag of coffee beans
<empty-block/>
### Day Trips {color="green"}
- [Europa Park](https://www.europapark.de/en) - just a 30 min drive/1 hr public transit away for a day of rollercoaster fun
- Titisee - Cute little town along the lake, 40 minutes from Freiburg
- Schluchsee - another lake near Titisee (get here by train), you can rent boats or walk around the lake and stop for a nice lunch along the way
- Colmar, France - picturesque town sits along the Alsace Wine Route just NW of Freiburg
<empty-block/>
### Hiking {color="green"}
- **Belchen**: take the cable car up and walk down
- Hike from **Feldberg Passhöhe** over **Grafenmatt** to **Herzogenhorn** and back
- Hike from **Schauinsland** to **Feldberg**, really good scenery → longer hike, requires taking public transport
- Hike to the [**Zweribach Waterfalls**](https://www.hochschwarzwald.de/en/tours/through-the-mystical-bannwald-to-the-zweribach-waterfall-415dba7fc0)
<empty-block/>
<empty-block/>
</content>

**Stadtgarten**
- Grab a coffee at Cafe Marcel and mosey around the rose garden or say hi to the ducks at the pond

	<column>
		![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/13c6b034-a45b-4b3e-b250-3cf323db8660/stadtgarten-fwtm-spiegelhalter19.jpg?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB4662BTBJC6F%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095851Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIAMZ8PkIZiEa1U%2Bnw9hGcYGGPTcATV3syD8LxUoIutjGAiAZGh3LKlC7EUIW6awa1SZAAcbg4Uh%2F6t8fYEbeNi4Eiir%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMQZTydkSCiEgn3mVJKtwDwEmmocssQre%2BS%2FL2NEaoIUUR2Ayp5GOYYvt%2FBdPItM5DTdAHsPprq1%2FvJZD6pWVB0%2F4SeogcxsSYQe%2Fu2eSPOTMyHiYya%2B2TRMwwWpeZKRfxUGcncOMMItyfRfWbR5trV7iQL8uukcAsN06h12h6P%2By833a16rOwtMebRKRkRAgxY0EDaOjhzNtefJ%2BiHdcPa%2BExxojNodbN4po4UT9EMLRbcxI%2FwlGCElF8VUQP5mSM3T6DRz8xCMbsQR00x6TYKr2tqea5Eat4AN%2F7di1sHC6ft37pM8%2BTV7qk8SsgvfJwR84T5FioSymt7QCvGkI8IEFoVgxrMGBbYj8pUNwaYEi39o3UnuoIqjlnRgiEYYakASZZ8yPGdqECg6JwQmvJLU34OsiEINSg46rx%2FNuvAFtyToAgPdrr5dXRKsW2WQA61oFkGCaMyz7aq%2BaZVfUkcICJV7%2BEvOGVARBS4hscnYm0MduaVv6hOKWeQ0mG%2Fj4ouQ%2Bws1F8glKxtL7WsId2m0plgFwAkpIsmmPG1pCmGe0x%2BhMRMuv%2FFV%2FjYvLjFwIEYYi5iWn3xXxYdIMPzgycVIxWD5lphC2NYBEb2v80XQ5OkF9wyUEA6Mykgwi%2F08mKmrsEXJAESC7wPv8wra%2BSzwY6pgGAciy2ekFXesBVN%2F%2B7bprhAfrkOQSR010%2BpcGKLPMb6pVSEbW8iPNfYxkzPYUX60OkYEowqKVDGzZeLdu%2FswfGz%2FZM8Murh6cYygjwuBSFKfbIHw8dDuECoQEummMT5ZAkOAz8ObZCrQYmTKay4Nz7TsMC7naK6ujZ%2Fu0VFdh5k6ZhttyZmsdbrUdw%2Fym4AZolgyOy2H8nN3sUEkA%2BUT5HZJJf%2FQsd&X-Amz-Signature=adb022427917475fc762778c83b908b7bdd9b4246f647da80d61f015627c9601&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject)
	</column>
	<column>
		- Take the tram (Schlossbergbahn) or walk up to the Schloßberg for a view of Freiburg and the Black Forest + see some castle ruins (from the year 1091 🤯)
		- From here there are access points into the Forest for a variety of trails
		- After, take the pedestrian foot bridge to cross over to Altstadt
	</column>
</columns>
<empty-block/>
**Freiburger Münster**
<columns>
	<column>
		![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/f1eb93d3-e373-45e2-880e-59635713351d/360_F_488878262_wOGyC4BJpw6DkSjvKUOW0tH3V4Mwnbht.jpg?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB4662BTBJC6F%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T095851Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJGMEQCIAMZ8PkIZiEa1U%2Bnw9hGcYGGPTcATV3syD8LxUoIutjGAiAZGh3LKlC7EUIW6awa1SZAAcbg4Uh%2F6t8fYEbeNi4Eiir%2FAwgCEAAaDDYzNzQyMzE4MzgwNSIMQZTydkSCiEgn3mVJKtwDwEmmocssQre%2BS%2FL2NEaoIUUR2Ayp5GOYYvt%2FBdPItM5DTdAHsPprq1%2FvJZD6pWVB0%2F4SeogcxsSYQe%2Fu2eSPOTMyHiYya%2B2TRMwwWpeZKRfxUGcncOMMItyfRfWbR5trV7iQL8uukcAsN06h12h6P%2By833a16rOwtMebRKRkRAgxY0EDaOjhzNtefJ%2BiHdcPa%2BExxojNodbN4po4UT9EMLRbcxI%2FwlGCElF8VUQP5mSM3T6DRz8xCMbsQR00x6TYKr2tqea5Eat4AN%2F7di1sHC6ft37pM8%2BTV7qk8SsgvfJwR84T5FioSymt7QCvGkI8IEFoVgxrMGBbYj8pUNwaYEi39o3UnuoIqjlnRgiEYYakASZZ8yPGdqECg6JwQmvJLU34OsiEINSg46rx%2FNuvAFtyToAgPdrr5dXRKsW2WQA61oFkGCaMyz7aq%2BaZVfUkcICJV7%2BEvOGVARBS4hscnYm0MduaVv6hOKWeQ0mG%2Fj4ouQ%2Bws1F8glKxtL7WsId2m0plgFwAkpIsmmPG1pCmGe0x%2BhMRMuv%2FFV%2FjYvLjFwIEYYi5iWn3xXxYdIMPzgycVIxWD5lphC2NYBEb2v80XQ5OkF9wyUEA6Mykgwi%2F08mKmrsEXJAESC7wPv8wra%2BSzwY6pgGAciy2ekFXesBVN%2F%2B7bprhAfrkOQSR010%2BpcGKLPMb6pVSEbW8iPNfYxkzPYUX60OkYEowqKVDGzZeLdu%2FswfGz%2FZM8Murh6cYygjwuBSFKfbIHw8dDuECoQEummMT5ZAkOAz8ObZCrQYmTKay4Nz7TsMC7naK6ujZ%2Fu0VFdh5k6ZhttyZmsdbrUdw%2Fym4AZolgyOy2H8nN3sUEkA%2BUT5HZJJf%2FQsd&X-Amz-Signature=32ce40dcfd6c904222ba99cf161ab2defa7fb566f3e552c7be38565041e421de&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject)
	</column>
	<column>
		- The market on the Münsterplatz is open everyday but Sunday until 2pm. Grab some fresh fruit, a sausage, or some souvenirs to take home
			- Order a Lange Rote (literally ‘long red’ - pork sausage)
			- find Stefan’s (bright yellow van) for Freiburg’s famous cheesecake
	</column>
</columns>
- Go inside the Münster - construction on Freiburg’s cathedral started in 1120. [Organ concerts](https://www.muensterorgelkonzerte.de/) happen nearly each week!
- Climb to the top of the Münster to see the bells - the cathedral holds 19 bells 🔔 altogether 25 tonnes, making it one of the largest peals in Germany. 
<empty-block/>

- Check out the Bächle (small canals along the streets which were used in the Middle Ages to supply cleaning water and extinguish fires). Dip your toes in on a hot day!
