	</column>
	<column>
		- Rathausplatz
		- Alexanderplatz
		- Martinstor
		- Schwabentor
	</column>
</columns>
<empty-block/>
### Activities {color="green"}
- Hike into the Black Forest (*see below for more hiking*)
- Cheer on [SC Freiburg](https://www.scfreiburg.com/en/stadium/europa-park-stadium/) at a Fußball match ⚽️ at the Europa-Park Stadium
- Take a soak/sauna at the [Keidel Mineral Thermal Bath](https://www.keideltherme.de/)
- Bike along the Dreisam River ([route inspo here](https://www.komoot.com/highlight/404674))
- Take [the cable car](https://www.schauinslandbahn.de/en/) up to the Schauinsland (stay/eat at [Die Halde](https://www.halde.com/) + more hiking if you like!)
- Go wine tasting in the Kaiserstuhl - Freiburg is best known for its white wine, if you’re lucky enough to be here in the Fall, try a glass of Neuer Süßer! 
<empty-block/>
### **Eating** {color="green"}
**Local Food:**
- Cafe Ruef
- Feierling Brauerei
- Martinsbräu
- Omas Küche
- Breisgauer Flammkuchen - SW German pizza
- Markthalle - variety of food options in a 19th century food hall
<empty-block/>
**More Delicious Food:**
- Primo Market - Italian
- Trattorio Cum Laude - Italian
- Chada Thai Nudelsuppe - by the Uni on Rempartstraße (there is another Chada Thai in the North part of town - also delicious but a much farther walk!!)
- Jeju Korean Bistro
- Umami Ramen 
- PIN Kitchen - Chinese
- Indian Curryhouse
- Bengal - Bangladeshi
- Lollo - brunch, burgers
<empty-block/>
**Cafes / Dessert:**
- Cafe Auszeit (right by the office, everyone’s go-to)
- Cafe Schmidt (down the street, with amazing cakes)
- Cafe Marcel (at the Stadtgarten, great coffee and croissants)
- Günter Coffee (grab a coffee - and a bag of coffee beans
<empty-block/>
### Day Trips {color="green"}
- [Europa Park](https://www.europapark.de/en) - just a 30 min drive/1 hr public transit away for a day of rollercoaster fun
- Titisee - Cute little town along the lake, 40 minutes from Freiburg
- Schluchsee - another lake near Titisee (get here by train), you can rent boats or walk around the lake and stop for a nice lunch along the way
- Colmar, France - picturesque town sits along the Alsace Wine Route just NW of Freiburg
<empty-block/>
### Hiking {color="green"}
- **Belchen**: take the cable car up and walk down
- Hike from **Feldberg Passhöhe** over **Grafenmatt** to **Herzogenhorn** and back
- Hike from **Schauinsland** to **Feldberg**, really good scenery → longer hike, requires taking public transport
- Hike to the [**Zweribach Waterfalls**](https://www.hochschwarzwald.de/en/tours/through-the-mystical-bannwald-to-the-zweribach-waterfall-415dba7fc0)
<empty-block/>
<empty-block/>
</content>
</page>

Product imagery at scale.","Type":"Enterprise","Video Use Case":"Possible","date:Date of session:is_datetime":0,"date:Date of session:start":"2026-04-02","url":"https://www.notion.so/314c370222d5817daef5c7515464061a"} **Post-Session Summary** **Date:** 4/2/2026 **Key Use Cases Identified (ranked by priority):** 1. **Lifestyle/Motion Graphics** - Walmart is generating lifestyle videos for key products. The input involves product details, and the output is a lifestyle video. This is actively being explored and expected to launch in the next 3-6 months. 2. **Interactive Video** - Creating interactive product videos, such as an air fryer with zoomable controls. The input is product details, and the output is an interactive video. These are pre-generated and not real-time. 3. **Promotional Marketing Videos** - Developing promotional videos for marketing purposes. The input is product details, and the output is a promotional video. Examples include "\$8.99 pizza" and "roses farm to table" for Sam’s Club. **Top Model Capabilities (ranked by importance):** 1. **Near-zero hallucination on text and logos** - Walmart requires high accuracy in text and logos to avoid misrepresentation of products. 2. **Sufficient output duration (up to \~45 seconds)** - Current models have a max duration of 8-15 seconds, which is insufficient for meaningful content. 3. **Ability to transform raw product images into inspirational marketing videos** - Walmart desires to convert raw warehouse product images into inspirational marketing videos without relying heavily on human prompting. **Top Pain Points (ranked by severity):** 1. **Hallucinations** - Affects Veo models. Misrepresentation of products, even slightly off logos, is unacceptable. Example shared: Y. 2. **Max duration too short** - Affects Veo models. Current models only allow 8-15 seconds, but up to 45 seconds is needed. Example shared: Y. 3. **Unnatural movement** - Affects Veo models. Human movements are slow and aimless, making it hard to catch with automated QC. Example shared: Y. **Video Importance Level:** High - Video is as important as images for Walmart, but the quality bar needs to be raised for production use. **Audio Relevance:** Yes — separate - Audio is a "nice to have" but not critical. Known issues include robotic voice and inconsistent sentiment. **Key Competitive Models Mentioned:** Veo **Visual Examples Received:** None (oskar to follow up) **Visual Examples Promised (follow up needed):** Oskar to share prompts and output examples with Sam. **Surprising Insights or Unmet Needs:** - Walmart wants to move away from prompting entirely, preferring templates or style-selection to increase volume without relying on human prompt-writing. - Needs 100% product consistency or they can’t use it - Legal pushback on using people in Walmart content, even with licensed images. **Follow-Up Actions:** - Oskar Radermecker to share document of failure examples and prompts with Sam — Oskar — No deadline specified. - Schedule a follow-up session focused on image generation and Flux use cases — Sam — No deadline specified. - Invite Walmart team as alpha testers when Flux 3 is ready — Sam — No deadline specified. **Notes for each question below:** ## 1 — Current State & Video Importance 1.1 How important is video generation to your product today vs. 6–12 months from now? Video is actively being explored but nothing is in production yet. Generative content creation is primarily image-based today. On a 3–6 month horizon, several video use cases are planned or in progress: lifestyle/motion graphics for key products, interactive video (e.g. air fryer with zoomable controls — pre-generated, not real-time), promotional/storyboard marketing videos (trialled but not yet past the quality bar), and Sam's Club promotional videos (e.g. "\$8.99 pizza," "roses farm to table"). Traditional video creation costs \~\$5K per shoot, making generative video compelling if the quality threshold can be met. 1.2 What role does audio play alongside video? Audio is a "nice to have," not critical. Workarounds exist (music overlay, separate generation). Known issues with current audio capabilities include robotic voice, inconsistent sentiment, lip-sync mismatches, and non-English-sounding output. 1.3 Which video/audio generation models or tools are you currently using? Primarily Veo (Google). Most pain points documented below are drawn from experience with Veo. 1.4 How does image generation fit into your video workflows today? They use image far more than video but didn’t detail how it’s used with video. They did mention transforming raw warehouse product images into inspirational marketing videos — suggesting a stills-first approach is the target direction. --- ## 2 — Use Cases & Applications 2.1 Top 3 video generation use cases (in priority order): 1. Lifestyle/motion graphics for key products - Input: Product images (including raw warehouse shots) - Output: Polished, inspirational marketing video - End user: Internal creative teams, eventually buyers and sellers 2. Interactive/shoppable video content - Input: Product images with detailed feature areas - Output: Pre-generated video with interactive elements (e.g. air fryer with zoomable controls) - End user: Walmart.com shoppers 3. Promotional marketing videos (incl. Sam's Club) - Input: Product/campaign brief and imagery - Output: Short-form promotional video (e.g. "\$8.99 pizza," "roses farm to table") - End user: Marketing/brand teams; Sam's Club has more flexibility than Walmart core brand 2.2 Reference examples of "great" output: *To be provided by Oskar post-call.* 2.3 Current outputs that fall short: *Failure examples and prompts to be shared by Oskar post-call.* 2.4 Abandoned use cases: 360-degree product spins were explored but shelved. Models only accept start/end frames, forcing hallucination of the entire product in between. Volume targets were aggressive (hundreds of thousands of assets); quality was insufficient to proceed. 2.5 What video durations matter most? Up to \~45 seconds for meaningful marketing content. However, they noted that this is very use case dependent and some things can be shorter. Longer videos have more risk of hallucinations. 2.6 Resolutions and aspect ratios needed: 2K minimum, 4K preferred. Nothing higher is needed (8K is only relevant for print/packaging, which is image not video). Standard marketing/social aspect ratios assumed. 2.7 Top 3 most important model capabilities: 1. Near-zero hallucination on text, logos, and product details 2. Sufficient output duration (up to \~45 seconds) 3. Template or style-selection interface to reduce reliance on manual prompting and increase throughput --- ## 3 — Pain Points with Existing Models 3.1 Top 3 frustrations with current models: 1. Hallucination on products, logos, and text — Even slightly off-brand logos are a hard no-go. More complex products increase hallucination risk. Text on screens (phones, watches) consistently renders as gibberish. Zero tolerance for misrepresentation. 2. Insufficient output duration — 8–15 second caps are not enough. Meaningful content requires up to \~45 seconds. 3. Slow iteration / high prompt friction — Averaging 4–5 attempts to get satisfactory output. "Time to asset" is a tracked OKR internally. The prompting interface itself is a bottleneck to scale. *Additional frustrations:* - Unnatural human movement (slow, aimless) — hard to catch with automated QC - Videos cut at awkward moments; scenes don't end naturally - SFW filters producing false positives (detergent videos blocked, children's content blocked even with filters deactivated) - Physics failures (fluid passing through closed lids, unrealistic ball bouncing) 3.2 Model ratings by dimension:
Dimension Rating Notes
Visual quality / realism Medium Acceptable for some uses; product fidelity is the blocker
Motion quality and naturalness Low Humans move slowly and unnaturally
Temporal consistency Low Core issue — 360° spins abandoned due to hallucination between frames
Text/typography rendering Very Low Consistently renders as gibberish on screens
Character/identity consistency N/A No people in Walmart content (legal restriction)
Prompt adherence Low–Medium 4–5 attempts average to hit acceptable output
Resolution and detail Medium 2K/4K capability needed but not always delivered
Speed / latency Medium Longer wait acceptable for offline 4K; \<30 sec needed for ideation flows
Audio quality and sync Low Robotic, inconsistent sentiment, lip-sync issues
3.3 Content types where models consistently fail: - Logo rendering (must be pixel-accurate) - Text on product screens (phones, watches, packaging) - 360° or continuous product rotation - Complex product details on higher-value SKUs - Children's content (false positives from SFW filters) - Household products like detergent (also triggering false positives) 3.4 Controllability issues: - No support for continuous camera paths (only start/end frame input) - Videos end abruptly rather than at natural scene completion points - Pacing and motion speed of subjects (humans appear slow/aimless) 3.5 Camera Controls & Conditioning - Said this wasn’t important to them and we were running out of time --- ## 4 — What "Winning" Looks Like 4.1 Magic wand — what would the perfect model do? - Near-zero hallucination on text, logos, and product details - Transform raw warehouse product images into polished marketing video automatically - Output up to \~45 seconds of content - Accessible to buyers and sellers, not just internal creative teams — template or style-selection UI, no prompting required - 2K minimum / 4K preferred resolution - Latency under 30 seconds for interactive/ideation workflows; longer acceptable for offline 4K batch jobs 4.2 Must-haves vs. nice-to-haves to switch primary workload to FLUX.3: *Must-haves:* - Logo and text pixel-accuracy (near-zero hallucination) - Duration up to \~45 seconds - Reduced / configurable moderation filters (custom endpoint for Walmart's use cases) - 2K+ resolution output *Nice-to-haves:* - 4K output - Audio generation (sync'd or separate) - Template/style-selection interface - Camera path control beyond start/end frames 4.3 Internal evaluation frameworks: QC is a mix of internal creative team review, Labelbox (third-party annotation), and an in-development LLM-based QC system. Oskar to share internal prompts and failure examples under NDA. 4.4 Current gold standard / competitive reference: Veo (Google) is the primary reference point, though it is the source of most documented pain points. No alternative cited as the gold standard. *Ask Oskar for sample outputs at follow-up.* --- ## 5 — Sample Collection 5.1–5.3 Oskar Radermecker to share a document of failure examples and prompts with Sam for the BFL research team. Follow-up scheduled. 5.4 Internal evaluation criteria: "Time to asset" is a tracked OKR. QC involves creative team, Labelbox, and an LLM-based QC system in development. Further detail to be gathered at follow-up. --- ## 6 — Pricing Model Preferences 6.1 Current billing method: Don’t care too much about pricing yet. 6.2 Most intuitive pricing unit:Not discussed 6.3 Resolution/duration pricing expectations: Latency tolerance (longer for 4K offline, faster for ideation) implies an expectation that 4K/longer clips are priced differently than quick ideation outputs. Specific pricing preferences to be discussed at follow-up. --- ## Next Steps

Sam Follow up to receive Oskar's prompt/output examples
Sam Schedule follow-up session focused on image generation and FLUX use cases (virtual try-on, product imagery)

Meaningful content requires up to \~45 seconds. 3. Slow iteration / high prompt friction — Averaging 4–5 attempts to get satisfactory output. "Time to asset" is a tracked OKR internally. The prompting interface itself is a bottleneck to scale. *Additional frustrations:* - Unnatural human movement (slow, aimless) — hard to catch with automated QC - Videos cut at awkward moments; scenes don't end naturally - SFW filters producing false positives (detergent videos blocked, children's content blocked even with filters deactivated) - Physics failures (fluid passing through closed lids, unrealistic ball bouncing) 3.2 Model ratings by dimension:
Dimension Rating Notes
Visual quality / realism Medium Acceptable for some uses; product fidelity is the blocker
Motion quality and naturalness Low Humans move slowly and unnaturally
Temporal consistency Low Core issue — 360° spins abandoned due to hallucination between frames
Text/typography rendering Very Low Consistently renders as gibberish on screens
Character/identity consistency N/A No people in Walmart content (legal restriction)
Prompt adherence Low–Medium 4–5 attempts average to hit acceptable output
Resolution and detail Medium 2K/4K capability needed but not always delivered
Speed / latency Medium Longer wait acceptable for offline 4K; \<30 sec needed for ideation flows
Audio quality and sync Low Robotic, inconsistent sentiment, lip-sync issues
3.3 Content types where models consistently fail: - Logo rendering (must be pixel-accurate) - Text on product screens (phones, watches, packaging) - 360° or continuous product rotation - Complex product details on higher-value SKUs - Children's content (false positives from SFW filters) - Household products like detergent (also triggering false positives) 3.4 Controllability issues: - No support for continuous camera paths (only start/end frame input) - Videos end abruptly rather than at natural scene completion points - Pacing and motion speed of subjects (humans appear slow/aimless) 3.5 Camera Controls & Conditioning - Said this wasn’t important to them and we were running out of time --- ## 4 — What "Winning" Looks Like 4.1 Magic wand — what would the perfect model do? - Near-zero hallucination on text, logos, and product details - Transform raw warehouse product images into polished marketing video automatically - Output up to \~45 seconds of content - Accessible to buyers and sellers, not just internal creative teams — template or style-selection UI, no prompting required - 2K minimum / 4K preferred resolution - Latency under 30 seconds for interactive/ideation workflows; longer acceptable for offline 4K batch jobs 4.2 Must-haves vs. nice-to-haves to switch primary workload to FLUX.3: *Must-haves:* - Logo and text pixel-accuracy (near-zero hallucination) - Duration up to \~45 seconds - Reduced / configurable moderation filters (custom endpoint for Walmart's use cases) - 2K+ resolution output *Nice-to-haves:* - 4K output - Audio generation (sync'd or separate) - Template/style-selection interface - Camera path control beyond start/end frames 4.3 Internal evaluation frameworks: QC is a mix of internal creative team review, Labelbox (third-party annotation), and an in-development LLM-based QC system. Oskar to share internal prompts and failure examples under NDA. 4.4 Current gold standard / competitive reference: Veo (Google) is the primary reference point, though it is the source of most documented pain points. No alternative cited as the gold standard. *Ask Oskar for sample outputs at follow-up.* --- ## 5 — Sample Collection 5.1–5.3 Oskar Radermecker to share a document of failure examples and prompts with Sam for the BFL research team. Follow-up scheduled. 5.4 Internal evaluation criteria: "Time to asset" is a tracked OKR. QC involves creative team, Labelbox, and an LLM-based QC system in development. Further detail to be gathered at follow-up. --- ## 6 — Pricing Model Preferences 6.1 Current billing method: Don’t care too much about pricing yet. 6.2 Most intuitive pricing unit:Not discussed 6.3 Resolution/duration pricing expectations: Latency tolerance (longer for 4K offline, faster for ideation) implies an expectation that 4K/longer clips are priced differently than quick ideation outputs. Specific pricing preferences to be discussed at follow-up. --- ## Next Steps
Owner Action
Oskar Radermecker Share document of failure examples and prompts with Sam for BFL research team
Sam Follow up to receive Oskar's prompt/output examples
Sam Schedule follow-up session focused on image generation and FLUX use cases (virtual try-on, product imagery)
Sam Invite Walmart team as alpha testers when FLUX.3 is ready

306c3702-22d5-81c7-8d27-ef3057923f87.title: Master Copy- AE Case Study — Your First 90 Days at BFL
306c3702-22d5-81c7-8d27-ef3057923f87.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/306c370222d581c78d27ef3057923f87 as of 2026-03-27T08:36:18.394Z: {"title":"Master Copy- AE Case Study — Your First 90 Days at BFL"} This first part is internal! ## How to Use This Case Study **Send to the candidate 3 days before their onsite.** They should prepare a **35-minute presentation** (see "Your Task" at the bottom). Allow **25 minutes for Q&A** after. Candidates are encouraged to research BFL online during prep. They are welcome to use AI tools (Claude, ChatGPT, etc.) during preparation — we care about the quality of thinking and conclusions, not whether the analysis was done by hand. This includes using AI to help process or analyze the attached data files — that's expected and encouraged. No internal materials will be provided beyond this document and the attached data files with mock-up data (inbound leads spreadsheet, API users spreadsheet, lost deals spreadsheet). **Why this case study works** This case study works because it mirrors the actual job. A mid-level AE joining BFL will face exactly this: too many accounts, messy data, no playbook, and more workstreams than they can handle at once. By giving candidates more information than they can possibly cover in 35 minutes, the exercise tests prioritization — the single most important skill for this role. The traps are subtle: accounts that should be escalated to partnerships or senior AEs, hidden gems buried in noisy API data that only surface if the candidate thinks to cross-reference, lost deals that are worth revisiting vs. dead ends, and an outbound campaign they should arguably deprioritize because they already have enough on their plate. Candidates who try to cover everything superficially fail. Candidates who pick 3-4 areas, go deep with data-backed reasoning, and clearly explain what they're deliberately not doing — those are the ones who can actually do this job. The 25-minute Q&A then stress-tests everything they parked, so there's nowhere to hide. From here onwards it’s the external facing case-study ## Context You've just joined **Black Forest Labs (BFL)** as an Account Executive — the company's **first mid-level AE hire**. BFL builds the FLUX family of state-of-the-art image generation models. The whole GTM team is \~15 people including sales, partnerships, SE/FDE and legal. There are three Senior AEs handling high-stakes, complex strategic deals (think: multi-million platform integrations, custom licensing structures). A separate **partnerships team of 3 Senior Partnerships Managers** handles channel partnerships, cloud platform relationships, and similar strategic motions. 5** SE / FDEs ****(Forward Deployed Engineers)** work alongside these teams on the biggest deals — building custom assets, implementations, and custom endpoints to create highly customized environments for large contracts or to unlock use cases at scale. That means **you own basically everything else** — a very large surface area of accounts, leads, and opportunities that need prioritization. Before your first day, familiarize yourself with BFL's products, models, and positioning by researching the company online. ### Commercial Motions BFL sells through three commercial motions: - **API** — customers call BFL's hosted endpoints and pay per image generated. FLUX.2 is priced by megapixels — more details can be found at [bfl.ai](http://bfl.ai) - **Weight Licensing** — customers license model weights and run inference on their own infrastructure. Current indicative tiers: FLUX.2 Dev (32B parameters, \~\$10K/month) and FLUX.2 Klein (9B parameters, \~\$5K/month). Note: the team is still figuring out the best pricing per customer segment and use case, so these are directional - **Mixed / Custom Deals** — some customers combine API usage with weight licensing depending on their use case ### Pricing Landscape BFL has evolved its pricing over time, so **different customers are on very different commercial structures:** - Some are on an **old waterfall pricing scheme** — no commitments, but they get increasing discounts the more they consume (volume tiers) - Some have **annual commitments** with locked-in pricing - Some have **discounts without any commitment** — BFL moved to this model at one point to close deals faster - Some have **prepaid credits** — either consumed at per-image pricing with a discount (e.g., 10% off list), or at a flat per-image rate across all models. The flat-rate structure is common with larger enterprises — they pay the same rate regardless of which model they use, which makes the effective deal value much larger than a simple PAYG customer who might only use cheaper models. Startups typically don't go for flat-rate prepaid deals As you review the account portfolio, pay attention to what pricing structure each customer is on — it affects expansion strategy significantly. ### Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) BFL has a small **FDE (Forward Deployed Engineering)** team — solutions engineers who work hands-on with license customers to fine-tune models, build custom workflows, and optimize inference pipelines. FDE is billed at **\$6.5K/day** and is a key upsell lever for license deals. However, the FDE team is small and should **only be deployed on major strategic implementation projects** — not sold as day-rate consulting to every license customer. ### FLUX.2 and Competitive Positioning - **FLUX.2** launched in Q4 2025 as BFL's flagship model. It competes head-to-head with **Nano Banana** (Google's image generation suite) - Being direct: FLUX.2 **might appear slightly worse than Nano Banana in some key areas**. Nano Banana benefits from Google's massive marketing machine, producing far more hype than BFL can match as a startup. Nano Banana also has the full Gemini suite behind it, making prompting very forgiving — users can write lazy, imprecise prompts and get good results - **FLUX.2's advantage** is that it can be **prompted much more precisely** — but users need to follow BFL's prompt guide (available on the website). Most users default to the same prompts they use with Nano Banana and then perceive FLUX.2 as worse. BFL knows this is a real onboarding friction point and is actively working on fixing it — but for now it's something you need to address proactively with customers - **FLUX.2 Klein** (9B) — fast, cheap, high quality. Near real-time inference. Ideal for preview/draft use cases, free-tier platform users, and high-volume applications where speed and cost matter more than maximum fidelity ### Upcoming Model Release BFL is launching a **new model in \~4 weeks** with significantly better prompt following and improved image quality at a slightly higher price point. It will be **API-only**. We don't know yet whether this model will beat the competition or simply close the gap a bit more — that's still to be seen. Historically, new model releases have driven significant API revenue spikes. Factor this into your planning — but be careful about counting unannounced product launches in your quota modeling. ### ICP (Ideal Customer Profile) BFL does not have a formally defined ICP yet. In general, the best-performing customer segments so far have been AI-native companies, digital-native platforms, large social media and e-commerce platforms, and photo/video editing tools — but this varies by product (API vs. license), model tier, and use case. We've also noticed that **slower-moving enterprises** (traditional industries, large corporates) are interesting because long-term they can become very sticky contracts. --- ## Part 1: Account List Your manager gives you access to BFL's account list. It's your job to figure out which ones are relevant for you to pursue. Among them are these 12 — there isn't much context around them apart from these notes you find yourself in the CRM and on internal Notion pages. Some of these might not be worth your time. Some might not even be "your" accounts. Part of the job is figuring that out. For most of these, BFL closed the deal and then had limited capacity to manage the relationship — so you don't necessarily know what the customer is actually doing with the model, what other models they're using, or where expansion opportunities exist. ### 1. Berta Benz (Weight License — Needs Upsell + Expansion) A major German car brand. Using FLUX internally for automotive design — fully secure, isolated environment. Currently on **all available FLUX.1 dev licenses at \$2.5K/month each**. They need to transition to FLUX.2 licensing (\$10K/month FLUX.2 Dev or \$5K/month Klein) — you can argue that FLUX.2 is meaningfully better in quality. **The challenge:** They're skeptical about the price increase and are actively evaluating **Qwen** (open-source alternative) as a fallback. Current usage is limited to one team, but they want the license available to all Berta Benz entities globally (even if most won't use it immediately). Some design teams in other countries are already pushing for access. Your primary contact is a senior designer who personally championed the project. The CIO stepped in to unblock procurement but has gone cold since (didn't reply to an email from BFL's co-founder a few weeks ago). The deal had to be structured through their US entity because the German parent company's legal team required BFL to fully indemnify for all model outputs — something BFL cannot accept when the customer hosts and can modify the model. ### 2. Berlin Motor Werke (Weight License + FDE) Another major German car brand. Using FLUX locally for advertising campaigns — putting cars into new backgrounds and environments. BFL's FDE team built custom workflows with them. Originally wanted a small \$1K license, then upsold with the FDE motion to \$35K/year. There's much more potential — multiple teams, multiple use cases — but nobody has mapped it. **Watch out:** Mid-project, they came up with the idea that the workflow they created with BFL should be **patented by them**. The workflow was actually picked up from a Reddit forum user and read by the BMW employee. This is a significant issue — they cannot patent a workflow built on open-weights models. ### 3. Eagle Motors (Small License — Zero Relationship) A major US automotive brand. Currently on a \$1K/month small FLUX.1 Dev license. The only history: their **Director of Design** reached out desperately to BFL's first GTM hire. Simply set up a small license as there was no capacity to go deeper. **No further contact since.** They'll need to transition to new pricing within the grace period or churn. Nobody knows what they're doing with the model or who the stakeholders are beyond whoever signed up. ### 4. Winter AI (Weight License — Stalled) A Korean mid-sized photo editing app. Long-standing dev license customer at \$10K/month. They've been using the weights steadily but haven't moved to broader production usage. Similar profile to other BFL dev license customers — solid baseline, potential to grow significantly if properly engaged. They also mentioned wanting to introduce BFL to their **Chinese entity**, but this was never properly followed up on. ### 5. GetPic (API — Transitioning) An AI image generation platform. They just requested cancellation of ALL their FLUX.1 licenses — the full suite: FLUX.1 Dev (\$10K/month), FLUX.1 Tools (\$5K/month), and FLUX.1 Kontext (\$5K/month). They want to shift entirely to FLUX.2 on API. This is a positive signal — they're consolidating on BFL's newest model — but nobody at BFL has capacity to help them ramp on API. If nobody engages soon, they'll ramp slowly on their own or get pulled by competitors. ### 6. Amazing-Corp (API — Major Revenue, Autopilot Risk) A Korean company. They signed up before the FLUX.2 launch on an **old waterfall pricing scheme** — no commitments, but increasing discounts the more they consume, starting at a 250K images/month threshold. They were expected to scale significantly but **haven't scaled up yet** — which could indicate competitive pressure (Nano Banana?) or internal blockers. They had billing questions early on that were only addressed sporadically. There's a **dormant Slack channel** with them that nobody monitors. Interestingly, Amazing-Corp's CEO is the wife of the Winter AI CEO — and apparently Amazing-Corp has more volume than Winter AI. This is a significant revenue account running on autopilot — a big risk and a big opportunity. Nobody at BFL has had capacity to properly manage them. ### 7. Estate-Texx (API — Needs Activation) A startup building AI-powered real estate listings. They've tested multiple times — once even spiked to **\$10K/day** in API spend — but never sustained production usage. Good CEO relationship exists. Their former engineering lead (the main technical contact) left the company and was replaced by someone new. They were historically very price-sensitive but recently shifted their own pricing model, so budget is less of a blocker now. **Key detail:** Their end customers are **major real estate platforms** (think ImmobilienScout24, Kleinanzeigen-type companies) — which would also be valuable BFL customers in their own right. ### 8. Hofer Market (Early Exploration) A major international grocery/discount retailer exploring FLUX for marketing content creation across **all their global operations, including the US market** (where they're a household name). Still very early — the tech team needs significant guidance, including basic prompting help. There's a project owner on the business side from an innovations team who is very positive — but likely doesn't have real decision-making power or budget authority. They haven't yet involved the "real" stakeholders (marketing leadership, brand team) who would need to see what FLUX can do to drive real adoption and budget. ### 9. StudioMax (Weight License — Unknown Status) A creative software company. BFL's first GTM hire closed a **\$150K/year** weight license deal 5 months ago and handed the account to you. There's been **no QBR, no check-in, and no structured follow-up** since the deal closed. You don't know what they're doing with the model, whether they've deployed it, what other models they're evaluating, or who the day-to-day contacts are. ### 10. SnapMagic (API — Declining) A photo enhancement startup. Was doing \~\$2K/month on API, but spend has declined to \~\$500/month over the last 3 months. Nobody has investigated why. Could be a product issue, a competitive switch, a use case that didn't work out, or simply seasonal. ### 11. Atelier Digital (Weight License — Agency / Partnerships Play) A creative agency with a \$5K/month dev license. They're a subsidiary of **Deccenture**, one of the world's largest consulting/agency conglomerates. They want to get a license for themselves ASAP, and best case want it to be available to all Deccenture subsidiaries — essentially wanting preferred pricing and terms for the entire Deccenture network. You stumble across this because they submitted an inbound lead. Digging into the CRM, you see that BFL's **partnerships team is actually in contact with Deccenture**, negotiating a broader framework deal for the parent company. The initial outreach from the partnerships team was a while back, but the conversation is active at the Deccenture level. ### 12a. ResearchLabs AI (API Opportunity — Reseller) Currently using **Laf** (a reseller that aggregates multiple AI model providers). Doing **\~500K FLUX images/month** via Laf. Their Laf contract is up for renewal and they've reached out to BFL directly. They simply tell you they get a **30% discount from Laf** and want to know if BFL can beat that price. No other context — pure price inquiry. ### 12b. CommerceFlow (API Opportunity — Reseller) Also currently on **Laf**, doing **\~500K FLUX images/month**. Their Laf contract is also up for renewal. Unlike ResearchLabs, CommerceFlow is more engaged — they want to explore a **direct strategic partnership** with BFL, including dedicated support, early access to new models, and custom integration work. ### 12c. HelloGen Today (API Opportunity — Reseller / Direct) Doing **\~100K FLUX generations/day via Laf** plus **\~200K generations/day on Nano Banana**. They want to come direct and would prefer hosting BFL's Pro and Max models directly on their own infrastructure. BFL is competing with **Laf** and **Runpath** on this account. The conversation is currently purely price-driven — no value discussion has happened. BFL's **partnerships team was in contact with HelloGen** but the account has been sitting in-stage for **8 weeks** with no movement. --- ## Part 2: Inbound Lead Backlog Your CRM shows **\~5,000+ leads** accumulated over the past 12 months. The vast majority were created automatically when someone filled out the contact form or signed up for the API. About **200-300 are from the last 90 days**. Historically, someone skimmed through them and responded to the obviously huge names, but the rest sit untouched. **Attached separately: BFL_Inbound_Leads_Sample.xlsx** — \~1,000 sample leads from the backlog. Skim through it. It's messy — that's realistic. You'll find a mix of: - Legitimate enterprise inquiries with clear budget signals - Mid-market companies with real use cases - Individual developers and freelancers - Spam and bot submissions - Support tickets that ended up in the sales queue - People who just want to know how to use the product - Duplicates and junk data Your manager says: *"I don't expect you to work all 5,000. I expect you to figure out which ones matter, build a system for the rest, and tell me what we should do with the backlog long-term. Think about how you would qualify these at scale — we absolutely cannot call every single one."* **Side note:** BFL's API currently generates **\~5 billion images per year** across all customers. The lead data is not cross-referenced with API usage data — you have no idea which of these leads (or other companies) are already spending money on the API. That data exists in a separate system. If you want it, we can pull a sample — see **BFL_API_Users_Sample.xlsx** (attached separately, \~200 users with monthly spend data). --- ## Part 3: Lost Deals (\~50) Your CRM shows approximately 50 lost deals from the past 6-9 months. CRM hygiene is not ideal — many deals are categorized under vague reasons because nobody filled in the details. **Summary by lost reason:**
Lost Reason Count Deal Size Range Notes
Other / Unknown \~12 \$50K–\$1M+ No notes, reason never logged, unclear what happened
Competition (mainly Nano Banana) 5 \$50K–\$500K Platforms chose Nano Banana for easier prompting and bundled Google features
Too early for customer 4 \$50K–\$300K Enterprise hadn't figured out AI strategy yet, "come back next quarter"
We were too late 3 \$100K–\$500K Enterprise was already in advanced talks or had signed with a competitor before BFL engaged. These were companies close to BFL's core business where earlier outreach could have made a difference
Too pricey 3 \$50K–\$250K Customer felt BFL was too expensive compared to alternatives
Quality / Model fit 3 \$50K–\$200K Customer felt the model didn't match their specific style requirements. Open question: did they not use it correctly (prompting issue)? Would they need a custom fine-tuned model (which BFL can sell as an expensive engagement)? Or was it a genuine quality gap?
API instability 2 \$100K–\$500K Experienced downtime during evaluation period in summer 2025
Built in-house 2 \$5M–\$50M Large tech companies decided to train own models. One deal (\~\$5M) was with a company that has actually shipped a competitive in-house model. Another deal (\~\$50M potential) was with a global tech company exploring platform-wide integration — they ultimately announced a partnership with Gemini instead, but there may still be potential
Legal blocker (indemnification) 1 \$200K Enterprise legal required full output indemnification for self-hosted
Legal blocker (other) 1 \$80K–\$250K Data processing terms
Too slow 1 \$100K Needed real-time inference — before FLUX.2 Klein existed
Reseller conflict 1 \$50K–\$100K Wanted to resell FLUX but terms didn't work
**Attached separately: BFL_Lost_Deals.xlsx** — the full anonymized lost deal list. Note: "—" in Close Date means no projected close date was logged. Many lost reasons are blank because CRM hygiene was not maintained. Some companies appear multiple times because different product lines or teams were evaluating separately. Your manager says: *"FLUX.2 is a meaningfully better model than what most of these companies evaluated. Some lost deals might be worth a second look — especially the ones lost on speed, quality, or 'too early.' But don't waste time on dead ends, and think carefully about which deals you should handle yourself versus which ones need to be escalated. Some of these are founder-level relationships."* --- ## Part 4: Outbound Campaign Your manager expects you to run at least one outbound campaign in your first month. BFL has just launched **FLUX.2 Klein** — a 9B parameter model offering: - Near real-time inference - Significantly lower cost per image than FLUX.2 Dev - High quality for its speed tier The target: **win high-volume image generation workloads away from competing models** (not cannibalizing FLUX.2's own premium tier — Klein is about capturing volume that's currently going to lower-tier competitors). Note: Klein 9B via API is **extremely cost-efficient** — check public pricing on [bfl.ai](http://bfl.ai) to understand the unit economics before building your campaign plan. You have access to: LinkedIn Sales Navigator, [customer.io](http://customer.io) (email sequencing — coordinate with marketing), and competitor comparison data. Remember the prompting challenge: FLUX.2 models require different prompting than Nano Banana. Your outbound messaging needs to address this proactively — maybe linking to the prompt guide, offering a comparison, or positioning the precision as a feature rather than a friction point. --- ## Your Task Prepare a **35-minute presentation**. You have a lot of information in front of you — intentionally more than you can cover in 35 minutes. **We don't expect you to address everything.** In fact, trying to cover all of it superficially would be a mistake. You are not expected to analyze all attached data files in depth. Use them to support your priorities, not to cover all of them. Pick the **2-4 areas you would prioritize in your first 90 days** and go deep. Show us your thinking: what data did you look at, what did you conclude, what would you actually do? For everything else, tell us what you'd deliberately deprioritize or defer — and why. Here are the areas you can choose from: 1. **First 90 Days Plan** — What do you do in Month 1, Month 2, Month 3? What do you deliberately NOT do? How do you prioritize across the workstreams — you can't do everything at once, so what gets your time first and what waits? 2. **Account Priorities** — From the account list, which accounts do you pursue and why? Which do you qualify out? What's your first action for each? 3. **Inbound System** — How would you triage 5,000+ leads? What's your qualification framework? How would you qualify these at scale — you can't call every single one. 4. **Lost Deal Reactivation** — Which lost deals are worth revisiting given FLUX.2's improvements? Which should you handle vs. escalate to leadership? 5. **Outbound Campaign** — What segment do you target? What's your message and value proposition? Consider the unit economics. 6. **Any Other Potential Revenue Stream** — Is there anything else in the data you've been given that could unlock revenue? What would you do with it? Pick 3-4 of these and go deep. For the rest, a sentence or two on why you're parking it is enough. We care about how you think and prioritize, not about covering everything. ### Quota & Pipeline Model (Required) Your annual quota is **\$5M in new + expansion ARR**. Based on everything you've seen across all the data — build a rough pipeline model. Where does the revenue come from? Is \$5M achievable? What's your biggest risk? This is not optional — every candidate should address this. **No complex financial model required** — napkin math is fine (e.g., X accounts × Y avg deal size = Z ARR). We want to see your logic and assumptions, not your spreadsheet skills. **Format:** 35-minute presentation + 25 minutes Q&A. Use whatever format works for you — slides, Notion doc, Google Doc, whiteboard, whatever. We care about your thinking, not your design skills. --- ## Appendix - Inbound leads: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1O55pxnicHvVzeo6JBiWdxQzaAsHjwNvf/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1O55pxnicHvVzeo6JBiWdxQzaAsHjwNvf/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true) - API user data sample: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1fK_UGRHbWlLS0GWJLOqj_K8FJE3-_GAQ/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1fK_UGRHbWlLS0GWJLOqj_K8FJE3-_GAQ/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true) - Lost deals: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1KArMnH5PwBKvjNeqsAS9j02bcN6mFgfN/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1KArMnH5PwBKvjNeqsAS9j02bcN6mFgfN/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true)

raw.title: Master Copy- AE Case Study — Your First 90 Days at BFL
raw.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/306c370222d581c78d27ef3057923f87 as of 2026-03-27T08:36:18.394Z: {"title":"Master Copy- AE Case Study — Your First 90 Days at BFL"} This first part is internal! ## How to Use This Case Study **Send to the candidate 3 days before their onsite.** They should prepare a **35-minute presentation** (see "Your Task" at the bottom). Allow **25 minutes for Q&A** after. Candidates are encouraged to research BFL online during prep. They are welcome to use AI tools (Claude, ChatGPT, etc.) during preparation — we care about the quality of thinking and conclusions, not whether the analysis was done by hand. This includes using AI to help process or analyze the attached data files — that's expected and encouraged. No internal materials will be provided beyond this document and the attached data files with mock-up data (inbound leads spreadsheet, API users spreadsheet, lost deals spreadsheet). **Why this case study works** This case study works because it mirrors the actual job. A mid-level AE joining BFL will face exactly this: too many accounts, messy data, no playbook, and more workstreams than they can handle at once. By giving candidates more information than they can possibly cover in 35 minutes, the exercise tests prioritization — the single most important skill for this role. The traps are subtle: accounts that should be escalated to partnerships or senior AEs, hidden gems buried in noisy API data that only surface if the candidate thinks to cross-reference, lost deals that are worth revisiting vs. dead ends, and an outbound campaign they should arguably deprioritize because they already have enough on their plate. Candidates who try to cover everything superficially fail. Candidates who pick 3-4 areas, go deep with data-backed reasoning, and clearly explain what they're deliberately not doing — those are the ones who can actually do this job. The 25-minute Q&A then stress-tests everything they parked, so there's nowhere to hide. From here onwards it’s the external facing case-study ## Context You've just joined **Black Forest Labs (BFL)** as an Account Executive — the company's **first mid-level AE hire**. BFL builds the FLUX family of state-of-the-art image generation models. The whole GTM team is \~15 people including sales, partnerships, SE/FDE and legal. There are three Senior AEs handling high-stakes, complex strategic deals (think: multi-million platform integrations, custom licensing structures). A separate **partnerships team of 3 Senior Partnerships Managers** handles channel partnerships, cloud platform relationships, and similar strategic motions. 5** SE / FDEs ****(Forward Deployed Engineers)** work alongside these teams on the biggest deals — building custom assets, implementations, and custom endpoints to create highly customized environments for large contracts or to unlock use cases at scale. That means **you own basically everything else** — a very large surface area of accounts, leads, and opportunities that need prioritization. Before your first day, familiarize yourself with BFL's products, models, and positioning by researching the company online. ### Commercial Motions BFL sells through three commercial motions: - **API** — customers call BFL's hosted endpoints and pay per image generated. FLUX.2 is priced by megapixels — more details can be found at [bfl.ai](http://bfl.ai) - **Weight Licensing** — customers license model weights and run inference on their own infrastructure. Current indicative tiers: FLUX.2 Dev (32B parameters, \~\$10K/month) and FLUX.2 Klein (9B parameters, \~\$5K/month). Note: the team is still figuring out the best pricing per customer segment and use case, so these are directional - **Mixed / Custom Deals** — some customers combine API usage with weight licensing depending on their use case ### Pricing Landscape BFL has evolved its pricing over time, so **different customers are on very different commercial structures:** - Some are on an **old waterfall pricing scheme** — no commitments, but they get increasing discounts the more they consume (volume tiers) - Some have **annual commitments** with locked-in pricing - Some have **discounts without any commitment** — BFL moved to this model at one point to close deals faster - Some have **prepaid credits** — either consumed at per-image pricing with a discount (e.g., 10% off list), or at a flat per-image rate across all models. The flat-rate structure is common with larger enterprises — they pay the same rate regardless of which model they use, which makes the effective deal value much larger than a simple PAYG customer who might only use cheaper models. Startups typically don't go for flat-rate prepaid deals As you review the account portfolio, pay attention to what pricing structure each customer is on — it affects expansion strategy significantly. ### Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) BFL has a small **FDE (Forward Deployed Engineering)** team — solutions engineers who work hands-on with license customers to fine-tune models, build custom workflows, and optimize inference pipelines. FDE is billed at **\$6.5K/day** and is a key upsell lever for license deals. However, the FDE team is small and should **only be deployed on major strategic implementation projects** — not sold as day-rate consulting to every license customer. ### FLUX.2 and Competitive Positioning - **FLUX.2** launched in Q4 2025 as BFL's flagship model. It competes head-to-head with **Nano Banana** (Google's image generation suite) - Being direct: FLUX.2 **might appear slightly worse than Nano Banana in some key areas**. Nano Banana benefits from Google's massive marketing machine, producing far more hype than BFL can match as a startup. Nano Banana also has the full Gemini suite behind it, making prompting very forgiving — users can write lazy, imprecise prompts and get good results - **FLUX.2's advantage** is that it can be **prompted much more precisely** — but users need to follow BFL's prompt guide (available on the website). Most users default to the same prompts they use with Nano Banana and then perceive FLUX.2 as worse. BFL knows this is a real onboarding friction point and is actively working on fixing it — but for now it's something you need to address proactively with customers - **FLUX.2 Klein** (9B) — fast, cheap, high quality. Near real-time inference. Ideal for preview/draft use cases, free-tier platform users, and high-volume applications where speed and cost matter more than maximum fidelity ### Upcoming Model Release BFL is launching a **new model in \~4 weeks** with significantly better prompt following and improved image quality at a slightly higher price point. It will be **API-only**. We don't know yet whether this model will beat the competition or simply close the gap a bit more — that's still to be seen. Historically, new model releases have driven significant API revenue spikes. Factor this into your planning — but be careful about counting unannounced product launches in your quota modeling. ### ICP (Ideal Customer Profile) BFL does not have a formally defined ICP yet. In general, the best-performing customer segments so far have been AI-native companies, digital-native platforms, large social media and e-commerce platforms, and photo/video editing tools — but this varies by product (API vs. license), model tier, and use case. We've also noticed that **slower-moving enterprises** (traditional industries, large corporates) are interesting because long-term they can become very sticky contracts. --- ## Part 1: Account List Your manager gives you access to BFL's account list. It's your job to figure out which ones are relevant for you to pursue. Among them are these 12 — there isn't much context around them apart from these notes you find yourself in the CRM and on internal Notion pages. Some of these might not be worth your time. Some might not even be "your" accounts. Part of the job is figuring that out. For most of these, BFL closed the deal and then had limited capacity to manage the relationship — so you don't necessarily know what the customer is actually doing with the model, what other models they're using, or where expansion opportunities exist. ### 1. Berta Benz (Weight License — Needs Upsell + Expansion) A major German car brand. Using FLUX internally for automotive design — fully secure, isolated environment. Currently on **all available FLUX.1 dev licenses at \$2.5K/month each**. They need to transition to FLUX.2 licensing (\$10K/month FLUX.2 Dev or \$5K/month Klein) — you can argue that FLUX.2 is meaningfully better in quality. **The challenge:** They're skeptical about the price increase and are actively evaluating **Qwen** (open-source alternative) as a fallback. Current usage is limited to one team, but they want the license available to all Berta Benz entities globally (even if most won't use it immediately). Some design teams in other countries are already pushing for access. Your primary contact is a senior designer who personally championed the project. The CIO stepped in to unblock procurement but has gone cold since (didn't reply to an email from BFL's co-founder a few weeks ago). The deal had to be structured through their US entity because the German parent company's legal team required BFL to fully indemnify for all model outputs — something BFL cannot accept when the customer hosts and can modify the model. ### 2. Berlin Motor Werke (Weight License + FDE) Another major German car brand. Using FLUX locally for advertising campaigns — putting cars into new backgrounds and environments. BFL's FDE team built custom workflows with them. Originally wanted a small \$1K license, then upsold with the FDE motion to \$35K/year. There's much more potential — multiple teams, multiple use cases — but nobody has mapped it. **Watch out:** Mid-project, they came up with the idea that the workflow they created with BFL should be **patented by them**. The workflow was actually picked up from a Reddit forum user and read by the BMW employee. This is a significant issue — they cannot patent a workflow built on open-weights models. ### 3. Eagle Motors (Small License — Zero Relationship) A major US automotive brand. Currently on a \$1K/month small FLUX.1 Dev license. The only history: their **Director of Design** reached out desperately to BFL's first GTM hire. Simply set up a small license as there was no capacity to go deeper. **No further contact since.** They'll need to transition to new pricing within the grace period or churn. Nobody knows what they're doing with the model or who the stakeholders are beyond whoever signed up. ### 4. Winter AI (Weight License — Stalled) A Korean mid-sized photo editing app. Long-standing dev license customer at \$10K/month. They've been using the weights steadily but haven't moved to broader production usage. Similar profile to other BFL dev license customers — solid baseline, potential to grow significantly if properly engaged. They also mentioned wanting to introduce BFL to their **Chinese entity**, but this was never properly followed up on. ### 5. GetPic (API — Transitioning) An AI image generation platform. They just requested cancellation of ALL their FLUX.1 licenses — the full suite: FLUX.1 Dev (\$10K/month), FLUX.1 Tools (\$5K/month), and FLUX.1 Kontext (\$5K/month). They want to shift entirely to FLUX.2 on API. This is a positive signal — they're consolidating on BFL's newest model — but nobody at BFL has capacity to help them ramp on API. If nobody engages soon, they'll ramp slowly on their own or get pulled by competitors. ### 6. Amazing-Corp (API — Major Revenue, Autopilot Risk) A Korean company. They signed up before the FLUX.2 launch on an **old waterfall pricing scheme** — no commitments, but increasing discounts the more they consume, starting at a 250K images/month threshold. They were expected to scale significantly but **haven't scaled up yet** — which could indicate competitive pressure (Nano Banana?) or internal blockers. They had billing questions early on that were only addressed sporadically. There's a **dormant Slack channel** with them that nobody monitors. Interestingly, Amazing-Corp's CEO is the wife of the Winter AI CEO — and apparently Amazing-Corp has more volume than Winter AI. This is a significant revenue account running on autopilot — a big risk and a big opportunity. Nobody at BFL has had capacity to properly manage them. ### 7. Estate-Texx (API — Needs Activation) A startup building AI-powered real estate listings. They've tested multiple times — once even spiked to **\$10K/day** in API spend — but never sustained production usage. Good CEO relationship exists. Their former engineering lead (the main technical contact) left the company and was replaced by someone new. They were historically very price-sensitive but recently shifted their own pricing model, so budget is less of a blocker now. **Key detail:** Their end customers are **major real estate platforms** (think ImmobilienScout24, Kleinanzeigen-type companies) — which would also be valuable BFL customers in their own right. ### 8. Hofer Market (Early Exploration) A major international grocery/discount retailer exploring FLUX for marketing content creation across **all their global operations, including the US market** (where they're a household name). Still very early — the tech team needs significant guidance, including basic prompting help. There's a project owner on the business side from an innovations team who is very positive — but likely doesn't have real decision-making power or budget authority. They haven't yet involved the "real" stakeholders (marketing leadership, brand team) who would need to see what FLUX can do to drive real adoption and budget. ### 9. StudioMax (Weight License — Unknown Status) A creative software company. BFL's first GTM hire closed a **\$150K/year** weight license deal 5 months ago and handed the account to you. There's been **no QBR, no check-in, and no structured follow-up** since the deal closed. You don't know what they're doing with the model, whether they've deployed it, what other models they're evaluating, or who the day-to-day contacts are. ### 10. SnapMagic (API — Declining) A photo enhancement startup. Was doing \~\$2K/month on API, but spend has declined to \~\$500/month over the last 3 months. Nobody has investigated why. Could be a product issue, a competitive switch, a use case that didn't work out, or simply seasonal. ### 11. Atelier Digital (Weight License — Agency / Partnerships Play) A creative agency with a \$5K/month dev license. They're a subsidiary of **Deccenture**, one of the world's largest consulting/agency conglomerates. They want to get a license for themselves ASAP, and best case want it to be available to all Deccenture subsidiaries — essentially wanting preferred pricing and terms for the entire Deccenture network. You stumble across this because they submitted an inbound lead. Digging into the CRM, you see that BFL's **partnerships team is actually in contact with Deccenture**, negotiating a broader framework deal for the parent company. The initial outreach from the partnerships team was a while back, but the conversation is active at the Deccenture level. ### 12a. ResearchLabs AI (API Opportunity — Reseller) Currently using **Laf** (a reseller that aggregates multiple AI model providers). Doing **\~500K FLUX images/month** via Laf. Their Laf contract is up for renewal and they've reached out to BFL directly. They simply tell you they get a **30% discount from Laf** and want to know if BFL can beat that price. No other context — pure price inquiry. ### 12b. CommerceFlow (API Opportunity — Reseller) Also currently on **Laf**, doing **\~500K FLUX images/month**. Their Laf contract is also up for renewal. Unlike ResearchLabs, CommerceFlow is more engaged — they want to explore a **direct strategic partnership** with BFL, including dedicated support, early access to new models, and custom integration work. ### 12c. HelloGen Today (API Opportunity — Reseller / Direct) Doing **\~100K FLUX generations/day via Laf** plus **\~200K generations/day on Nano Banana**. They want to come direct and would prefer hosting BFL's Pro and Max models directly on their own infrastructure. BFL is competing with **Laf** and **Runpath** on this account. The conversation is currently purely price-driven — no value discussion has happened. BFL's **partnerships team was in contact with HelloGen** but the account has been sitting in-stage for **8 weeks** with no movement. --- ## Part 2: Inbound Lead Backlog Your CRM shows **\~5,000+ leads** accumulated over the past 12 months. The vast majority were created automatically when someone filled out the contact form or signed up for the API. About **200-300 are from the last 90 days**. Historically, someone skimmed through them and responded to the obviously huge names, but the rest sit untouched. **Attached separately: BFL_Inbound_Leads_Sample.xlsx** — \~1,000 sample leads from the backlog. Skim through it. It's messy — that's realistic. You'll find a mix of: - Legitimate enterprise inquiries with clear budget signals - Mid-market companies with real use cases - Individual developers and freelancers - Spam and bot submissions - Support tickets that ended up in the sales queue - People who just want to know how to use the product - Duplicates and junk data Your manager says: *"I don't expect you to work all 5,000. I expect you to figure out which ones matter, build a system for the rest, and tell me what we should do with the backlog long-term. Think about how you would qualify these at scale — we absolutely cannot call every single one."* **Side note:** BFL's API currently generates **\~5 billion images per year** across all customers. The lead data is not cross-referenced with API usage data — you have no idea which of these leads (or other companies) are already spending money on the API. That data exists in a separate system. If you want it, we can pull a sample — see **BFL_API_Users_Sample.xlsx** (attached separately, \~200 users with monthly spend data). --- ## Part 3: Lost Deals (\~50) Your CRM shows approximately 50 lost deals from the past 6-9 months. CRM hygiene is not ideal — many deals are categorized under vague reasons because nobody filled in the details. **Summary by lost reason:**
Lost Reason Count Deal Size Range Notes
Other / Unknown \~12 \$50K–\$1M+ No notes, reason never logged, unclear what happened
Competition (mainly Nano Banana) 5 \$50K–\$500K Platforms chose Nano Banana for easier prompting and bundled Google features
Too early for customer 4 \$50K–\$300K Enterprise hadn't figured out AI strategy yet, "come back next quarter"
We were too late 3 \$100K–\$500K Enterprise was already in advanced talks or had signed with a competitor before BFL engaged. These were companies close to BFL's core business where earlier outreach could have made a difference
Too pricey 3 \$50K–\$250K Customer felt BFL was too expensive compared to alternatives
Quality / Model fit 3 \$50K–\$200K Customer felt the model didn't match their specific style requirements. Open question: did they not use it correctly (prompting issue)? Would they need a custom fine-tuned model (which BFL can sell as an expensive engagement)? Or was it a genuine quality gap?
API instability 2 \$100K–\$500K Experienced downtime during evaluation period in summer 2025
Built in-house 2 \$5M–\$50M Large tech companies decided to train own models. One deal (\~\$5M) was with a company that has actually shipped a competitive in-house model. Another deal (\~\$50M potential) was with a global tech company exploring platform-wide integration — they ultimately announced a partnership with Gemini instead, but there may still be potential
Legal blocker (indemnification) 1 \$200K Enterprise legal required full output indemnification for self-hosted
Legal blocker (other) 1 \$80K–\$250K Data processing terms
Too slow 1 \$100K Needed real-time inference — before FLUX.2 Klein existed
Reseller conflict 1 \$50K–\$100K Wanted to resell FLUX but terms didn't work
**Attached separately: BFL_Lost_Deals.xlsx** — the full anonymized lost deal list. Note: "—" in Close Date means no projected close date was logged. Many lost reasons are blank because CRM hygiene was not maintained. Some companies appear multiple times because different product lines or teams were evaluating separately. Your manager says: *"FLUX.2 is a meaningfully better model than what most of these companies evaluated. Some lost deals might be worth a second look — especially the ones lost on speed, quality, or 'too early.' But don't waste time on dead ends, and think carefully about which deals you should handle yourself versus which ones need to be escalated. Some of these are founder-level relationships."* --- ## Part 4: Outbound Campaign Your manager expects you to run at least one outbound campaign in your first month. BFL has just launched **FLUX.2 Klein** — a 9B parameter model offering: - Near real-time inference - Significantly lower cost per image than FLUX.2 Dev - High quality for its speed tier The target: **win high-volume image generation workloads away from competing models** (not cannibalizing FLUX.2's own premium tier — Klein is about capturing volume that's currently going to lower-tier competitors). Note: Klein 9B via API is **extremely cost-efficient** — check public pricing on [bfl.ai](http://bfl.ai) to understand the unit economics before building your campaign plan. You have access to: LinkedIn Sales Navigator, [customer.io](http://customer.io) (email sequencing — coordinate with marketing), and competitor comparison data. Remember the prompting challenge: FLUX.2 models require different prompting than Nano Banana. Your outbound messaging needs to address this proactively — maybe linking to the prompt guide, offering a comparison, or positioning the precision as a feature rather than a friction point. --- ## Your Task Prepare a **35-minute presentation**. You have a lot of information in front of you — intentionally more than you can cover in 35 minutes. **We don't expect you to address everything.** In fact, trying to cover all of it superficially would be a mistake. You are not expected to analyze all attached data files in depth. Use them to support your priorities, not to cover all of them. Pick the **2-4 areas you would prioritize in your first 90 days** and go deep. Show us your thinking: what data did you look at, what did you conclude, what would you actually do? For everything else, tell us what you'd deliberately deprioritize or defer — and why. Here are the areas you can choose from: 1. **First 90 Days Plan** — What do you do in Month 1, Month 2, Month 3? What do you deliberately NOT do? How do you prioritize across the workstreams — you can't do everything at once, so what gets your time first and what waits? 2. **Account Priorities** — From the account list, which accounts do you pursue and why? Which do you qualify out? What's your first action for each? 3. **Inbound System** — How would you triage 5,000+ leads? What's your qualification framework? How would you qualify these at scale — you can't call every single one. 4. **Lost Deal Reactivation** — Which lost deals are worth revisiting given FLUX.2's improvements? Which should you handle vs. escalate to leadership? 5. **Outbound Campaign** — What segment do you target? What's your message and value proposition? Consider the unit economics. 6. **Any Other Potential Revenue Stream** — Is there anything else in the data you've been given that could unlock revenue? What would you do with it? Pick 3-4 of these and go deep. For the rest, a sentence or two on why you're parking it is enough. We care about how you think and prioritize, not about covering everything. ### Quota & Pipeline Model (Required) Your annual quota is **\$5M in new + expansion ARR**. Based on everything you've seen across all the data — build a rough pipeline model. Where does the revenue come from? Is \$5M achievable? What's your biggest risk? This is not optional — every candidate should address this. **No complex financial model required** — napkin math is fine (e.g., X accounts × Y avg deal size = Z ARR). We want to see your logic and assumptions, not your spreadsheet skills. **Format:** 35-minute presentation + 25 minutes Q&A. Use whatever format works for you — slides, Notion doc, Google Doc, whiteboard, whatever. We care about your thinking, not your design skills. --- ## Appendix - Inbound leads: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1O55pxnicHvVzeo6JBiWdxQzaAsHjwNvf/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1O55pxnicHvVzeo6JBiWdxQzaAsHjwNvf/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true) - API user data sample: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1fK_UGRHbWlLS0GWJLOqj_K8FJE3-_GAQ/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1fK_UGRHbWlLS0GWJLOqj_K8FJE3-_GAQ/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true) - Lost deals: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1KArMnH5PwBKvjNeqsAS9j02bcN6mFgfN/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1KArMnH5PwBKvjNeqsAS9j02bcN6mFgfN/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=108864865833676927548&rtpof=true&sd=true)

31fc3702-22d5-805f-b836-e132110d52cd.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/31fc370222d5805fb836e132110d52cd as of 2026-03-25T23:31:28.077Z: {"title":"FLUX for outpainting"} **Expand any image beyond its borders** — straight from the API. Set `auto_crop=true` to gracefully handle cases where the positioned image extends beyond the canvas edges. ```bash IMAGE_BASE64="$(base64 < /path/to/input.png | tr -d '\n')" B64_TMP=$(mktemp) echo "$IMAGE_BASE64" > "$B64_TMP" jq -n \ --rawfile img "$B64_TMP" \ '{ prompt: "expand background, woman standing in front of greek temple.", input_image: ($img | rtrimstr("\n")), width: 1024, height: 1024, bbox_x1: 100, bbox_y1: 50, auto_crop: false, output_format: "png" }' > /tmp/outpaint_request.json rm -f "$B64_TMP" curl -sk -X POST "https://labs.us2.bfl.ai/partners/$PARTNER/outpainting" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-Key: $BFL_API_KEY" \ --data-binary @/tmp/outpaint_request.json ``` This returns a task ID and a polling URL: ```json {"id": "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx", "polling_url": "..."} ``` **3. Poll for your result** ```bash curl -sk "https://labs.us2.bfl.ai/v1/get_result?id=YOUR_TASK_ID" \ -H "X-Key: $BFL_API_KEY" ``` When `status` is `"Ready"`, grab the expanded image URL from `result.sample` — it's a full-resolution PNG with seamlessly generated content filling the new canvas area. --- ## Python quick start ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import base64 import os import time import requests API_KEY = os.environ["BFL_API_KEY"] BASE = "https://labs.us2.bfl.ai" PARTNER = "" HEADERS = {"X-Key": API_KEY, "Content-Type": "application/json"} # Prompt is optional; the backend prepends "OUTPAINT" automatically. PROMPT = "expand background, woman standing in front of greek temple." IMAGE_PATH = "" WIDTH, HEIGHT = 1024, 1024 BBOX_X1 = 100 # None = center horizontally BBOX_Y1 = 50 # None = center vertically AUTO_CROP = False OUTPUT = "output.png" with open(IMAGE_PATH, "rb") as f: image_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() payload = { "prompt": PROMPT, "input_image": image_b64, "auto_crop": AUTO_CROP, "output_format": "png", } payload.update({"width": WIDTH, "height": HEIGHT}) if BBOX_X1 is not None: payload["bbox_x1"] = BBOX_X1 if BBOX_Y1 is not None: payload["bbox_y1"] = BBOX_Y1 resp = requests.post( f"{BASE}/partners/{PARTNER}/outpainting", headers=HEADERS, json=payload, verify=False, ).json() try: task_id = resp["id"] except Exception as e: print(f"Error getting task id: {e}") print(resp) exit(1) poll_url = resp.get("polling_url", f"{BASE}/v1/get_result?id={task_id}") print(f"Task submitted: {task_id}") while True: result = requests.get(poll_url, headers={"X-Key": API_KEY}, verify=False).json() if result["status"] == "Ready": img_url = result["result"]["sample"] with open(OUTPUT, "wb") as f: f.write(requests.get(img_url).content) print(f"Saved: {OUTPUT}") break if result["status"] in ("Error", "Request Moderated", "Content Moderated", "Task not found"): print(f"Failed: {result['status']}") break time.sleep(1) ``` --- ## Details: API and Training: The `pydantic` model used to construct the outpainting request. You have three options: - **Let the endpoint handle padding (centered)** — provide your image, set `width` and `height`, and leave `bbox_x1` / `bbox_y1` as `None`. The image will be centered on the new canvas automatically (legacy behaviour). - **Place the image at a custom position** — set `bbox_x1` and `bbox_y1` to control exactly where the top-left corner of your input image lands on the canvas (negative values are allowed). Optionally enable `auto_crop=True` to crop any overflow instead of raising an error. ```python class PartnerOutpaintingInputs(BaseModel): """Input model for partner outpainting endpoint. The caller provides a prompt, an input image, and target dimensions. The image is placed on a white canvas at (width, height) before being sent to the Flex finetuned model. bbox_x1 / bbox_y1 set the top-left corner of the input image on the canvas in pixels (may be negative). When both are None the image is centered (legacy behaviour). """ prompt: Optional[str] = Field( default=None, description=( "Text prompt for outpainting. The trigger word 'OUTPAINT' is prepended " "automatically if absent. Defaults to a quality-focused outpainting prompt." ), ) input_image: str = Field(description="Base64-encoded input image.") width: Optional[int] = Field( default=None, ge=64, description="Target output width." ) height: Optional[int] = Field( default=None, ge=64, description="Target output height." ) bbox_x1: Optional[int] = Field( default=None, description=( "Left offset (px) of input image top-left corner on the canvas. " "Negative values are allowed. None = center horizontally." ), ) bbox_y1: Optional[int] = Field( default=None, description=( "Top offset (px) of input image top-left corner on the canvas. " "Negative values are allowed. None = center vertically." ), ) auto_crop: bool = Field( default=False, description=( "If True, crop the input image to the canvas bounds when it " "extends beyond the edges. If False, an error is raised instead." ), ) output_format: Optional[OutputFormat] = Field(default=OutputFormat.png) ``` The model was trained on green, blue, and magenta masks and performs best with those colors. In practice, however, any solid color with sufficient contrast against the rest of the image should work reliably. ```python MASK_COLORS = { "GREEN": (0, 255, 0), "BLUE": (0, 0, 255), "MAGENTA": (255, 0, 255), } ``` ## Key details
**Endpoint** `https://labs.us2.bfl.ai/partners/$PARTNER/outpainting`
**Auth** `X-Key` header with your BFL API key
**Output** PNG & JPG (RGB)
