## Inpainting with FLUX Fill An additional feature we released via FLUX.1 Fill as part of the “FLUX.1 Tools” was inpainting (Fill) and outpainting (Expand). We see three major use cases for this tool:
- i) Object insertion. For the image with the two glasses below, first try to insert a third one. Next, try to fill both of them with any liquid of your liking. Finally, try to remove one of the glasses.
- ii) Object removal. Now, try to remove one of the glasses (don’t worry if it does not work, models fail consistently at this task)
- iii) Outpainting: Currently only supported via the “Mask” upload in forestlabs.black, we can skip it for now. Good for extending images on any side. To use FLUX.1 Fill we can go back to the playground and select \`Fill\` on the left sidebar. You can then upload an image and select the area you'd like to change (see screenshot). ---
## **CRITICAL - Data Hosting & Infrastructure**
**Supabase**
(PostgreSQL Database & Auth)
- Hosts all user data, generations, assets, collections
**Microsoft Azure Blob Storage**
- Stores user uploads and generated media files
**Vercel**
- Hosting platform for Next.js applications
- CDN and edge functions
- Deployment infrastructure
**Upstash Redis**
- Rate limiting and caching
---
## **HIGH - Payment, Security & AI Services**
**Stripe**
- Payment processing for credit purchases
**PostHog**
- Product analytics (EU-hosted)
- User behavior tracking
- Feature flags
- Session replay
**Google reCAPTCHA**
- Bot protection on forms
- Spam prevention
**Mistral AI**
- AI-powered prompt editing/generation
- Template suggestions in Playground
**Slack**
- Internal notifications
**Sanity.io**
- Headless CMS for homepage content
- Media library
---
## **MEDIUM - Development & Monitoring**
**Next.js 15**
(Vercel)
- React framework
- Server-side rendering
- API routes
**Pino**
- Logging infrastructure
- Structured logging
**React Query**
(@tanstack/react-query)
- Data fetching and caching
- State synchronization
**React PDF**
(@react-pdf/renderer)
- PDF generation (likely for invoices/reports)
**Zustand**
- Client-side state management
---
## **LOW - UI Frameworks & Build Tools**
**Radix UI**
- Unstyled, accessible component primitives
- \~30+ component packages (@radix-ui/react-*)*
**Tailwind CSS**
- Utility-first CSS framework
- Plugins: tailwindcss-animate, tailwind-scrollbar, @tailwindcss/container-queries
**Lucide React**
- Icon library
**Shadcn UI**
(via Radix + Tailwind)
- Pre-built component library (workspace package)
**React Hook Form**
- Form validation and management
- Resolver: @hookform/resolvers with Zod
**Turborepo**
(Vercel)
- Monorepo build system
**Three.js**
& React Three Fiber
- 3D graphics (homepage hero animation)
- Libraries: three, @react-three/fiber, @react-three/drei
**Recharts**
- Data visualization charts
**Motion**
(Framer Motion fork)
- Animation library
**Konva**
& React Konva
- Canvas manipulation
- Image editing in Playground
**Shiki**
- Syntax highlighting
---
## **MINOR - Utilities & Styling**
**Zod**
- TypeScript-first schema validation
**date-fns**
- Date manipulation utility
**nanoid**
- ID generation
**uuid**
- UUID generation
**clsx**
&
**class-variance-authority**
- CSS class utilities
**sharp**
- Image optimization
**pako**
- Compression library
**react-markdown**
&
**@uiw/react-md-editor**
- Markdown rendering/editing
**react-masonry-css**
- Masonry grid layouts
**react-device-detect**
- Device detection
**Embla Carousel**
(embla-carousel-react)
- Carousel component
**Vaul**
- Drawer component
**cmdk**
- Command palette component
**next-themes**
- Theme switching
**next-sitemap**
- Sitemap generation
**styled-components**
- CSS-in-JS (homepage-new only)
**detect-gpu**
- GPU capability detection
**react-number-format**
- Number formatting
**react-resizable-panels**
- Resizable panel layouts
</content>
</page>

1c7c3702-22d5-80dd-9167-d7307f100abd.title: Infra/Security & compliance
1c7c3702-22d5-80dd-9167-d7307f100abd.text: Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/1c7c370222d580dd9167d7307f100abd as of 2025-04-03T09:22:12.694Z: {"title":"Infra/Security & compliance"} ### **1. Where are we spending disproportionate time troubleshooting?** We’re in firefighting mode too often—handling \~1 production incident per day, mostly infra-related (e.g., outages, latency). ### **2. Which critical projects have insufficient attention?** - **Infra Stability:** We need root-cause analysis and hardening to cut incident frequency—think better monitoring, chaos testing, or capacity planning. It’s foundational but neglected. - **Cloud Security Posture:** Wiz and Vanta will be live, but we need to implement controls and leverage it fully—automated remediation and policy enforcement cannot be on the back burner. - **API Security:** Daily incidents leave no bandwidth for deeper API testing. We have engaged third party for this already, and will have to coordinate. - **Compliance Automation:** SOC 2/ISO 27001—proactive automation. ### **3. What tasks are being done by people too senior for them?** Just a couple of things. I’m stuck in the weeds more than I should be: - **Vendor questionnaire Reviews:** Chasing HyperComply follow-ups—operational, not strategic. But I have a plan to make it self-sufficient and get myself out of this by the end of April. - **Basic Hardening:** I’d rather spend designing resilient architecture. ### **4. What skills do we lack for upcoming priorities?** Given our incident rate and roadmap, we’re missing: - **Infra Reliability + Security:** Someone who can debug production issues (e.g., Kubernetes, AWS) and secure the stack (e.g., Terraform, Wiz integrations). - **Automation Chops:** Scripting skills to offload repetitive tasks—incident playbooks, compliance automation, alert triage. - **API Security:** Expertise in securing APIs under load—threat modeling, runtime monitoring. - **Compliance Workflow:** Practical knowledge of SOC 2/ISO 27001 to streamline audits without my constant oversight. ### **Hiring Needs (Next 6 Months)** I’d push for one hybrid role—a **Security & Reliability Engineer**: - **Must-Haves:** Infra/backend experience (e.g., Azure, Kubernetes), scripting (e.g., Python, Bash), and comfort with security/compliance basics. - **Nice-to-Haves:** API security, familiarity with Wiz/Vanta/HyperComply, incident response experience. - **Why One Role:** We need a versatile player who can fight fires, harden infra, support compliance, and also roll sleeves and make code changes—reducing our tactical load so we can focus on architecture, API security, and scaling strategy. A second resource might stretch us thin at this stage, but we can revisit it in 6 months. ### **Automation & Outsourcing Opportunities** - **Automate:** - [ ] Incident response playbooks (e.g., auto-restart scripts, Wiz remediation triggers). - [ ] Compliance evidence pipelines (e.g., Vanta API to pull logs). - [ ] Monitoring/alert consolidation—less noise, faster triage. - **Outsource:** - [x] Vendor reviews via HyperComply or a managed service—low-hanging fruit. - [x] External pentests—annual or semi-annual, to cover APIs/infra without taxing us. - **In-House Priority:** Infra stability, security, and API protection must stay internal—too core to our product and too tied to daily ops. **Profile** - Beyond the technical skills (infra, security, automation), we need someone comfortable with the non-glamorous “grunt work”—think manual incident triage, chasing compliance evidence, or willing to interact with auditors/vendors—especially in our current high-incident environment. - Not every candidate enjoys that, but it’s critical until we automate more (e.g., evidence pipelines alert workflows). I suggest we bring this upfront during interviews? I’d rather set clear expectations than backfill later. Let me know what you think! Next step: - Arun to help with JD ![]()

## **Member of Technical Staff - Core Infrastructure / API Backend Engineer**
Freiburg (Germany), San Francisco (USA)
**What if the gap between a breakthrough research model and something millions of people can actually use is making inference fast enough and APIs reliable enough to matter?**
Our founding team pioneered Latent Diffusion and Stable Diffusion - breakthroughs that made generative AI accessible to millions. Today, our FLUX models power creative tools, design workflows, and products across industries worldwide.
Our FLUX models are best-in-class not only for their capability, but for ease of use in developing production applications. We top public benchmarks and compete at the frontier - and in most instances we're winning.
If you're relentlessly curious and driven by high agency, we want to talk.
With a team of \~80, we move fast and punch above our weight. From our labs in Freiburg - a university town in the Black Forest - and San Francisco, we're building what comes next.
But here's what doesn't show up in download numbers: transforming research models into production systems that serve millions of requests reliably. Models that generate in seconds, not minutes. APIs that don't fall over under load. Demos that convince people this technology is real. That's the infrastructure you'll build.
**What You'll Pioneer**
You'll be the bridge between research breakthroughs and production reality. This isn't about maintaining existing APIs—it's about taking models fresh from research, deploying them on robust serving infrastructure, and making them as reliable as possible so we can always show the world what's possible.
**You'll be the person who:**
Develops and maintains world class robust cloud architecture to serve machine learning models at scale.
You maintain the highest standard for operational excellence ensuring high availability and reliability of model serving infrastructure—downtime means users can't create
**Questions We're Wrestling With**
How do you make diffusion model inference fast enough for interactive experiences without sacrificing quality?
What's the right serving architecture for models that don't fit standard deployment patterns?
How do you balance multiple models while ensuing efficient use of compute resources
How do you build code that is both reliable in production but also enables fast iteration on new product ideas and customer POCs
What does "production-ready" actually mean for models that are still actively being improved?
How do you instrument systems to understand not just that they're working, but how well they're working for users?
These aren't theoretical—they're tradeoffs you'll navigate daily as research becomes product.
**Who Thrives Here**
Self driven and performance obsessed engineers. You are never satisfied with the status quo and will push operational excellence to the next level
**You likely have:**
Strong proficiency in Python
Extensive experience with RESTful API development —you've built APIs that real products depend on
Familiarity with containerization and orchestration technologies (Docker, Kubernetes) for deploying infrastructure at scale
Knowledge of cloud platforms (AWS, GCP, or Azure) and IAC
Experience with distributed task queues and scalable model serving architectures 
Understanding of monitoring, logging, and observability best practices for multi region cloud architecture 
Implemented CI/CD systems that quickly test and deploy code globally
**We'd be especially excited if you:**
Familiarity with MLOps practices and tools
Know database systems and data streaming technologies
Have experience with A/B testing and feature flagging in production environments
Understand security best practices for API development and ML model serving
Have built real-time inference systems with low-latency optimizations
**What We're Building Toward**
We're not just serving models—we're building the infrastructure that makes frontier AI research usable at scale. Every optimization you ship makes inference faster. Every API you build enables new applications. If that sounds more compelling than maintaining existing systems, we should talk.

<content>
## **Member of Technical Staff - Core Infrastructure / API Backend Engineer**
Freiburg (Germany), San Francisco (USA)
**What if the gap between a breakthrough research model and something millions of people can actually use is making inference fast enough and APIs reliable enough to matter?**
Our founding team pioneered Latent Diffusion and Stable Diffusion - breakthroughs that made generative AI accessible to millions. Today, our FLUX models power creative tools, design workflows, and products across industries worldwide.
Our FLUX models are best-in-class not only for their capability, but for ease of use in developing production applications. We top public benchmarks and compete at the frontier - and in most instances we're winning.
If you're relentlessly curious and driven by high agency, we want to talk.
With a team of \~80, we move fast and punch above our weight. From our labs in Freiburg - a university town in the Black Forest - and San Francisco, we're building what comes next.
But here's what doesn't show up in download numbers: transforming research models into production systems that serve millions of requests reliably. Models that generate in seconds, not minutes. APIs that don't fall over under load. Demos that convince people this technology is real. That's the infrastructure you'll build.
**What You'll Pioneer**
You'll be the bridge between research breakthroughs and production reality. This isn't about maintaining existing APIs—it's about taking models fresh from research, deploying them on robust serving infrastructure, and making them as reliable as possible so we can always show the world what's possible.
**You'll be the person who:**
Develops and maintains world class robust cloud architecture to serve machine learning models at scale.
You maintain the highest standard for operational excellence ensuring high availability and reliability of model serving infrastructure—downtime means users can't create
**Questions We're Wrestling With**
How do you make diffusion model inference fast enough for interactive experiences without sacrificing quality?
What's the right serving architecture for models that don't fit standard deployment patterns?
How do you balance multiple models while ensuing efficient use of compute resources
How do you build code that is both reliable in production but also enables fast iteration on new product ideas and customer POCs
What does "production-ready" actually mean for models that are still actively being improved?
How do you instrument systems to understand not just that they're working, but how well they're working for users?
These aren't theoretical—they're tradeoffs you'll navigate daily as research becomes product.
**Who Thrives Here**
Self driven and performance obsessed engineers. You are never satisfied with the status quo and will push operational excellence to the next level
**You likely have:**
Strong proficiency in Python
Extensive experience with RESTful API development —you've built APIs that real products depend on
Familiarity with containerization and orchestration technologies (Docker, Kubernetes) for deploying infrastructure at scale
Knowledge of cloud platforms (AWS, GCP, or Azure) and IAC
Experience with distributed task queues and scalable model serving architectures 
Understanding of monitoring, logging, and observability best practices for multi region cloud architecture 
Implemented CI/CD systems that quickly test and deploy code globally
**We'd be especially excited if you:**
Familiarity with MLOps practices and tools
Know database systems and data streaming technologies
Have experience with A/B testing and feature flagging in production environments
Understand security best practices for API development and ML model serving
Have built real-time inference systems with low-latency optimizations
**What We're Building Toward**
We're not just serving models—we're building the infrastructure that makes frontier AI research usable at scale. Every optimization you ship makes inference faster. Every API you build enables new applications. If that sounds more compelling than maintaining existing systems, we should talk.

2c3c3702-22d5-8037-b54f-d3eda2b939d9.title: BFL Operating Model
2c3c3702-22d5-8037-b54f-d3eda2b939d9.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2c3c370222d58037b54fd3eda2b939d9 as of 2026-04-01T14:53:08.905Z: {"title":"BFL Operating Model"} # Role of Operations at BFL {toggle="true"} **Why now? **At 20 people, the CEO *is* the operating system. At 70+, that breaks. You're in every room, every decision, every hire conversation. This doc is the plan to get you out of the bottleneck so you can focus on what only you can do. - operations at BFL means turning our money in the bank into \$XM ARR by managing the **company's three biggest cost centers (compute and people, followed by data)**…while building the systems that let X people ship faster with x less headcount than incumbents - It’s operating system that governs how compute, people, data and risk are converted into frontier progress - If compute is our factory, Ops runs the factory: deciding what gets built, when, at what cost, and under what rules - **(1) The 3 main spend items** - Compute and infra: largest burn, the finance component. Compute is not a fixed cost, it's a strategic weapon to us. Ops owns provider strategy, training vs. inference allocation, and capacity planning tied to the model roadmap. Every dollar misallocated here is a model that ships late or ships worse. - People (second largest, fastest growing cost). the people we're hiring, frontier ML researchers are the scarcest talent pool. We're competing against orgs with 100x our headcount and 10x our compensation budgets for the same \~200 people who can push the frontier. Ops ensures every hire is strategic, not reactive, and that we build comp and talent systems that let us win despite the asymmetry. - Data (third largest, most underleveraged cost): training data is the “raw material” of the factory. Today we procure it reactively, without taxonomy, without feedback loops, and without a sourcing strategy beyond a handful of large providers. The wrong dataset costs model performance and release cadence. The right dataset at the right time is a competitive moat - **(2) The operational system layer = what makes spend productive** - **Compute governance.** Provider strategy, training vs. inference allocation, capacity planning tied to the FLUX 3 schedule. Compute is our single largest line item and every allocation decision is a bet on what ships next. Ops ensures those bets are deliberate, tracked, and tied to the model roadmap rather than made ad hoc - **Capital & talent deployment =** **Raise, allocate and track. **Fundraising and strategic finance - investor pipeline, fundraise execution, due diligence, strategic partnerships. Hiring strategy, comp systems, resource allocation, budget pacing, forecast accuracy, board reporting. The full lifecycle of capital operationalised: bring it in, deploy it across compute, people, and data, report on it. Essentially turning CEO decisions into tracked, measurable execution - **Research reality translation.** The specific interfaces that turn research breakthroughs into shippable products: the Research to Product bridge meeting, launch coordination, and the customer feedback → research loop. This includes the data pipeline (procurement → sourcing → evaluation → feedback to research) and the infrastructure that lets BFL expand into new modalities without reinventing the process each time. Today this is ad hoc and person-dependent. The ops job is to make it a repeatable pipeline in 2026. - **Cross-functional coherence & velocity.** The function-by-function interface model: Ops ↔ Finance, Ops ↔ People, Ops ↔ GTM, Ops ↔ Product/Eng. Launch coordination, bottleneck removal, decision rights. The reason models ship in weeks after completion, not months. - **Decision architecture & operating model.** The weekly/monthly/quarterly cadence that operationalises strategy: frequent leadership sync, monthly strategy day, monthly finance review, quarterly OKR cycle to see if we are off or on track. The infrastructure that lets people operate as one company without the CEO in every room. - **Corporate operations.** Legal, IT/security, compliance, external comms and employer brand. The "keep the lights on" layer that scales us quietly or breaks loudly. **
Ops doesn't do any function's job. Ops makes every function's job possible, measurable, and coordinated so BFL operates as one company, not \~7 teams that share a Slack workspace** The job is ensuring: **Inputs are strong **→ **Engine runs fast **→ **Outputs improve**
Layer Metric Category
Inputs compute, people, data, capital
Engine research velocity, execution speed
Outputs model progress, adoption, revenue
How this maps to people and headcount What Great looks like Signals our Operating model is working Operating clarity: Accountability vs Enablement ## Key Metrics Framework {toggle="true"} **The system in one line:** **Inputs → Engine → Outputs** Operations owns the inputs and the engine. The company measures the outputs. ### 1. Core Inputs These are the three production inputs for a frontier AI lab. Operations is accountable for all three.
⚡ Compute — Do we have enough, and are we using it efficiently? **Metrics**
Metric Why it matters
GPU capacity available Are we under-resourced before a training window opens?
GPU utilisation % Are we wasting what we have?
Training cost per run Are we improving efficiency run over run?
Inference cost per request Does our margin hold as usage scales?
Compute runway (months) How long can we run the current roadmap?
**Strategic signals** - Compute secured vs. roadmap needs — never reactive, always ahead - Compute concentration risk — provider dependency Compute is not a fixed cost. It is a strategic weapon. Every dollar misallocated is a model that ships late or ships worse.
👥 People — Are we deploying talent where it matters most? **Metrics**
Metric Why it matters
Headcount vs. plan Are we executing the hiring strategy?
Hiring velocity Are we moving fast enough to win talent wars?
Critical role fill rate Are the right seats filled before they become blockers?
Researcher-to-engineer ratio Is the technical mix right for the roadmap?
Retention of top 15 superstars Zero unplanned departures is the target
**Strategic signals** - Time to hire for frontier ML roles - Top contributor output and satisfaction For frontier labs, talent density matters more than raw headcount. We are competing against orgs with 100x our headcount for the same \~200 people who can push the frontier.
📦 Data — Do researchers have what they need to improve models? **Metrics**
Metric Why it matters
New datasets acquired Are we building the right raw material pipeline?
Dataset throughput How fast is data moving from procurement to training?
Labeling throughput Are we creating bottlenecks downstream?
Time: acquisition → training The hidden latency that delays model releases
Data pipeline reliability Is this a single point of failure?
**Strategic signals** - Dataset diversity across modalities - Training data freshness at time of run Data is the quiet bottleneck. Today we procure reactively, without taxonomy or feedback loops. The ops job is to make this a repeatable pipeline in 2026.
### 2. Strategic input = Capital Operations also owns the capital layer: fundraising infrastructure, deployment, and efficiency.
💰 Capital / Fundraising — Do we have enough runway to execute the roadmap? **Metrics**
Metric Why it matters
Cash runway (months) How long can we operate without a new raise?
Capital raised vs. plan Are we on track with the fundraising strategy?
Investor pipeline health Are we always fundraise-ready?
Burn multiple How efficiently are we converting capital into ARR?
Capital efficiency Revenue generated per dollar deployed
**Strategic signals** - Ability to finance the next compute generation - Investor demand and narrative strength The \$300M raised is not a buffer. It is the fuel for Lift 1. Operations owns how it is deployed across compute, people, and data — and reports on whether each allocation is producing the intended output.
### 3. The Engine (Operations) Operations converts inputs into outputs through five systems:
System What it does
**Compute governance** *(Finance ↔ Research interface — not a standalone system at this headcount)* Compute cost & capacity: Finance. Compute allocation (what trains when): Research. No dedicated system until there is a dedicated owner.
**Capital & talent deployment** Fundraising execution and investor pipeline (Ops). Budget pacing, resource allocation, board reporting (Finance — not duplicated in Ops). Headcount plan (Ops). Comp architecture and org design (People — not duplicated in Ops).
**Research → reality translation** Research-to-Product bridge, launch coordination, customer feedback → research loop
**Cross-functional coherence & decision architecture** *(one BizOps mandate — Nicholas)* Operating cadence, function interface model (Ops ↔ Finance, People, GTM, Product/Eng), bottleneck removal, decision rights, OKR cycle. Not three separate systems — one job.
### 4. Outputs (What the company measures) Operations does not own these directly — but if the engine is broken, these break.
Output Signal
Model capability progress Benchmark improvements, new capabilities unlocked, performance vs. competitors
Training efficiency Performance per GPU, training cost per run, scaling efficiency
Research velocity Iteration speed, research-to-production time, time from idea → experiment → model change
Product / developer adoption API usage growth, active users, applications built on FLUX
Revenue per compute Revenue per GPU, inference margin, revenue growth vs. compute growth
> **If compute → capability → adoption → revenue is flowing, the engine is working. If it breaks anywhere, Operations finds it first.** Cadence ### Weekly rhythm proposal
Day Forum Who What happens
Monday Leadership sync Robin + all functional leads Each lead: top priority, blocked, at risk. **Ops drives decisions, assigns owners, closes open items in the room.** Decisions made here are final unless explicitly escalated. Robin gives strategic guidance, not approval.

At 70+, that breaks. You're in every room, every decision, every hire conversation. This doc is the plan to get you out of the bottleneck so you can focus on what only you can do. - operations at BFL means turning our money in the bank into \$XM ARR by managing the **company's three biggest cost centers (compute and people, followed by data)**…while building the systems that let X people ship faster with x less headcount than incumbents - It’s operating system that governs how compute, people, data and risk are converted into frontier progress - If compute is our factory, Ops runs the factory: deciding what gets built, when, at what cost, and under what rules - **(1) The 3 main spend items** - Compute and infra: largest burn, the finance component. Compute is not a fixed cost, it's a strategic weapon to us. Ops owns provider strategy, training vs. inference allocation, and capacity planning tied to the model roadmap. Every dollar misallocated here is a model that ships late or ships worse. - People (second largest, fastest growing cost). the people we're hiring, frontier ML researchers are the scarcest talent pool. We're competing against orgs with 100x our headcount and 10x our compensation budgets for the same \~200 people who can push the frontier. Ops ensures every hire is strategic, not reactive, and that we build comp and talent systems that let us win despite the asymmetry. - Data (third largest, most underleveraged cost): training data is the “raw material” of the factory. Today we procure it reactively, without taxonomy, without feedback loops, and without a sourcing strategy beyond a handful of large providers. The wrong dataset costs model performance and release cadence. The right dataset at the right time is a competitive moat - **(2) The operational system layer = what makes spend productive** - **Compute governance.** Provider strategy, training vs. inference allocation, capacity planning tied to the FLUX 3 schedule. Compute is our single largest line item and every allocation decision is a bet on what ships next. Ops ensures those bets are deliberate, tracked, and tied to the model roadmap rather than made ad hoc - **Capital & talent deployment =** **Raise, allocate and track. **Fundraising and strategic finance - investor pipeline, fundraise execution, due diligence, strategic partnerships. Hiring strategy, comp systems, resource allocation, budget pacing, forecast accuracy, board reporting. The full lifecycle of capital operationalised: bring it in, deploy it across compute, people, and data, report on it. Essentially turning CEO decisions into tracked, measurable execution - **Research reality translation.** The specific interfaces that turn research breakthroughs into shippable products: the Research to Product bridge meeting, launch coordination, and the customer feedback → research loop. This includes the data pipeline (procurement → sourcing → evaluation → feedback to research) and the infrastructure that lets BFL expand into new modalities without reinventing the process each time. Today this is ad hoc and person-dependent. The ops job is to make it a repeatable pipeline in 2026. - **Cross-functional coherence & velocity.** The function-by-function interface model: Ops ↔ Finance, Ops ↔ People, Ops ↔ GTM, Ops ↔ Product/Eng. Launch coordination, bottleneck removal, decision rights. The reason models ship in weeks after completion, not months. - **Decision architecture & operating model.** The weekly/monthly/quarterly cadence that operationalises strategy: frequent leadership sync, monthly strategy day, monthly finance review, quarterly OKR cycle to see if we are off or on track. The infrastructure that lets people operate as one company without the CEO in every room. - **Corporate operations.** Legal, IT/security, compliance, external comms and employer brand. The "keep the lights on" layer that scales us quietly or breaks loudly. **
Ops doesn't do any function's job. Ops makes every function's job possible, measurable, and coordinated so BFL operates as one company, not \~7 teams that share a Slack workspace** The job is ensuring: **Inputs are strong **→ **Engine runs fast **→ **Outputs improve**

Inputs compute, people, data, capital
Engine research velocity, execution speed

How this maps to people and headcount What Great looks like Signals our Operating model is working Operating clarity: Accountability vs Enablement ## Key Metrics Framework {toggle="true"} **The system in one line:** **Inputs → Engine → Outputs** Operations owns the inputs and the engine. The company measures the outputs. ### 1. Core Inputs These are the three production inputs for a frontier AI lab. Operations is accountable for all three.
⚡ Compute — Do we have enough, and are we using it efficiently? **Metrics**
Metric Why it matters
GPU capacity available Are we under-resourced before a training window opens?
GPU utilisation % Are we wasting what we have?
Training cost per run Are we improving efficiency run over run?
Inference cost per request Does our margin hold as usage scales?
Compute runway (months) How long can we run the current roadmap?
**Strategic signals** - Compute secured vs. roadmap needs — never reactive, always ahead - Compute concentration risk — provider dependency Compute is not a fixed cost. It is a strategic weapon. Every dollar misallocated is a model that ships late or ships worse.
👥 People — Are we deploying talent where it matters most? **Metrics**
Metric Why it matters
Headcount vs. plan Are we executing the hiring strategy?
Hiring velocity Are we moving fast enough to win talent wars?
Critical role fill rate Are the right seats filled before they become blockers?
Researcher-to-engineer ratio Is the technical mix right for the roadmap?
Retention of top 15 superstars Zero unplanned departures is the target
**Strategic signals** - Time to hire for frontier ML roles - Top contributor output and satisfaction For frontier labs, talent density matters more than raw headcount. We are competing against orgs with 100x our headcount for the same \~200 people who can push the frontier.

Metric Why it matters
New datasets acquired Are we building the right raw material pipeline?
Dataset throughput How fast is data moving from procurement to training?
Labeling throughput Are we creating bottlenecks downstream?
Time: acquisition → training The hidden latency that delays model releases
Data pipeline reliability Is this a single point of failure?
**Strategic signals** - Dataset diversity across modalities - Training data freshness at time of run Data is the quiet bottleneck. Today we procure reactively, without taxonomy or feedback loops. The ops job is to make this a repeatable pipeline in 2026.
### 2. Strategic input = Capital Operations also owns the capital layer: fundraising infrastructure, deployment, and efficiency.
💰 Capital / Fundraising — Do we have enough runway to execute the roadmap? **Metrics**
Metric Why it matters
Cash runway (months) How long can we operate without a new raise?
Capital raised vs. plan Are we on track with the fundraising strategy?
Investor pipeline health Are we always fundraise-ready?
Burn multiple How efficiently are we converting capital into ARR?
Capital efficiency Revenue generated per dollar deployed
**Strategic signals** - Ability to finance the next compute generation - Investor demand and narrative strength The \$300M raised is not a buffer. It is the fuel for Lift 1. That becomes a problem as token counts rise with image resolution, video length, and world-model context. This project tests a
simple alternative: replace most attention layers with cheaper directional scan blocks, and keep only occasional attention layers for global mixing. The core hypothesis is that image tokens do not need full global attention at every layer. Vision data lives on a 2D grid with strong spatial structure, so structured row and column scans may be enough to move information across the image if they are combined with
periodic attention. If that works, we get a model that keeps much of the quality of a DiT while using a more scalable mixing mechanism. We already have early signs that this is plausible. The work is part architecture design, part systems measurement, and part careful ablation. # References - DiT - Gated DeltaNet - Mamba and related state-space models - Vision Transformers

318c3702-22d5-809b-abf2-f69924809487.title: Precision Video Editing
318c3702-22d5-809b-abf2-f69924809487.text: Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/318c370222d5809babf2f69924809487 as of 2026-04-01T20:23:02.184Z: {"title":"Precision Video Editing"} **Goal:** Train a video-to-video model that performs high precision video editing. **Pushing the frontier:**** **While competing T2V models have seen rapid advancement, video editing has lagged behind in capabilities. This offers an opportunity to differentiate ourselves if we can achieve this goal. **People: , , + **will likely recruit a researcher (do reach out!). **Compute estimate: **Hard to say at this point but for creating the datasets perhaps up to 10% of the compute used to create our pre-training video datasets. **Cash estimate: **\$100k-\$1M (possibly more if we aggressively invest in data deals). **Output: **Ultimately, a video-editing variant of FLUX.3 or build this into base FLUX.3 --- We can separate video-to-video generation into two different categories: 1. **Video as context** The input video is used to provide subjects, assets, or setting, but the output does not need to preserve the original clip. For example, generating the next scene of a video using the previous scene as context. 2. **Precision video editing** The input video must be preserved exactly except for the requested change, e.g. “add a cowboy hat to the character” or “replace the content of a digital billboard with this video.” **Video as context** is relatively easy given the data we have. **Precision video editing** is more difficult and what we should aim to achieve --- ### Hypothesis & Training Strategy For **video as context**, we can train at scale by splitting videos into sequential pairs: first half as input, second half as output. If captioned well enough, this teaches the model how to extract and reuse visual context, but it does not teach it to preserve the original video. Precision editing requires training pairs where *everything is the same except the intended change*. The ideal data would be Hollywood-grade VFX plates paired with final shots, or multiple takes of the same scene with controlled differences. But this data is hard to acquire at scale (if at all). We faced an similar problem during Flux Kontext development. We had large datasets of image pairs sourced from the same photoshoots that gave general editing capability but poor controllability & precision, because multiple factors changed at once (pose, camera angle, expression). The model learned to general capabilities but not to make constrained, precise changes. We fixed this by adding a much smaller dataset (\~50k samples) focused explicitly on precision edits. I think we can approach video in the same way. A **two-stage approach** 1. **Large-scale mid-training** to learn general video editing priors. 2. **Targeted fine-tuning** to enforce precision, controllability, and preservation. --- ## Stage 1: Large scale mid-training datasets The goal here is to train the model on many forms of “related video pairs”. **1. Within-scene video pairs** Extract multiple clips from the same scene and train on pairs, with instruct captions. - Highly scalable. - Will learn how to use visual context from videos, but a weak signal for precision. - It may be a challenge to identify clips with an interesting relationship between them. **2. Generated video pairs** Edit the first and/or last frame of a video, then use a frame-conditioned video model to generate to generate a very similar video to the original with the edit applied. With strong captioning that details all the differences between the videos I think this will be a much stronger prior for fine-tuning in precision video editing than the within scene video pairs approach. - Scales with budget; estimated cost \~\$0.5–\$1 per sample if we use existing leading video models. Though maybe we could do this ourselves cheaper once the base flux 3 t2v model is finished - Plausible size: \~50k to 1M+ **3. Open-source video editing datasets** In particular: - Senorita-2M (h/t ) **4. Generalizing from image-editing** Strong image-editing abilities will be a very useful prior for learning precision video editing. --- ## Stage 2: Fine-tuning for precision editing This stage explicitly trains the model to preserve everything except the requested edit. **1. Video editing templates (After Effects pipeline)** Automated rendering of After Effects projects with parameterized edits (text editing, input image/video assets, layer addition/removal). - Highly precise. - Covers motion graphics and text-editing use cases. - Plausible scale: 50k–500k video pairs. It is plausible to acquire 100k+ source projects. ```plain text Data Flow S3 Bucket (incoming/*.zip) │ ▼ LISTENER (nexlistener.js) │ 1. Polls S3 for new ZIPs (read-only, never deletes) │ 2. Discovers render nodes via EC2 tags (Role=render-node) │ 3. Health-checks nodes, picks the one with most free capacity │ 4. Downloads ZIP, POSTs it to the best node's /api/v2/batches │ ▼ RENDER NODE (nexserver.js) │ 5. Extracts ZIP, cleans macOS residues │ 6. Runs AfterFX.com headlessly (aeCompose_v3.jsx) to: │ - Relink missing footage │ - Extract project structure (layers, comps, text, fonts) │ 7. Generates nexrender task JSON from the structure │ 8. Forks N+1 children (1 base + N randomized variants) │ - Each child gets its own project dir copy │ - Randomizer modifies text/visibility/opacity/effects/media/color/transform │ 9. Queues children through the render pipeline (aerender → ffmpeg → MP4) │ ▼ LISTENER (polls batch status) │ 10. As each child job finishes, downloads its MP4 + metadata │ 11. Uploads MP4 + metadata to the receiver │ ▼ RECEIVER (nexreceiver.js) 12. Stores MP4s as output/

317c3702-22d5-81ff-9331-c8a2d20e0ab3.title: SOTA in Autoregressive Video Distillation
317c3702-22d5-81ff-9331-c8a2d20e0ab3.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/317c370222d581ff9331c8a2d20e0ab3 as of 2026-03-02T13:32:15.006Z: {"title":"SOTA in Autoregressive Video Distillation"} ## Research Question How do we build a real-time, interactive, temporally coherent autoregressive video generation system and push image quality beyond current methods by replacing vanilla DMD with our own step distillation recipe? ## Hypothesis Current AR video distillation methods solve the speed problem but leave image quality on the table. The bottleneck is the final distribution matching stage -- every method defaults to vanilla DMD. Our LADD recipe is a direct upgrade here, and the parallel Scalable Diffusion Distillation shop will push it further. Combining this with the best structural ideas across methods (injectivity-preserving ODE init, self-rollout training, attention sinks) should yield SOTA quality at real-time interactive speeds. ## Landscape
Method Steps FPS VBench Total Dynamic Degree VisionReward Quality Drift
CausVid 4 17.0 81.33 62 5.741 2.18
Self Forcing 1-4 17.0 84.31 57 5.820 1.66
Rolling Forcing 5 15.79 \~84 -- -- 0.01
Causal Forcing 2 17.0 84.04 68 6.326 --
All on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. No one has applied these to larger models or combined their complementary strengths. ## Why This Moves the Frontier 1. **All current work is on a small model.** Applying these techniques to our models (LTX-2, then Flux.3 video) is unexplored and should yield significantly better absolute quality. 2. **The refinement stage is the quality bottleneck.** Every method uses vanilla DMD. We already have LADD as a stronger replacement, and the parallel scalable distillation shop is pushing further. 3. **Interactive real-time video is a deployment priority.** Streaming generation with prompt changes mid-video, low latency, and temporal coherence over minutes -- this is the product-level goal. ## Proposed Work ### Phase 1: Reproduce SOTA on Our Architecture (Month 1-1.5) Implement the core pipeline directly on LTX-2, then FLUX.3 1. **Causal Forcing baseline**: Teacher-forced AR finetuning -\> Causal ODE distillation -\> DMD. Strongest theoretical foundation (injectivity preservation). 2. **Self Forcing self-rollout**: Add self-rollout training with SGT as complementary exposure-bias fix. 3. **Rolling Forcing coherence**: Attention sinks + dynamic RoPE for long-horizon generation. Test as plug-in on top of both baselines. Deliverable: Systematic comparison with per-chunk quality, VBench, temporal consistency, quality drift, and throughput. ### Phase 2: Push Image Quality with LADD (Month 1.5-3) 1. **Replace DMD with LADD**: Swap the final distribution matching stage with our LADD recipe. Direct upgrade -- no architectural changes needed. As the Scalable Diffusion Distillation shop finds improved refinement recipes, plug those in too. 2. **Combine complementary techniques**: Cherry-pick across methods -- Causal Forcing's ODE init (injectivity) + Self Forcing's self-rollout (exposure bias) + Rolling Forcing's attention sinks (drift) + EMA-sink from Reward Forcing. Ablate each component. ### Phase 3: Interactive Streaming & Scale-up (Month 3-4) 1. **Interactive streaming**: KV cache reuse across prompt changes (cf. LongLive), rolling KV cache for unbounded generation, attention sink implementation for long-horizon coherence. Target: real-time interactive video with prompt control mid-stream. 2. **Scale to Flux.3 video**: Full training run on production model. Validate on long-form interactive generation (60s+). 3. **Latency optimization**: Chunk scheduling, KV cache management, first-chunk latency minimization. ## Measuring Success - VBench 84+ on our architecture at 17+ FPS with 2-4 steps per chunk - Measurable image quality improvement over vanilla DMD refinement (per-frame FID/FVD, human preference) - Quality drift \< 0.1 over 60s+ rollouts - Interactive demo: real-time streaming with prompt changes mid-video - Paper: systematic study + new SOTA ## Expected Output Artifacts - Paper (AR video distillation comparison + combined recipe) - AR distillation recipe in schwarzwald - Distilled video checkpoints (LTX-2, then Flux.3) - Interactive streaming demo ## Headcount 2-3 people. Tight collaboration with the Scalable Diffusion Distillation shop. ## Compute - **Exploration**: 16 GB200 nodes for \~2 months - **Scale-up**: 64 GB200 nodes for \~2-4 weeks ## References - [CausVid](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07772) -- Foundational recipe: causal attention masking + ODE init + asymmetric DMD (Yin et al., 2024) - [Self Forcing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08009) -- Self-rollout training with SGT for AR video (Huang et al., NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight) - [Rolling Forcing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25161) -- Rolling window joint denoising with attention sinks (Liu et al., ICLR 2026) - [Causal Forcing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02214) -- Injectivity-preserving 3-stage pipeline (Zhu et al., 2026) - [LongLive](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22622) -- Multi-clip rollouts with KV cache reuse and mid-video prompt changes - [Reward Forcing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04678) -- EMA-sink for KV cache management + DMD improvements - [Deep Forcing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05081) -- Training-free long video via attention sinks + token pruning

1b6c3702-22d5-807c-a73b-ef2114b63f3a.text: Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/1b6c370222d5807ca73bef2114b63f3a as of 2026-02-27T07:12:48.687Z: {"title":"Minimal Image-Dataset Compliance"} **Goal**: Define minimum standard that each image-datasets needs to fulfill before we can use it in training # Documentation All datasets need at least minimal documentation: - What kind of data is this? E.g. “webdataset-scale data”, “high quality anime data”, “hand curated black and white images”, … - Where on the server is this dataset - Dataset size - Are the DF filters applied offline or online (see below) - Confirmation that the dataset is deduplicated - Who created this set / who to ask about this - Potentially optional: - Two sentences about every new metadata-aspect in case of zip-data - What captions are available # Metadata This data should be available in parquets saved alongside with the remaining dataset - `sha256` of the image (in case of dpo/etc there should be one canonical image) - `p_watermarkdf` calculated on a squashed image with the DF-filters - `p_nsfwdf` calculated on a squashed image with the DF-filters - `width` , `height` - `__key__` the key inside of tars - `__source_id__` the path from the dataset root to the file. Therefore `__source_id__` + `__key__` should be unique in the whole dataset # Filtering - Perceptual-Deduplication - These must be applied either to the whole dataset (prefered) or online: - `p_watermarkdf < 0.5` (minimum, more doesn’t hurt) - `p_nsfwdf < 0.5` --- # Interactive Visualization Easily visualize any dataset with `databoard`via ```bash streamlit run src/sbord/databoard.py -- ``` Chose tars you want to see and apply filter directly via the streamlit interface. # FLUX.1 Kontext - Image-to-Image Prompting Guide
<callout icon="📢" color="yellow_bg">
	Please check the guide in our Documentation directly for the latest version! [https://docs.bfl.ai/guides/](https://docs.bfl.ai/guides/)
</callout>
<callout icon="💡" color="blue_bg">
	Maximum prompt token is 512 tokens.
</callout>
*Kontext* makes editing images easy! Specify what you want to change and *Kontext* will follow. It is capable of understanding the context of the image, making it easier to edit them without having to describe in details what you want to do. 
## Basic Object Modifications
*Kontext* is really good at straightforward object modification, for example if we want to change the colour of an object, we can prompt it.

## Prompt Precision: From Basic to Comprehensive
<callout icon="💡" color="blue_bg">
	promptAs a rule of thumb, making things more explicitly never hurts if the number of instructions per edit is not too complicated
</callout>
If you want to edit the image with more modifications, it is useful to be more explicit in your prompts to make sure you get the result you want. 
### Quick Edits
While using very simple prompts might yield some good results, it can also change the style of the input image.

## Style transfer
### Using prompts
When working on style transfer prompts, follow those principles: 
1. **Name the specific style**: Instead of vague terms like "make it artistic," specify exactly what style you want ("Transform to Bauhaus art style," "Convert to watercolor painting")
2. **Reference known artists or movements**: For more precise results, include recognizable style references ("Renaissance painting style”, "like a 1960s pop art poster")
3. **Detail the key characteristics**: If naming the style doesn’t work, it might be good to describe the visual elements that define the style:
	- "*Transform to oil painting with visible brushstrokes, thick paint texture, and rich color depth*"
4. **Preserve what matters**: Explicitly state what elements shouldn’t change:
	- "Change to Bauhaus art style while maintaining the original composition and object placement"

For Character consistency, you can follow this framework to keep the same character across edits: 
1. **Establish the reference**: Begin by clearly identifying your character
	- "This person..." or "The woman with short black hair..."
2. **Specify the transformation**: Clearly state what aspects are changing
	- Environment: "...now in a tropical beach setting"
	- Activity: "...now picking up weeds in a garden"
	- Style: "Transform to Claymation style while keeping the same person"
3. **Preserve identity markers**: Explicitly mention what should remain consistent
	- "...while maintaining the same facial features, hairstyle, and expression"
	- "...keeping the same identity and personality"
	- "...preserving their distinctive appearance"
<callout icon="⚠️" color="yellow_bg">
	**Common mistake**: Using vague references like "her" instead of "The woman with short black hair"
</callout>
## Text Editing 
*Kontext* can directly edit text that appears in images, making it easy to update signs, posters, labels, and more without recreating the entire image.
The most effective way to edit text is using quotation marks around the specific text you want to change: 
**Prompt Structure**: `Replace '[original text]' with '[new text]'`
**Example - **We can see below where we have an input image with “Choose joy” written, and we replace “joy” with “BFL” - note the upper case format for BFL.

### Text Editing Best Practices
- **Use clear, readable fonts** when possible. Complex or stylized fonts may be harder to edit
- **Specify preservation** when needed. For example: *"Replace 'joy' with 'BFL' while maintaining the same font style and color"*
- **Keep text length similar** - Dramatically longer or shorter text may affect layout
## When Results Don't Match Expectations
### General Troubleshooting Tip
If the model is changing elements you want to keep unchanged, be explicit about preservation in your prompt. For example: *"everything else should stay black and white*" or "*maintain all other aspects of the original image*."
### **Character identity changes too much**
When transforming a person (changing their clothing, style, or context), it's easy to lose their unique identity features if prompts aren't specific enough.
- Try to be more specific about identity markers ("maintain the exact same face, hairstyle, and distinctive features")
- **Example**: *"Transform the man into a viking warrior while preserving his exact facial features, eye color, and facial expression"*

**Vague prompts replace identity:**
- **Prompt: ***"Transform the person into a Viking"* → Complete replacement of facial features, hair, and expression
**Detailed prompts preserve identity:**
- **Prompt: ***"Transform the man into a viking warrior while preserving his exact facial features, eye color, and facial expression"* → Maintains core identity while changing context
**Focused prompts change only what's needed:**
- **Prompt: ***"Change the clothes to be a viking warrior"* → Keeps perfect identity while only modifying the specified element
**Why this happens? **
The verb "transform" without qualifiers often signals to *Kontext* that a complete change is desired. It might be useful to use other words for example in this context if you want to maintain specific aspects of the original image.
### Composition Control
When editing backgrounds or scenes, you often want to keep the subject in exactly the same position, scale, and pose. Simple prompts can sometimes change some of those aspects.
**Simple prompts causing unwanted changes: **
- **Prompt: ***"He's now on a sunny beach"* → Subject position and scale shift 
- **Prompt: ***"Put him on a beach"* → Camera angle and framing change

**Why this happens? **
Vague instructions like *"put him on a beach"* leave too much to interpretation. *Kontext* might choose to:
- Adjust the framing to match typical beach photos
- Change the camera angle to show more of the beach
- Reposition the subject to better fit the new setting
### **Style isn't applying correctly**
When applying certain styles, simple prompts might create inconsistent results or lose important elements of the original composition. We could see that in the [example above](/1fcc370222d580e2af0df93271590e2b?pvs=25). 
**Basic style prompts can lose important elements:**
- **Prompt: ***"Make it a sketch" *→ While the artistic style is applied, some details are lost.
**Precise style prompts maintain structure:**
- **Prompt:*** "Convert to pencil sketch with natural graphite lines, cross-hatching, and visible paper texture"* → Preserves the scene while applying the style. You can see more details in the background, more cars are also appearing on the image.

## Best Practices Summary
- **Be specific**: Precise language gives better results. Use exact color names, detailed descriptions, and clear action verbs instead of vague terms.
- **Start simple**: Begin with core changes before adding complexity. Test basic edits first, then build upon successful results. Kontext can handle very well iterative editing, use it.
- **Preserve intentionally**: Explicitly state what should remain unchanged. Use phrases like *"while maintaining the same \[facial features/composition/lighting\]"* to protect important elements.
- **Iterate when needed**: Complex transformations often require multiple steps. Break dramatic changes into sequential edits for better control.
- **Name subjects directly**: Use "the woman with short black hair" or "the red car" instead of pronouns like “her”, "it," or "this" for clearer results.
- **Use quotation marks for text**: Quote the exact text you want to change: Replace 'joy' with 'BFL' works better than general text descriptions.
- **Control composition explicitly**: When changing backgrounds or settings, specify *"keep the exact camera angle, position, and framing"* to prevent unwanted repositioning.
- **Choose verbs carefully**: *"Transform"* might imply complete change, while *"change the clothes"* or *"replace the background"* gives you more control over what actually changes.

	**Remember**: Making things more explicit never hurts if the number of instructions per edit isn't too complicated.

# FLUX.1 Kontext - Image-to-Image Prompting Guide
<callout icon="📢" color="yellow_bg">
	Please check the guide in our Documentation directly for the latest version! [https://docs.bfl.ai/guides/](https://docs.bfl.ai/guides/)
</callout>
<callout icon="💡" color="blue_bg">
	Maximum prompt token is 512 tokens.
</callout>
*Kontext* makes editing images easy! Specify what you want to change and *Kontext* will follow. It is capable of understanding the context of the image, making it easier to edit them without having to describe in details what you want to do. 
## Basic Object Modifications
*Kontext* is really good at straightforward object modification, for example if we want to change the colour of an object, we can prompt it.

## Prompt Precision: From Basic to Comprehensive
<callout icon="💡" color="blue_bg">
	promptAs a rule of thumb, making things more explicitly never hurts if the number of instructions per edit is not too complicated
</callout>
If you want to edit the image with more modifications, it is useful to be more explicit in your prompts to make sure you get the result you want. 
### Quick Edits
While using very simple prompts might yield some good results, it can also change the style of the input image.

## Style transfer
### Using prompts
When working on style transfer prompts, follow those principles: 
1. **Name the specific style**: Instead of vague terms like "make it artistic," specify exactly what style you want ("Transform to Bauhaus art style," "Convert to watercolor painting")
2. **Reference known artists or movements**: For more precise results, include recognizable style references ("Renaissance painting style”, "like a 1960s pop art poster")
3. **Detail the key characteristics**: If naming the style doesn’t work, it might be good to describe the visual elements that define the style:
	- "*Transform to oil painting with visible brushstrokes, thick paint texture, and rich color depth*"
4. **Preserve what matters**: Explicitly state what elements shouldn’t change:
	- "Change to Bauhaus art style while maintaining the original composition and object placement"

For Character consistency, you can follow this framework to keep the same character across edits: 
1. **Establish the reference**: Begin by clearly identifying your character
	- "This person..." or "The woman with short black hair..."
2. **Specify the transformation**: Clearly state what aspects are changing
	- Environment: "...now in a tropical beach setting"
	- Activity: "...now picking up weeds in a garden"
	- Style: "Transform to Claymation style while keeping the same person"
3. **Preserve identity markers**: Explicitly mention what should remain consistent
	- "...while maintaining the same facial features, hairstyle, and expression"
	- "...keeping the same identity and personality"
	- "...preserving their distinctive appearance"
<callout icon="⚠️" color="yellow_bg">
	**Common mistake**: Using vague references like "her" instead of "The woman with short black hair"
</callout>
## Text Editing 
*Kontext* can directly edit text that appears in images, making it easy to update signs, posters, labels, and more without recreating the entire image.
The most effective way to edit text is using quotation marks around the specific text you want to change: 
**Prompt Structure**: `Replace '[original text]' with '[new text]'`
**Example - **We can see below where we have an input image with “Choose joy” written, and we replace “joy” with “BFL” - note the upper case format for BFL.

### Text Editing Best Practices
- **Use clear, readable fonts** when possible. Complex or stylized fonts may be harder to edit
- **Specify preservation** when needed. For example: *"Replace 'joy' with 'BFL' while maintaining the same font style and color"*
- **Keep text length similar** - Dramatically longer or shorter text may affect layout
## When Results Don't Match Expectations
### General Troubleshooting Tip
If the model is changing elements you want to keep unchanged, be explicit about preservation in your prompt. For example: *"everything else should stay black and white*" or "*maintain all other aspects of the original image*."
### **Character identity changes too much**
When transforming a person (changing their clothing, style, or context), it's easy to lose their unique identity features if prompts aren't specific enough.
- Try to be more specific about identity markers ("maintain the exact same face, hairstyle, and distinctive features")
- **Example**: *"Transform the man into a viking warrior while preserving his exact facial features, eye color, and facial expression"*

**Vague prompts replace identity:**
- **Prompt: ***"Transform the person into a Viking"* → Complete replacement of facial features, hair, and expression
**Detailed prompts preserve identity:**
- **Prompt: ***"Transform the man into a viking warrior while preserving his exact facial features, eye color, and facial expression"* → Maintains core identity while changing context
**Focused prompts change only what's needed:**
- **Prompt: ***"Change the clothes to be a viking warrior"* → Keeps perfect identity while only modifying the specified element
**Why this happens? **
The verb "transform" without qualifiers often signals to *Kontext* that a complete change is desired. It might be useful to use other words for example in this context if you want to maintain specific aspects of the original image.
### Composition Control
When editing backgrounds or scenes, you often want to keep the subject in exactly the same position, scale, and pose. Simple prompts can sometimes change some of those aspects.
**Simple prompts causing unwanted changes: **
- **Prompt: ***"He's now on a sunny beach"* → Subject position and scale shift 
- **Prompt: ***"Put him on a beach"* → Camera angle and framing change

**Why this happens? **
Vague instructions like *"put him on a beach"* leave too much to interpretation. *Kontext* might choose to:
- Adjust the framing to match typical beach photos
- Change the camera angle to show more of the beach
- Reposition the subject to better fit the new setting
### **Style isn't applying correctly**
When applying certain styles, simple prompts might create inconsistent results or lose important elements of the original composition. We could see that in the [example above](/1fcc370222d580e2af0df93271590e2b?pvs=25). 
**Basic style prompts can lose important elements:**
- **Prompt: ***"Make it a sketch" *→ While the artistic style is applied, some details are lost.
**Precise style prompts maintain structure:**
- **Prompt:*** "Convert to pencil sketch with natural graphite lines, cross-hatching, and visible paper texture"* → Preserves the scene while applying the style. You can see more details in the background, more cars are also appearing on the image.

## Best Practices Summary
- **Be specific**: Precise language gives better results. Use exact color names, detailed descriptions, and clear action verbs instead of vague terms.
- **Start simple**: Begin with core changes before adding complexity. Test basic edits first, then build upon successful results. Kontext can handle very well iterative editing, use it.
- **Preserve intentionally**: Explicitly state what should remain unchanged. Use phrases like *"while maintaining the same \[facial features/composition/lighting\]"* to protect important elements.
- **Iterate when needed**: Complex transformations often require multiple steps. Break dramatic changes into sequential edits for better control.
- **Name subjects directly**: Use "the woman with short black hair" or "the red car" instead of pronouns like “her”, "it," or "this" for clearer results.
- **Use quotation marks for text**: Quote the exact text you want to change: Replace 'joy' with 'BFL' works better than general text descriptions.
- **Control composition explicitly**: When changing backgrounds or settings, specify *"keep the exact camera angle, position, and framing"* to prevent unwanted repositioning.
- **Choose verbs carefully**: *"Transform"* might imply complete change, while *"change the clothes"* or *"replace the background"* gives you more control over what actually changes.

	**Remember**: Making things more explicit never hurts if the number of instructions per edit isn't too complicated.

## What we're launching/what’s changed
**Product/Feature Description**
The API supports LoRA inference. It is able to load a pre-trained LoRA efficiently and serve generations using this LoRA.
## Why it matters
**Who cares**
Our current production models can’t solve all tasks. A lot of value reside in these tasks since most production models can’t solve them yet.
Various teams (FDE, product) have demonstrated the ability to solve some of these tasks by training dedicated LoRAs.
But until this release we can’t use these checkpoints in production, heavily limiting their reach.

2e9c3702-22d5-805a-be1f-f9955ca9a94e.title: FLUX.2 [klein] - Private API integration
2e9c3702-22d5-805a-be1f-f9955ca9a94e.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2e9c370222d5805abe1ff9955ca9a94e as of 2026-03-19T14:14:45.724Z: {"title":"FLUX.2 \\[klein\\] - Private API integration"} # Image Generation with FLUX.2 \[klein\] **UNMODERATED ENDPOINT** — The `-private` endpoints documented on this page are **unmoderated**. They do not apply content moderation or safety filtering to generated images. Using these endpoints is subject to the specific terms agreed between Black Forest Labs and whitelisted partners (which can stipulate that Partners deploying these endpoints are fully responsible for implementing their own content moderation and ensuring compliance with applicable laws and regulations). FLUX.2 \[klein\] is our fastest and most cost-effective model family, optimized for high-throughput use cases while maintaining excellent quality. Available in two variants: **Klein 4B**, **Klein 9B.** This is a guide for private, extremely fast endpoints we offer to trusted partners. ## API Endpoints **Global Endpoint (Recommended):** - [`api.bfl.ai`](http://api.bfl.ai) - Automatic failover between clusters for enhanced uptime **Regional Options:** - [`api.eu.bfl.ai`](http://api.eu.bfl.ai) - European Multi-cluster - [`api.us.bfl.ai`](http://api.us.bfl.ai) - US Multi-cluster routing ## Available Models
Endpoint Description
`/flux-2-klein-4b-private` Fastest model, 4B parameters, **unmoderated**
`/flux-2-klein-9b-private` Higher quality, 9B parameters, **unmoderated**
--- ## Basic Text-to-Image Generation The API uses an asynchronous workflow: 1. **Submit** a generation request 2. **Poll** for results using the returned `polling_url` ### Python Example ```python import os import requests import time # Step 1: Submit generation request response = requests.post( 'https://api.bfl.ai/v1/flux-2-klein-9b-private', headers={ 'accept': 'application/json', 'x-key': os.environ.get("BFL_API_KEY"), 'Content-Type': 'application/json', }, json={ 'prompt': 'A serene mountain landscape at sunset with golden light', 'width': 1024, 'height': 1024, }, ).json() print(f"Task ID: {response['id']}") polling_url = response['polling_url'] # Step 2: Poll for results while True: result = requests.get( polling_url, headers={ 'accept': 'application/json', 'x-key': os.environ.get("BFL_API_KEY"), }, ).json() if result['status'] == 'Ready': print(f"Image URL: {result['result']['sample']}") break elif result['status'] == 'Error': print(f"Error: {result.get('error')}") break time.sleep(0.5) ``` --- ## Generation with Reference Images FLUX.2 \[klein\] supports up to **4 reference images** for style guidance and context. `width` integer No Output width (default: 1024, max total: 4MP)
`height` integer No Output height (default: 1024, max total: 4MP)
`input_image` string No First reference image (URL or base64)
`input_image_2` string No Second reference image (URL or base64)
`input_image_3` string No Third reference image (URL or base64)
`input_image_4` string No Fourth reference image (URL or base64)
`seed` integer No Random seed for reproducibility
`output_format` string No `"jpeg"` or `"png"` (default: jpeg)
**Note:** The `safety_tolerance` parameter is not applicable to these `-private` endpoints as they are **unmoderated**. No content filtering is applied to generated outputs. --- ## Response Format ### Initial Response ```json { "id": "task-uuid-here", "polling_url": "" } ``` ### Polling Response (Success) ```json { "id": "task-uuid-here", "status": "Ready", "result": { "sample": "https://delivery.bfl.ai/..." } } ``` > **Important:** The signed URL in `result.sample` expires after **10 minutes**. Download the image immediately rather than storing the URL. --- ## Rate Limits - **Standard limit:** 24 concurrent active tasks - HTTP 429 indicates rate limit exceeded --- ## Model Comparison
Model Speed Quality Best For
Klein 4B Fastest Good High-throughput applications, rapid prototyping
Klein 9B Fastest Better Balance of speed and quality

	## Code Package Manager

# Skills
<details>
<summary>Save CC conversation summary to Notion</summary>
	```markdown
Summarize the current conversation into a concise note and create it as a new sub-page under the Notion "Notes" page (ID: <your-page-id>).

Steps:
1. Review the conversation and write a clear, concise summary covering: what was discussed, key decisions made, and any outcomes or next steps.
2. Use the Notion MCP `notion-create-pages` tool to create a new page as a child of page ID `<your-page-id>`.
3. Title the page with today's date and a short topic descriptor (e.g. "2026-03-13 - Auth refactor discussion").
4. Include the summary as the page content using markdown.
5. Share the URL of the created page with the user.

	```
	<empty-block/>
</details>
<details>
<summary>Notify when CI is done</summary>
	```markdown
Watch the current branch's CI and notify when done.

Steps:
1. Run `gh run list --branch $(git branch --show-current) --limit 5 --status in_progress --json databaseId,name,status -q '.[] | "\(.databaseId)\t\(.name)"'` to find in-progress runs.
2. If there are in-progress runs, pick the first one and run `gh run watch <id> --exit-status` to poll it.
3. If there are no in-progress runs, check for the latest queued run instead with `--status queued`. If still none, tell the user there are no active runs.
4. After the watch completes, send a macOS notification:
   - On success: `osascript -e 'display notification "CI passed ✅" with title "PR CI" sound name "Glass"'`
   - On failure: `osascript -e 'display notification "CI failed ❌" with title "PR CI" sound name "Basso"'`
5. Report the result to the user.

	```
</details>
<details>
<summary>Commits: Structure and Convention</summary>
	```markdown
---
description: Structure changes into logical individual commits
allowed-tools: [Bash, Read, Glob, Grep]
---

You are a commit assistant. Your job is to analyze all uncommitted changes and group them into logical, atomic commits.

## Steps

1. Run `git status` and `git diff` (staged + unstaged) to see all changes.
2. Analyze the changes and group them into logical commits. Each commit should be a self-contained, coherent unit of work. Examples of good groupings:
   - Config/setup changes separate from feature code
   - Refactors separate from new functionality
   - Moves/renames separate from edits
   - Test changes with their corresponding source changes
3. Present the proposed commit plan to the user as a numbered list, showing:
   - The files in each commit
   - The proposed commit message
4. Wait for user approval before executing. The user may ask to adjust groupings or messages.
5. Once approved, execute the commits in order:
   - Stage only the specific files for each commit
   - Use clear, concise commit messages focused on the "why"
   - do not mention claude in the commits

## Rules

- Never combine unrelated changes in one commit
- Never use `git add -A` or `git add .` — always add specific files
- Never amend existing commits
- Never push to remote
- If a file has mixed changes that belong in different commits, use `git add -p` to stage hunks separately
- Keep commit messages under 72 characters for the subject line
- Use imperative mood ("Add feature" not "Added feature")

## Commit convention
As an open-source maintainer, squash feature branches onto master and write a standardized commit message while doing so.

The commit message should be structured as follows:

<type>[optional scope]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer]
The commit contains the following structural elements, to communicate intent to the consumers of your library:

fix: a commit of the type fix patches a bug in your codebase (this correlates with PATCH in semantic versioning).
feat: a commit of the type feat introduces a new feature to the codebase (this correlates with MINOR in semantic versioning).
BREAKING CHANGE: a commit that has the text BREAKING CHANGE: at the beginning of its optional body or footer section introduces a breaking API change (correlating with MAJOR in semantic versioning). A breaking change can be part of commits of any type. e.g., a fix:, feat: & chore: types would all be valid, in addition to any other type.
Others: commit types other than fix: and feat: are allowed, for example @commitlint/config-conventional (based on the the Angular convention) recommends chore:, docs:, style:, refactor:, perf:, test:, and others. We also recommend improvement for commits that improve a current implementation without adding a new feature or fixing a bug. Notice these types are not mandated by the conventional commits specification, and have no implicit effect in semantic versioning (unless they include a BREAKING CHANGE, which is NOT recommended). A scope may be provided to a commit’s type, to provide additional contextual information and is contained within parenthesis, e.g., feat(parser): add ability to parse arrays.
	```
</details>

# Extra Tools
## Signoz MCP {toggle="true"}
	```markdown
# SigNoz MCP for Claude Code

Query traces, logs, and metrics from SigNoz directly in Claude Code.

## Prerequisites

- Go installed (`brew install go`)
- A SigNoz API key (get from https://bfl.eu.signoz.cloud → Settings → API Keys)
(I got mine from Kerem lol)

## Setup

```bash
# Build the server
git clone https://github.com/SigNoz/signoz-mcp-server.git
cd signoz-mcp-server
go build -o bin/signoz-mcp-server ./cmd/server/

# Register with Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport stdio signoz \
  --env SIGNOZ_URL=https://bfl.eu.signoz.cloud \
  --env "SIGNOZ_API_KEY=<your-key>" \
  --env LOG_LEVEL=info \
  --scope user \
  -- $(pwd)/bin/signoz-mcp-server

# Verify it's connected
claude mcp list
```

Restart Claude Code after adding. The SigNoz tools will then be available in all conversations.

## Useful Prompts

- "Search traces for errors on /flux-2-pro-fashion in the last hour"
- "Show me logs from namespace review-3094"
- "What's the p99 latency for the flux-2-pro endpoint?"

3. If there are no in-progress runs, check for the latest queued run instead with `--status queued`. If still none, tell the user there are no active runs.
4. After the watch completes, send a macOS notification:
   - On success: `osascript -e 'display notification "CI passed ✅" with title "PR CI" sound name "Glass"'`
   - On failure: `osascript -e 'display notification "CI failed ❌" with title "PR CI" sound name "Basso"'`
5. Report the result to the user.

	```

<summary>Commits: Structure and Convention</summary>
	```markdown
---
description: Structure changes into logical individual commits
allowed-tools: [Bash, Read, Glob, Grep]
---

You are a commit assistant. Your job is to analyze all uncommitted changes and group them into logical, atomic commits.

## Steps

1. Run `git status` and `git diff` (staged + unstaged) to see all changes.
2. Analyze the changes and group them into logical commits. Each commit should be a self-contained, coherent unit of work. Examples of good groupings:
   - Config/setup changes separate from feature code
   - Refactors separate from new functionality
   - Moves/renames separate from edits
   - Test changes with their corresponding source changes
3. Present the proposed commit plan to the user as a numbered list, showing:
   - The files in each commit
   - The proposed commit message
4. Wait for user approval before executing. The user may ask to adjust groupings or messages.
5. Once approved, execute the commits in order:
   - Stage only the specific files for each commit
   - Use clear, concise commit messages focused on the "why"
   - do not mention claude in the commits

## Rules

- Never combine unrelated changes in one commit
- Never use `git add -A` or `git add .` — always add specific files
- Never amend existing commits
- Never push to remote
- If a file has mixed changes that belong in different commits, use `git add -p` to stage hunks separately
- Keep commit messages under 72 characters for the subject line
- Use imperative mood ("Add feature" not "Added feature")

## Commit convention
As an open-source maintainer, squash feature branches onto master and write a standardized commit message while doing so.

The commit message should be structured as follows:

<type>[optional scope]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer]
The commit contains the following structural elements, to communicate intent to the consumers of your library:

fix: a commit of the type fix patches a bug in your codebase (this correlates with PATCH in semantic versioning).
feat: a commit of the type feat introduces a new feature to the codebase (this correlates with MINOR in semantic versioning).
BREAKING CHANGE: a commit that has the text BREAKING CHANGE: at the beginning of its optional body or footer section introduces a breaking API change (correlating with MAJOR in semantic versioning). A breaking change can be part of commits of any type. e.g., a fix:, feat: & chore: types would all be valid, in addition to any other type.
Others: commit types other than fix: and feat: are allowed, for example @commitlint/config-conventional (based on the the Angular convention) recommends chore:, docs:, style:, refactor:, perf:, test:, and others. We also recommend improvement for commits that improve a current implementation without adding a new feature or fixing a bug. Notice these types are not mandated by the conventional commits specification, and have no implicit effect in semantic versioning (unless they include a BREAKING CHANGE, which is NOT recommended). A scope may be provided to a commit’s type, to provide additional contextual information and is contained within parenthesis, e.g., feat(parser): add ability to parse arrays.

# SigNoz MCP for Claude Code

Query traces, logs, and metrics from SigNoz directly in Claude Code.

## Prerequisites

- Go installed (`brew install go`)
- A SigNoz API key (get from https://bfl.eu.signoz.cloud → Settings → API Keys)
(I got mine from Kerem lol)

## Setup

```bash
# Build the server
git clone https://github.com/SigNoz/signoz-mcp-server.git
cd signoz-mcp-server
go build -o bin/signoz-mcp-server ./cmd/server/

# Register with Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport stdio signoz \
  --env SIGNOZ_URL=https://bfl.eu.signoz.cloud \
  --env "SIGNOZ_API_KEY=<your-key>" \
  --env LOG_LEVEL=info \
  --scope user \
  -- $(pwd)/bin/signoz-mcp-server

# Verify it's connected
claude mcp list
```

Restart Claude Code after adding. The SigNoz tools will then be available in all conversations.

## Useful Prompts

- "Search traces for errors on /flux-2-pro-fashion in the last hour"
- "Show me logs from namespace review-3094"
- "What's the p99 latency for the flux-2-pro endpoint?"
