327c3702-22d5-80bb-9741-ed8d504f84cd.title: Robin Snap meeting brief - April 19, 2026
327c3702-22d5-80bb-9741-ed8d504f84cd.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/327c370222d580bb9741ed8d504f84cd as of 2026-03-19T19:51:05.978Z: {"title":"Robin Snap meeting brief - April 19, 2026"} ## Post-Meeting Update — Mar 19 call completed ✅ Key outcomes: Robin walked Dhritiman through FLUX.3 architecture. Snap confirmed they need architectural access, not just synthetic data rights. Alexei Stolier (key contract stakeholder) couldn't join — fast follow call needed. Commercial scoping to happen in parallel between Seb and Michael. --- ## Agenda
Time Who Focus
0–30 min Robin + Michael only FLUX.3 architecture walkthrough, Self-Flow paper, real-time video, model variants
30–60 min Robin + Michael + Dhritiman (+Seb dialled in) Technical deep dive — distillation pipeline, use cases, what they actually need from the architecture
--- ## TL;DR Snap's research team has largely moved off FLUX image to Chinese open source. Michael flagged it himself and reached out to save the partnership. The renewal hinges entirely on FLUX.3 to include video — without a credible path there, he can't defend the contract internally. Budget is genuinely tight (stock at all-time lows). He's motivated to make it work and has offered PR support, investor testimonials, and a joint launch announcement in return for a good deal. We didn't touch exact numbers yet - but I've mentioned that there are other deals way bigger to set an anchor (he understood and mentioned Meta). In this meeting, we need to show them the F3 arch, get the researchers excited, and lay the foundation for a successful deep collaboration (how deep depending on capacity). Michael is open to boiling down the agreement to exactly what they need - so this also needs to be a bit of a research discovery. Show them F3 as the stepping stone into world models - they're keen to hear it as well (relevant for AR - Specs has its own budget we could explore as part of this!) Once they're excited - get the message across that we cannot give them F3 dev at the \$4.99M renewal and probe for budget. Look at their pain points - we can give them what they need, nobody else can. --- ## Situation Snap's research team reported they'd almost completely stopped using FLUX for image — Chinese open source filled the gap without anyone asking permission. Michael was surprised, reached out to Robin, and that's what kicked all of this off. Two things the meeting hinges on: 1. **FLUX.3 video** — Robin had signalled "video coming last summer, then Q4." It didn't land. Open source video (Wan 2.2, LTX-2, Hunyuan) is now filling the gap. Michael's alarm bell: if there's no credible FLUX.3 video path, he can't extend the relationship. 2. **What they actually need** — Seb flagged BFL is hesitant to offer a blanket FLUX.3 Dev license. The right moment to dig into which components their pipeline actually requires, so we can scope the agreement properly. --- ## Why competitors aren't good enough Snap is currently using VO3 Fast, Kling variants, and Chinese open source models. Shortcomings Michael flagged: - **Audio alignment issues** — problems syncing audio across models - **Spatio-temporal conformity** — Chinese models struggle to maintain consistent spatial relationships and temporal coherence across frames - **Constellation problem** — each model has different gaps; they end up using multiple models, which is expensive and operationally painful - **No architectural access** — the decisive one: "I can't break apart the internal transformer architecture and leverage it for distillation. Google's not giving me distilled variants." VO3, Kling etc. are black boxes. FLUX is the only model family where Snap can get inside the architecture and build on top of it. --- ## Stakeholder map
Name Role Notes
Michael Greenberg Head of AI Strategy Primary commercial contact. Candid, motivated, has Robin's trust since Stability AI days
Dhritiman Sagar Head of Applied AI Leads all third-party model work and distillation pipeline
Alexei Stolier Above Dhritiman One of the contract stakeholders, more abstracted. Couldn't join Mar 19 — fast follow needed
Bobby (CTO) CTO On paternity leave but in the loop and a BFL fan
Sergei Tulyakov Research Director Pure research, conservative — less relevant for commercial track
Michael wants 30 min with just the two of you at the end. --- ## Non-cash value on the table Michael explicitly offered: - PR support and joint announcement at FLUX.3 launch (open to it if collaboration goes deep) - Investor testimonials — spoke to Temasek on BFL's behalf during the raise - Quiet conversations with prospects / strategic introductions - "Whatever we do, we won't leak pricing or undercut your go-to-market" Note: public naming of Snap currently requires written approval per §11(o) of the contract — making this an explicit deal condition is the right move. --- ## Key questions to probe 1. Which components of FLUX.3 does their pipeline actually need — full model, or could a scoped access work? 2. Is there budget outside Michael's pocket — specifically the Specs org, which has its own experimental budget? 3. What's their honest read on the open source alternatives — are they genuinely considering switching, or is this leverage? 4. Can they share more on what "video for Lens" means in practice — real-time generation, distillation target size, latency requirements? --- ## Commercial context - Current contract: \$3.99M Year 2 auto-renews May 8 — **image only** - Termination window closes **April 8** — 20 days left - Video explicitly excluded under current agreement (§1c, §2h) — a new Order Form is required - Any deal must be in writing and signed (§11j) --- ## What We Learned — Mar 19 Call **Snap's distillation targets** - Image: 300–500M params on-device - Video: \~800M params on-device; 4–9 seconds server-side - Running on H100s for server inference; on-device for most scalable/free tier use cases - Cost threshold: sub-penny per generation to unlock freemium scale **How they currently use FLUX Dev** Two separate use cases confirmed: 1. Synthetic data generation for distillation pipeline 2. Direct hosting of FLUX Dev for **premium/subscription products** (gated, behind paywall) — not just distillation. Important for pricing. **Distillation approach** - Historically: their own architecture + synthetic data from teacher model - Now considering: pruning the teacher model itself down to target size - CFG distillation can cause problems — they want flexibility (step distillation preferred) - They would want to try intermediate activations from teacher too **Architectural access — still needed** Robin surfaced the key question: synthetic data only, or architectural access? Dhritiman: architectural access still has value. Important hedge, especially given they're now considering teacher model pruning. A pure "synthetic data only" license likely won't be enough. **Audio confirmed relevant** Speech + sound effects + atmospheric audio. Gaming/mini-games flagged as an emerging use case. Audio AE more relevant than initially assumed. **Specs / action encoder — separate budget potential** Michael flagged Specs org has its own experimental budget. Action encoder + real-time video = Genie-style interactive Lens experiences. Could unlock a second commercial conversation separate from the renewal. **FLUX.3 timeline:** \~June target. Open weight Dev variant \~99% confirmed. Commercial distillation + premium product use still requires license. --- ## Next Steps (agreed on call) 1. Robin shares FLUX.3 architecture slides with Dhritiman 2. Fast follow call with **Alexei Stolier** (missed Mar 19 — was in Evan Spiegel meeting) to scope commercial shape 3. Technical follow-up with Dhritiman's team next week 4. Seb + Michael working commercial construct in tight loop — before it goes wider internally at Snap 5. Specs/action encoder angle: park for now, revisit as separate budget conversation

Can they share more on what "video for Lens" means in practice — real-time generation, distillation target size, latency requirements? --- ## Commercial context - Current contract: \$3.99M Year 2 auto-renews May 8 — **image only** - Termination window closes **April 8** — 20 days left - Video explicitly excluded under current agreement (§1c, §2h) — a new Order Form is required - Any deal must be in writing and signed (§11j) --- ## What We Learned — Mar 19 Call **Snap's distillation targets** - Image: 300–500M params on-device - Video: \~800M params on-device; 4–9 seconds server-side - Running on H100s for server inference; on-device for most scalable/free tier use cases - Cost threshold: sub-penny per generation to unlock freemium scale **How they currently use FLUX Dev** Two separate use cases confirmed: 1. Synthetic data generation for distillation pipeline 2. Direct hosting of FLUX Dev for **premium/subscription products** (gated, behind paywall) — not just distillation. Important for pricing. **Distillation approach** - Historically: their own architecture + synthetic data from teacher model - Now considering: pruning the teacher model itself down to target size - CFG distillation can cause problems — they want flexibility (step distillation preferred) - They would want to try intermediate activations from teacher too **Architectural access — still needed** Robin surfaced the key question: synthetic data only, or architectural access? Dhritiman: architectural access still has value. Important hedge, especially given they're now considering teacher model pruning. A pure "synthetic data only" license likely won't be enough. **Audio confirmed relevant** Speech + sound effects + atmospheric audio. Gaming/mini-games flagged as an emerging use case. Audio AE more relevant than initially assumed. **Specs / action encoder — separate budget potential** Michael flagged Specs org has its own experimental budget. Action encoder + real-time video = Genie-style interactive Lens experiences. Could unlock a second commercial conversation separate from the renewal. **FLUX.3 timeline:** \~June target. Open weight Dev variant \~99% confirmed. Commercial distillation + premium product use still requires license. --- ## Next Steps (agreed on call) 1. Robin shares FLUX.3 architecture slides with Dhritiman 2. Fast follow call with **Alexei Stolier** (missed Mar 19 — was in Evan Spiegel meeting) to scope commercial shape 3. Technical follow-up with Dhritiman's team next week 4. Seb + Michael working commercial construct in tight loop — before it goes wider internally at Snap 5. Specs/action encoder angle: park for now, revisit as separate budget conversation

# **OKRs (Q4 2025 → Q1 2026)**
## Objective 1: Build growth loops beyond releases
1. KR: Launch & maintain 1 online competition/month (≥ 4 by next offsite)
2. KR: 5+ landmark case studies published (top customers & integrations) — Work with SA on those!
3. KR: Achieve 30% of API signups via community/competition funnels
4. KR: Whenver there is an update in playground or API, promote changelog and talk about it on socials
## **Objective 2: Own the market narrative & build brand equity**
1. KR: We keep on telling narrative with our unique story, showing the world why it matters what we are building and how it creates economic opportunities (investor comms, website, launches, candidate comms, enterprise buyer comms) 
2. KR: X high-profile press features (target: newsletters, US media, German outlets, policy makers, “EU AI Champion”)
3. KR: 1 celebrity/creative campaign executed (Scorsese-type)
4. KR: Every release follows the 4-phase “Flood the Zone” playbook, 1M+ views organic reach
## **Objective 3: Strengthen developer love & community**
1. KR: 90% of DevRel produced docs/tutorials score ≥ 90% feedback
2. KR: ≥ 50% of competition participants active 2 weeks later
## **Objective 4: Data-driven growth & analytics-first culture** 
1. KR: Posthog fully implemented across BFL → Playground → API funnel
2. KR: Track conversion “Homepage → Signup → API Key → First Call” with ≥ 25% conversion
3. KR: Monthly growth dashboard reviewed in team syncs (traffic, conversions, virality)

2e6c3702-22d5-8053-a3a2-e86cc4788600.title: What success looks likes, Bizops vs  CoS
2e6c3702-22d5-8053-a3a2-e86cc4788600.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2e6c370222d58053a3a2e86cc4788600 as of 2026-03-25T13:42:59.768Z: {"title":"What success looks likes, Bizops vs CoS"} ## BizOps in 5 simple terms 1. **Strategy & planning.** Develops company strategy, OKRs, and planning cadences so we're aligned on what matters and not debating priorities every week 2. **Systems that drive revenue.** Builds and optimizes company-wide systems (RevOps, forecasting, pricing), so commercial outcomes aren't accidental 3. **Resource allocation.** Owns the models for headcount, budget, and investment decisions so we know where to put money and people. 4. **Cross-functional coordination.** Runs projects that span Finance, GTM, Product, Research so things don't fall between the cracks. 5. **Metrics & KPIs.** Tracks what matters and surfaces what's broken so leadership makes decisions with data, not gut feel. **Bonus (when we're ready):** 1. **Incubates new growth motions.** Tests new commercial approaches (FDE, enterprise, partnerships) — then hands them off once they work. —\> BizOps makes sure we have a plan, the systems to execute it, and the data to know if it's working ## What great looks like ### At 6 Months **Theme: Own the data, build trust, install foundations**
Area Success looks like
**Strategy & planning** Monthly bfl business review running, you own prep, agenda, follow-ups. our first quarterly OKR cycle supported
**Systems that drive revenue** RevOps foundations in place, pipeline stages standardized, deal qualification exists for each motion (API, licensing, etc)
**Resource allocation** Headcount model built and maintained. You can answer "can we afford this hire?" in 24 hours
**Cross-functional coordination** Running at least one cross-functional project independently. Stakeholders see you as a partner
**Metrics & KPIs** Some form of real-time dashboard live where we get insights into analysis (current API dashboard is not enough) leadership uses it weekly or monthly. Pipeline forecast accurate
Board deck data prep \<5 days
**Incubating new motions** Not yet, focus is on foundations first
**Dept deep-dive** 1 "fix and scale" cycle complete (likely GTM/RevOps) — diagnosed, built v1, documented playbook
2 company level priorities tracking and making sure they are being achived cross functionally
**Automation** At least 1 manual workflow automated (e.g., weekly pipeline report, company wide KPI tracking, board data pull)
We tell a consistent story across board deck, town hall meetings + any external or fundraising materials
**Behaviors:** - Flags risks proactively - Great communications skills - Brings data to unblock decisions, not opinions - Leaves behind documentation, not just fixes - Running independently, CoS close collab, has to do final 10%, not 80% --- ### At 12 Months **Theme: Drive strategic impact, own the rhythm, be indispensable**
Area Success Looks Like
**Strategy & planning** Quarterly OKR process runs without heroics. Monthly strategy meetings have pre-reads 48h before, decisions documented.
**Systems that drive revenue** RevOps humming — forecast accuracy ±10%, Finance and Sales use the same numbers, no "gut feel" discounting. Customer health scoring in place.
**Resource allocation** Model is the source of truth for hiring decisions. Scenario planning (base/upside/downside) maintained and used.
**Cross-functional coordination** Decision rights documented for top 20 recurring decisions. Bottlenecks resolved in days, not weeks. Escalations rare.
**Metrics & KPIs** Concentration risk dashboard live. Usage-based early warning catches at-risk accounts before renewal. Leadership reflex: "what does the data say?"
**Incubating new motions** At least 1 new motion tested or supported (e.g., FDE, enterprise expansion playbook, partnership model).
**Dept deep-dives** 2-3 functions "fixed and scaled" you've moved on and they run without you.
**Automation** 3-5 workflows automated. Team not dependent on you for recurring data pulls.
**Major initiative shipped** Led one high-impact cross-functional project end-to-end (launch, pricing change, acquisition eval) — it moved the needle.
**Behaviors:** - Surfaces hard strategic questions with data and frameworks - Protects own time; says no to low-leverage asks - Trusted to represent BizOps in exec discussions - When something ambiguous and high-stakes lands, leadership's reflex is "get \[you\] on this" --- ### Quick Reference: 6 vs. 12 Month Shift
Dimension 6 Months 12 Months
**Strategy & planning** Support the cadence Own the cadence
**Systems** Build v1 Systems run without you
**Resource allocation** Build the model Model drives decisions
**Cross-functional** Run assigned projects Self-directed; others come to you
**Metrics** Get the numbers right Numbers drive decisions
**Incubation** Not yet Testing new motions
**Dept deep-dives** 1 complete 2-3 complete, handed off
**Automation** 1 workflow 3-5 workflows
**Relationship to CoS** Execute with light oversight True thought partner
--- ### Department "Fix, Build, Scale, Leave" Cycle **This is core to the role:** They go into a function, diagnose what's broken, build the system, make it run, then hand it off and move on.
Phase What You Do Time
**1. Diagnose** Shadow the team, map workflows, find the bottleneck 1-2 weeks
**2. Fix** Solve the immediate pain — manual if needed 2-4 weeks
**3. Build** Design the scalable system (process + tool + owner) 4-6 weeks
**4. Document** Playbook, SOP, training — so it runs without you 1-2 weeks
**5. Hand off** Transfer ownership to function or new hire Ongoing
**Expected cadence:** - **6 months:** 1 full cycle complete (likely GTM/RevOps) - **12 months:** 2-3 cycles complete; functions running independently --- ### Build & Automation Expectations
Timeframe Automation Wins
**By 6 months** At least 1 manual workflow automated (e.g., weekly pipeline report, board data pull, usage alerts)
**By 12 months** 3-5 workflows automated; team not dependent on you for recurring data tasks
**Examples of "automate and move on":** - Pipeline reporting: from manual CRM pulls → automated weekly snapshot - Usage monitoring: from reactive → automated alerts when customer hits 60% threshold - Board deck data: from 3-day scramble → templated pull with live data - AR reconciliation: from monthly chaos → Finance owns clean process - OKR tracking: from quarterly fire drill → self-serve dashboard --- ### Quick Reference: 6 vs. 12 Month Shift
Dimension 6 Months 12 Months
**Mode** Build foundations, earn trust Drive strategy, own outcomes
**Data** Get the numbers right Use numbers to drive decisions
**Cadence** Install the rhythm Run the rhythm independently
**Scope** Assigned projects Self-directed priorities
**Relationship to CoS** Execute with light oversight True thought partner
**Dept deep-dives** 1 complete 2-3 complete, handed off
**Automation** 1 workflow automated 3-5 workflows; not needed for recurring pulls
**Legacy** Fixes problems Leaves behind systems
## BizOps vs. CoS vs. COO
**BizOps** **CoS** **COO**
**Core job** Build the systems & get the numbers right Extend the CEO's reach Make the business run
**Orientation** Analytical / operational CEO leverage / alignment Organizational accountability
**Time horizon** This quarter's data & next quarter's systems CEO's priorities this week/month 12-24 month operational health
**Authority** Influence through data Borrowed authority from CEO Direct authority over functions
**Typical output** Models, dashboards, playbooks Memos, prep docs, alignment Decisions, org design, accountability
--- --- ### When Roles Blur At earlier stages (like BFL now), these roles overlap heavily: - **No COO yet?** CoS does COO work - **No BizOps yet?** CoS does BizOps work ### Scenario 1: BizOps + CoS Only (No COO) *CoS absorbs COO responsibilities, common at earlier stage*
Flow BizOps CoS (+ COO duties)
**Resource allocation** Builds the model Frames for CEO **+ Decides**
**Board prep** Tracks pipeline, owns data Preps CEO, owns narrative **+ Accountable for revenue**
**Bottleneck resolution** Diagnoses with data Aligns execs **+ Owns the fix**
**Planning** Builds OKRs, tracks metrics Manages CEO priorities **+ Sets org accountability**
**Cross-functional projects** Runs tracking, surfaces blockers Owns if CEO priority **+ Accountable for outcomes**
**What changes:** - CoS is stretched thin, doing CEO leverage work AND operational accountability - BizOps becomes more critical as the "engine" CoS relies heavily on BizOps output - Decision-making can bottleneck at CoS/CEO ### Scenario 2: BizOps + COO Only (No CoS) *BizOps absorbs CoS responsibilities, less common but possible*
Flow BizOps (+ CoS duties) COO
**Resource allocation** Builds the model **+ Frames for CEO** Decides
**Board prep** Tracks pipeline, owns data **+ Preps CEO, owns narrative** Accountable for revenue
**Bottleneck resolution** Diagnoses with data **+ Aligns execs** Owns the fix
**Planning** Builds OKRs, tracks metrics **+ Manages CEO priorities** Sets org-level accountability
**Cross-functional projects** Runs tracking **+ Owns if CEO priority** Accountable for outcomes
**What changes:** - BizOps has more CEO exposure and strategic framing responsibility - BizOps needs stronger exec communication skills (not just analytical) - COO focuses on operational accountability and decisions, but if there is no COO and no COs, - BizOps gets pulled into CEO orbit, systems building suffers ### Summary: Who Absorbs What
Missing Role Who Absorbs Risk
**No COO** CoS does COO work CoS stretched; decisions bottleneck
**No CoS** BizOps does CoS work BizOps pulled strategic; systems suffer
**No BizOps** CoS does BizOps work CoS drowning in data work; no leverage
## **What *isn’t* getting built or done without BizOps ** ### **Strategic gaps** - No single owner for **cross-functional diagnosis** - Tradeoffs debated emotionally instead of analytically - Planning assumptions go stale quickly - Headcount growth not tied tightly to outcomes - Initiatives stall between functions ### **Org health gaps** - VP Ops becomes over relied on - CEO absorbs synthesis work unconsciously - Finance pulled into decisions they’re not designed to own

<properties>

</properties>
<content>
**Compute governance**
- This sits between Finance / FP&A (cost tracking) and Research (allocation decisions), as compute spend grows we will likely need a dedicated Compute/Infra Ops person, someone who can model provider economics, negotiate cloud contracts, and tie capacity planning to the research roadmap. - WIP
**Capital & talent deployment**
- FP&A / Strategic Finance: budget pacing, resource allocation models, forecast accuracy, board reporting. This is our financial planning engine. - WIP
- People (Head of People): The systems side of the people cost center. - DONE
- Talent: recruiting strategy and execution. The pipeline side of the people cost center. - DONE
**Research ↔ reality translation**
- BizOps / Strategy = the bridge between research, finance and GTM - DONE 
- Data Procurement: the data pipeline specifically. Sourcing strategy, vendor management, taxonomy, evaluation loops with the research team - DONE 
**Cross-functional coherence & velocity**
- BizOps & Strategy = the core BizOps job. Running the interface model across functions, removing bottlenecks, enforcing decision rights. - DONE 
**Decision architecture & operating model**
- BizOps / Strategy = owns the cadence design and runs it. Leadership syncs, strategy days, OKR cycles. - DONE 
**Corporate operations**
- Legal: contracts, IP, compliance, regulatory, policy. - DONE 
- Security/IT (CISO): infosec, SOC2, tooling. - DONE 
- Comms: external narrative, press, investor comms, employer brand - WIP
</content>
</page>

336c3702-22d5-809b-9e5d-f2dcfbe53a39.title: Walmart Flux.3 Summary 4/2/26
336c3702-22d5-809b-9e5d-f2dcfbe53a39.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/336c370222d5809b9e5df2dcfbe53a39 as of 2026-04-02T23:42:48.462Z: {"title":"Walmart Flux.3 Summary 4/2/26"} **Post-Session Summary** **Date:** 4/2/2026 **Attendees:** - **Sam** ([sam@blackforestlabs.ai](mailto:sam@blackforestlabs.ai)) — Go-to-market team, Black Forest Labs - **Mingqiang Zhang** ([mingqiang.zhang@walmart.com](mailto:mingqiang.zhang@walmart.com)) - **Stephanie Tsai** ([stephanie.tsai@walmart.com](mailto:stephanie.tsai@walmart.com)) — Product Manager, leading generative content creation initiatives - **Oskar Radermecker** ([oskar.radermecker@walmart.com](mailto:oskar.radermecker@walmart.com)) - **Henry Phillips** ([henry.phillips@walmart.com](mailto:henry.phillips@walmart.com)) — Interface between the team and Walmart's content studio **Key Use Cases Identified (ranked by priority):** 1. **Lifestyle/Motion Graphics** - Walmart is generating lifestyle videos for key products. The input involves product details, and the output is a lifestyle video. This is actively being explored and expected to launch in the next 3-6 months. 2. **Interactive Video** - Creating interactive product videos, such as an air fryer with zoomable controls. The input is product details, and the output is an interactive video. These are pre-generated and not real-time. 3. **Promotional Marketing Videos** - Developing promotional videos for marketing purposes. The input is product details, and the output is a promotional video. Examples include "\$8.99 pizza" and "roses farm to table" for Sam’s Club. **Top Model Capabilities (ranked by importance):** 1. **Near-zero hallucination on text and logos** - Walmart requires high accuracy in text and logos to avoid misrepresentation of products. 2. **Sufficient output duration (up to \~45 seconds)** - Current models have a max duration of 8-15 seconds, which is insufficient for meaningful content. 3. **Ability to transform raw product images into inspirational marketing videos** - Walmart desires to convert raw warehouse product images into inspirational marketing videos without relying heavily on human prompting. **Top Pain Points (ranked by severity):** 1. **Hallucinations** - Affects Veo models. Misrepresentation of products, even slightly off logos, is unacceptable. Example shared: Y. 2. **Max duration too short** - Affects Veo models. Current models only allow 8-15 seconds, but up to 45 seconds is needed. Example shared: Y. 3. **Unnatural movement** - Affects Veo models. Human movements are slow and aimless, making it hard to catch with automated QC. Example shared: Y. **Video Importance Level:** High - Video is as important as images for Walmart, but the quality bar needs to be raised for production use. **Audio Relevance:** Yes — separate - Audio is a "nice to have" but not critical. Sam's Club) - Input: Product/campaign brief and imagery - Output: Short-form promotional video (e.g. "\$8.99 pizza," "roses farm to table") - End user: Marketing/brand teams; Sam's Club has more flexibility than Walmart core brand 2.2 Reference examples of "great" output: *To be provided by Oskar post-call.* 2.3 Current outputs that fall short: *Failure examples and prompts to be shared by Oskar post-call.* 2.4 Abandoned use cases: 360-degree product spins were explored but shelved. Longer videos have more risk of hallucinations. 2.6 Resolutions and aspect ratios needed: 2K minimum, 4K preferred. Nothing higher is needed (8K is only relevant for print/packaging, which is image not video). Standard marketing/social aspect ratios assumed. 2.7 Top 3 most important model capabilities: 1. Temporal consistency Low Core issue — 360° spins abandoned due to hallucination between frames

2a3c3702-22d5-804c-a9e2-d49fdc0bbfd9.title: What is BizOps - A Primer
2a3c3702-22d5-804c-a9e2-d49fdc0bbfd9.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2a3c370222d5804ca9e2d49fdc0bbfd9 as of 2026-03-04T20:17:42.056Z: {"title":"What is BizOps - A Primer"} ## **BizOps, aka Business Operations, aka Office of the COO** You see "Strategy & Operations" on the org chart and wonder if Sarah just made up a fancy title because "Chief of Staff" felt too *West Wing (in the white house)*. Or maybe you think it's corporate speak for "does random stuff CEO doesn't want to do." ## **BizOps - aka Strategy & Operations, aka Business Operations- is the team that helps us build a well-functioning organization = defining and delivering company priorities.** We act as a strategic partner across the company, providing data-driven strategy, optimizing how we work, and fostering new growth initiatives. We help leadership make informed decisions by providing a holistic view of the business, aligning strategies with execution, and incubating new growth opportunities for BFL. **Everything ladders up to actual business outcomes. It is never presentations**, workshops, or optimisations, for their own sake. BizOps key stakeholder is the CEO. As such, Biz Ops has a great opportunity and a big responsibility: - Align around a coherent strategy and plan, by **developing clear company strategy(ies), and OKRs** - **Deep functional fixes** — diving into specific areas that need automation or repair (like RevOps), rather than spreading thin across everything - Drive commercial outcomes by **building and optimising company-wide systems** - Cross functional project coordination - Resource allocation decisions - **Metrics and KPIs tracking ** - Unlock new areas of commercial growth by **incubating new motions** [**Unfiltered chatgpt version: how VP Ops, ceo, bizops, finance work together **](https://chatgpt.com/share/698f8bc4-9358-8006-a455-ca52855f2f62) ## Why BizOps is even more critical at AI-native companies Here's what makes BFL different from traditional tech companies: we're not bolting AI onto an existing business model. **AI isn't just a feature or enhancement for us - it's the foundation of our identity and how we operate. **And this fundamentally changes how we need to build and scale the company. But here's the harder part, and the part that makes my job as CoS both fascinating and occasionally maddening: **BFL is research-focused at its core. We're not a typical product company that happened to use AI. We're researchers who are building a company. And we need to stay that way - research DNA is our competitive advantage, our moat, the reason FLUX models are best-in-class.**
**The challenge? We need to be both.** **We need to keep our research DNA as our core *and* build a well-functioning organization** that delivers business outcomes. This isn't "pick one" - we have to do both, simultaneously, or we lose what makes us special. Think about what this actually means: - Research teams need freedom to explore and push at the frontier, *and* we need higher release velocity, predictable roadmaps - We value academic rigor and peer review, *and* we need to ship fast enough to compete with Google and OpenAI - Our founders are researchers with limited business experience, *and* we're scaling to \$300M+ ARR with institutional investors who expect operational excellence - We want to maintain open philosophy and community credibility, *and* we need to build sustainable commercial revenue streams - We're headquartered in Freiburg, Germany, *and* we need to build a global business that competes with San Francisco and London-based companies These aren't just tensions to manage - they're fundamental contradictions we're designing a new type of company around. And this is exactly why BizOps matters more here than at a traditional company. **Traditional playbooks don't work, the pace is faster, and the org structure needs to be continuously redesigned as AI capabilities evolve. Without BizOps, you either move too slow (trying to run like a traditional company) or you fly apart (moving fast with no systems).** 1. **The pace is different.** We went from 0 to \$100M ARR in 14 months. Traditional operating models can't keep up with that velocity. BizOps designs systems that scale at some speed. 2. **The org structure is different.** We can't just copy the SaaS playbook. When your product is research heavy and your operations are or should be AI powered, you need someone constantly evaluating: What should be automated? What needs human judgment? Where do we need traditional functions vs. AI augmented workflows? That's not a one-time exercise, it's continuous strategic work. 3. **The commercial model is evolving in real-time.** API vs. licensing vs. prosumer. Usage-based vs. subscription. Open weights vs closed. We're figuring out the business model *while* scaling revenue. Traditional ops teams execute a known playbook. BizOps at an AI-native company is writing the playbook while running the race. 4. **Cross-functional complexity is higher.** At BFL, our research team ships product. Our product influences our commercial strategy. Our commercial strategy shapes our research priorities. These aren't siloed functions, they're deeply interconnected. Someone needs to see the whole board and make sure the moves align. **That's where BizOps comes in.** We're not just optimizing existing processes; we're designing systems and operations with AI first architecture and mental models from day one. We're figuring out how to make a 50-person team punch like a 200-person company because we've automated the right things and kept human strategic judgment where it counts. ## **The Three Superpowers of BizOps** 1. **Single threaded leadership:** BizOps tackles strategic initiatives that are too important to be someone's 20% project. If left to business-as-usual owners, these get ignored - or worse, the stuff keeping the lights on breaks while everyone's distracted. We answer questions like: - "How do we scale to 150+ people without losing our research culture?" - "What compute model do we need as we grow, and how do we structure those partnerships?” - "How do we design compensation and equity incentives that work for researchers and business hires across multiple countries?" - "Can we shift to consumption-based pricing, and when, without undermining API research access?" - "What do we do about these inbound partnership requests that might compromise our open-source credibility?" - "How do we build a global business from Freiburg—enterprise sales, customer support, partnerships - without losing our German research base?" - "What's our actual growth plan that investors will believe in, given our unique structure?" These questions deserve *real* answers, not gut feelings or whoever-shouted-loudest-in-the-meeting decisions. 2. **Independence (We're Switzerland, Baby)** Projects and initiatives that sit in BizOps are protected from commercial pressure, roadmap interference, or political maneuvering. Our analysis doesn't fit—by definition—with any one leader's wishful thinking or biased views. **When I tell you the numbers don't support a timeline, or that a strategy needs adjustment, it's not personal. It's because I've looked at the data without the emotional investment of the team executing it. (And yes, this is why sometimes people don't love hearing from me.)** 3. **Flexibility in structure** Early on, BizOps is like a Swiss Army knife like a CoS. As we grow, it evolves with the org. For us at BFL, that means: - Right now: Our CoS built the zero to 1 of many functions from finance to HR, talent, marketing, ops, incubating growth initiatives - Some of these functions have already graduated: We hired Dave to run Finance, Adam built out a legal team, our GTM function is maturing. - Soon: More of these functions our CoS covered will "graduate" and become independent (hello, Head of People and CISO we're hiring) - Future state: BizOps will focus strategic planning, and new motion incubation, RevOps etc The structure follows where the business needs the most leverage. ## Where BizOps sits in the Org BizOps reports directly to the CEO - and in more mature orgs, to the COO. There are three reasons this matters: 1. **Executive oversight**: We're shaping company strategy and operational excellence, which requires C-level access and authority 2. **Cross-functional coordination**: We're the glue between research, engineering, and business teams, which means we need to be peers with department heads. Which is why we attend cross functional meetings. If we don’t, we cant do our job well. 3. **Centralized view**: While individual "ops" people might sit in marketing or finance, BizOps sees across all of it to deliver cross-functional initiatives. ### How do we measure BizOps success? Here's the trap: *If BizOps is seen as some mysterious force - it gets easily overlooked.* We end up in the shadows, "invisible when things work," and then... forgotten when budget cuts from Dave come around. **BizOps wins when everyone else wins. We pick a few leading indicators of success focused on the parts of the business we can actually influence. Then we design initiatives to move those metrics.** Right now for example at BFL, that means: - Speed of decision-making and release velocity - Working on compute plans - Building out revenue operations rigor - Cross-functional alignment on strategy - Evaluating new tools to help us grow - Investor confidence and fundraising outcomes - …. ## A Chief of Staff scales a person A BizOps function scales a company. A CoS is designed to: - Amplify the CEO (or COO) - Track priorities - Push alignment - Handle cross-functional chaos But once you double from 50 → 100 people, the problem shifts from: > “Are we aligned?” to: > “Do we have systems that work without constant executive intervention?” That’s where BizOps comes in. --- ## Complexity grows non-linearly At 50 people: - Informal communication works - Decisions happen in a room - Founders still touch everything At 100 people: - Layers emerge (managers of managers) - Budgeting becomes real - Headcount planning matters - Metrics matter - Hiring mistakes get expensive - Misalignment costs millions BizOps builds: - Planning cycles - KPI frameworks - Budget models - Org design processes - Hiring capacity models - Cross-functional workflows Those are durable systems, not just follow-ups. We need more of those at BFL who can do this.

raw.title: What is BizOps - A Primer
raw.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/2a3c370222d5804ca9e2d49fdc0bbfd9 as of 2026-03-04T20:17:42.056Z: {"title":"What is BizOps - A Primer"} ## **BizOps, aka Business Operations, aka Office of the COO** You see "Strategy & Operations" on the org chart and wonder if Sarah just made up a fancy title because "Chief of Staff" felt too *West Wing (in the white house)*. Or maybe you think it's corporate speak for "does random stuff CEO doesn't want to do." ## **BizOps - aka Strategy & Operations, aka Business Operations- is the team that helps us build a well-functioning organization = defining and delivering company priorities.** We act as a strategic partner across the company, providing data-driven strategy, optimizing how we work, and fostering new growth initiatives. We help leadership make informed decisions by providing a holistic view of the business, aligning strategies with execution, and incubating new growth opportunities for BFL. **Everything ladders up to actual business outcomes. It is never presentations**, workshops, or optimisations, for their own sake. BizOps key stakeholder is the CEO. As such, Biz Ops has a great opportunity and a big responsibility: - Align around a coherent strategy and plan, by **developing clear company strategy(ies), and OKRs** - **Deep functional fixes** — diving into specific areas that need automation or repair (like RevOps), rather than spreading thin across everything - Drive commercial outcomes by **building and optimising company-wide systems** - Cross functional project coordination - Resource allocation decisions - **Metrics and KPIs tracking ** - Unlock new areas of commercial growth by **incubating new motions** [**Unfiltered chatgpt version: how VP Ops, ceo, bizops, finance work together **](https://chatgpt.com/share/698f8bc4-9358-8006-a455-ca52855f2f62) ## Why BizOps is even more critical at AI-native companies Here's what makes BFL different from traditional tech companies: we're not bolting AI onto an existing business model. **AI isn't just a feature or enhancement for us - it's the foundation of our identity and how we operate. **And this fundamentally changes how we need to build and scale the company. But here's the harder part, and the part that makes my job as CoS both fascinating and occasionally maddening: **BFL is research-focused at its core. We're not a typical product company that happened to use AI. We're researchers who are building a company. And we need to stay that way - research DNA is our competitive advantage, our moat, the reason FLUX models are best-in-class.**
**The challenge? We need to be both.** **We need to keep our research DNA as our core *and* build a well-functioning organization** that delivers business outcomes. This isn't "pick one" - we have to do both, simultaneously, or we lose what makes us special. Think about what this actually means: - Research teams need freedom to explore and push at the frontier, *and* we need higher release velocity, predictable roadmaps - We value academic rigor and peer review, *and* we need to ship fast enough to compete with Google and OpenAI - Our founders are researchers with limited business experience, *and* we're scaling to \$300M+ ARR with institutional investors who expect operational excellence - We want to maintain open philosophy and community credibility, *and* we need to build sustainable commercial revenue streams - We're headquartered in Freiburg, Germany, *and* we need to build a global business that competes with San Francisco and London-based companies These aren't just tensions to manage - they're fundamental contradictions we're designing a new type of company around. And this is exactly why BizOps matters more here than at a traditional company. **Traditional playbooks don't work, the pace is faster, and the org structure needs to be continuously redesigned as AI capabilities evolve. Without BizOps, you either move too slow (trying to run like a traditional company) or you fly apart (moving fast with no systems).** 1. **The pace is different.** We went from 0 to \$100M ARR in 14 months. Traditional operating models can't keep up with that velocity. BizOps designs systems that scale at some speed. 2. **The org structure is different.** We can't just copy the SaaS playbook. When your product is research heavy and your operations are or should be AI powered, you need someone constantly evaluating: What should be automated? What needs human judgment? Where do we need traditional functions vs. AI augmented workflows? That's not a one-time exercise, it's continuous strategic work. 3. **The commercial model is evolving in real-time.** API vs. licensing vs. prosumer. Usage-based vs. subscription. Open weights vs closed. We're figuring out the business model *while* scaling revenue. Traditional ops teams execute a known playbook. BizOps at an AI-native company is writing the playbook while running the race. 4. **Cross-functional complexity is higher.** At BFL, our research team ships product. Our product influences our commercial strategy. Our commercial strategy shapes our research priorities. These aren't siloed functions, they're deeply interconnected. Someone needs to see the whole board and make sure the moves align. **That's where BizOps comes in.** We're not just optimizing existing processes; we're designing systems and operations with AI first architecture and mental models from day one. We're figuring out how to make a 50-person team punch like a 200-person company because we've automated the right things and kept human strategic judgment where it counts. ## **The Three Superpowers of BizOps** 1. **Single threaded leadership:** BizOps tackles strategic initiatives that are too important to be someone's 20% project. If left to business-as-usual owners, these get ignored - or worse, the stuff keeping the lights on breaks while everyone's distracted. We answer questions like: - "How do we scale to 150+ people without losing our research culture?" - "What compute model do we need as we grow, and how do we structure those partnerships?” - "How do we design compensation and equity incentives that work for researchers and business hires across multiple countries?" - "Can we shift to consumption-based pricing, and when, without undermining API research access?" - "What do we do about these inbound partnership requests that might compromise our open-source credibility?" - "How do we build a global business from Freiburg—enterprise sales, customer support, partnerships - without losing our German research base?" - "What's our actual growth plan that investors will believe in, given our unique structure?" These questions deserve *real* answers, not gut feelings or whoever-shouted-loudest-in-the-meeting decisions. 2. **Independence (We're Switzerland, Baby)** Projects and initiatives that sit in BizOps are protected from commercial pressure, roadmap interference, or political maneuvering. Our analysis doesn't fit—by definition—with any one leader's wishful thinking or biased views. **When I tell you the numbers don't support a timeline, or that a strategy needs adjustment, it's not personal. It's because I've looked at the data without the emotional investment of the team executing it. (And yes, this is why sometimes people don't love hearing from me.)** 3. **Flexibility in structure** Early on, BizOps is like a Swiss Army knife like a CoS. As we grow, it evolves with the org. For us at BFL, that means: - Right now: Our CoS built the zero to 1 of many functions from finance to HR, talent, marketing, ops, incubating growth initiatives - Some of these functions have already graduated: We hired Dave to run Finance, Adam built out a legal team, our GTM function is maturing. - Soon: More of these functions our CoS covered will "graduate" and become independent (hello, Head of People and CISO we're hiring) - Future state: BizOps will focus strategic planning, and new motion incubation, RevOps etc The structure follows where the business needs the most leverage. ## Where BizOps sits in the Org BizOps reports directly to the CEO - and in more mature orgs, to the COO. There are three reasons this matters: 1. **Executive oversight**: We're shaping company strategy and operational excellence, which requires C-level access and authority 2. **Cross-functional coordination**: We're the glue between research, engineering, and business teams, which means we need to be peers with department heads. Which is why we attend cross functional meetings. If we don’t, we cant do our job well. 3. **Centralized view**: While individual "ops" people might sit in marketing or finance, BizOps sees across all of it to deliver cross-functional initiatives. ### How do we measure BizOps success? Here's the trap: *If BizOps is seen as some mysterious force - it gets easily overlooked.* We end up in the shadows, "invisible when things work," and then... forgotten when budget cuts from Dave come around. **BizOps wins when everyone else wins. We pick a few leading indicators of success focused on the parts of the business we can actually influence. Then we design initiatives to move those metrics.** Right now for example at BFL, that means: - Speed of decision-making and release velocity - Working on compute plans - Building out revenue operations rigor - Cross-functional alignment on strategy - Evaluating new tools to help us grow - Investor confidence and fundraising outcomes - …. ## A Chief of Staff scales a person A BizOps function scales a company. A CoS is designed to: - Amplify the CEO (or COO) - Track priorities - Push alignment - Handle cross-functional chaos But once you double from 50 → 100 people, the problem shifts from: > “Are we aligned?” to: > “Do we have systems that work without constant executive intervention?” That’s where BizOps comes in. --- ## Complexity grows non-linearly At 50 people: - Informal communication works - Decisions happen in a room - Founders still touch everything At 100 people: - Layers emerge (managers of managers) - Budgeting becomes real - Headcount planning matters - Metrics matter - Hiring mistakes get expensive - Misalignment costs millions BizOps builds: - Planning cycles - KPI frameworks - Budget models - Org design processes - Hiring capacity models - Cross-functional workflows Those are durable systems, not just follow-ups. We need more of those at BFL who can do this.

314c3702-22d5-8041-9c94-f6900de02437.text: Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/314c370222d580419c94f6900de02437 as of 2026-03-30T15:51:19.056Z: {"title":"FLUX.3 Midtraining Goals"} # General questions - [ ] Multi-task training: - [ ] how are we balancing the tasks vs each other, i.e how much image editing, how much image to video, how much text to video? - [ ] what does more conditioning (image(s), camera, video) beyond text mean for noise schedule? - [ ] already start building specialized models? - [ ] Which discriminative tasks can we add? - [ ] Which tasks to add? - t2i: ✅ - i2i single: ✅ - i2i multi: ✅ - t2v: ✅ - i2v: ✅  - specific frames → video 🚧 - reference editing (if time) - single ref ❌ - multi ref ❌ - t2v+a: ✅ - i2v+a: ✅ - v2v: 🚧 - camera control (can be used for basic action prediction conditioning) - discriminative outputs - masks - bounding boxes - more explicit action conditioning? (What exactly?) - [ ] Evaluation pipeline : - [ ] build extensive evaluation for each task, which methods to use for*:* - [ ] t2i: - [ ] human ✅: /blob/eval/maksim/benchmarks/t2i_bench_2026-02-13/ - [ ] i2i single: - [ ] i2v+a: → VAbench - [ ] human ✅ (needs to be copied though): /blob/eval/maksim/benchmarks/i2av_bench_2026-03-30 - [ ] auto: pending - [ ] v2v: - [ ] camera control: - [ ] discriminative outputs - [ ] masks - [ ] bounding boxes - [ ] action prediction/conditioning - [ ] prompt upsampling (initial variant should be ready by then): different prompt upsamplers, task dependent? ## Steps to take (during pretraining) We already want to be evaluating during pretraining to assess if continued pretraining gives us further improvements after adding all the new tasks - [ ] set up evaluation pipeline - [ ] set up midtraining config with all the tasks mentioned above - [ ] consistent finetuning using that config to see if we gain more performance through further pretraining (can be lower res than the actual pretraining but should contain all the tasks # Data ## Video **Goal:** - Increase length of generation (5s, 10s, 15s) - Increase resolution (from 190p/360p in pretraining to 360p+ in midtraining) - Build path for interactive prompting. - interactive prompting needs specific captions - some of the caption pairs should be in instruct/change format instead of t2v - Frame(s) conditioning/image to video - Camera control - video-to-video - Precise time control - e.g. timestamped captions (for the above) - camera trajectories - cut conditioning? **Compared to FLUX.2: **new modality **What we need:** - **General video data** - [ ] more filtering needed? - possibilities: - better watermark detection - higher motion filtering (available on the fly, decide based on pretraining performance) - [ ] video resolution? - [ ] going beyond 360p? - **general** - [ ] *captions: determine captioning ratio between 5s, 10s, 15s *(Owner ) - [ ] Answer question ‘Does training on longer captions improve motion understanding in general’? → ablation - [ ] get training speed perspective on this - **prompting interactivity (Owner + to conduct experiments)** - [ ] * identify switch between actions / semantic difference (switching captions)* - option: check for consecutive frames with low motion - option: check for frames with high difference to the start in some similarity space - option: base it on cuts - option: literature review - **procedure:** collect data for each options and ablate - [ ] *conduct captioning* - [ ] *transform captions into “instruct style”* - **frame conditioning (Owner since captions similar to interactive prompting)** - [ ] *get frame-aware captions* - conditioning formats: - start, - mid - end - start + end - alternative: random frame at t for combination with precise time control - [ ] *reference image(s) to video* - [ ] single ref: - [ ] multi ref: - **Camera control (Owner **❌) - [ ] *input format: *decide whether to - “distill” camera positions into prompt - leave as coord - do both - [ ] *combine with time* —\> camera trajectories - **Time control (Owner **❌) - [ ] *discuss options* - timed cut conditioning - timed captions → yes for interactivity of prompting - timed camera coordinates → yes for precise camera control and trajectories 🤖 - **Discriminative Tasks (Owner **❌) ## Image **Goal:** - Improve common weak points with target datasets - Improve instruction-alignment - Lay the foundation for specific product features - Final Resolution **Compared to FLUX.2: **bigger focus on typography, maybe some different product focus, better captions **What we need:** - Large scale, general image data with hierarchical captions - Base pumpkin - Status: ongoing - improved captions - … ## Image Editing **Goal:** - Introduce Editing as a task - Build strong general capability for referencing & local editing **Compared to FLUX.2: **better scaled datasets, local editing focus **What we need:** - local editing - inpainting dataset including captions (up to 200M): Ready to run, needs gpus - Referencing - products (60M) + posts (40M): ready to train - sstk-ref - TODO: May need stronger filters → only keep if faces are sufficiently large - inat: should be fine to train - \[likely out-of-scope/time\] video → editing pairs - \[likely out-of-scope\] pumpkin pairs - TODO make the pipeline work well - local + Referencing: - inpainting on posts → estimated at least 6M suitable samples - TODO needs finalization - TODO running it - discriminative tasks: - image to mask - image to bounding box ## Video Editing # Audio - # Open Questions: - Should we try to include “control-net” tasks either as a general helper, or as a potential to flywheel with tighter control? - Should we try to bring in explicit cut conditioning here? This has the risk, that our cut detection method might be flawed and provide a bad signal to the model. But is the chance for a good feature in general and a contender for a strong timestamp signal. Also a native starting point for mid generation prompt change - Exact captioning scheme and timestamps for captions? We want interactive prompting so need to annotate time segments of a video clip with captions. - Do we want to create explicit negations in prompts? E.g. “The man isn’t wearing a hat”. Can mostly be solved already by prompt rewriting, but might be awkward “The man has a bald head”. Interesting for “there are no cuts” - Will we have enough high quality data to include video editing - how about audio? - Do hierarchical captions help us? - Do we want to add some additional quality filtering for videos and if so what? - Do we want to invest more on color-ref? Likely needs bigger scale, maybe some changed approach - Can we do explicit camera position conditioning in a sensible way? - Do we want to include 15s clips as well? - make ablation - How much compute do we need? - work back from 1 month midtraining with the decided # Out of Scope

“distill” camera positions into prompt - leave as coord - do both - [ ] *combine with time* —\> camera trajectories - **Time control (Owner **❌) - [ ] *discuss options* - timed cut conditioning - timed captions → yes for interactivity of prompting - timed camera coordinates → yes for precise camera control and trajectories 🤖 - **Discriminative Tasks (Owner **❌) ## Image **Goal:** - Improve common weak points with target datasets - Improve instruction-alignment - Lay the foundation for specific product features - Final Resolution **Compared to FLUX.2: **bigger focus on typography, maybe some different product focus, better captions **What we need:** - Large scale, general image data with hierarchical captions - Base pumpkin - Status: ongoing - improved captions - … ## Image Editing **Goal:** - Introduce Editing as a task - Build strong general capability for referencing & local editing **Compared to FLUX.2: **better scaled datasets, local editing focus **What we need:** - local editing - inpainting dataset including captions (up to 200M): Ready to run, needs gpus - Referencing - products (60M) + posts (40M): ready to train - sstk-ref - TODO: May need stronger filters → only keep if faces are sufficiently large - inat: should be fine to train - \[likely out-of-scope/time\] video → editing pairs - \[likely out-of-scope\] pumpkin pairs - TODO make the pipeline work well - local + Referencing: - inpainting on posts → estimated at least 6M suitable samples - TODO needs finalization - TODO running it - discriminative tasks: - image to mask - image to bounding box ## Video Editing # Audio - # Open Questions: - Should we try to include “control-net” tasks either as a general helper, or as a potential to flywheel with tighter control? - Should we try to bring in explicit cut conditioning here? This has the risk, that our cut detection method might be flawed and provide a bad signal to the model. But is the chance for a good feature in general and a contender for a strong timestamp signal. Also a native starting point for mid generation prompt change - Exact captioning scheme and timestamps for captions? We want interactive prompting so need to annotate time segments of a video clip with captions. - Do we want to create explicit negations in prompts? E.g. “The man isn’t wearing a hat”. Can mostly be solved already by prompt rewriting, but might be awkward “The man has a bald head”. Interesting for “there are no cuts” - Will we have enough high quality data to include video editing - how about audio? - Do hierarchical captions help us? - Do we want to add some additional quality filtering for videos and if so what? - Do we want to invest more on color-ref? Likely needs bigger scale, maybe some changed approach - Can we do explicit camera position conditioning in a sensible way? - Do we want to include 15s clips as well? - make ablation - How much compute do we need? - work back from 1 month midtraining with the decided # Out of Scope

317c3702-22d5-8177-9274-c8a92e456453.title: Scalable Diffusion Distillation
317c3702-22d5-8177-9274-c8a92e456453.text:
Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/317c370222d581779274c8a92e456453 as of 2026-03-02T13:13:04.074Z:
<page url="https://www.notion.so/317c370222d581779274c8a92e456453">
<ancestor-path></ancestor-path>
<properties>
{"title":"Scalable Diffusion Distillation"}
</properties>
<content>
## Research Question
What is the simplest recipe that achieves SOTA few-step (and ultimately 1-step) diffusion generation across modalities? Can a straightforward mode-covering initialization + well-engineered refinement phase match or beat the growing zoo of distillation methods that are complex both mathematically and in engineering (consistency models needing specialized sampling and JVP tricks, shortcut models with level conditioning, TwinFlow, RCM, MeanFlow, ...)?
## Hypothesis
Simplicity is a first-class citizen alongside performance because simplicity enables scalability. The field has accumulated layers of mathematical and engineering complexity (JVP computation, EMA schedules, progressive curricula, level conditioning, per-sample CFG sampling, logvar tricks) that are hard to tune, debug, and transfer to new modalities. A two-stage approach of (1) cheap mode-covering initialization followed by (2) a well-engineered refinement phase can potentially match or beat complex methods while being far easier to scale. 
## Why This Moves the Frontier
Distillation is a required step in Flux3 post-training. While 4-step distillation works for T2I (our SD+LADD recipe already beats the multi-step teacher), it remains unproven for multimodal generation (video, editing, audio) and 1-step quality is still far from solved. Current methods look great on ImageNet 64/256 but struggle at production scale. The** north star is 1-step multimodal generation.**
## Preliminary Results
Systematic comparison of 10+ methods on Klein 9B (soft-TIFA GM, FDD, UnifiedReward, 800 GenEval2 prompts):
- **LADD (4-step) already surpasses the 30-step Klein 9B teacher** on all three metrics (soft-TIFA 33.35 vs 31.55, FDD 115 vs 118, UR 3.32 vs 3.29)
- **Distribution-matching methods (DMD, LADD) reach high text-alignment fastest** but DMD scores are inflated by saturation artifacts -- metric alone is misleading
- **Mode-covering methods plateau or diverge**: SCM caps at \~24, RCM diverges at 12k, Shortcut IG plateaus at \~28, MeanFlow peaks at 34 but collapses
- **Vanilla step distillation is a surprisingly strong simple baseline** (SD-direct peaks at 31.6) -- progressive distillation does not help
- **SD + LADD is already our winning recipe** and outperforms more complex methods (SCM, RCM, TwinFlow) on our benchmarks. The question is: can we push performance even further while maintaining this simplicity advantage, and extend it to 1-step and across modalities?
![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/ea8f4867-eca3-4d33-ade7-8d3ce24cf18c/image.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB4666HFOIO5J%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T100108Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJIMEYCIQD3mTqSoeMU5zWzOHg8j56B83x2sSEeidi56YvuiRXMEAIhALEwUtAbqPPR40jaOtEGlIWH55kxnMGKxkBtz1UijqhZKv8DCAIQABoMNjM3NDIzMTgzODA1IgyZZkoJIgqoLdLllcgq3AOtxkuCbAg8m0OKRtLuiFuVplJiGkWrDbKJjMSJFuNuKswTHJb7pk2DRbT7o4uUwpBCC314QcQbgYalKM6i%2FoePE2NGKwK%2By0DXnS%2BnwO9i431rK3BxziQL8vhnNIw%2BlSg%2BzlfsJY0xV%2BK37pDbFPsEGEpQziKu88BTWZHqAma3N1MZ9JGvsqZT48vifzUTm3WzSEisTGFMiNYEYm3%2B2fytCTXvALjaP%2BJa2kUxNKM6ZkuvtqJoywPEX4QlQYuOUviHXgh%2FATvNVIkuuJE1nnDbCP6mdZeHCTVaCHZwTy0sW9J8InQO%2F3TkmIFOPi3spQo6Xbh%2FGnJBDCAQD0xJQ%2BnjMCg%2FyO%2BYEhhl834bP%2BScRmyRilYxi3Q0JsDByIZh9elnaGMIyAJuAAE1Y5QQ0lc3wz1h7BaeUsN2VWUGScH4LMnq%2F430Y1SOwdpIbKOVgxGwBm%2FxU2mhRJRxDD1H24XGaLJBRCIFQNiz2FNDlenLN%2BSWo7QPUvKUWsAX8ukhqQDSVjUMAeNgJ%2BUYf43sJJDJvsGyRJnJoPOFRxDOraKZkXTFOWGlJgRvua0NdN5FHcUMVrDXRqC3V6VVSXg46bI%2BLZvCbbfUyN8dNhJoGMWKJUH2yonnrL2gF9JWbTC1sJLPBjqkASnoXRzoWkjDi%2FJsUUF83gVj78N8Wni2HnGIA8a%2BmYnB9QI%2B4QDEqJWLxgZIU9sptP%2B4v5tZHZgK7r8Hb2wn6h6DZLu1N%2FQsTUIwojHqyne9sEIskN97oaUGB9egsJS1MVmJ6w4PCbCAKrLcc2RbD%2BVcK5pziaiLOBsF60bDlfu2kMZfDNnimfb%2FDRFxRNsookyeSyHqf2vpB5o9DMZHi400ukcD&X-Amz-Signature=be7c3695d45023c3d756b432763c08388855a5aa0872b3da8a542b0c61080e77&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject)
- Disclaimer: These are prelim results
	- LADD is much simpler than our standard recipe (no pre-step-distill phase, full ft instead of lora, no teacher target)
	- Metrics is decent but not perfect
		- Meanflow & DMD achieve higher soft-tifa than Klein-9B, but look significantly worse
		- especially DMD scores are inflated by saturation/artifacts
		- soft-TIFA measures text alignment, not image quality, so a saturated mess that happens to contain "a red car" scores well
	- Longer training: SC-IG, SCM stay flat, RCM diverges at 12k
	- Current plot is not quite fair to LADD, DMD, and RCM, they have fewer student updates due to a discriminator phase, RCM does even 4x more discriminator steps than student steps.
## Proposed Work
### Exploration Phase (Months 1-2)
**Goal**: Find the optimal 1-2 step recipe, with simplicity as a design constraint. Not blocked on Flux3 -- exploration starts immediately on Klein 9B (T2I) and LTX-2 (video/audio).
1. **1-step generation deep dive**: Current results are at 4 steps. Push to 1-2 steps -- where does quality collapse? What breaks first (text alignment, detail, diversity)?
2. **Best mode-covering init**: What is the cheapest initialization that gives the refinement phase a good starting point? SD-direct vs meanflow vs nothing (train from pretrained directly). Does it even matter for 1-step?
3. **Best refinement method**: This is the core research question. Candidates:
	- Adversarial / distribution matching (LADD, DMD, combinations)
	- Perceptual losses (latent perceptual loss + reflow as a simple baseline)
	- Reward-based fine-tuning (VLM rewards, human preference models)
	- Novel combinations
4. **Modular vs joint**: Can stages be trained independently and components swapped? If yes, huge win for practitioners and scaling to new modalities.
5. **Diversity preservation**: Adversarial training is mode-seeking -- measure per-prompt diversity loss vs base model. Can we maintain diversity at 1 step?
### Scale-up Phase (Months 2-4)
Apply the winning recipe to Flux3 post-training across modalities:
- Text-to-image
- Video generation
- Image/video editing
- Audio generation
For video, this shop delivers per-chunk distillation; combined with the parallel SOTA in Autoregressive Video Distillation shop for rollout-robust autoregressive generation.
### Paper: "Scalable Diffusion Distillation"
The goal is to push each distillation approach as far as possible, then build the winning recipe optimizing for both performance and scalability:
- Push all major distillation families to their limits at production scale
- Identify what actually matters for 1-step quality and what is unnecessary complexity
- Deliver a practical, scalable recipe for 1-step and few-step generation across modalities
## Measuring Success
- **1-step Flux3 T2I** matches multi-step Flux3 on human preference evals 
- Recipe generalizes to video, editing, audio
- Paper accepted at top venue
## Expected Output Artifacts
- Paper (pushing all approaches + winning recipe + scaling analysis)
- Distillation recipe and code integrated into schwarzwald
- Distilled Flux3 checkpoints across modalities (1-step and few-step)
## Headcount
1 person.
## Compute
- **Exploration**: 8-16 GB200 nodes for \~2 months
- **Scale-up**: 32 GB200 nodes for \~2-4 weeks per modality
## References
- [LADD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12015) -- Latent Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (Sauer et al., 2024)
- [DMD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.18828) / [DMD2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14867) -- Distribution Matching Distillation (Yin et al., 2024)
- [sCM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11081) -- Simplifying, Stabilizing & Scaling Continuous-Time Consistency Models (Lu & Song, 2024)
- [rCM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08431) -- Score-Regularized Continuous-Time Consistency (combining sCM + DMD at scale)
- [MeanFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13447) -- Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling (Geng et al., 2025)
- [Shortcut Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12557) -- One Step Diffusion via Shortcut Models (Frans et al., 2025)
- [TwinFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01075) -- Self-adversarial consistency distillation
- [Sana Sprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09899) -- Hybrid mode-covering + adversarial (LADD) distillation
- [T2I-Distill](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13006) -- Few-Step Distillation benchmark on FLUX.1-lite (Alibaba DAMO, 2025)
</content>
</page>

26ac3702-22d5-8083-8a72-d5051ec1d6a4.title: Moderation Roadmap 2025
26ac3702-22d5-8083-8a72-d5051ec1d6a4.text: Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/26ac370222d580838a72d5051ec1d6a4 as of 2026-02-03T08:31:48.127Z: {"title":"Moderation Roadmap 2025"} Moderation Projects # 2025 Q3 Offsite Session ## Takeaways Great Presentation by Ben: [https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1Gs-N4dXrF84335ZuCLchB_mr4EuaBZbHHyk3hXsKw4g/edit?slide=id.g37bfcc759f5_0_0#slide=id.g37bfcc759f5_0_0](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1Gs-N4dXrF84335ZuCLchB_mr4EuaBZbHHyk3hXsKw4g/edit?slide=id.g37bfcc759f5_0_0#slide=id.g37bfcc759f5_0_0) - We should distinguish between Liability Risks and Reputational Risks - Liability exposure is greater in T2I and T2V, in that these are the modes in which we generate content (rather than edit existing content) - Liability Risks are the priority - CSAM, NCII, Unlawful Use of Likeness, Unlawful Use of IP - (In some Key Jurisdictions) Pornographic Material, Unlawful use of Private Data, Synthetic Content without Labeling - Reputational Risks are lower priority, but have the potential of viral brand harm (ie a bad model output shared on X) - Politically sensitive deepfakes, Pro-Terror material, Pro-Crime material, Pro-Violence material, Glorification of Self-Harm, Impact on fundamental rights (e.g. nondiscrimination, civic discourse, mental health) - While some classes can easily be modeled with standard classifiers, others require a higher-level system - Hate speech, violence, self-harm and sexual content can be modeled as is - CSAM - Cannot collect training/eval data - Can be modeled as a combination of underage + sexual content - NCII - This is extremely complicated. If a sexual image with a face is generated, we need to know if they person represented gives their consent - Likeness and IP - These classes are very knowledge based, not semantic - Better modeled using some RAG-like system - How much mitigation is “enough”? - We need to demonstrate a **good faith effort** to verify and comply with these thresholds before release - There is a sliding trade-off between safety and performance. Having some ability to justify the level we chose is important - Maintaining consistency with industry standard practices - We must implement mitigations for both model releases and API releases - Mitigations for model releases - Data filtering during pre-training - Fine-tuning against CSAM and NCII during post-training - Mitigations for API releases - Filtering outputs using classifiers - Prompt re-writing - Requesting consent if a face is detected - Imperceptible marking - Continuous Evaluation and Benchmarking - Internal - Use our test sets to evaluate model releases - External - Use third-parties to evaluate both model and API releases ## Talking Points - Which classes should we moderate/How do we decide which classes to moderate? - Subtopic: Which languages should we support? Is it okay to have lower standards for non-en languages? - How much control should be given to users? - In terms of both granularity (e.g. subclasses) and severity - What parts of moderation are our “product” (ie. offered in licensing etc.)? What parts are to fulfill our legal policy and moral duties? - Ideal system design of moderation workers - Should we move moderation inference into a separate worker/micro-service to improve GPU usage? - Shared primitives with future VLLM development (reusable training, eval and deployment framework) ## Action Items - [ ] Engineering folks decide micro-service design - [ ] Collect documentation around current moderation stack (for internal education and legal paper trail) - [ ] Alex sync with Adam - [ ] Create roadmap of moderation solutions - [ ] new stuff - [ ] optimization ## Notes - CSAM - Training and evaluating csam classifiers will be difficult/impossible - A workaround is training a child presence detector and using it with a sexual content classifier. - IP filter? - Some onus is on the user. If the user inputs IP in their image and uses Kontext as an “editor” (analogous to using photoshop), that’s probably fine. It’s generative use cases. - RAG solution? - Provenance ai? (look at bfl-provenance channel) - They build a dataset of copyrighted images. Does matching against this database and return closest images. - Reasonably fast. - At the very least good for eval and benchmarking. - NCII? - How do we distinguish between simple NSFW and NCII? Facial recognition? Identity verification? Text prompt intent classification? - Limited by sexual classifier anyway - Jonas and Yam experimented with redteaming. We nuked Kontext dev to keep it safe. - Sexual content training data filtering model - CLIP linear probe. Deep Floyd NSFW score `DeepFloydHandler` - nsfw and watermark scores - todo: eval deep floyd on my benchmarking dataset - Memorization - Hash Dedup - SSCD embedding dedup - Multilingual support - Analyze language distribution of PG prompts - Decide on set of “supported” languages, collect eval data and benchmark - Public persona - Pre-filtering on [top 10000 celebrities dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/madhuripanchakshri/top-10000-celebrities-dataset) ## Moderation at Discord ![](https://prod-files-secure.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/d47c9781-7a36-4f60-98ec-c16fd7b286a6/0b7d28de-5d28-401c-9cf5-c3723e0658e5/Screenshot_2025-09-10_at_2.10.37_PM.png?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Content-Sha256=UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD&X-Amz-Credential=ASIAZI2LB46634GDWD3D%2F20260419%2Fus-west-2%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Date=20260419T100113Z&X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEDkaCXVzLXdlc3QtMiJHMEUCIG%2BnfUSQ1U7rd8xtLE6S8u%2F0KicyL42QGOTfmv8m5dFtAiEAwNbeyBRw40kqeigwxoVVvOOjoLU3C0XcDc9l%2BLc6h3cq%2FwMIAhAAGgw2Mzc0MjMxODM4MDUiDAAlZYG2AuxIssC1SyrcA3gTdya9TQvEpVbXD4p3EOf%2BRhlGoElettZVAz%2FPR0USudy7xnX5nay55u%2FEIHq18adWESmWkkTanjo8d9xqToaDctctFCIEndvvIOZeWVMyWEX2WbIR0Yw0MclfqgLDtGg30Ti%2BuctjCQnU6xs6bNAn%2Bk%2F6J2RbejMvcHy2yTiuLAAjkIr%2BrFfnEf%2BPbCPhIFo6%2BvbAqScV4iRK0g2y%2BJF2cklKHeAo%2F%2FCIuos5%2BiZWxLXdiu%2FWT793zSFsBQKM2EFNngs16YR58T%2BpplrqRe8h74etjwfN%2FnQ%2F%2FC0wnVRT1VXm3vEjqqLI%2FIkY58%2BXry3osGQWQE3el3ly03eQEchKAgY5RgigcupXQay2BfeQLkXVBdIc4UAu97taLozpgQLaQRspRs65fybLBOICMFprqWGTi9qtODjx44VbtLu36aqzMiUsEVjiK8oCaqjrcTmUKjoqp1yXo8PSKkaxUx3LX58vE7XhPg7Pf3IPmgI7F4Jlfd8miO8EuaS4SfylNeFuGK3G2iy8PPakR4pa6ZP1ViOv%2BnRqbDzqquU%2BfY2SGiTuwZZY6bHIKF6wnpHj1YaQNpOfqjlWt8hJBTDiFcpZIVFMxKJepANhJLjVneng7nXttfD%2BoW3r%2Bo47MKyvks8GOqUBfTVwWDETLjau%2BRwj7hRfPmOAygRHn6%2BZDqeQu%2FDkev8gzfz5L27fSLBR8QKbEC75zdp2qJ7pf%2F9%2BiHbrQ1wRpl%2FhbboJE62pZe4XmRQOBGxMGX0wf7lOYYyM8TJ872RyXXs7D7DQyoz7VF25B2cAxecZGNHlgJgWkwBJHsMzajM%2BBU%2BwG6%2B9%2BKBPa8G8pSsHBdJueikQidL1i8sJCH0z%2FFlSHGyl&X-Amz-Signature=0bc1b91a0f0ca72246d05884fa7f665e8dc90f5e16ca1a94a33ffb40e22d5e54&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&x-amz-checksum-mode=ENABLED&x-id=GetObject) - Extremely Cross-Functional Space - Safety Engineering, Safety ML, ML Infra, Outsourcers/Labelers, Policy - The advantage we have as a startup is that I can be as many of these “teams” as possible, and if I have to collaborate the decision turnaround should be fast. - Data is king - Historical data can be mined and sampled for training/eval - Data with signal from users is even better. At Discord these are reports. At BFL this can be user feedback. - Online monitoring is crucial. Is there offline-online data drift? Are the models working as expected? Where are our weak points? - Moderation should be adaptable, and third-party models will always be a part of an adaptable system - This can be APIs or off-the-shelf models (already using both at BFL) - Child Safety is owned by Safety Engineering, not Safety ML - Powered by Hash-Match (PhotoDNA) - Heuristics + Sexual Classifiers - The baseline to beat is the status quo, not the ideal - Having precision *and *recall targets is not helpful. Releasing the best model you have is better than none at all. - Except for prioritizing iteration and improvements. But tbh it’s all vibes anyway. - Each class having a precision *or *recall target is practical (e.g. hate speech needs 95% recall, maximize precision given this). - Calibration/consistency is annoying but necessary. Invest early in a layer to automate this away. - Fine-tuning an open source model overtakes third-party models at surprisingly low magnitude of training data (\~500 positive samples), probably due to domain/policy alignment. - Basically better in every way: accuracy, speed, cost, customizability, reliability. - We should be as agnostic as possible to the base model used. New open-source safety models are frequently released. - Classes used at Discord: - Hate Speech - CSAM - Self-harm - Split into self-harm risk/depictions and self-harm encouragement - SHR is a special case where we want to report/support users. SHE is standard abuse - Threats of Violence - Doxxing - Bullying and Harassment - Non-Consensual Pornography (leaks and deepfakes) - Dangerous Goods (Regulated by “pro-crime” category) - Cybercrime (Regulated by “pro-crime” category) - Classes not used at Discord that we should moderate: - Violence and Gore - General Sexual Content - Copyrighted IP - Celebrity Likeness
